lax.hook: A lax rule is like a loose shoelace: it slips, and nobody bothers to tighten it.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite of lax.
Lax can sound relaxed, but it is about rules, not being tired.
Generous is a kind, positive word; lax means carelessly not enforcing rules.

syn1.tip: Lax hides inside "relax." Rules that are relaxed too much are lax, or loose.

traps.why: Far too harsh is the opposite of lax.
Lax is about rules not being enforced, not about moving slowly.
Kind and gentle is praise; lax is a complaint about carelessness.

syn2.tip: Think of "lax security": guards who never check bags are not strict enough.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite; the new babysitter is unlike the strict one.
A babysitter serious about rules would not allow midnight ice cream.
Worry about rules would not lead kids to stay up past midnight.

sc1.tip: "Unlike" sets her against a "strict" babysitter, and midnight ice cream shows she barely enforced any rules.

sc2.sentence: Coach Rivera was famously _____ about practice; players wandered in late, skipped drills, and never heard a single word of complaint from him.

traps.why: Strict is the opposite; a strict coach would complain about skipped drills.
Punctual is about being on time, and his players wandered in late.
Nothing shows he was nervous; the examples show he never enforced rules.

sc2.tip: The examples after the semicolon, late players, skipped drills, and "never heard a single word of complaint," show rules weren't enforced.

simultaneous.hook: A simulcast is a show aired on TV and radio at the same moment: a simultaneous broadcast.

traps.why: Consecutive means one after another, not at the same time.
Similar looks close, but it means alike, not at the same time.
Sudden is about timing, but it means unexpected, not at the same time.

syn1.tip: Think of a "simulcast," one show aired on two channels at once. Concurrent also means running at the same time.

traps.why: Taking turns is the opposite of happening at the same time.
That is similar, a lookalike word, not simultaneous.
Speed is about timing too, but simultaneous means at the same moment.

syn2.tip: The ending sounds like "instantaneous." Simultaneous things share the same instant, so they happen at once.

traps.why: Separate events would not both start at exactly noon.
Similar looks close, but alike events wouldn't force Rafael to choose.
Big events can be crowded, but crowds wouldn't make him pick one.

sc1.tip: The phrase "both starting at exactly noon" means the events happen at the same time, which is why Rafael "had to choose."

sc2.sentence: At most concerts the two drummers take turns soloing, but tonight they will play _____ solos, so the crowd should expect twice the noise at once.

traps.why: Separate solos are the usual plan; "but" says tonight is different.
Alternating means taking turns, which is what "but" says they won't do.
Similar looks close, but alike solos wouldn't make twice the noise at once.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with drummers who "take turns," and "twice the noise at once" tells you both solos happen together.

brawl.hook: Picture a cartoon brawl: a spinning dust cloud with fists, feet, and stars flying out of it.

traps.why: A truce is an agreement to stop fighting, the opposite of a brawl.
Crawl looks like brawl but means a slow creep.
Brawls can break out at games, but a game is not a fight.

syn1.tip: Think of a cowboy movie "barroom brawl": chairs flying, everyone swinging. That is a fight.

traps.why: A peaceful meeting is the opposite of a brawl.
That is bawl, which sounds like brawl but means to cry.
An argument is only words; a brawl uses fists, so it's stronger.

syn2.tip: A brawl uses fists, not just words. If a choice is only shouting, it's too mild.

traps.why: A handshake is friendly, the opposite of a shoving match growing wild.
An argument is milder than shoving, but the fight "grew" bigger.
Benches clear for celebrations too, but a shoving match doesn't become a party.

sc1.tip: A "shoving match" that "grew into" something "wild" with "both entire benches" must be bigger and rougher than shoving.

sc2.sentence: The lunchroom argument began politely, but after someone shoved a tray, it became a messy _____, and three teachers had to pull the students apart.

traps.why: A debate is just talking; teachers pulling students apart means real fighting.
An apology ends trouble; this scene got worse after the shove.
Picnics involve food, but nobody pulls students apart at a picnic.

sc2.tip: "But" shows the talk stopped being polite, and teachers who "had to pull the students apart" means it turned physical.

conform.hook: Conform is con (with) plus form: you shape yourself into the same form as everyone around you.

traps.why: To rebel is to fight the rules, the opposite of conform.
Confirm looks like conform but means to make sure something is true.
People may complain about rules, but conform means following them.

syn1.tip: Picture a cookie cutter: con- means "with," so you match the same form as everyone else. That means following, or complying.

traps.why: Breaking the rules is the opposite of conforming.
That means confirm, a lookalike word, not conform.
Conform holds "form," but it means following rules, not reshaping something.

syn2.tip: A "nonconformist" refuses to fit in, so conform means the reverse: to go along with the crowd.

traps.why: Objecting is what Jade actually did; "rather than" needs the opposite.
Confess starts like conform, but admitting to a trend makes no sense here.
You hear about trends, but the clue is about copying everyone's style.

sc1.tip: "Rather than" tells you Jade did the opposite of the blank. She stood out, so the blank means going along "as everyone else" does.

sc2.sentence: To look perfectly matched on stage, every band member must _____ to the uniform rules: white shirts, black pants, and absolutely no flashy jewelry.

traps.why: Objecting to the rules would ruin the goal of looking matched.
Bands play music for dancing, but the sentence is about following rules.
Confess starts like conform but means admitting something, which doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: The goal is to "look perfectly matched," and the colon lists rules everyone has to follow. So the blank means go along with them.

turmoil.hook: Picture a kitchen in turmoil: pots boiling over, the smoke alarm beeping, and three cooks yelling at once.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of turmoil.
Toil looks similar but means hard work, not wild confusion.
Turmoil can make people sad, but it means confusion and disorder.

syn1.tip: Turmoil ends with the same letters as "boil." Picture a boiling pot: everything churning and messy. That's chaos.

traps.why: Peace is the opposite of turmoil.
Turnover starts like turmoil but means a pastry or a change of people.
Worry is a mild feeling; turmoil is a whole scene of wild confusion.

syn2.tip: Things are "thrown into turmoil," like a room tossed upside down. Look for the choice meaning a big mess.

traps.why: Shouting and crying are the opposite of silence.
Plays get applause, but a fire alarm causes panic, not clapping.
Disappointment is too mild for shouting, crying, and running.

sc1.tip: The list after the comma, "shouting," "crying," and "running offstage," paints wild confusion, not one quiet feeling.

sc2.sentence: The library was usually calm and orderly, but after a pipe burst overnight it was in total _____, with soggy books, buckets everywhere, and workers rushing around.

traps.why: Order describes the usual library; "but" says things changed.
Burst pipes can cut power, but the clues describe mess, not darkness.
Comfort is a pleasant feeling; soggy books and rushing workers are stressful.

sc2.tip: "But" flips the "calm and orderly" library, and "buckets everywhere" with "workers rushing around" describe wild disorder.

fluent.hook: Fluent shares a Latin root with "fluid" and "flow": a fluent speaker's words flow like water.

traps.why: Stumbling over words is the opposite of fluent.
Fluffy starts like fluent but means soft and puffy.
Loudness is about speaking too, but fluent means easy and smooth.

syn1.tip: Fluent shares a root with "fluid." Speech that flows like water is smooth.

traps.why: Stumbling over words is the opposite of being fluent.
The root means flow, but fluent describes speech, not actual liquid.
Fluent starts with "flu," but it has nothing to do with illness.

syn2.tip: You've heard "fluent in Spanish." It means you can speak the language easily, without stopping to search for words.

traps.why: Confused speakers hesitate, but he switched "without any hesitation."
Shyness is about speaking too, but it doesn't explain easy switching.
Average is too weak for switching languages without hesitation.

sc1.tip: "Having grown up speaking both" explains why he switched "without any hesitation." Easy, smooth speaking is the answer.

sc2.sentence: My little brother is only learning French, so he pauses after every word, but my aunt is _____ and chats with the waiter in Paris at full speed.

traps.why: Hesitant describes the brother; "but" shows the aunt is different.
A waiter suggests food, but the clue is about how she speaks.
Quiet doesn't fit someone chatting "at full speed."

sc2.tip: "But" sets the aunt against a brother who "pauses after every word," and "at full speed" shows she speaks French easily.

uphold.hook: Uphold is up plus hold: picture judges holding a rule up high so nobody can knock it down.

traps.why: To overturn a rule is to throw it out, the opposite.
Upset also starts with "up" but means to disturb or knock over.
Up plus hold sounds like lifting, but uphold means keeping a rule strong.

syn1.tip: Up plus hold: you hold a rule up so it stays standing. "Uphold the law" means support it.

traps.why: Abandon means give up on, the opposite of uphold.
The parts suggest raising up, but uphold means keeping a rule in place.
A holdup is a robbery, but uphold means keeping a rule standing.

syn2.tip: Courts "uphold a decision" when they keep it in place. Think of keeping something standing, not tossing it out.

traps.why: The council exists to stop the code from being ignored.
Rewriting changes a code; the council's job is making students follow it.
Up plus hold sounds like lifting, but you can't lift a code of honesty.

sc1.tip: "Making sure every student follows it rather than letting it be ignored" tells you the council keeps the code strong.

sc2.sentence: Grandma insists that every family member _____ our tradition of Sunday pancakes, so even my busy cousins rush home each weekend to flip them together.

traps.why: If they abandoned it, the cousins wouldn't rush home every weekend.
You can't invent a tradition that already exists.
Upset also starts with "up" but means to disturb, which doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: Because of Grandma, "even my busy cousins rush home" every weekend. That effect shows everyone keeps the tradition going.

collaborate.hook: Collaborate is co (together) plus labor (work): two classes working together on one giant mural.

traps.why: Competing means working against each other, the opposite.
Elaborate looks similar but means to add more detail.
Teammates talk, but communicating isn't the same as working together.

syn1.tip: Spot "labor" (work) inside collaborate, plus co- for "together." Working together is cooperating.

traps.why: Working alone is the opposite of collaborating.
That is collapse, a lookalike word, not collaborate.
Collaborate contains the letters "lab," but it means teamwork, not science labs.

syn2.tip: Co- means "together" in "coworker" and "cooperate." A collaborator is a teammate.

traps.why: "Instead of competing" rules this out; they did the opposite.
Rivals might argue, but sharing ideas and parts is teamwork.
Elaborate looks similar but means to explain in more detail.

sc1.tip: "Instead of competing" flips the meaning, and "sharing ideas, parts, and practice time" describes teamwork.

sc2.sentence: The science project was too big for one person, so Maya and Leo agreed to _____, with Maya building the volcano and Leo writing the report.

traps.why: Competing is the opposite of splitting the jobs on one project.
A huge project might tempt you to quit, but they each did a job.
Collapse looks similar but means to fall down.

sc2.tip: "Too big for one person" causes the plan, and splitting jobs, one "building" and one "writing," means they work together.

speculate.hook: Speculate comes from a Latin word for watching from a lookout: picture sailors squinting at a far ship, guessing what it is.

traps.why: To prove is to show for certain, the opposite of guessing.
Speak starts like speculate but just means to talk.
Calculating works things out exactly; speculating is guessing without facts.

syn1.tip: When sports reporters "speculate" about a game, they're guessing before the facts come in. Speculation is guesswork.

traps.why: Knowing for sure is the opposite of speculating.
The root spec means look, but speculate now means guessing.
Rumors involve guesses, but speculating doesn't mean spreading gossip.

syn2.tip: Detectives speculate when they form a theory before they have proof. Look for building an idea without all the facts.

traps.why: Bragging is boasting; one tooth gives nothing to boast about.
Sharks can be scary, but the clue is about missing facts.
Forgetting doesn't connect to having only one tooth to study.

sc1.tip: "Only a single fossil tooth" means they lacked the full facts, so they "could only" make guesses.

sc2.sentence: Since the coach has not announced the starting lineup yet, players can only _____ about who will start, trading hunches in the locker room.

traps.why: Nothing has been announced, so there is nothing to read yet.
Complaining is grumpy, but the players are just trading hunches.
Players trading hunches are clearly thinking about it, not forgetting.

sc2.tip: The lineup is "not announced yet," and "trading hunches" restates the blank. Hunches are guesses made without facts.

innate.hook: Innate shares a Latin root with "natal," as in prenatal: an innate trait is one you were born with.

traps.why: Learned means picked up later, the opposite of innate.
Inner looks similar but means inside, not present from birth.
Talent can be innate, but innate just means born with it.

syn1.tip: Innate sounds like "in-born": built into you from the start, like a spider's natural knack for webs.

traps.why: Taught skills are learned, the opposite of innate.
In- here means "in," not "not"; innate means born with.
That is inmate, a lookalike word, not innate.

syn2.tip: Babies grab fingers without lessons; that is an innate behavior. Look for the choice about being born with it.

traps.why: "No one ever teaches" them, so the instinct isn't learned.
Newly hatched turtles haven't had time to practice anything.
Ornate looks similar but means fancy and decorated.

sc1.tip: "No one ever teaches" them and it works "from the moment they hatch," so the instinct is something they're born with.

sc2.sentence: Although Dad took years of lessons to play piano, my sister seems to have an _____ sense of rhythm; she tapped perfect beats before she could walk.

traps.why: Acquired means gained over time, like Dad's lessons; "although" signals a contrast.
Her perfect beats were real, so her rhythm isn't imaginary.
Ornate looks similar but means fancy and decorated.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts Dad's "years of lessons" with your sister, who had rhythm "before she could walk," so hers came naturally.

advocate.hook: Advocate holds the root voc, meaning voice or call: you use your voice for a cause you believe in.

traps.why: Oppose is the opposite: it means to fight against something.
Allocate looks similar but means to hand out or divide up.
You can discuss an idea without being for it at all.

syn1.tip: Inside advocate is voc, meaning voice. To advocate is to use your voice for something you support.

traps.why: Arguing against something is the opposite of advocating for it.
Voc means call, but advocate means supporting a cause, not calling someone.
Voting happens around causes, but advocating means speaking up for one.

syn2.tip: A lawyer is sometimes called an advocate because she speaks up for her client.

traps.why: The club worries about plastic, so it would push for the ban, not against it.
Letters and speeches push for a ban; they are not just studying it.
Mention is too weak for writing letters and giving speeches.

sc1.tip: "Worried about plastic" plus "writing letters and giving speeches" shows the club is pushing hard for the ban.

sc2.sentence: Although Marco disliked giving speeches, he stood up at the town meeting to _____ for a new skate park, because he believed his friends needed a safe place to ride.

traps.why: Apologizing shows regret, but Marco believes in the park.
Waiting is too passive; he stood up and spoke.
Paying is about money, but the clue is about speaking up.

sc2.tip: "Stood up at the town meeting" and "because he believed his friends needed" show he is speaking in favor of the park.

chronic.hook: Chronic contains chron, meaning time, as in chronological: a chronic problem sticks around for a long time.

traps.why: Short-lived is the opposite: it means ending quickly.
Chron means time, but chronic is not about good timing.
Chronic problems can hurt, but chronic means lasting long.

syn1.tip: Chron means time, as in chronological. Chronic things take up lots of time because they keep going or coming back.

traps.why: Brief and sudden is the opposite of something that keeps lasting.
A chronic problem can be mild; chronic is about how long.
Chron means time, but chronic does not mean well timed.

syn2.tip: Doctors call an illness chronic when it lasts for months or keeps returning, unlike a quick cold.

traps.why: Temporary means short, but this pain has lasted three years.
Sharp describes how pain feels, not how long it lasts.
Chron means time, but timely means well timed, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: "Unlike a cold that goes away in a week" and "for over three years" tell you the pain lasts a long time.

sc2.sentence: Because Leo's cough was _____, returning every winter for five years, his doctor finally sent him to a specialist to find the cause.

traps.why: Brief is the opposite of returning every winter for five years.
Spreading to others is a different idea from coming back for years.
Loud describes sound, but the clue is about how long it lasts.

sc2.tip: "Returning every winter for five years" restates the blank, so you need a word for something that keeps coming back.

devoted.hook: Picture a devoted dog greeting you at the door every single day, no matter what.

traps.why: Faithless is the opposite: it means not loyal.
Divided looks a bit like devoted but means split apart.
A devoted person may feel grateful, but devoted means loving and loyal.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "devote your time." A devoted person gives their heart and time to someone again and again.

traps.why: Coldly distant is the opposite of warm, loyal love.
This turns loyalty into something negative, but devoted is a warm word.
Mildly interested is far too weak for devoted.

syn2.tip: Devoted carries a warm feeling of strong love and loyalty, so look for the choice that is both warm and strong.

traps.why: A disloyal dog would not wait every single day.
A stray dog has no owner to wait for.
Devious looks similar but means sneaky.

sc1.tip: "Every afternoon" and "never missing a single day" show a dog that loves its owner and stays faithful.

sc2.sentence: Although the team lost every game that season, its _____ fans still packed the bleachers each Saturday, cheering as loudly as ever.

traps.why: Unfaithful fans would stop coming, but these still packed the bleachers.
Former fans have stopped supporting the team, but these still show up.
Angry fans would boo, not cheer loudly every week.

sc2.tip: "Although the team lost every game" contrasts with "still packed the bleachers," so the fans stayed loyal.

notion.hook: Notion and notice both come from a Latin word meaning to know; a notion is something your mind believes.

traps.why: Motion looks like notion but means movement.
A notion is something believed, which may not be a fact.
A question asks something; a notion is something you think.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "I have no notion of what you mean." A notion is something in your mind.

traps.why: Doubt means not believing, the opposite of a notion.
Proof shows something is true; a notion is only believed.
Nation looks like notion but means a country.

syn2.tip: In "the notion that bats are blind," notion means something people believe, whether or not it is true.

traps.why: "In fact" shows the idea is wrong, so it cannot be a fact.
Motion looks like notion but means movement.
Truth is too strong; the sentence says this belief is wrong.

sc1.tip: "But in fact" shows that what people believe is wrong, so the blank must be a belief, not something true.

sc2.sentence: Jake gave up the silly _____ that he could finish his science project in one night after he stayed up until midnight and was only half done.

traps.why: A fact can't be silly or wrong, and Jake's idea was wrong.
Motion looks like notion but means movement.
Finishing quickly is something Jake hoped for, not feared.

sc2.tip: "Gave up the silly" plus "that he could finish" shows he dropped a mistaken belief once he was only half done.

preliminary.hook: Pre means before, so preliminary rounds come before the big final, like tryouts before the real show.

traps.why: Final is the opposite: it means coming last.
Primary looks similar but means main or most important.
The middle looks like limit, but preliminary means coming first.

syn1.tip: Start with pre, meaning before. Preliminary things happen first, before the main event.

traps.why: Coming last is the opposite of preliminary.
The main event matters most; preliminary steps only lead up to it.
Preliminary only looks like limit; it means coming before.

syn2.tip: You may have heard "preliminary results" on the news: early numbers that come before the final count.

traps.why: The final is on Saturday; these heats come before it.
Preliminary looks like limit, but limited heats makes no sense here.
Friday heats come earlier than Saturday's final, not later.

sc1.tip: "Friday morning" heats lead to the "championship final on Saturday night," so the blank describes rounds that come before.

sc2.sentence: The architect showed us only a _____ sketch of the new library, a rough first drawing she would improve many times before building began.

traps.why: She will improve it many times, so it is not final.
Detailed doesn't fit a rough drawing that still needs work.
Primary means main, but this sketch is just a rough first try.

sc2.tip: The phrase "a rough first drawing" restates the blank, telling you the sketch comes before the real plans.

vocal.hook: Vocal comes from voc, meaning voice: vocal people use their voices to say exactly what they think.

traps.why: Silent is the opposite of speaking up freely.
Vocal music means singing, but here vocal means speaking your mind.
Local rhymes with vocal but means nearby.

syn1.tip: Voc means voice. A vocal person lets everyone hear their opinions.

traps.why: Vocal people complain openly, so this is the opposite.
That's vocal as in singing, not speaking your opinions.
Vocal people speak openly, but not always in an angry shout.

syn2.tip: Picture parents who are vocal about a crosswalk: they speak up at every meeting until someone listens.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with the quiet students, so these ones were loud.
Calm doesn't match complaining loudly at every assembly.
Vocal can mean singing, but these students were complaining.

sc1.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "quietly accepted," and "complaining loudly" tells you these students spoke up.

sc2.sentence: Because Grandpa was so _____ about his dislike of loud music, everyone at the reunion knew exactly how he felt before the band even started playing.

traps.why: If he kept it secret, nobody would know how he felt.
Vocal can describe singing, but Grandpa was sharing an opinion.
Being confused would not make everyone know exactly how he felt.

sc2.tip: "Everyone knew exactly how he felt" is the effect, so Grandpa must have spoken his opinion openly.

immune.hook: Your immune system is your body's guard, keeping germs from making you sick.

traps.why: Vulnerable is the opposite: it means easily harmed.
Healthy people can still catch a disease; immune means protected from it.
Immobile looks similar but means unable to move.

syn1.tip: Think of your "immune system," which fights off germs so they can't make you sick.

traps.why: Exposed means open to harm, the opposite of protected.
Contagious means able to spread a disease, not safe from it.
Immortal looks similar but means never dying.

syn2.tip: Immune things are shielded. When something can't affect you, like a virus after a vaccine, you are protected from it.

traps.why: Vulnerable means easily harmed, but she did not get sick.
Allergies are about the body too, but the vaccine kept her safe.
A vaccine doesn't make you exposed; it explains why she stayed well.

sc1.tip: "Because she had received the measles vaccine" is the cause, and "did not get sick" is the effect, so she was protected.

sc2.sentence: Most of the class giggled at every joke in the play, but Oscar seemed _____ to the humor, sitting with a straight face the whole time.

traps.why: Sensitive means easily affected, but the jokes didn't affect Oscar.
Everyone heard the jokes; the point is they had no effect on him.
Being drawn to the humor would make him laugh, not keep a straight face.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Oscar with the giggling class, and "a straight face the whole time" shows the jokes had no effect on him.

excessive.hook: Excessive is what you get when something goes past enough, like frosting piled three inches high on a cupcake.

traps.why: Moderate means a sensible amount, the opposite of excessive.
Expensive is about cost; excessive means too much of anything.
Exciting starts the same way but means thrilling.

syn1.tip: Inside excessive is "excess," meaning extra. Excessive amounts go beyond what is sensible.

traps.why: Just enough is the opposite of going past the limit.
A bit extra is too weak; excessive means far too much.
Costly is about price, not about having too much.

syn2.tip: Think of "excess baggage," luggage over the limit. Excessive means more than the limit or more than needed.

traps.why: Twenty miles a day is not moderate, and moderate training rarely injures.
Useful training would make players stronger, not hurt them.
Cost isn't the problem here; the amount of running is.

sc1.tip: "Twenty miles every day" and "cause injuries rather than make the players stronger" show the training goes far past what is reasonable.

sc2.sentence: Mom said a little salt makes popcorn tasty, but the _____ amount Leo poured on made it so salty that nobody could eat a single bite.

traps.why: A tiny amount would not make the popcorn too salty to eat.
Perfect is positive, but nobody could eat the popcorn.
Salt's cost isn't the point; the amount ruined the popcorn.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "a little salt" with Leo's amount, and "nobody could eat a single bite" shows he used way too much.

fatal.hook: Fatal comes from the same Latin word as fate: a fatal mistake seals someone's fate, bringing death or disaster.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite: it means causing no harm.
Final looks similar but means last.
Painful is too weak; fatal means causing death.

syn1.tip: You may know the phrase "a fatal accident," one in which someone died. Fatal means causing death.

traps.why: Giving life is the opposite of causing death.
Minor harm is far too weak for fatal.
Fatal is related to fate, but it means deadly, not destined.

syn2.tip: Fatal goes with words like "fatal crash" or "fatal disease," all about something that kills or ruins.

traps.why: Healthy berries wouldn't need such a strict warning.
Delicious is a happy word, but the guide is warning of danger.
Messy is far too mild for a warning never to taste anything.

sc1.tip: "So the guide warned them never to taste anything" is the effect, so the berries must be dangerous enough to kill.

sc2.sentence: Most mistakes in a chess game can be fixed later, but leaving your queen unguarded is often a _____ error that ends the game within a few moves.

traps.why: A minor error could be fixed, but this one ends the game.
Clever is positive, but this error ruins the game.
Being common doesn't explain why the error ends the game.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts mistakes that "can be fixed later" with one that "ends the game," so the blank means disastrous.

animated.hook: Animated cartoons are drawings brought to life; an animated person seems bursting with life too.

traps.why: Dull is the opposite: it means lacking life or energy.
Animated films are drawn, but an animated person is full of energy.
Animated people are excited, not angry.

syn1.tip: Animated cartoons make drawings move as if alive. An animated person is full of that same life and energy.

traps.why: Low on energy is the opposite of animated.
That fits animated movies, not lively people.
Slightly interested is too weak; animated means excited and lively.

syn2.tip: Think of an animated conversation: people talking fast, waving their hands, and clearly excited.

traps.why: She was talking excitedly, so she was not silent.
Bored is the wrong feeling; she was waving her hands with excitement.
Nervous people may fidget, but she was talking excitedly, not worrying.

sc1.tip: "Usually quiet" contrasts with "waving her hands and talking excitedly," so she suddenly became full of life.

sc2.sentence: The tour guide was so _____ as she described the dinosaur bones, jumping and making roaring sounds, that even the sleepy kids sat up and paid attention.

traps.why: A dull guide would not make sleepy kids sit up.
Animated cartoons are drawn, but here the guide is full of energy.
Her roaring was for fun; frightened is the wrong feeling.

sc2.tip: "Jumping and making roaring sounds" made "even the sleepy kids" pay attention, so the guide must have been full of energy.

guile.hook: Guile hides inside beguile, which means to charm or trick someone, just like a sly fox grinning at a lion.

traps.why: Honesty is the opposite of guile, which is all about tricking people.
Guilt looks like guile but means the bad feeling after doing wrong.
Force is another way to get what you want, but guile uses tricks instead.

syn1.tip: Guile is inside beguile, meaning to charm or fool someone. Picture a sly fox's sneaky plan.

traps.why: Sincerity means being truthful, the opposite of sneaky guile.
Ingenuity is honest cleverness; guile is clever trickery meant to fool someone.
Power gets results through strength, while guile gets results through trickery.

syn2.tip: Guile has a sly, negative feeling. Look for the choice that means sneaky cleverness, not honest smarts.

traps.why: The sentence says strength alone was not enough, so muscle cannot be the answer.
Flattery and a clever lie are the opposite of honesty.
Luck is chance, but flattery and a lie are a planned trick.

sc1.tip: The clues are "Unable to win by strength alone" and "fooling the mighty lion with flattery and a clever lie." Fooling with lies is clever trickery.

sc2.sentence: The con artist in the movie won the old man's trust through pure _____, pretending to be a long-lost nephew so he could steal the family fortune.

traps.why: Pretending to be someone else is the opposite of sincerity.
Con artists may be patient, but pretending and stealing point to trickery.
Guilt looks like guile but means feeling bad, which does not win trust.

sc2.tip: The clue is "pretending to be a long-lost nephew so he could steal." That is a sneaky trick, so the blank means clever trickery.

beseech.hook: Beseech comes from an old form of seek: you seek help so badly that you drop to your knees and beg.

traps.why: Refusing turns a request down; beseeching is begging for something.
Screech rhymes with beseech but means to make a harsh, high cry.
You might thank someone after they agree, but beseeching is the begging first.

syn1.tip: Beseech comes from the same old word as seek. Picture someone seeking help so desperately they beg.

traps.why: Commanding means ordering someone, not begging them.
Suggesting is a gentle idea; beseeching is urgent, desperate begging.
To grant is to give what someone begs for, the other side of beseeching.

syn2.tip: Beseech sounds old and serious, like a knight on his knees asking a king for mercy. That is urgent pleading.

traps.why: Scolding is angry blaming, not kneeling and pleading.
Thanking would come after she agreed; the kneeling and pleading is begging.
Pleading with someone over and over is the opposite of ignoring them.

sc1.tip: The clues "dropped to their knees" and "pleading over and over" describe begging someone urgently.

sc2.sentence: Rather than calmly asking for a later bedtime, my little brother chose to _____ our dad, clasping his hands and crying 'please' twenty times in a row.

traps.why: Asking is too mild; the sentence says he did not calmly ask.
Obeying means doing what Dad says, not begging him for something.
Teasing is playful mocking, not crying please with clasped hands.

sc2.tip: "Rather than calmly asking" signals something stronger than asking, and "clasping his hands" and saying please twenty times show urgent begging.

recuperate.hook: Recuperate starts with re-, meaning back: after the flu, you recuperate by getting your strength back.

traps.why: Weakening is losing strength, the opposite of recuperating.
Cooperate looks like recuperate but means to work together.
Exercise is about the body, but recuperating means resting to get well.

syn1.tip: Find re-, meaning back, at the start. To recuperate is to get your health or strength back.

traps.why: Getting worse is the opposite of recuperating.
Sleep can help you heal, but recuperate means the healing itself.
The re- here means back, as in getting health back, not trying again.

syn2.tip: You often hear recuperate after an illness or surgery: someone stays home to recuperate. That means getting well.

traps.why: Resting for a week helps players regain strength, not collapse.
Training is hard work, but the week off was for rest.
Players might celebrate, but rest after exhaustion points to regaining strength.

sc1.tip: The clues are "exhausting three-day tournament" and "rest." Exhausted players rest so they can get their strength back.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa was pale and weak when he left the hospital, but after a month of good meals and naps he had begun to _____ and was gardening again.

traps.why: The word but shows a change for the better, so decline is wrong.
Retiring means stopping work; gardening again after weakness shows getting well.
Complaining is grumpy; meals, naps, and gardening show he was healing.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "pale and weak" with "gardening again," so the blank must mean getting healthy and strong again.

genial.hook: Genial sounds a bit like genie: picture a cheerful genie warmly greeting you with a big friendly smile.

traps.why: Grumpy is the opposite of genial, which means warm and friendly.
Genuine looks like genial but means real or honest.
Talkative people talk a lot, but genial means warm and cheerful.

syn1.tip: Genial has a warm, positive feeling. Picture a genial host who smiles and makes everyone feel welcome.

traps.why: Gloomy means sad and dark, the opposite of genial.
General looks like genial but means overall or not specific.
Giddy is wildly excited and dizzy, much more than calm, warm genial.

syn2.tip: A genial person is pleasant to be around. Think of a smiling, good-natured neighbor who always waves hello.

traps.why: A stern shopkeeper would not smile warmly and hand out free candy.
A shy shopkeeper would not chat with every customer about their families.
A greedy shopkeeper would not give away free candy.

sc1.tip: The clues "warm smile," "asked about their families," and "free candy" all describe a friendly, cheerful person.

sc2.sentence: Unlike her grumpy older brother, who barely nodded at guests, Mia was _____, chatting happily with every visitor and making sure no one felt left out.

traps.why: Sulky describes the grumpy brother, but "Unlike" tells you Mia is different.
Bossy people order others around; making sure no one feels left out is kind.
Nervous people feel uneasy; chatting happily shows relaxed, warm friendliness.

sc2.tip: "Unlike her grumpy older brother" means Mia is the opposite of grumpy, and "chatting happily" confirms she is friendly and cheerful.

whimper.hook: Whimper sounds like what it is: the small, shaky cry of a puppy left alone at night.

traps.why: A roar is loud and strong; a whimper is soft and weak.
Whisper looks like whimper but means to speak very quietly, not cry.
Giggling is a happy sound; whimpering is a sad, scared one.

syn1.tip: Say whimper aloud; it sounds soft and shaky. Picture a sad puppy making small crying noises at the door.

traps.why: Shouting is loud and strong; whimpering is soft and weak.
Sobbing loudly is too strong; a whimper is a small, quiet cry.
Speaking quietly is soft, but whimpering is crying, not talking.

syn2.tip: A whimper is quiet and weak, the sound a hurt or scared animal makes. Look for soft crying.

traps.why: Purring is a happy sound, but this kitten is frightened and crying.
Kittens hiss when angry, but the sentence describes tiny crying sounds.
Whisper looks like whimper, but kittens do not whisper; they cry.

sc1.tip: The clues "frightened" and "making tiny crying sounds" describe a soft, weak cry.

sc2.sentence: The toddler did not scream or throw a tantrum when his balloon floated away; instead he began to _____, his lip trembling as quiet little sobs escaped.

traps.why: Wailing is loud crying, but the sentence says he did not scream.
A trembling lip and sobs show sadness, not laughter.
Chasing the balloon is an action; "quiet little sobs" describes a sound.

sc2.tip: "Did not scream" and "instead" rule out loud crying, and "quiet little sobs" points to soft, weak crying.

unearth.hook: Unearth means taking something out of the earth, like a dog digging up a bone it buried last week.

traps.why: To bury is to put something in the ground, the opposite of unearth.
Earn hides inside unearth, but earning means getting paid for work.
Planting is also about soil, but it puts things into the ground.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: earth. To unearth is to take something out of the earth, or uncover it.

traps.why: Covering up hides something, the opposite of unearthing it.
Dig in sounds close but means to start eating, not to uncover.
Unearth is not leaving the earth; it means pulling something out of the ground.

syn2.tip: Archaeologists unearth old coins and bones. Picture them digging something up out of the earth.

traps.why: The bottle was already buried; the children found it by digging.
Glass can break, but the clue is about digging up something buried.
They might polish it later, but digging tells you they found it first.

sc1.tip: The clues "While digging" and "buried there for a century" show the children dug the bottle up.

sc2.sentence: After weeks of reading old newspapers in the library, the student reporter managed to _____ a long-forgotten secret about who had founded our town.

traps.why: Weeks of research lead to finding a secret, not hiding it.
Inventing means making something up; the reporter found something real in old newspapers.
Research brings forgotten facts back, the opposite of erasing them.

sc2.tip: "Weeks of reading old newspapers" leads to a "long-forgotten secret," so the blank means discover something hidden.

tardy.hook: A tardy slip is what schools hand out when you stroll in after the bell has already rung.

traps.why: Early is the opposite of tardy.
Tidy looks like tardy but means neat and clean.
A lazy student might be late, but tardy only means arriving late.

syn1.tip: Think of a tardy slip at school. You get one when you arrive after the bell, so tardy means late.

traps.why: Ahead of schedule means early, the opposite of tardy.
Absent means not coming at all; tardy means coming, just late.
Tardy students may run, but tardy is about time, not breathing.

syn2.tip: Schools mark you tardy if you show up after the bell. It is about arriving later than expected.

traps.why: They missed only ten minutes, so they came late, not stayed away.
Prompt means on time, but a broken bus made them late.
A quiz can make students nervous, but the bus problem is about time.

sc1.tip: "Because the bus broke down" gives the cause, and "missed the first ten minutes" shows they arrived late.

sc2.sentence: Although Jaden usually arrives at soccer practice ten minutes early, he was _____ on Saturday, jogging onto the field after warm-ups had already ended.

traps.why: Punctual means on time; "Although" signals Saturday was different from usual.
Jogging might look eager, but arriving after warm-ups ended means late.
Nothing mentions an injury; he jogged in after warm-ups were over.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a change from "ten minutes early," and "after warm-ups had already ended" shows he arrived late.

dauntless.hook: To daunt is to scare; add -less and dauntless means without fear, like a climber pushing on through a storm.

traps.why: Timid means shy and easily scared, the opposite of dauntless.
Doubtless looks similar but means certainly, not brave.
Reckless is careless bravery, a criticism; dauntless is admiring praise.

syn1.tip: Split it: daunt plus -less. Daunting things are scary, so dauntless means without fear.

traps.why: Cowardly is the opposite of dauntless.
Careless also ends in -less but means not paying attention.
Boastful people brag about being brave; dauntless people actually are brave.

syn2.tip: You may know "a daunting task," one that scares you. Someone dauntless faces such tasks without fear.

traps.why: A hesitant explorer would hold back, but she refused to give up.
A lazy explorer would not keep trying after two failed attempts.
Careless ends like dauntless, but nothing shows she was careless.

sc1.tip: "Despite freezing winds and two failed attempts" and "refused to give up" show someone who keeps going without fear.

sc2.sentence: Because she was completely _____, the young firefighter rushed into the smoky building to rescue the trapped puppy while others stood frozen in fear.

traps.why: Terrified describes the others who stood frozen, not the firefighter who rushed in.
Firefighters get tired, but exhaustion would not make her rush in.
Feeling lonely does not explain rushing into a smoky building.

sc2.tip: "Because" links the blank to rushing into smoke "while others stood frozen in fear," so she must be without fear.

judicious.hook: Judicious comes from the same root as judge: a judicious person judges carefully before acting.

traps.why: Foolish is the opposite of judicious.
Judicial looks similar but means having to do with courts and judges.
Stingy is a negative word for saving; judicious is praise for good sense.

syn1.tip: Find judge in judicious. A good judge thinks carefully, so judicious means showing good judgment.

traps.why: Reckless means acting without thinking, the opposite of judicious.
Judicious comes from judge, but it means wise, not harsh or strict.
Suspicious ends with a similar sound but means distrustful.

syn2.tip: Judicious is a positive word for choices made with care. Think of a judicious use of your allowance.

traps.why: Comparing prices at three stores is careful, not hasty.
The sentence is about money, but she avoided spending her whole budget.
Comparing prices is careful planning, not selfishness.

sc1.tip: "Instead of spending her whole budget on the first costume" contrasts with "comparing prices at three stores," which shows careful, sensible judgment.

sc2.sentence: Since the hiking trail was icy and the sun was setting, our guide made the _____ decision to turn back early rather than risk a dangerous climb in the dark.

traps.why: Turning back to avoid real danger is smart, not a cowardly insult.
A daring choice would be to keep climbing, not turn back.
Judicial means about courts, which has nothing to do with hiking.

sc2.tip: "Since the hiking trail was icy and the sun was setting" gives the cause, and avoiding "a dangerous climb" shows good sense.

rejuvenate.hook: Rejuvenate holds re-, again, and juven, young, as in juvenile: it makes you feel young and lively again.

traps.why: Exhaust means to wear out, the opposite of rejuvenate.
The re- means again, but rejuvenate is being made fresh, not doing something twice.
Decorating changes how something looks; rejuvenating gives it new life.

syn1.tip: Juven is in juvenile, meaning young. Re- means again, so rejuvenate means to make young and fresh again.

traps.why: Wearing out drains energy, the opposite of rejuvenating.
Juven means young, but rejuvenate is regaining energy, not acting childish.
Sleep can refresh you, but rejuvenate means the fresh feeling itself.

syn2.tip: Think of a vacation that rejuvenates tired parents. They come back full of energy, as if young again.

traps.why: Planting flowers and repairing the fountain is caring for the park, not neglecting it.
Towns may sell land, but planting and repairs bring the park back to life.
Adding a playground makes the park bigger and livelier, not smaller.

sc1.tip: "Run-down" shows the park was worn out, and "planting new flowers, repairing the old fountain" shows bringing it back to life.

sc2.sentence: Dad trudged in from his double shift looking gray and worn out, but a hot shower and a bowl of soup seemed to _____ him, and soon he was laughing with us.

traps.why: The word but shows Dad felt better, so drain is the opposite.
A hot shower could burn, but laughing afterward shows he felt fresh again.
Nothing here causes worry; laughing soon after shows he felt lively again.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "gray and worn out" with "laughing with us," so the shower and soup made him lively again.

pessimistic.hook: A pessimistic person sees the glass as half empty and packs an umbrella on a sunny day.

traps.why: Hopeful is the opposite of pessimistic.
Persistent starts like pessimistic but means not giving up.
Angry is a bad mood too, but pessimistic means expecting the worst.

syn1.tip: Think of the opposite, optimistic, which means hopeful. Pessimistic is the gloomy side: always expecting things to go wrong.

traps.why: Expecting the best describes an optimist, the opposite of a pessimist.
Planning is sensible; pessimistic is about gloomy expectations, not careful planning.
A little unsure is too weak; a pessimist is sure things will go badly.

syn2.tip: Picture the person who says "This will never work" before anything starts. That gloomy forecasting is being pessimistic.

traps.why: Optimistic is the opposite; he expects rain, not a nice day.
Cheerful has a happy feeling, but Grandpa is gloomily sure of rain.
Uncertain is too weak; the sentence says he "was sure" it would rain.

sc1.tip: "Although" signals a contrast: the forecast says sunshine, yet he packs three umbrellas and is "sure" of rain. He expects the worst.

sc2.sentence: After losing the first five games of the season, Maya grew so _____ that she stopped practicing, convinced her soccer team would never win again.

traps.why: Hopeful is the opposite; she thinks her team will never win.
Determined is a positive reaction, but she quit practicing.
Losing can tire you out, but the clue is about expecting more losses.

sc2.tip: Look at the result: she stopped practicing, "convinced her soccer team would never win again." Expecting only bad results is the meaning you need.

submissive.hook: Sub means under: a submissive dog puts itself under the bigger dog, rolling over to show it gives in.

traps.why: Defiant means refusing to obey, the opposite of submissive.
Sub means under, but submissive isn't about being underwater.
Shy means nervous around people, not ready to obey them.

syn1.tip: Submissive comes from submit, as in "submit to the rules." Someone who submits goes along with what they're told.

traps.why: Taking charge is the opposite of giving in to others.
Kind and helpful sounds positive; submissive means giving in too easily.
Shyness is about nerves, not about obeying whoever is in charge.

syn2.tip: Look inside the word for submit. A submissive person submits, giving in and following orders, often a bit too easily.

traps.why: Dominant describes the leader, the opposite of the wolves giving in.
Young wolves do play, but lowering heads shows accepting authority.
Protective means guarding others, not bowing to a leader.

sc1.tip: The clue is "lowering their heads and tails to show that they accept its authority." Accepting someone's power over you means giving in to them.

sc2.sentence: Unlike her bold older sister, who argued with every rule, Lila was quiet and _____, doing exactly what the babysitter said without a word of complaint.

traps.why: Rebellious means fighting rules, the opposite of what Lila does.
Stubborn describes the arguing sister, not Lila.
Forgetful kids miss instructions, but Lila does exactly what she's told.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets up a contrast with the sister who "argued with every rule." Lila does "exactly what the babysitter said," so she obeys easily.

jargon.hook: Doctors say "stat" and gamers say "noob": every group has its own jargon that outsiders can't follow.

traps.why: Gossip is talk about people, not a group's special words.
Language is too broad; jargon is one group's special vocabulary.
Jargon can be confusing like a riddle, but it means special words.

syn1.tip: Think of "computer jargon" or "legal jargon." It's the special set of words one group uses that outsiders don't understand.

traps.why: Everyday words are the opposite of jargon, which outsiders can't follow.
This is too broad; jargon belongs to a particular group or job.
Jargon isn't rude; it's just technical words for insiders.

syn2.tip: Jargon usually comes with a field in front of it: "sports jargon," "science jargon." That tells you it's words special to one group.

traps.why: Jokes aren't technical terms like "bandwidth throttling."
The terms aren't mistakes; they're real technical words Grandma doesn't know.
Praise is positive, and it wouldn't confuse Grandma.

sc1.tip: The examples after "like" are "bandwidth throttling" and "DNS cache," special computer terms. Words only experts understand are what fills the blank.

sc2.sentence: The science fair judges understood the student's _____ perfectly, but the younger visitors needed her to explain her project again using plain, everyday words.

traps.why: If she spoke simply, no one would need plain words explained again.
An accent is how words sound, but the fix was different words.
Handwriting isn't fixed by explaining with everyday words.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "plain, everyday words." The blank must be the opposite: special terms only experts like the judges understand.

enigma.hook: Enigma was the name of a famous World War II code machine whose secret messages were a puzzle to crack.

traps.why: A solution answers a puzzle; an enigma is still unsolved.
Enemy starts with "en" too, but means a foe, not a mystery.
A detective solves mysteries but isn't a mystery itself.

syn1.tip: You may know the phrase "a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma." An enigma is something nobody can figure out.

traps.why: Easy to explain is the opposite of an enigma.
Lost things are hard to find; an enigma is hard to understand.
Enigmas can be spooky, but the word means puzzling, not frightening.

syn2.tip: People say a quiet, unusual person "is an enigma" when nobody can figure them out. Think puzzling, not lost or scary.

traps.why: Scientists "cannot explain" it, so it isn't an explanation.
Nature teaches lessons, but the clue says the navigation is unexplained.
Proof settles a question, but this question is still open.

sc1.tip: The clue is "scientists still cannot explain" and "baffling." Something nobody can explain is a mystery.

sc2.sentence: Our new neighbor never speaks to anyone, leaves only at midnight, and has no name on his mailbox, so to the whole street he is a complete _____.

traps.why: Everyone knows a celebrity; nobody knows anything about this neighbor.
He never speaks to anyone, so he can't be everyone's friend.
Hero is strongly positive, and he has done nothing heroic.

sc2.tip: The clues come before "so": he never speaks, goes out at midnight, and has no name. Because nobody can figure him out, he's a puzzle.

secluded.hook: A secluded spot is shut away from the crowd, like a hidden beach only you know about.

traps.why: Crowded is the opposite of secluded.
Excluded looks similar but means left out on purpose by others.
Secluded places are often peaceful, but secluded means hidden away.

syn1.tip: Think of "a secluded beach" or "a secluded corner." These are places tucked far away from other people.

traps.why: Out in the open is the opposite of hidden away.
Jail separates people too, but secluded means tucked away, not imprisoned.
Secluded is neutral; it says nothing about feeling sad.

syn2.tip: Secluded describes a place, like a cabin or a beach, that is tucked out of sight where few people go.

traps.why: Miles from the nearest neighbor can't be crowded.
Spacious is about room inside, not being far from people.
Modern is about how new it is, not where it is.

sc1.tip: The clue is "deep in the woods, miles from the nearest neighbor and reachable only by a narrow dirt road." That describes a cabin hidden away.

sc2.sentence: Most of the lake's shore was packed with noisy swimmers, but we found a _____ cove behind the rocks where we could read in total quiet.

traps.why: Popular means many people come, but this cove was quiet.
A cove can be sandy, but the clue is about having no people.
Dangerous is negative, but the cove was a pleasant, quiet spot.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the shore "packed with noisy swimmers" with a spot "behind the rocks" in "total quiet." You want a word meaning tucked away.

blight.hook: Picture healthy green leaves turning black and slimy overnight: that is a blight wiping out a crop.

traps.why: A cure ends a disease; a blight is the disease.
Flight rhymes with blight but means flying.
A blight ruins the harvest, but it isn't the harvest.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of the Irish potato blight. A blight is a sickness that kills plants and crops.

traps.why: A healthy crop is the opposite of one hit by blight.
Fertilizer helps plants grow; blight destroys them.
A drought also harms crops, but blight is a disease.

syn2.tip: Farmers fear "potato blight" and "tomato blight." Link the word with crops getting sick and rotting.

traps.why: A harvest gathers crops; it doesn't blacken and rot them.
Drought dries plants out, but this rotted crops in the ground.
A celebration is happy, but this was "terrible" and destroyed crops.

sc1.tip: The clue is "turning the leaves black and rotting the crops." Something that sweeps through fields and rots plants is a plant disease.

sc2.sentence: Every elm tree on our street once stood tall and green, but after a _____ spread from tree to tree, workers had to cut down all the dying elms.

traps.why: A cure would save the trees, not leave them dying.
Fertilizer helps trees grow and doesn't spread from tree to tree.
A rainstorm doesn't spread from tree to tree and kill elms.

sc2.tip: Follow cause and effect: something "spread from tree to tree" and left them "dying." A sickness that spreads among plants fits.

abrasive.hook: Sandpaper is abrasive, and so is a person whose words rub you the wrong way.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of abrasive.
Evasive ends the same way but means avoiding answers.
Firm is a positive word; abrasive means unpleasantly rough.

syn1.tip: Sandpaper and scouring powder are called abrasive because they scrape. An abrasive person scrapes at people's feelings.

traps.why: Kind and polite is the opposite of abrasive.
Honest and direct sounds positive; abrasive is rough in a hurtful way.
Abrasive people may be loud, but the word means harsh, not noisy.

syn2.tip: Think of scrubbing with something scratchy. Abrasive means rough like that, whether it's a surface or a person's manner.

traps.why: Shouting and insults are the opposite of gentle.
Cheerful is positive, but players wanted to quit.
A shy coach wouldn't be constantly shouting.

sc1.tip: The clues are "constant shouting," "cutting insults," and "rubbed the players the wrong way." A manner that rubs people raw is harsh.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the soft cotton towels in the bathroom, the scrubbing pad in the kitchen is so _____ that it can scrape burned food right off a pan.

traps.why: Something smooth couldn't scrape burned food off a pan.
Absorbent looks similar but means soaking up water, like the towels.
Clean is about dirt, not the rough surface that scrapes.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the soft cotton towels" tells you the pad is the opposite of soft, and "scrape burned food" shows it's rough and scratchy.

enlighten.hook: To enlighten is to switch on a light in someone's mind so they finally see and understand.

traps.why: Confuse is the opposite of enlighten.
Light is inside it, but enlighten means give understanding, not add light.
Entertaining amuses people; enlightening teaches them.

syn1.tip: Picture a light bulb over someone's head when they finally get it. To enlighten someone is to give them that understanding.

traps.why: Leaving someone puzzled is the opposite of enlightening them.
Testing checks what you know; enlightening adds to it.
Lighten up sounds like cheer up, but enlighten is about understanding.

syn2.tip: People say "Please enlighten me" when they want something explained. It means to help someone understand.

traps.why: They were already confused; they wanted the opposite.
The travelers wanted answers given to them, not to be questioned.
Mislead means giving false ideas; they wanted the truth.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Confused by the strange symbols." Because they were confused, they asked for someone to explain "what each mark meant."

sc2.sentence: Our librarian loves to _____ curious students, and she always explains hard topics until everyone in the room finally understands.

traps.why: Puzzling students is the opposite of making them understand.
Scold is negative, but the librarian patiently explains.
Quizzing checks knowledge, but the clue is about explaining.

sc2.tip: The second half restates the first: she "explains hard topics until everyone in the room finally understands." The blank means giving understanding.

calamity.hook: A calamity is no small oops; think flood, earthquake, or a volcano burying a whole city.

traps.why: A blessing is a good thing, the opposite of a calamity.
Calmness starts like calamity but means peace and quiet.
Problem is too weak; a calamity is a terrible disaster.

syn1.tip: News reports use calamity for huge events like floods and earthquakes. It's a strong word for a terrible disaster.

traps.why: A lucky break is good fortune, the opposite of a calamity.
Small is far too weak; a calamity causes great harm.
Calamity starts like calm, but it means disaster.

syn2.tip: Calamity sounds dramatic, and it is. It names something terrible that causes great damage or suffering.

traps.why: A triumph is a great success, not a city destroyed.
Inconvenience is far too weak for losing a whole city.
Pompeii was a famous discovery later, but the eruption destroyed it.

sc1.tip: The clue is "destroying the entire city in a single day." Something that wipes out a whole city is a terrible disaster.

sc2.sentence: Everyone feared the burst pipe would be a _____ that ruined every book in the library, but the janitor shut off the water just in time.

traps.why: No one fears a blessing or expects it to ruin books.
Celebration is happy, but people "feared" this.
A hiccup is a tiny problem, but this would ruin every book.

sc2.tip: Don't be fooled by the happy ending after "but." The blank is what people "feared": something that "ruined every book." That's a disaster.

wield.hook: A knight wields a sword, a chef wields a knife, and a president wields power.

traps.why: Drop means let go, the opposite of wielding a tool.
Weld looks almost the same but means join metal with heat.
Yield rhymes with wield but means give way or give up.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "wield a sword" or "wield power." It means to hold something and use it with control.

traps.why: Fumbling clumsily is the opposite of wielding with skill.
Carrying is too general; wielding means actually using it with skill.
That describes weld, which looks like wield but means something else.

syn2.tip: A warrior who "wields a sword" isn't just holding it; she's swinging it with control. Wield means to use something skillfully.

traps.why: Fumbling is clumsy, but he worked "so skillfully."
Lifting alone can't carve petals; he had to use it skillfully.
Yield sounds like wield but means give up.

sc1.tip: The clues are "so skillfully" and "carved delicate flower petals." He's not just holding the chisel; he's using it with great control.

sc2.sentence: At first the new drummer could barely hold his sticks, but after a summer of lessons he could _____ them with the speed and control of a professional.

traps.why: Dropping sticks shows no control, but he plays like a professional.
Painting sticks has nothing to do with speed and control.
Weld looks like wield but means join metal with heat.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "could barely hold his sticks" with "speed and control of a professional." The blank means using them with skill.

contagious.hook: One person yawns, then another, then the whole room: a contagious yawn jumps from person to person.

traps.why: Contained means kept in one place, the opposite of spreading.
Contiguous looks similar but means touching or next to something.
Illnesses can be curable, but contagious is about spreading, not healing.

syn1.tip: Think of a contagious yawn or laugh. It spreads from one person to the next, just like a cold you can catch.

traps.why: Something contagious moves to others; this means it stays put.
Germs can be contagious, but so can laughter, which makes no one sick.
The tag inside contagious has nothing to do with tagging along.

syn2.tip: Germs, giggles, and moods can all be contagious. The key idea is spreading from one person to another.

traps.why: Hidden excitement could not spread to the whole bus.
Contiguous means touching or next to, which makes no sense for excitement.
Tiresome excitement would annoy people, not get them cheering.

sc1.tip: "So _____ that within minutes the entire bus was cheering" shows his excitement spread to everyone. You need a word meaning able to spread.

sc2.sentence: Unlike a broken arm, which stays with one patient, the flu is _____, so the nurse asked sick students to stay home.

traps.why: Broken arms hurt too, so painful gives no contrast with a broken arm.
Contained means kept in one place, but the flu spreads to others.
If the flu were harmless, the nurse would not send sick students home.

sc2.tip: "Unlike a broken arm, which stays with one patient" sets up a contrast. The flu must be the kind of illness that spreads to others.

discourage.hook: Discourage takes the courage out of you: dis plus courage means losing the heart to try.

traps.why: Cheering someone on makes them more eager, the opposite of discourage.
Discouraging lowers eagerness; scaring to death is far too strong.
Disagree starts with dis too, but it means having a different opinion.

syn1.tip: Split it: dis plus courage. To discourage someone takes away their courage or eagerness, so they feel put off.

traps.why: Making someone more eager is encouraging, the opposite.
Discouraging lowers eagerness, but a ban stops something completely.
Embarrassment might discourage you, but it means shame, not losing eagerness.

syn2.tip: People say "don't get discouraged" when you want to give up. Discourage means lowering someone's eagerness to try.

traps.why: Inspiring her would match motivating, so "instead" would make no sense.
Discover looks similar but means find, and scores cannot find Ayana.
Dismiss means send away, which test scores cannot do to a student.

sc1.tip: "Did not _____ Ayana; instead, they motivated her" signals a contrast. The blank is the opposite of motivating, a word for making someone want to quit.

sc2.sentence: The coach worried that one bad loss might _____ the younger players, making them lose confidence and want to quit the team.

traps.why: Motivating players makes them want to keep going, not quit.
Reward is a happy word, but the players lose confidence here.
Dissolve starts with dis but means melt away, like sugar in water.

sc2.tip: The phrase "making them lose confidence and want to quit" explains the blank. You need a word meaning take away someone's eagerness.

oasis.hook: Picture a ring of palm trees around a cool blue pool in the middle of endless sand dunes.

traps.why: A wasteland is empty and barren, the opposite of a welcoming oasis.
A mirage is fake water you imagine; an oasis is real.
Basis looks similar but means the foundation of an idea.

syn1.tip: An oasis is a safe green spot in a harsh desert. People call any peaceful escape an oasis, like a quiet library on a noisy day.

traps.why: An oasis is the wet, green break from dry sand.
That describes a mirage; an oasis has real water.
An oasis has water, but it is a small spot inside a desert.

syn2.tip: Think of desert travelers spotting palm trees in the distance. An oasis is real water and green plants surrounded by dry sand.

traps.why: Dunes are in deserts, but they are hills of dry sand, not water.
The travelers really reached the water, so it was not a mirage.
A wasteland is barren, not full of spring water and palm trees.

sc1.tip: "Cool spring water" and "shady palm trees" in a "hot, dusty" place describe one thing: a green, watered spot in dry land.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the crowded, noisy cafeteria, the school library felt like a calm _____ where students could read in peace.

traps.why: A madhouse is wild and noisy, the reverse of calm and peaceful.
A mirage is not real, but students really read in the library.
Basis looks like oasis but means a foundation, not a place.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the crowded, noisy cafeteria" sets up a contrast. The library must be a peaceful escape, the way an oasis is an escape in a desert.

amend.hook: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments: changes added to improve the U.S. Constitution.

traps.why: Amending makes something better; worsen means make it worse.
Amaze looks similar but means surprise someone greatly.
Lawmakers approve or amend rules, but approving accepts something as it is.

syn1.tip: Amendments to the Constitution are changes that fix or improve it. To amend something is to revise it.

traps.why: Damaging harms something; amending improves it.
Amending changes part of something; replacing swaps out the whole thing.
You obey rules as they are; amending changes them.

syn2.tip: Hidden inside amend is "mend," as in mending a torn shirt. Amending fixes or corrects something.

traps.why: Enforcing makes people follow a rule; adding an exception changes it.
Canceling gets rid of the rule, but she kept it and added an exception.
Defending keeps the rule unchanged, but she changed it.

sc1.tip: "Unfair" and "by adding an exception" tell you the principal changed the rule to fix it. You need a word meaning improve or correct.

sc2.sentence: Rather than throwing out her entire essay, Priya decided to _____ it, fixing a few weak sentences and adding a stronger conclusion.

traps.why: Discarding means throwing it out, which "rather than" rules out.
She might submit it later, but fixing sentences is improving it.
Amass looks similar but means collect a large amount.

sc2.tip: "Rather than throwing out her entire essay" means she kept it, and "fixing a few weak sentences" tells you she improved it.

intricate.hook: Picture a snowflake under a magnifying glass: so many tiny, detailed parts that it looks intricate.

traps.why: Simple means plain and easy, the opposite of intricate.
Intimate looks similar but means close and personal.
Intricate things are often delicate, but delicate means easily broken.

syn1.tip: Intricate things have lots of small parts woven together, like a detailed drawing or a maze. Think complicated, not plain.

traps.why: Plain means having few details, the opposite of intricate.
Intricate things may cost a lot, but intricate is about many parts.
Intricate things are complicated but still possible to make or understand.

syn2.tip: Picture an intricate quilt pattern of tiny stars carefully stitched. Intricate means full of fine details.

traps.why: A basic clock would not need the one expert repairman.
Value does not explain why only one person could fix it.
Intimate means close and personal, which does not describe a clock.

sc1.tip: "Hundreds of tiny gears fitting together" and "only one repairman" who could fix it point to something with many complicated parts.

sc2.sentence: Maya's first paper airplane was simple to fold, but the dragon in her origami book was far more _____, requiring forty-two careful folds and tiny tucks.

traps.why: Basic would fit only if you missed the contrast word "but."
Origami can be colorful, but the clue is about the number of folds.
Dragons can be scary, but the clue is about careful folds and tucks.

sc2.tip: "Simple to fold, but" signals a contrast, and "forty-two careful folds and tiny tucks" shows the dragon has many complicated steps.

rampant.hook: Picture weeds swallowing a garden and vines climbing everything while nobody stops them: that wild growth is rampant.

traps.why: Controlled means kept in check, the opposite of rampant.
Rampant things are often harmful, but rampant means spreading wildly.
Radiant looks a bit similar but means glowing or bright.

syn1.tip: You often hear "rampant" with bad things that spread, like "rampant cheating" or "rampant weeds." It means growing with nothing to stop it.

traps.why: Kept in check means controlled, the opposite of rampant.
Rampant spreading is fast and wild, not slow.
Rampage looks similar, but rampant is about spreading, not anger.

syn2.tip: Rampant describes something spreading wildly, like rumors racing around school. Ask yourself whether anything is stopping it. If not, it is rampant.

traps.why: Limited growth would not smother plants faster than volunteers worked.
Beautiful is positive, but smothering native plants is a bad thing.
Plants grow in seasons, but the clue is about growth nobody can stop.

sc1.tip: "Smothering native plants faster than volunteers could pull it up" shows nothing could stop the vine. The blank needs a word for wild, uncontrolled growth.

sc2.sentence: Last month only a couple of students believed the rumor about a four-day school week, but by Friday it was _____, repeated in every hallway and classroom.

traps.why: Rare would fit only if you missed "but" and "every hallway."
Rumors are often false, but the clue is about how far it spread.
The clue is about the rumor spreading everywhere, not how fun it felt.

sc2.tip: "Only a couple of students... but by Friday" signals a big change, and "repeated in every hallway" shows the rumor spread wildly.

spirited.hook: Think of school spirit: a spirited crowd jumps, chants, and cheers with energy that fills the whole gym.

traps.why: Dull means lacking energy, the opposite of spirited.
Spiritual looks similar but is about religion or the soul.
Spirit can mean ghost, but spirited means full of energy.

syn1.tip: Think of "school spirit." Fans with school spirit cheer loudly. Spirited means full of that kind of energy.

traps.why: Sluggish means slow and tired, the opposite of spirited.
Frantic is wild and panicked, much stronger than spirited.
Rowdy is negative and unruly; spirited is a positive word.

syn2.tip: Spirited is a positive word for having lots of pep. A spirited team or debate is full of energy, not wild or out of control.

traps.why: Gloomy fits only if you miss "although"; the fans kept cheering.
Spiritual is about religion or the soul, not cheering fans.
The team was losing, but cheering fans did not act defeated.

sc1.tip: "Although the team was losing badly" sets up a contrast, and "cheering, chanting, and waving banners" shows the fans stayed full of energy.

sc2.sentence: After a long nap and a big snack, the puppy was suddenly _____, racing around the yard, chasing its tail, and pouncing on every leaf.

traps.why: Drowsy means sleepy, but the puppy is racing and pouncing.
It just had a big snack, and racing around shows energy.
Spirit can mean ghost, but the puppy is full of energy.

sc2.tip: "After a long nap and a big snack" explains the change, and "racing," "chasing," and "pouncing" describe a puppy full of energy.

ambush.hook: Ambush comes from an old French word meaning to hide in the woods, exactly where attackers wait.

traps.why: A warning tells you danger is coming; an ambush gives no warning.
An ambush can start a battle, but it is specifically a hidden surprise.
Ambulance starts the same way but is a vehicle for sick people.

syn1.tip: Picture attackers crouched out of sight, waiting to spring on someone passing by. An ambush is a hidden trap.

traps.why: An ambush is a hostile surprise, not a friendly heads-up.
A retreat is moving away from a fight, not springing an attack.
A war is huge and long; an ambush is one sudden attack.

syn2.tip: An ambush depends on surprise. The attackers stay hidden, then strike suddenly, so ambush means a surprise attack.

traps.why: A truce stops a fight, but they leaped out throwing snowballs.
Snowmen fit the snowy scene, but you cannot leap out from one.
Ambulance looks similar but is a vehicle for sick people.

sc1.tip: "Hid behind the hedge" and "leaping out to surprise their cousins" describe a hidden attack. That sneak attack is the missing word.

sc2.sentence: Instead of charging openly across the field, the soldiers hid quietly in the forest, planning their _____ for when the enemy troops marched down the road.

traps.why: A charge is an open attack, which "instead of" rules out.
Troops march in parades, but hiding soldiers are planning an attack.
Ambition starts like ambush but means a strong goal or dream.

sc2.tip: "Instead of charging openly" tells you the attack was not open, and "hid quietly in the forest" shows it was a hidden surprise.

articulate.hook: Articulate comes from Latin for jointed: an articulate speaker joins words together smoothly, like well-fitted joints.

traps.why: Tongue-tied means unable to find words, the opposite of articulate.
Artistic starts with art too but means skilled at art.
Talkative people talk a lot, but not always clearly.

syn1.tip: Articulate people put their thoughts into clear words. If someone explains a hard idea so everyone gets it, they are articulate.

traps.why: Articulate people explain things well, the reverse of this.
Articulate is a compliment; loud and pushy is negative.
Articulate begins with art, but it is about speaking, not painting.

syn2.tip: Think of the verb: you articulate ideas when you put them into words. An articulate person does that clearly and well.

traps.why: A shy child would not win applause for a persuasive speech.
Artistic is about art, but the clue is about explaining clearly.
Stubborn is negative, but the adults applauded her clear explanation.

sc1.tip: "Explaining her recycling plan so clearly and persuasively" is the clue. The blank must describe someone who expresses ideas well in words.

sc2.sentence: Usually Marcus mumbled and lost his place during reports, but at the science fair he was surprisingly _____, describing his volcano project in clear, confident sentences.

traps.why: Tongue-tied fits only if you miss "but"; he spoke clearly here.
Volcanoes are explosive, but the clue is about how Marcus spoke.
Boastful is negative; clear, confident sentences show skill, not bragging.

sc2.tip: "Usually Marcus mumbled... but" signals a contrast, and "clear, confident sentences" tells you he spoke well.

covert.hook: Covert comes from an old French word meaning covered: a covert plan is covered up so nobody sees it.

traps.why: Public means open for all to see, the opposite of covert.
Coveted looks similar but means strongly wanted, like a coveted trophy.
Spy missions can be dangerous, but covert means hidden.

syn1.tip: Covert looks like "covered." A covert plan is covered up so others cannot see it, like a spy mission.

traps.why: Overt means out in the open, the reverse of covert.
Covert actions can be harmless, like a surprise party; illegal is negative.
Secret plans may be clever, but covert means kept hidden.

syn2.tip: Think of "covert operations" in spy movies. Agents stay hidden so nobody knows what they are doing.

traps.why: A public mission would not need whispering or waiting until she left.
Decorating might be hard, but the clue is about keeping it hidden.
Coveted means strongly wanted, which does not explain the whispering.

sc1.tip: "Whispering in hallways" and "meeting only after she had left the building" show the students kept their plan hidden from their teacher.

sc2.sentence: Most of the soccer team's plays were obvious, but the coach also taught a _____ signal, a tiny tug on her ear that the other team never noticed.

traps.why: A loud signal would be noticed, but the other team never noticed.
A tiny ear tug is simple; the clue is about it being unnoticed.
Friendliness has nothing to do with the other team never noticing.

sc2.tip: "Most... were obvious, but" sets up a contrast, and "the other team never noticed" tells you the signal was hidden.

credible.hook: Credible shares its Latin root cred, meaning believe, with words like credit and credentials.

traps.why: Doubtful is the opposite of credible; it means hard to believe.
Popular things are liked by many, but that doesn't make them believable.
Impressive is close to what incredible often means, but credible means believable.

syn1.tip: Look for cred, which means believe, plus -ible, which means able to be. Credible means able to be believed.

traps.why: Unreliable is the opposite; a credible source is one you can rely on.
Gullible describes someone who believes too easily, not something worth believing.
Edible means safe to eat; it only shares the -ible ending.

syn2.tip: Think of credit: a bank gives credit to people it trusts. Credible things deserve your trust.

traps.why: The article was flawed, so saying it was not flawed contradicts the clue.
Popularity has nothing to do with missing sources and spelling errors.
Recent is about the date, but the clue is about whether it can be trusted.

sc1.tip: The words "cited no sources" and "full of spelling errors" show the article can't be trusted, so it is not a believable source.

sc2.sentence: Although Marco's excuse about a dog eating his homework sounded silly at first, it became _____ when he showed the teacher the chewed, soggy pages.

traps.why: The excuse sounded silly at first; the chewed pages changed that, so ridiculous is backward.
Edible means safe to eat; it only looks like credible.
The pages made the story easier to believe, not more complicated.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a change: the excuse "sounded silly at first," but the chewed pages proved it, so it became believable.
