catalyst.hook: In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction; in life, it is the spark that gets big changes going.

traps.why: An obstacle blocks change; a catalyst gets change started.
A catalog is a list of items for sale; it only looks like catalyst.
A result comes after a change; a catalyst comes first and causes it.

syn1.tip: Think of science class: a catalyst makes a reaction happen faster. Anything that sets off change is a catalyst.

traps.why: A barrier stops things from moving forward; a catalyst pushes change ahead.
An outcome is what happens at the end, not what starts the change.
In science a catalyst can be a chemical, but the word means a trigger.

syn2.tip: A catalyst is the thing that starts something happening, like pulling a trigger. Picture a match lighting a fire.

traps.why: A setback slows things down, but the discovery made change happen fast.
Gold sounds like a reward, but the clue is about what started rapid change.
California was the place, but the discovery itself is what set off the change.

sc1.tip: "Causing thousands of people to rush west" shows the discovery started the change, so it was the spark.

sc2.sentence: Mia's science fair win was the _____ that turned her quiet interest in robots into a real passion; in other words, it set everything in motion.

traps.why: An obstacle would block her passion, but the win set everything in motion.
A catalog is a list of products; it only looks like catalyst.
A reminder brings back the past; it doesn't set things in motion.

sc2.tip: "In other words, it set everything in motion" restates the blank: the win was what started the change.

prestige.hook: Prestige once meant a magic trick; today it means the dazzling respect that comes with big success.

traps.why: Disgrace means loss of respect, the opposite of prestige.
Rich people may have prestige, but prestige is respect, not money.
Pride is a feeling inside you; prestige is respect others give you.

syn1.tip: Think of a prestigious school or award: it is admired because of its success and high rank.

traps.why: Public shame is the opposite of the respect that prestige brings.
A fortune is money, but prestige is respect, which money can't guarantee.
Hard work may earn prestige, but it isn't the respect itself.

syn2.tip: Prestige is how highly others rank you. Picture a trophy that makes everyone look up to the winner.

traps.why: Shame would not bring invitations and admiration from musicians.
Risk is a worried, negative idea; the clue shows only good results.
Concerts can cost money, but the clue is about admiration, not cost.

sc1.tip: "Earning them invitations and admiration from musicians everywhere" shows the honor brought respect, which is prestige.

sc2.sentence: Though the small art school had little money and few buildings, its famous graduates gave it more _____ than many larger colleges, and students competed hard to get in.

traps.why: Students would not compete to join a school that embarrasses them.
Graduates can't add buildings or room; the clue is about reputation.
Trouble is negative, but famous graduates and eager students show something good.

sc2.tip: "Though" sets up a contrast: little money, but "famous graduates" and students who "competed hard to get in" show the school was highly respected.

arrogant.hook: Picture someone with their nose in the air, strutting past everyone as if the whole world were their throne.

traps.why: Humble people don't think they are better than others; it's the opposite.
Confident is the positive version; arrogant means looking down on others.
Ignorant means lacking knowledge; it only looks like arrogant.

syn1.tip: Arrogant has a negative feeling. Picture a show-off who won't listen to anyone because he thinks he knows best.

traps.why: Modest people play down their success, the opposite of arrogant.
Arrogant people may be rude, but arrogant specifically means acting superior.
Self-assured is a positive word; arrogant is negative.

syn2.tip: An arrogant person acts superior, like a snob who thinks others are beneath them.

traps.why: A shy person wouldn't brag to everyone.
Winning shows some skill, but bragging and refusing advice show an attitude.
Excited is a happy feeling; refusing expert advice shows something worse.

sc1.tip: "Bragged to everyone" and "refused to take advice" from experienced players show Derek thinks he is better than others.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his _____ older brother, who sneered at anyone who could not keep up, Leo patiently helped the younger kids learn to skateboard at the park.

traps.why: Leo is the helpful one; "unlike" means his brother is different.
A clumsy brother would not sneer at people who can't keep up.
Quiet doesn't explain sneering; the clue is about looking down on others.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts the brother with patient Leo, and "sneered at anyone who could not keep up" shows the brother thinks he's better.

contempt.hook: In "contempt of court," someone openly disrespects a judge; contempt means looking down on someone as worthless.

traps.why: Admiration means looking up to someone, the opposite of contempt.
Contentment means feeling satisfied; it only looks like contempt.
Anger can be hot and quick; contempt means thinking someone is worthless.

syn1.tip: You may know "contempt of court," when someone disrespects a judge. Contempt is a sneering, looking-down feeling.

traps.why: Honor shows high respect, the opposite of contempt.
Attempt rhymes with contempt, but it means a try.
Jealousy means wanting what someone has; contempt means thinking they're worthless.

syn2.tip: Picture a sneer or an eye roll. Contempt is the feeling that someone isn't worth your respect.

traps.why: Refusing a handshake and smirking are not kind.
He acts as if she doesn't deserve to be there, not as if she scares him.
Smirking can look amused, but acting like she doesn't deserve the court is scornful.

sc1.tip: "Refusing to shake her hand" and "smirking as if she did not deserve" to be there show he thinks she is worthless.

sc2.sentence: Because the bully had laughed at her drawings for weeks, Nora felt nothing but _____ for him and would not even look at him when he apologized.

traps.why: Sympathy means caring about someone's feelings; Nora won't even look at him.
Gratitude is a thankful feeling, but the bully gave her nothing to thank.
Envy means wanting what he has; Nora wants nothing from the bully.

sc2.tip: "Because" the bully "laughed at her drawings for weeks," Nora "would not even look at him." She thinks he is worthless.

vain.hook: Picture a peacock admiring its feathers in a mirror; that is vain. Don't confuse it with vein or weather vane.

traps.why: Modest people don't show off their looks, the opposite of vain.
"In vain" means uselessly, but a vain person is too proud of themselves.
Pretty describes looks; vain describes being too proud of your looks.

syn1.tip: Think of a vain person staring into a mirror all day. The word is about too much pride in yourself.

traps.why: Truly humble is the opposite of vain.
That fits "in vain," but a vain person is too proud of themselves.
A vain person thinks they are attractive, but they may not be.

syn2.tip: Picture the queen in Snow White asking her mirror who is fairest. Being vain means too much pride in your looks.

traps.why: A careless person wouldn't spend an hour styling her hair.
Checking every window and styling for an hour isn't relaxed.
Curious means wanting to learn; checking every reflection shows pride, not curiosity.

sc1.tip: "Checked her reflection in every window" and "an hour styling it each morning" show too much pride in her looks.

sc2.sentence: The famous actor was surprisingly modest in interviews, but his costar was so _____ that she demanded mirrors in every room and talked only about her own beauty.

traps.why: "But" shows the costar is unlike the modest actor, so humble is backward.
That fits "in vain," but the sentence is about her pride in her beauty.
Talent doesn't explain demanding mirrors and talking only about her beauty.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the costar with the "modest" actor, and "talked only about her own beauty" shows too much pride in her looks.

condemn.hook: Picture a judge banging the gavel and declaring for all to hear that something is wrong; that is what condemn means.

traps.why: Praise means saying something is good, the opposite of condemn.
Condense means to make smaller or thicker; it only looks like condemn.
You can discuss something without saying it is wrong.

syn1.tip: Condemn has a strong negative feeling. Think of leaders who condemn cruelty: they say loudly that it is wrong.

traps.why: Warmly praise is the opposite of saying something is wrong.
Ignoring says nothing at all; condemning speaks out against something.
Mildly question is far too weak; condemning is strong disapproval.

syn2.tip: A building that is "condemned" is declared unsafe. To condemn is to declare strongly that something is bad or wrong.

traps.why: Calling the dumping harmful is not defending it.
Condone means to allow or excuse; it looks like condemn but is nearly opposite.
Advertising promotes something; calling it harmful does the opposite.

sc1.tip: "Calling it harmful and irresponsible" is strong public disapproval, so the scientists said the dumping was wrong.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the many people who praised the new law, the mayor chose to _____ it in a fiery speech, calling it cruel and unfair to families.

traps.why: Applauding agrees with the people who praised it, but "unlike" means the mayor disagreed.
Mayors sign laws, but calling it cruel shows she spoke against it.
Doubting is much weaker than calling something cruel in a fiery speech.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets the mayor against people who "praised" the law, and "calling it cruel and unfair" shows strong disapproval.

volatile.hook: Picture a volcano that might erupt any minute: volatile things, and people, can blow up or change suddenly.

traps.why: Steady means staying the same, the opposite of volatile.
Valuable means worth a lot; it only looks a little like volatile.
A volatile person might turn violent, but volatile means likely to change suddenly.

syn1.tip: You may hear about a volatile temper or volatile weather. Both can change in a flash.

traps.why: Always the same is the opposite of volatile.
Volatile comes from a Latin word for fly, but it means likely to change.
That describes fragile things; volatile things change suddenly instead.

syn2.tip: Think of a volatile mood that flips from happy to furious. Volatile means it can change in a moment.

traps.why: Stable weather wouldn't turn from sun to hail within an hour.
Mountains can be cold, but the clue is about sudden change.
A surprise hailstorm isn't pleasant; the clue warns hikers to be ready.

sc1.tip: "A sunny morning can turn into a hailstorm within an hour" shows the weather changes suddenly.

sc2.sentence: Sam's older dog was calm around strangers, but his new puppy was so _____ that it could be licking someone's hand one moment and growling at them the next.

traps.why: "But" shows the puppy is unlike the calm dog, so gentle is backward.
Puppies are playful, but growling suddenly shows quick changes, not play.
Versatile means able to do many things well; it only looks like volatile.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the puppy with the "calm" dog, and licking "one moment" then growling "the next" shows sudden change.

perceive.hook: Your eyes, ears, and nose help you perceive the world, like smelling smoke before you ever see the fire.

traps.why: Overlook means to miss something, the opposite of perceive.
Receive means to get something; it only looks and rhymes like perceive.
Believing means accepting something as true; perceiving means noticing it.

syn1.tip: Think of perception, how your senses take in the world. To perceive is to notice through seeing, hearing, or feeling.

traps.why: Fail to see is the opposite of perceive.
Thinking hard about something is different from first noticing it.
Deceive rhymes with perceive, but deceive means to trick.

syn2.tip: Perceive is about your senses picking something up. If you perceive a sound, you become aware of it.

traps.why: Bats find their prey, so they don't ignore the insects.
Bats may scare insects, but the clue is about finding them without seeing.
Receive means to be given something; it only looks like perceive.

sc1.tip: "Finding their prey even when they cannot see it" shows bats become aware of insects by using echoes.

sc2.sentence: The change in the music was so tiny that most listeners missed it, but the trained conductor was able to _____ it right away and stopped the orchestra.

traps.why: Most listeners overlooked it; "but" shows the conductor did the opposite.
Conductors work with music, but he stopped the orchestra because he noticed something.
Deceive rhymes with perceive, but it means to trick.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the conductor with listeners who "missed it," and he "stopped the orchestra," so he noticed the change.

retrieve.hook: Golden retrievers got their name because they retrieve, bringing back ducks and tennis balls their owners send flying.

traps.why: Abandon means to leave behind, the opposite of retrieve.
Relieve means to ease pain or worry; it only looks like retrieve.
You throw a ball for a dog, but the dog retrieves it by bringing it back.

syn1.tip: Think of a golden retriever bringing back a stick. The re- means back: retrieve means get it back.

traps.why: Leave behind is the opposite of getting something back.
Re- can mean again, but here it means back, not trying again.
You may search first, but retrieve means actually getting it back.

syn2.tip: The re- in retrieve means back, as in return. A retriever dog gets the ball and brings it back.

traps.why: She already forgot it; she races to the depot to get it back.
Nothing says the project is broken; she just left it on the bus.
Replacing means getting a new one; Isabel wants her own project back.

sc1.tip: "Left her science project on the bus" causes her to race to the depot, so she wants to get it back.

sc2.sentence: Instead of leaving his kite tangled in the tall oak tree, Jamal borrowed a long ladder from his neighbor to _____ it.

traps.why: "Instead of leaving" means Jamal does not abandon the kite.
Kites get launched, but a ladder in a tree is for getting it down.
Relieve means to ease pain or worry; it only looks like retrieve.

sc2.tip: "Instead of leaving his kite" signals a contrast: Jamal climbs a ladder so he can get the kite back.

plaintive.hook: Plaintive shares its origin with complaint, so picture a sad, mournful complaint set to a voice.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of plaintive, which sounds sad.
Plain means simple; it only looks like the start of plaintive.
A plaintive cry may be loud, but plaintive is about sadness, not volume.

syn1.tip: Think of complaint, which shares its origin with plaintive. A plaintive sound is like a sad complaint.

traps.why: Joyful is the opposite of plaintive.
Angry cries complain too, but plaintive sounds sad, not mad.
A plaintive sound can be faint or loud; plaintive is about sadness.

syn2.tip: Picture a lost kitten crying for its mother. That sad, mournful sound is plaintive.

traps.why: Joyful is the opposite of the sorrowful sound described.
Puppies can sound playful, but this whimper is called sorrowful.
Plain looks like plaintive but means simple, not sad.

sc1.tip: The phrase "so sorrowful" tells you the whimper sounded sad and mournful.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the happy barking at the park, the old dog's _____ howl at the empty doorway showed how much he missed his owner, who had left for college.

traps.why: Excited fits happy barking, but the sentence contrasts that with missing someone.
Playful is a happy feeling; missing his owner makes the howl sad.
Howls can be fierce, but missing someone sounds sad, not threatening.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the happy barking" signals a contrast, and "missed his owner" tells you the howl sounded sad.

morose.hook: Picture a kid slumped at the dinner table after a loss, scowling and refusing to speak. That is morose.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of morose.
Moral means good and right; it only looks like morose.
Both are bad moods, but furious is hot anger, not sulky gloom.

syn1.tip: Morose describes a sulky, gloomy mood. Picture someone who won't smile or talk after bad news.

traps.why: Bright and lively is the opposite of morose.
Calm is a pleasant quiet; morose is an unhappy, sullen quiet.
A morose person may be quiet, but from gloom, not shyness.

syn2.tip: Morose people sulk. If you can picture someone slumped and silent after losing, that is morose.

traps.why: Bubbly fits "usually cheerful," but she changed after her friend left.
Relieved is a good feeling; sulking and refusing to talk are not.
Moral means good and honest; it doesn't describe a sulky mood.

sc1.tip: "Usually cheerful" signals a change, and "sulking" and "refusing to talk" describe a gloomy mood.

sc2.sentence: Because the rain canceled the beach trip he had looked forward to all month, Theo stayed _____ all afternoon, staring out the window and barely speaking.

traps.why: Thrilled is the opposite of how a canceled trip would make him feel.
Relaxed is a pleasant calm; a canceled trip and silence suggest gloom.
Staring out a window might look curious, but the canceled trip points to gloom.

sc2.tip: "Because the rain canceled" a trip he had waited for, and "barely speaking" shows a sulky, gloomy mood.

rambunctious.hook: Picture rambunctious puppies tumbling, yapping, and knocking over the water bowl all at once.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of rambunctious.
Rambling means wandering or talking on and on, not wild and noisy.
Rambunctious kids are wild, but violent is far too strong.

syn1.tip: Say it out loud: rambunctious bounces and bumps like the noisy, wild energy it describes.

traps.why: Quiet and still is the opposite of rambunctious.
Rambunctious kids may knock things over, but from energy, not slowness.
Rambunctious describes lively energy, not meanness.

syn2.tip: Think of a playground after a sugary snack: running, shouting, bumping. That wild, noisy energy is rambunctious.

traps.why: Sleepy kids don't race around shrieking; that's the opposite.
Rambling means wandering in talk; it doesn't explain racing and shrieking.
Sugar might make kids queasy, but queasy kids don't race around shrieking.

sc1.tip: "Raced around," "shrieking," and "knocking over chairs" all describe wild, noisy energy.

sc2.sentence: The twins sat silently through the long wedding ceremony, but once the music started at the party, they turned _____, sliding across the dance floor and shouting with glee.

traps.why: Bashful fits the silent ceremony, but "but" signals they changed.
Dancing can be graceful, but sliding and shouting show wild energy.
Shouting can be angry, but "with glee" shows happy energy.

sc2.tip: "But once the music started" signals a change from silence, and "sliding" and "shouting with glee" show wild energy.

corrode.hook: Corrode shares a Latin root with rodent, meaning gnaw: picture rust slowly gnawing an old car's fender.

traps.why: Polishing makes metal shine, the opposite of corroding it.
Correct means fix a mistake; it only looks like corrode.
Heat melts metal quickly; corroding is a slow chemical wearing away.

syn1.tip: Corrode is what happens to a bike chain left out in the rain: it rusts and slowly wears away.

traps.why: Build up is the opposite of wearing something away.
Smashing breaks things fast by force; corroding wears them away slowly.
Heat can change metal, but corroding is a slow chemical wearing away.

syn2.tip: Corrode shares a root with rodent, meaning gnaw. Rust slowly eats away metal the way a mouse gnaws.

traps.why: Protecting the metal is the opposite of eating away at the chains.
Correct looks like corrode but means fix, which makes no sense here.
Ocean air feels cool, but cooling doesn't make chains crumble.

sc1.tip: "Eating away at the chains" and "turn orange and crumble" describe slow chemical damage to metal.

sc2.sentence: Dad wiped the old grill clean and gave it a fresh coat of paint, so rain would not _____ the metal and leave it full of crumbly orange holes.

traps.why: Strengthening is the opposite of leaving metal full of holes.
Rain does dampen things, but dampness alone doesn't leave crumbly holes.
Decorating is pleasant; crumbly orange holes are damage.

sc2.tip: Paint protects metal, "so" shows the reason, and "crumbly orange holes" describes rust damage.

brusque.hook: A brusque reply is short and sharp, like a door shut in your face: "Not now."

traps.why: Polite is the opposite of brusque.
A brusque person isn't necessarily giving orders; brusque means short and curt.
Cruel means wanting to hurt; brusque is only short and rude.

syn1.tip: Brusque sounds like a quick brush-off. A brusque answer is cut short and rude.

traps.why: Warm and friendly is the opposite of brusque.
Brusque is curt, not raging; loud and furious is much too strong.
Brusque people say little, but from rudeness, not shyness.

syn2.tip: Picture a busy clerk who says "Next" without looking up. That clipped, rude manner is brusque.

traps.why: A patient helper would look up and explain, the opposite of this.
A clever answer is smart, but turning away without looking shows rudeness.
He seemed rude, not enraged; furious is much too strong.

sc1.tip: "Two-word answer" and "without even looking up" show a short, rude manner.

sc2.sentence: Coach Patel is usually _____ with new players, barking orders without a smile; in other words, she is curt and impatient until they earn her trust.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of barking orders without a smile.
Generous is a kind word, but curt and impatient are not kind.
No smile could seem shy, but barking orders is rude, not shy.

sc2.tip: "In other words, she is curt and impatient" restates the blank, so it means short and rude.

enrage.hook: Enrage puts you in a rage: picture a bad call turning a calm crowd into a roaring mob.

traps.why: To calm someone is the opposite of enraging them.
Engage means involve or hold attention; one letter separates it from enrage.
Annoy is too weak; enrage means make extremely angry.

syn1.tip: Find rage inside enrage. To enrage someone is to fill them with rage.

traps.why: Making someone peaceful is the opposite of enraging them.
Jealousy is a strong feeling too, but enrage means make furious.
Grumpy is too mild; enraged people are extremely angry.

syn2.tip: En- can mean put into, as in endanger. Enrage puts someone into a rage.

traps.why: Litter on their clean park would not please them; that's the opposite.
Amuse is a happy feeling; ruined hard work brings anger.
The weekend's work might tire them, but seeing litter would make them furious.

sc1.tip: "Who had spent the whole weekend picking up trash" explains why fresh litter would make them furious.

sc2.sentence: Losing a board game usually just makes Marco shrug, but cheating will _____ him so much that he storms out of the room shouting.

traps.why: Relaxing is the opposite of storming out shouting.
Engage looks like enrage but means hold interest, not make furious.
Cheating might puzzle someone, but storming out shouting shows fury.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts a calm shrug with "storms out of the room shouting," so cheating makes him furious.

spurn.hook: Picture a cat sniffing cheap food, lifting its nose, and stalking away: it spurns the meal.

traps.why: Accept is the opposite of spurn.
To spur is to urge on, like a rider and horse; spurn means reject.
Postponing puts off a decision; spurning firmly turns it down.

syn1.tip: Spurn means turning something down with a sniff. Picture a proud person waving away a gift.

traps.why: Gladly welcome is the opposite of spurn.
Politely declining is gentle; spurning is rude and scornful.
Urge forward is what spur means; spurn is a different word.

syn2.tip: Spurn carries scorn. It is not a polite no but a proud, insulting refusal.

traps.why: He laughs at the offers, so he certainly doesn't accept them.
Considering means thinking offers over; laughing at them shows scorn.
Requesting means asking for offers; he laughs at them instead.

sc1.tip: "Laughing at even the largest sums" shows he rejects the offers with scorn.

sc2.sentence: Because Jordan had teased her all year, Mia decided to _____ his invitation to the party, tossing the card in the trash with a roll of her eyes.

traps.why: Tossing the card in the trash is the opposite of accepting.
Forgetting is accidental; tossing it with an eye roll is a deliberate rejection.
Answer is too general; the eye roll shows a scornful rejection.

sc2.tip: "Because Jordan had teased her" gives the reason, and "tossing the card" with an eye roll shows a scornful no.

credulous.hook: Credulous holds cred, meaning believe, as in credit: a credulous person believes almost anything.

traps.why: Suspicious is the opposite of credulous.
Credible means believable; a credulous person believes too easily.
Cred means believe, but credulous describes believing others, not being worth believing.

syn1.tip: Cred means believe, as in credit. A credulous person believes things too easily, even silly stories.

traps.why: Hard to fool is the opposite of credulous.
Credulous people may believe scary tales, but credulous is about believing, not fear.
Cred means believe, but credulous describes the believer, not the story.

syn2.tip: Credulous people fall for tricks. Picture someone believing a friend who says there's a dragon in the basement.

traps.why: Doubtful students would not believe such an unlikely rumor.
Credible means believable; it describes the rumor, not trusting students.
Studious students work hard; believing a silly rumor shows being too trusting.

sc1.tip: "Only the most" and a rumor about video games replacing homework point to students who believe too easily.

sc2.sentence: While her older sister instantly saw through the prank, _____ little Rosa really believed the cat had learned to talk.

traps.why: Suspicious fits the sister, but "while" sets Rosa against her.
Clever is praise, but believing a cat can talk is not clever.
Curious kids ask questions; believing the cat talks shows trusting too easily.

sc2.tip: "While" contrasts Rosa with a sister who "saw through the prank," so Rosa believes too easily.

scornful.hook: Scornful means full of scorn: picture a nose in the air and an eye roll at someone's cheap sneakers.

traps.why: Admiring is the opposite of scornful.
Scolding means telling someone off; scornful means looking down on them.
Disappointment is sadness at a letdown; scornful means looking down on someone.

syn1.tip: Split it: scorn plus -ful, full of. Scornful means full of scorn, sneering at what seems beneath you.

traps.why: Respectful is the opposite of scornful.
Scornful people may be calm; scorn is looking down on, not rage.
Playful teasing is friendly; scornful is cold and superior.

syn2.tip: Picture a curled lip and a sniff. That sneering, superior look is what a scornful person wears.

traps.why: She thinks the pizza is beneath her, so she is not delighted.
Pizza is about eating, but the clue is her looking down on it.
A polite sniff makes no sense when she thinks the pizza is beneath her.

sc1.tip: "As if the very idea of eating something so cheap were beneath her" shows she looks down on the pizza.

sc2.sentence: Since Jake thought he was the best skater in town, he gave a _____ laugh whenever younger kids fell, which made many of them quit coming to the park.

traps.why: A kindly laugh wouldn't drive kids away; that's the opposite.
A nervous laugh shows worry, but Jake thought he was the best.
A cheerful laugh wouldn't make kids quit; his laugh was mean.

sc2.tip: "Since Jake thought he was the best" explains why he looked down on others, and kids quitting shows the laugh mocked them.

admonish.hook: Picture a lifeguard blowing her whistle and wagging a finger at a running kid: she admonishes him.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite of admonish.
Punishing hands out a penalty; admonishing only warns or scolds.
Admire starts like admonish but means to look up to.

syn1.tip: Admonish is what a teacher does with a stern finger wag: a firm warning, not a punishment.

traps.why: Compliment is the opposite of admonish.
Admit means confess; it only shares a start with admonish.
Explain is too general; admonish means a stern correction.

syn2.tip: Admonish has a stern feeling. Think of a librarian's sharp "Shh" after you talk too loudly.

traps.why: Praise doesn't fit "sternly" or a threat of sitting on the bus.
Entertaining is fun; a stern reminder of consequences is not.
Teachers count students on trips, but a stern reminder is a warning.

sc1.tip: "Sternly" and "anyone who wandered off would spend the day on the bus" point to a firm warning.

sc2.sentence: Although the puppy looked adorable chewing his new sneakers, Mateo had to _____ it with a firm 'No' and take the shoe away.

traps.why: A firm 'No' and taking the shoe away is the opposite of rewarding.
Cuddling fits adorable, but a firm 'No' is a scolding.
Admire looks like admonish, and fits adorable, but not a firm 'No'.

sc2.tip: "Although" warns that cuteness won't win, and "a firm 'No'" shows Mateo scolds the puppy.

deplorable.hook: Deplorable comes from a Latin word meaning to weep bitterly: it describes things so bad they make you want to cry.

traps.why: Admirable means deserving praise, the opposite of deplorable.
Adorable looks similar but means cute and lovable.
Imperfect is far too mild; deplorable means very bad.

syn1.tip: Deplorable contains deplore, which means to strongly disapprove. Its feeling is very negative, so look for a choice that sounds like strong blame.

traps.why: Deserving praise is the opposite of deserving strong disapproval.
Slightly untidy is much too weak for something deplorable.
You might feel sorry about something deplorable, but the word describes the thing itself.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "deplorable conditions," used for terrible places. The word judges something as very bad, so pick the choice that blames.

traps.why: Spotless means perfectly clean, but the cages were filthy.
Adorable looks similar but means cute, not terrible.
Modern describes how new a place is, not how badly animals are treated.

sc1.tip: The examples after the colon, "filthy," "empty," and "clearly underfed," all describe conditions that are very bad and deserve disapproval.

sc2.sentence: Ms. Ortiz praises good sportsmanship, so she called the player's behavior _____ when he shoved an opponent and then mocked him after the game.

traps.why: Admirable means worthy of praise, but shoving and mocking are not.
Athletic fits the sports topic but says nothing about bad behavior.
Mocking someone is on purpose, so the behavior was not accidental.

sc2.tip: She values "good sportsmanship," and the player "shoved" and "mocked" someone. That cause leads to strong disapproval.

defer.hook: Students who defer college take a gap year first: they put starting school off until later.

traps.why: Rush means hurry, the opposite of putting something off.
Differ looks similar but means to be different.
Cancel ends a plan for good; defer only moves it later.

syn1.tip: Think of the word deferred, as in "a deferred payment": the payment still happens, just later. Look for a choice about waiting.

traps.why: Hurry up means do it sooner, the opposite of defer.
Call off means cancel completely, but deferred things still happen later.
The word's Latin parts can suggest carrying away, but defer means postpone.

syn2.tip: When something is deferred, it gets pushed to a later date. Pick the choice that means moving it later, not ending it.

traps.why: Sick players mean the coach would not begin the tournament now.
"Until the following weekend" shows the tournament still happens later.
Hurrying makes no sense when half the team is sick.

sc1.tip: "Because half the team was sick" is the cause, and "until the following weekend" shows the tournament was moved later, not ended.

sc2.sentence: Maya wanted to answer the hard question right away, but she chose to _____ her reply until she had checked her notes and felt sure.

traps.why: Speeding up her reply goes against waiting until she checked her notes.
Shout is about how loudly she answers, not when.
Prefer rhymes with defer but means to like better.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "right away" with "until she had checked her notes," so she put her answer off.

onslaught.hook: Picture a wave of zombies charging all at once from every side: that overwhelming rush is an onslaught.

traps.why: A retreat is pulling back, the opposite of a fierce attack.
Onset looks similar but means the beginning of something.
Weapons are used in attacks, but a weapon is not an attack.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "an onslaught of questions": they come fast and hard. The word means a fierce rush, so look for an attack word.

traps.why: A gentle trickle is slow and small, the opposite of an onslaught.
A slight nudge is far too weak for a fierce attack.
Armies attack, but a camp is a place, not a rush.

syn2.tip: An onslaught comes on hard and all at once, like a flood of attackers. Choose the phrase that sounds powerful and overwhelming.

traps.why: A trickle is a small amount, but millions crashed the site.
Millions of buyers is the opposite of a shortage.
Discounts belong to shopping, but buyers can't be a discount.

sc1.tip: "Crashed," "millions of eager buyers," and "all trying to order at once" describe a huge, overwhelming rush.

sc2.sentence: The goalie stayed calm during the first few shots, but she was soon overwhelmed by an _____ of kicks that her tired team could not stop.

traps.why: An absence of kicks could not overwhelm anyone.
Games have audiences, but an audience doesn't kick at the goal.
An ovation is a happy burst of applause, not a fierce attack.

sc2.tip: "But" marks a change from "calm," and "overwhelmed" and "could not stop" show a fierce, unstoppable rush of kicks.

unveil.hook: To unveil is to pull off the veil, like the sheet yanked off a new statue so everyone sees it.

traps.why: Conceal means hide, the opposite of unveil.
Unravel looks similar but means to come apart, like yarn.
You might unveil an invention, but inventing is creating, not showing.

syn1.tip: Unveil is un plus veil: take off the cover. Think of a company unveiling a new phone. Pick the word meaning show.

traps.why: Keep secret is the opposite of showing something to everyone.
Pull apart fits unravel, a lookalike word, not unveil.
Unveiled things may be pretty, but unveil means show, not decorate.

syn2.tip: A veil hides a face. Taking it off lets people see what was hidden, so pick the choice about letting people know.

traps.why: The sheet already hid it; pulling it down shows the mural.
Murals are painted, but this one is finished and was hidden for weeks.
Unravel looks similar but means come apart, which murals don't do.

sc1.tip: "By pulling down the giant sheet that has hidden it for weeks" tells you the mural is being shown for the first time.

sc2.sentence: For months the company kept its new phone a secret, but at the big launch event it will finally _____ the design to millions of watching fans.

traps.why: Concealing goes with keeping a secret, but "but" signals a change.
The phone was already made; the event is about showing it.
Unravel looks similar but means come apart.

sc2.tip: "Kept... a secret, but" sets up a contrast, and "finally" with "watching fans" shows the phone is shown for the first time.

demeanor.hook: Before a teacher says a word, her demeanor shows you everything: her face, her posture, the way she walks in.

traps.why: Demeanor has "mean" inside it, but it is not about being unkind.
A misdemeanor looks similar but is a minor crime.
A mood is an inside feeling; demeanor is how you look and act.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a calm demeanor": it describes how someone comes across to others. Pick the word for a way of acting.

traps.why: Thoughts are hidden inside, but demeanor is what others can see.
The "mean" inside demeanor doesn't make it about unkindness.
Minor crime is a misdemeanor, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Demeanor is what people notice about you from the outside: your face, posture, and actions. Choose the phrase about what shows.

traps.why: She hid her fear, so she did not show panic.
An audition may have songs, but a song can't be calm and confident.
Misdemeanor looks similar but means a minor crime.

sc1.tip: "Although she was terrified" contrasts her inside with her outside. "Smiling" and "walking steadily" describe how she looked and acted.

sc2.sentence: The new librarian's warm, friendly _____ made shy students feel welcome, since she greeted everyone with a smile and spoke in a gentle voice.

traps.why: Rudeness can't be warm and friendly or make students feel welcome.
A misdemeanor is a minor crime, not a friendly way of acting.
Librarians have schedules, but a schedule doesn't smile or speak gently.

sc2.tip: "Greeted everyone with a smile" and "spoke in a gentle voice" restate how she behaved, which is her demeanor.

complacent.hook: A complacent runner slows down near the finish, so pleased with the lead that a rival zooms right past.

traps.why: Driven people keep pushing, the opposite of complacent.
Complaining looks similar but means grumbling.
Content is a positive calm; complacent means too pleased to keep trying.

syn1.tip: Complacent has a negative feeling: too pleased with yourself to keep working. Think of a team that "got complacent" and lost.

traps.why: Eager to improve is the opposite of being too satisfied to try.
Complaining looks like complacent but means grumbling.
Boastful people brag out loud; complacent people quietly stop trying.

syn2.tip: A complacent person feels so satisfied that they stop trying hard. Look for the choice that shows too much satisfaction.

traps.why: Determined players would keep practicing, not stop.
Tired players might stop, but the clue is easy wins, not tiredness.
Anxious players worry, but these players felt too comfortable.

sc1.tip: "Winning... easily" caused them to stop "practicing hard," and then they lost. They felt too satisfied to keep trying.

sc2.sentence: Unlike her teammates, who relaxed after one good season, Priya never grew _____; she kept training every morning as if she had something to prove.

traps.why: Training every morning shows she was driven, so "never grew driven" contradicts it.
Daily training would make her stronger, so "never grew stronger" doesn't fit.
Hopeful is positive; the blank is the lazy comfort she avoided.

sc2.tip: "Unlike her teammates, who relaxed" tells you Priya avoided that comfort, and "kept training every morning" confirms she never got too satisfied.

augment.hook: Augmented reality adds digital pictures to the real world you see, making it bigger and richer.

traps.why: Reduce means make smaller, the opposite of augment.
Argue looks a bit like augment but means to disagree.
Measuring is about amounts, but it doesn't make anything larger.

syn1.tip: Think of "augmented reality," which adds extra images to what you see. Augment means add more, so pick the growing word.

traps.why: Take from is the opposite of adding to something.
Augment looks a bit like argue, but it is not about disagreeing.
Trading swaps one thing for another; augmenting makes it bigger.

syn2.tip: When you augment something, you add more to it so it grows. Look for the phrase about adding.

traps.why: You spend allowance, but spending doesn't double your money.
His money nearly doubled, so he wasn't trying to lower it.
Wasting money is about allowance too, but his money grew.

sc1.tip: "Nearly doubled the money he had" shows his small allowance got bigger, so the blank means make larger.

sc2.sentence: Our class wanted to _____ the garden, adding six new tomato plants and a row of sunflowers to the few herbs already growing there.

traps.why: Adding plants makes the garden bigger, not smaller.
Weeding is garden work, but it removes plants instead of adding them.
Harvesting picks plants, but the class is adding new ones.

sc2.tip: "Adding six new tomato plants" to the herbs "already growing there" restates the idea of making the garden larger.

renounce.hook: When a king renounces the throne, he publicly declares that he is giving it up for good.

traps.why: Hold onto means keep, the opposite of give up.
Renounce looks like re plus announce, but it means give up.
People may argue about claims, but renounce means let go of one.

syn1.tip: Think of a prince who "renounced the throne": he no longer wanted to be king. Choose the phrase about letting go.

traps.why: Embrace means accept gladly, the opposite of renounce.
Pronounce looks similar but means say a word aloud.
Renouncing is often public, but proclaim just means announce.

syn2.tip: To renounce a belief or claim is to formally turn your back on it. Look for the choice that means push it away.

traps.why: He gave everything away, so he did not collect possessions.
Packing keeps your things; he gave his away.
Announce sounds like renounce but means tell people news.

sc1.tip: "Giving away his books, his clothes, and even his bicycle" shows him letting go of everything he owned.

sc2.sentence: Ben had always insisted that ghosts were real, but after the 'haunted' noise turned out to be a raccoon, he decided to _____ that belief.

traps.why: Finding a raccoon would weaken his belief, not strengthen it.
Announce sounds like renounce, but he didn't proclaim ghosts were real.
Re can mean again, but renounce doesn't mean say again.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change: once the noise "turned out to be a raccoon," Ben gave up the belief he had "always insisted" on.

repulsive.hook: Something repulsive pushes you back: one whiff of a rotten egg and you step away fast.

traps.why: Delightful means very pleasing, the opposite of repulsive.
Repetitive looks similar but means happening again and again.
Annoying is too weak; repulsive means strong disgust.

syn1.tip: Repulsive is related to repel, which means push away. Something repulsive is so gross it pushes you back.

traps.why: Attractive things pull you in; repulsive things push you away.
Impulsive looks and sounds similar but means acting without thinking.
Frightening is also unpleasant, but it is about fear, not disgust.

syn2.tip: Think of magnets that repel each other. Repulsive things push you away with disgust, so pick the choice about feeling sick.

traps.why: A smell like rotting meat is not sweet.
Faint means weak, but this "stink" is strong and gross.
The smell attracts flies, but visitors find it disgusting.

sc1.tip: "Like rotting meat" and "the stink" tell you how visitors feel. Don't be fooled by "attracts": that is about flies, not people.

sc2.sentence: My little brother thinks slugs are cute, but my sister finds their slimy trails so _____ that she shrieks and runs whenever she sees one.

traps.why: Adorable matches the brother's view, but "but" signals the sister disagrees.
Fascinating is positive, but shrieking and running show disgust.
Slugs are small, but size doesn't explain shrieking and running.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the sister with the brother who thinks slugs are "cute," and "shrieks and runs" shows strong disgust.

rectify.hook: Rect means right, as in a rectangle's right angles; to rectify a mistake is to make it right.

traps.why: Ruin means destroy, the opposite of fixing.
Verify also ends in ify but means check that something is true.
You notice a mistake before you fix it, but noticing isn't fixing.

syn1.tip: Rect means right, and ify means to make. Put them together: rectify means to make right.

traps.why: Make worse is the opposite of setting something right.
Pointing out an error shows it but does not correct it.
Rect appears in rectangle, but rectify is about correcting, not shapes.

syn2.tip: Rect means right and ify means make. Think of a bank rectifying an error on your account: it corrects it.

traps.why: He hurried after her to help, not to make things worse.
Chasing the customer shows he wanted to correct it, not hide it.
He already noticed; "realizing" happened before he hurried.

sc1.tip: "Realizing he had given the customer the wrong change" is the cause, and "hurried after her" shows he wanted to correct it.

sc2.sentence: Instead of blaming her little brother for the broken vase, Nia chose to _____ the situation by gluing the pieces together and admitting she had bumped the table.

traps.why: Gluing the vase and telling the truth make things better, not worse.
Ignoring would leave it broken, but she glued it and admitted the truth.
Verify also ends in ify but means check, not correct.

sc2.tip: "Instead of blaming" sets up a contrast, and "gluing the pieces together" and "admitting" show her setting things right.

consolidate.hook: Consolidate has con (together) and solid inside: you press loose pieces together into one solid whole.

traps.why: Separate is the opposite of consolidate, which joins things together.
Console looks similar but means to comfort someone who is sad.
The solid inside might suggest freezing, but consolidate means joining things.

syn1.tip: Find solid inside and con- (together) at the front: consolidate means putting pieces together into one solid whole.

traps.why: Divide is the opposite; consolidating turns many parts into one.
Arranging puts things in order but does not join them into one.
Consolidating makes something stronger, so weaken points the wrong way.

syn2.tip: Think of companies that consolidate: two businesses merge into one bigger, stronger company.

traps.why: Dividing splits notes apart, but he wants them in a single binder.
Console looks like consolidate but means to comfort, and notes need no comfort.
Throwing notes away would not put them into an organized binder.

sc1.tip: The words "from three notebooks into a single, organized binder" tell you he is joining scattered notes into one.

sc2.sentence: Instead of keeping three separate lemonade stands on different corners, the cousins decided to _____ them into one big stand near the park entrance.

traps.why: Split means break apart, but they end up with one big stand.
Advertising helps a stand sell, but it doesn't turn three stands into one.
Consult looks similar but means ask for advice.

sc2.tip: The contrast "Instead of keeping three separate" stands and the phrase "into one big stand" show they joined them together.

pinnacle.hook: Picture the thin, pointed top of a church tower reaching for the sky: that spire is a pinnacle, the highest point.

traps.why: Bottom is the lowest point, the opposite of a pinnacle.
Barnacle rhymes with pinnacle but is a shellfish stuck to rocks.
Mountains have peaks, but a pinnacle is only the very top point.

syn1.tip: Picture a pinnacle as the pointed tip of a tower or mountain. When you reach the pinnacle, nothing is higher.

traps.why: The lowest point is the opposite of a pinnacle.
The pin inside is a coincidence; a pinnacle is a top, not a pin.
A turning point is when things change, not when they are at their best.

syn2.tip: People say someone reached the pinnacle of success, meaning the very top, the best they ever did.

traps.why: Bottom means worst, but nothing later matched this solo, so it was his best.
The clue is about how good the solo was, not when it happened.
Barnacle sounds like pinnacle but is a sea creature, not a high point.

sc1.tip: The phrase "no later concert ever matched it" tells you this solo was his best moment, the very top.

sc2.sentence: Reaching the state finals was the _____ of our soccer season; it was the farthest our team had ever gone, and every practice had led to it.

traps.why: A downfall is a collapse, but reaching the finals was their greatest success.
An opening is a start, but every practice led up to this, so it came at the top.
Pinwheel starts like pinnacle but is a spinning toy.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon restates the blank: "the farthest our team had ever gone" means the highest point.

stature.hook: Stature can mean how tall you stand; a person of great stature stands tall in other people's respect.

traps.why: Disgrace is losing respect, the opposite of high stature.
Statue looks like stature but is a carved figure.
Posture is how your body stands; stature is how others respect you.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a person of great stature": someone whose achievements earned them high standing and respect.

traps.why: Shame means losing respect, the opposite of stature.
Statute looks like stature but means a written law.
Confidence is how you see yourself; stature is how others see you.

syn2.tip: Stature is earned by achievement. When a scientist's stature grows, her reputation grows.

traps.why: Statue looks like stature but is a sculpture, not a reputation.
Competing with other writers would not make fans travel to hear her.
Awards bring respect, so a negative word like embarrassment has the wrong feeling.

sc1.tip: The cause is "three award-winning novels" and the effect is writers traveling "across the country to hear her." Her reputation grew.

sc2.sentence: Although the coach was new to our town, her _____ as a former Olympic swimmer meant parents trusted her right away and signed their kids up for her lessons.

traps.why: Being new might suggest inexperience, but an Olympic past earns trust.
Posture is how she stands, which would not make parents trust her.
Shyness is a weakness here, but parents trusted her right away.

sc2.tip: The word "Although" sets up a contrast: she was new, yet "former Olympic swimmer" gave her respect that made parents trust her.

nostalgic.hook: Nostalgic is the warm ache you feel flipping through old photos and wishing you could visit those days again.

traps.why: Futuristic looks ahead; nostalgic looks fondly back at the past.
Historic means important in history; nostalgic is a personal feeling.
Bitter about the past is resentful; nostalgic is fond and warm.

syn1.tip: Think of a song that makes your parents say "that takes me back." Nostalgic is that warm, emotional longing for the past.

traps.why: Wanting change looks ahead, the opposite of longing for the past.
Studying history is facts; nostalgia is a fond personal feeling.
Nostalgia is fond, so anger has the wrong feeling.

syn2.tip: Nostalgic is the feeling of fondly looking back, like rewatching a show you loved when you were little.

traps.why: Ambitious people look ahead, but Jamal wishes to go back.
Relieved would mean glad those days are over, but he wants them back.
The drawings are art, but the clue is about longing for the past.

sc1.tip: The words "wishing he could return to those carefree days" show a fond longing for the past.

sc2.sentence: Most kids at the reunion couldn't wait to talk about high school plans, but Lena felt _____ and kept telling stories about their old second-grade classroom.

traps.why: Impatient fits the other kids looking ahead, but Lena looked back.
She did tell stories, but the blank names her feeling about the past.
Nothing shows anger; telling old stories shows fond memories.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts Lena with kids talking about the future. She told stories "about their old second-grade classroom," so she longed for the past.

audible.hook: Audible splits into aud (hear, as in audio) and -ible (able to be): able to be heard.

traps.why: Silent means making no sound, the opposite of audible.
Visible means able to be seen; audible is about hearing.
Edible looks like audible but means safe to eat.

syn1.tip: The root aud means hear, as in audio and audience. Audible means a sound is able to be heard.

traps.why: Too quiet to hear is the opposite of audible.
You can hear words without understanding them; audible is only about hearing.
Audible just means you can hear it, not that it hurts your ears.

syn2.tip: Find aud, the hearing root in audio and audience, plus -ible, meaning able to be. Audible sounds can just be heard.

traps.why: Visible is about seeing, but the students were trying to hear her.
Edible looks like audible but means safe to eat.
The problem was hearing her at all, not whether her voice sounded nice.

sc1.tip: The effect "kept asking each other what she had said" shows the students could hardly hear her voice.

sc2.sentence: The tiny kitten's cry was so faint that it was hardly _____, yet Maya, with her sharp ears, noticed it from across the yard.

traps.why: Adorable looks a bit like audible but means cute.
Kittens cry when hungry, but the clue is about how faint the sound was.
Visible is about seeing, but the clue is "sharp ears."

sc2.tip: The words "so faint" and "sharp ears" point to hearing: the cry could hardly be heard.

invincible.hook: Invincible is in (not) plus vinc (conquer) plus ible (able): a hero no one is able to conquer.

traps.why: Vulnerable means easy to hurt, the opposite of invincible.
Invisible looks like invincible but means unable to be seen.
Victorious means you won once; invincible means you can't be beaten.

syn1.tip: Split it: in- (not) plus vinc (conquer) plus -ible (able to be). Invincible means not able to be conquered.

traps.why: Easy to defeat is the exact opposite of invincible.
That describes invisible, a lookalike word.
Winning most games is too weak; invincible means never able to lose.

syn2.tip: Think of a video game power-up that makes you invincible: nothing can hurt or beat you while it lasts.

traps.why: Four years without a loss is far from ordinary.
Invisible looks like invincible but means unable to be seen.
Talented is too weak; one loss does not prove they lacked talent.

sc1.tip: The clues "had not lost a single match in four years" and "until a rookie team finally beat them" show they seemed unbeatable.

sc2.sentence: Superheroes in movies often seem _____, but even the strongest ones have a secret weakness, like Superman losing his powers near kryptonite.

traps.why: Helpless is the opposite; the strongest heroes seem unbeatable.
Heroes are brave, but the contrast is about having a weakness.
Inventive starts like invincible but means good at creating things.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "a secret weakness," so the blank means having no weakness at all, impossible to beat.

frenzy.hook: Think of sharks in a feeding frenzy, thrashing and snapping: frenzy is wild, out-of-control excitement.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of a wild frenzy.
Interest is far too mild; a frenzy is wild, out-of-control excitement.
Frenzies often happen in crowds, but a frenzy is a state, not people.

syn1.tip: Picture shoppers rushing a store on sale day, pushing and grabbing. A frenzy is that wild madness.

traps.why: Quiet peace is the opposite of a frenzy.
Mild curiosity is much too weak for a frenzy.
A gathering is a group of people, not their wild state of mind.

syn2.tip: The phrase "feeding frenzy" shows sharks going wild over food. A frenzy is excitement that goes out of control.

traps.why: Screaming fans are not silent; that is the opposite.
A smile is too mild for screaming, jumping, and pushing.
A chorus is singing together, not pushing toward barriers.

sc1.tip: The examples "screaming, jumping, and pushing" show excitement so wild it's out of control.

sc2.sentence: The classroom was calm all morning, but when the principal announced an early dismissal for snow, the class erupted into a _____ of cheering and backpack-grabbing.

traps.why: Hush fits the calm morning, but the word "but" signals a change.
A murmur is too quiet for a class that erupted.
Lessons happen in class, but this blank describes wild cheering.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "calm," and "erupted" signals an explosion of wild excitement.

simulate.hook: A flight simulator lets pilots practice in a fake cockpit; to simulate is to make something act like the real thing.

traps.why: Stimulate looks almost the same but means to excite or wake up.
Inventing creates something new; simulating copies something that already exists.
Simulate is related to similar, but it means copying, not comparing.

syn1.tip: Think of a flight simulator, a machine that copies the feel of flying a real plane. Simulate means to imitate.

traps.why: Originate means to start something new, the opposite of copying.
Simplify starts like simulate but means to make easier.
Simulators help you practice, but simulate itself means to copy.

syn2.tip: Video games simulate real things like driving or flying. They copy how the real thing looks and works.

traps.why: Stimulate looks like simulate but means to excite.
Astronauts explore space, but pools can't explore anything; they copy conditions.
The pools create a weightless feeling; they don't remove it.

sc1.tip: The phrase "floating as they would in orbit" shows the pools copy the feeling of space on Earth.

sc2.sentence: Our science teacher used a fan and a tub of water to _____ a hurricane, creating a tiny version of its wind and waves right on her desk.

traps.why: Forecasters predict hurricanes, but she built a tiny model of one.
She created hurricane wind and waves; she did not stop them.
Stimulate looks like simulate but means to excite.

sc2.tip: The phrase after the comma restates the blank: "creating a tiny version" means copying how a hurricane looks and works.

discreet.hook: Discreet sounds like discrete, but discreet is the quiet one: it keeps secrets and stays out of the spotlight.

traps.why: Gossipy people spread secrets, the opposite of discreet.
Discrete sounds the same but means separate.
Shy is feeling nervous; discreet is choosing to be careful.

syn1.tip: Discreet people choose their words carefully so they don't spill secrets or embarrass anyone.

traps.why: Gossiping spreads secrets, the opposite of being discreet.
That defines discrete, which sounds the same but means something else.
Discreet people can talk freely; they just don't reveal private things.

syn2.tip: When someone says "please be discreet," they're asking you to keep something quiet and not draw attention.

traps.why: Talkative fits someone who spills news, but she revealed nothing.
Honest means telling the truth, but she changed the subject instead.
She acted "politely," so a rude, negative word doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: The clues "keep her friend's news private" and "without revealing anything" show she was careful not to spill the secret.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his brother, who announced every surprise before the party even started, Leo was _____ and never let a single hint slip about the gift.

traps.why: Careless fits his brother; Leo is the opposite and kept quiet.
He may be excited, but the clue is that he never gave a hint.
Discrete sounds the same but means separate, not secret-keeping.

sc2.tip: The word "Unlike" contrasts Leo with a brother who spoils surprises, and "never let a single hint slip" shows he kept secrets.

stringent.hook: Picture rules pulled as tight as a guitar string, no slack at all: that's stringent, like stringent safety rules in labs.

traps.why: Relaxed rules are loose, the opposite of stringent.
String inside might suggest tangled, but stringent means very strict.
Stringent rules can be fair; they are just very strict.

syn1.tip: You often hear "stringent safety standards." Picture rules pulled tight with no wiggle room.

traps.why: Loosely enforced is the opposite of stringent.
Slightly picky is too weak; stringent means very strict.
Clear rules aren't always strict; stringent is about how tight they are.

syn2.tip: Stringent rules leave no slack, like a rope pulled tight. Breaking even a small one is not allowed.

traps.why: Full-body suits and zero dust are not relaxed rules.
Basic is too weak for rules where one speck of dust stops work.
Space labs are modern, but the clue is about how strict the rules are.

sc1.tip: The examples "full-body suits" and "even a single speck of dust can halt the work" show extremely strict rules.

sc2.sentence: At home, Nina's bedtime was flexible on weekends, but summer camp had _____ rules: lights out at nine sharp, and counselors checked every cabin.

traps.why: Loose fits her home bedtime, but "but" signals camp was different.
Lights out at nine sharp with cabin checks sounds strict, not fun.
The camp rules were clear; they were just very strict.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "flexible," and "nine sharp" plus "checked every cabin" show very strict rules.

mentor.hook: In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor was the wise friend trusted to guide young Telemachus while his father was away.

traps.why: A beginner is the one who needs a mentor, the opposite role.
Monitor looks similar but means someone who watches, not someone who guides.
A classmate learns beside you; a mentor has more experience and guides you.

syn1.tip: Think of a coach or an older student who shows you the ropes. That person guides you.

traps.why: A beginner is the learner, not the experienced person giving advice.
A critic judges harshly; a mentor helps kindly.
A fellow student is at your level; a mentor knows more than you.

syn2.tip: A mentor gives advice from experience. Look for the choice that means someone wise you can turn to.

traps.why: Ms. Chen is the new one; the experienced teacher is helping her, not learning.
A rival competes against you; this teacher was helping her.
Monitor looks similar but means someone who watches, not someone who advises.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank right after the comma: "an experienced teacher" who "gave her advice." That is a guide.

sc2.sentence: Because Jada had never played chess before, she asked an older club member to be her _____, and he spent every lunch teaching her new openings.

traps.why: An opponent plays against you; he spent lunches teaching her instead.
An apprentice is a learner; Jada is the learner here, not him.
A critic finds faults; he patiently taught her.

sc2.tip: Jada "had never played," so she needed help, and he spent lunches "teaching her." The blank is an experienced helper.

enthusiastic.hook: Picture a fan leaping off the bleachers, face painted, screaming before the ball even lands.

traps.why: Indifferent means not caring at all, the opposite of excited.
Nervous is a worried feeling, not a happy, excited one.
Agreeable means willing to go along, much weaker than excited.

syn1.tip: Think of an "enthusiastic crowd" cheering. The word is full of energy and excitement.

traps.why: Bored and tired is the opposite of excited.
Excited people may be loud, but enthusiastic is a positive word.
Mildly curious is far too weak for great excitement.

syn2.tip: Enthusiastic fans cheer the whole game. Pick the choice with the most energy and good feeling.

traps.why: Reluctant describes the groaning brother, and Zoe is unlike him.
Sulky is a gloomy feeling; Zoe was busy planning happily.
A forgetful person would not have planned which exhibits to visit.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her brother, who groaned" signals Zoe felt the opposite. She "had already planned" exhibits, so she was excited.

sc2.sentence: Marcus was so _____ about joining the robotics club that he showed up an hour early and asked a dozen questions before the first meeting began.

traps.why: A hesitant person holds back; Marcus rushed in an hour early.
Calm is too mild for someone arriving an hour early.
Upset is an unhappy feeling, but Marcus could not wait to start.

sc2.tip: "So ... that he showed up an hour early" shows cause and effect. Only great excitement explains arriving that early.

disclose.hook: Dis-close means un-close: open up the box and let the secret out.

traps.why: Conceal means to hide, the opposite of making something known.
Enclose looks similar but means to shut something inside.
Dis-close is not "move away from close"; it means to open up.

syn1.tip: Dis- undoes close, the way dislike undoes like. To un-close a secret is to open it up.

traps.why: Keeping something hidden is the opposite of disclosing it.
Shut is the meaning of close, but dis- reverses it.
Guessing is about secrets too, but disclosing means telling them.

syn2.tip: Companies "disclose" information when they tell the public. Find the choice that means telling what was secret.

traps.why: He refused, so the blank must be the thing he would not do: tell.
Magicians rehearse tricks, but the sentence is about sharing a secret.
He already did the trick; the question is whether he would share how.

sc1.tip: He said "a secret once shared is no longer a secret," so he refused to share it. The blank means make known.

sc2.sentence: Nina kept her diary locked for months, but tonight she finally decided to _____ its secrets, reading every page aloud to her best friend.

traps.why: Guarding is what she did before; "but" signals a change to sharing.
She read every page aloud, so she did not erase anything.
Enclose looks similar but means to shut in, not to share.

sc2.tip: "Locked for months, but" signals a change. "Reading every page aloud" shows she shared the secrets.

envy.hook: "Green with envy" pictures your face turning green as you stare at a friend's shiny new phone.

traps.why: Contentment means being happy with what you have, the opposite of envy.
Envoy looks similar but means a messenger sent by a government.
Admiration is a warm feeling; envy is wanting what others have.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "green with envy." It is the bad feeling of wanting someone else's things.

traps.why: Being happy for someone is the opposite of envying them.
Respect is a positive feeling; envy is an unhappy one.
Envy is about wanting what someone has, not missing what you lost.

syn2.tip: When you envy someone, you want what they have. Pick the choice about wanting another person's things.

traps.why: Pride is a feeling about your own things, not wishing for a friend's.
Gratitude is a thankful feeling, but Kofi wanted what his friend had.
Satisfied people do not wish they had something else.

sc1.tip: The clue is "wished he had one just like it." Wanting what a friend has is that feeling.

sc2.sentence: Rosa tried to hide her _____, but everyone could tell how badly she wanted her cousin's new phone; she stared at it all through dinner.

traps.why: Someone bored would not stare at the phone all dinner.
Curiosity is wondering about something; Rosa badly wanted it for herself.
Generosity is a giving feeling, but Rosa wanted to have, not give.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "how badly she wanted her cousin's new phone." That is the feeling.

notorious.hook: Al Capone was a notorious gangster: everyone knew his name, and none of the reasons were good.

traps.why: Unknown means nobody has heard of it, the opposite of notorious.
Celebrated means famous for good things; notorious is famous for bad things.
Nutritious looks similar but means healthy to eat.

syn1.tip: You hear of a "notorious criminal," never a notorious hero. It means well known for something bad.

traps.why: Being admired is good fame; notorious fame is bad.
Notorious things are talked about a lot.
The word starts like note, but it does not mean having notes.

syn2.tip: Notorious is a negative word: think of a "notorious villain." Look for the choice about being known for bad things.

traps.why: Sailors everywhere knew its sails, so it was not unknown.
Sailors feared meeting it, so it was not loved.
Old ships can be abandoned, but sailors feared meeting this one at sea.

sc1.tip: Two clues work together: "sailors everywhere knew" it, and they "feared meeting it." Known widely and feared means famous for bad things.

sc2.sentence: Though the diner was _____ for slow service and cold fries, people still lined up every weekend for its famous milkshakes.

traps.why: Nobody praises slow service and cold fries.
People do not recommend a place for its cold fries.
Nutritious looks similar but means healthy, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Though" and "still" set up a contrast: people come despite the diner's bad reputation. The blank is known for bad things.

imply.hook: When a friend says "Nice shoes" with a smirk, the smirk implies she doesn't mean it.

traps.why: To state is to say it directly; to imply is to hint.
The speaker implies; the listener infers, or figures it out.
Apply looks similar but means to put on or to request.

syn1.tip: Think of "Are you implying I'm wrong?" It means hinting at something without saying it outright.

traps.why: Spelling something out means saying it clearly, the opposite of hinting.
Figuring out a hint is inferring; implying is giving the hint.
Apply looks like imply, but applying for something means requesting it.

syn2.tip: Imply means saying something without words, like a look or a tone. Choose the phrase about a quiet signal.

traps.why: Her eyebrow showed she knew, so it did not deny it.
Ms. Lopez gives the hint; the student would infer it.
Declaring is saying out loud, but she "never said" it.

sc1.tip: "Never said out loud ... but her raised eyebrow" shows she sent a message without words. That is hinting.

sc2.sentence: Grandma's question, 'Did you finish your homework already?', was meant to _____ something; she was hinting that the video game should wait.

traps.why: Forbidding is a firm order, but Grandma was only hinting.
Grandma gives the hint; you would infer what she meant.
Announcing is saying it plainly, but she only asked a question.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon the sentence restates the blank: "she was hinting." A question that hints at something suggests it.

decisive.hook: A decisive referee blows the whistle at once, makes the call, and never changes it.

traps.why: Hesitant people hold back from choosing, the opposite of decisive.
Divisive looks similar but means causing people to disagree.
Stubborn is the negative word for refusing to change your mind.

syn1.tip: Decisive is inside the word decide. A decisive person decides quickly and stands by it.

traps.why: Being unable to choose is the opposite of decisive.
That describes divisive, a lookalike word about causing disagreement.
That is a negative trait; decisive is a positive word.

syn2.tip: Look inside decisive for decide. The answer should describe someone who makes up their mind fast.

traps.why: She chose in seconds, so she did not hesitate.
Divisive looks similar but means causing arguments, not choosing quickly.
The other captains did the talking; Keisha chose fast.

sc1.tip: "While the other captains wasted time debating" sets up a contrast. She "chose ... in seconds and never second-guessed it."

sc2.sentence: Because Coach Ruiz was so _____, the team never wasted time in the huddle; she picked a play in seconds and everyone ran it with confidence.

traps.why: An uncertain coach would waste time, but this team never did.
Being liked does not explain picking plays in seconds.
Deceptive looks a bit similar but means tricky or misleading.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals cause and effect: the team "never wasted time" because she "picked a play in seconds."

confront.hook: Con-front: you put your front toward someone and stand face to face.

traps.why: Avoiding means staying away, the opposite of facing something.
Comfort looks similar but means to make someone feel better.
Confronting means facing directly, not fighting or hurting.

syn1.tip: Look for front inside confront. You confront a fear by turning your front toward it.

traps.why: Steering clear means avoiding, the opposite of confronting.
Front is in the word, but confront does not mean leading the way.
Confronting someone is facing them, not fighting them.

syn2.tip: People "confront their fears." That means facing a problem directly instead of running from it.

traps.why: "Instead of avoiding" means he did not ignore the classmate.
Comfort looks similar, but he wanted the rumors to stop.
He only asked him to stop, which is far milder than punishing.

sc1.tip: "Instead of avoiding" signals the opposite of avoiding. He went straight to the classmate to "ask him to stop."

sc2.sentence: Mia's fear of the deep end kept her out of the pool all summer, so this year she has decided to _____ it by taking swimming lessons.

traps.why: Taking lessons is facing the fear, not running from it.
Confirm looks similar, but lessons would not prove her fear right.
Sharing a fear means telling others; lessons are how she tackles it.

sc2.tip: "So" shows cause and effect: the fear kept her out, so now she is "taking swimming lessons" to meet it directly.

rivalry.hook: Think Yankees versus Red Sox: two teams that have battled to beat each other for over a century.

traps.why: Cooperation means working together, the opposite of competing.
Revelry sounds similar but means noisy partying.
A rivalry is the contest itself, not winning it.

syn1.tip: A rival is someone you try to beat. A rivalry is the contest between rivals.

traps.why: Teamwork means working together, the opposite of a rivalry.
One game is too narrow; a rivalry lasts over many contests.
Rivals compete, but a rivalry can be friendly, not hateful.

syn2.tip: Find rival inside rivalry. Rivals keep trying to beat each other, often for years.

traps.why: The towns compete fiercely, so they are not partners.
The sentence calls it "friendly," so hatred is far too strong.
Pumpkins are harvested, but the sentence is about towns competing.

sc1.tip: "Compete fiercely" every year describes the blank. A friendly, ongoing competition between two sides is the answer.

sc2.sentence: Although the twins share a room and finish each other's sentences, their _____ on the soccer field is intense; each one is desperate to score more goals than the other.

traps.why: "Although" signals a contrast with being close, so the blank is about competing.
Each twin wants to outscore the other, which is not teamwork.
Revelry sounds similar but means partying, not competing.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts their closeness at home with the field, where "each one is desperate to score more goals than the other."

prejudice.hook: Pre-judice means judging before: deciding what someone is like before you have even met them.

traps.why: Fairness means judging evenly, the opposite of prejudice.
Both start with pre-, but prediction is a guess about the future.
Judges give punishments, but prejudice is an unfair opinion.

syn1.tip: Split it: pre (before) plus judge. Judging people before you know them is an unfair, one-sided view.

traps.why: An open mind waits for facts, the opposite of prejudice.
Courts make judgments, but prejudice is a personal unfair opinion.
Pre- means before, but prejudice is not a warning ahead of time.

syn2.tip: Look for pre- and judge in prejudice. It means judging too early, before the facts, which is unfair.

traps.why: Calling a team lazy is an insult, not a compliment.
He decided "before meeting any of the players," so he had observed nothing.
Judging people before meeting them is not fair.

sc1.tip: "Before meeting any of the players" he "had already decided." An opinion formed before the facts is the answer.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa called video games silly without ever trying one, but after an hour of puzzle games with me, his _____ disappeared and he asked for a rematch.

traps.why: If his enthusiasm vanished, he would not ask for a rematch.
He had never tried one, so he had no experience to lose.
Asking for a rematch shows interest, so his curiosity did not disappear.

sc2.tip: "Without ever trying one" shows he judged too soon. "But" signals that the unfair opinion vanished once he played.

endearing.hook: Picture a puppy tripping over its own ears: that is endearing, because it makes you feel it is dear to you.

traps.why: Annoying is the opposite of endearing; it pushes people away.
Enduring means lasting a long time; it only looks like endearing.
Dear can mean costly, but endearing means making people love you.

syn1.tip: Find the word dear inside endearing. Something endearing makes people hold it dear.

traps.why: Irritating is the opposite; endearing things make you smile.
Adoring means giving love; endearing means drawing love from others.
Endless means without end; it only looks like endearing.

syn2.tip: Think of how you feel about a clumsy kitten. Endearing describes the thing that wins your affection.

traps.why: Alarming tumbles would cause gasps of worry, not smiles and sighs of Aww.
Tiresome things bore people, but visitors crowded around smiling.
Acrobatic means skillful, but the sentence says the tumbles were clumsy.

sc1.tip: The clue is "smiling and sighing, 'Aww!'" People react that way to something that makes them feel affection.

sc2.sentence: Although my little brother's habit of mispronouncing spaghetti as "pasketti" should have been annoying, everyone in the family found it _____ and secretly hoped he would never learn.

traps.why: Irritating fits only if you miss "although"; the family wanted the habit to stay.
Mispronouncing can confuse people, but hoping he never learns shows affection.
Unusual does not explain why the family hoped the habit would last.

sc2.tip: "Although" flips "annoying," and "secretly hoped he would never learn" shows the family loved the habit.

strenuous.hook: A strenuous climb makes you strain every muscle, puffing and sweating all the way to the top.

traps.why: Effortless is the opposite of strenuous, which needs great effort.
Tenuous means weak or thin; it only looks like strenuous.
Hard climbs can be dangerous, but strenuous is about the effort needed.

syn1.tip: Strenuous sounds like strain. A strenuous workout strains your body and leaves you worn out.

traps.why: Easy is the opposite of strenuous.
Long tasks are not always hard; strenuous means needing great effort.
Stern means strict and serious; it only looks like strenuous.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "strenuous exercise," the kind that leaves you panting. Look for a word about hard effort.

traps.why: A relaxing hike would not leave fit hikers out of breath.
Scenic means pretty to look at, which would not make anyone gasp.
Mild effort would not force even the fittest to stop every few minutes.

sc1.tip: Look at "even the fittest members" and "catch their breath." If strong people need rests, the hike took great effort.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the light stretching we did in gym on Monday, Friday's workout was _____, leaving the whole class drenched in sweat and gasping after endless sprints.

traps.why: Gentle describes Monday's stretching, the thing Friday's workout is unlike.
Endless sprints rule out brief; the clue is about hard effort.
Whether a workout is required says nothing about the sweat and gasping.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the light stretching" sets up a contrast, and "drenched in sweat and gasping" shows the workout took great effort.

trespass.hook: A No Trespassing sign on a fence means stay out: you may not cross onto this land without permission.

traps.why: Withdraw means pull back out, the opposite of going in uninvited.
Pass in the word does not mean go past; trespass means enter without permission.
Sin is an older meaning of trespass, not entering someone's land.

syn1.tip: Think of a "No Trespassing" sign on a fence. It tells you not to go where you are not invited.

traps.why: Staying off property is exactly what a trespasser does not do.
Pass inside trespass does not mean hand something on.
Visiting is entering too, but trespassing means no permission.

syn2.tip: Picture the "No Trespassing" signs you see on fences and gates. They warn people not to go in uninvited.

traps.why: Farmhands work with permission; the clue says walking through without permission.
Building is not walking through fields; the clue describes entering uninvited.
