Reporting on land means describing it, not walking through it uninvited.

sc1.tip: The phrase "walking through his fields without permission" restates the blank. Look for a verb meaning going onto land you are not allowed on.

sc2.sentence: Kids who knock and ask first may play in the garden, but those who climb the wall and _____ without asking get a stern lecture.

traps.why: Knocking is what the polite kids do; the "but" points the other way.
Apologizing is polite; the lecture shows these kids did something wrong.
Waiting keeps you outside; these kids go in without being allowed.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the polite kids with "those who climb the wall," and "without asking" plus the lecture shows they entered without permission.

affliction.hook: Chicken pox, a broken arm, a terrible toothache: each is an affliction, something that makes you suffer.

traps.why: Comfort is the opposite of affliction, which causes pain.
Affection means fondness; it only looks like affliction.
Medicine treats an illness; an affliction is the suffering itself.

syn1.tip: People say someone is "afflicted" with a disease. An affliction is whatever is causing them pain or misery.

traps.why: Relief takes pain away; an affliction brings pain.
An infection is just one kind; affliction means any cause of suffering.
An annoyance is too mild; an affliction causes real pain or suffering.

syn2.tip: Affliction is a heavy, negative word, as in "afflicted with illness." Pick the choice that means real suffering.

traps.why: A cure would stop the itching, not keep campers awake.
Camps have activities, but a rash is not one; it causes suffering.
Itching so bad you cannot sleep is much worse than an inconvenience.

sc1.tip: Look at "itching so severe that many of them could not sleep." The blank names something that causes real suffering.

sc2.sentence: For most students the spelling bee was fun, but for shy Tomas, standing on stage in front of the whole school was a true _____ that made his hands shake.

traps.why: Delight fits only if you miss "but"; his shaking hands show suffering.
Affection means fondness; it only looks like affliction.
The bee is a contest, but the blank describes how Tomas suffered.

sc2.tip: "But for shy Tomas" contrasts with "fun," and "made his hands shake" shows that being on stage was painful for him.

momentous.hook: The first moon landing was momentous: one moment that changed history forever.

traps.why: Trivial means unimportant, the opposite of momentous.
Momentary means lasting only a moment; it only looks like momentous.
Famous means well known; momentous means having big effects.

syn1.tip: Think of "a momentous day in history." Momentous events matter a lot and change what comes after.

traps.why: Minor means small and unimportant, the opposite of momentous.
Momentous is not about a short moment of time; it means very important.
Exciting is about feelings; momentous is about lasting importance.

syn2.tip: Do not let the word moment fool you into thinking short. Momentous decisions and events carry great weight.

traps.why: An ordinary day would not be when "everything began to change."
Momentary means brief; the town still talks about that day's effects.
A noisy opening would not explain why everything began to change.

sc1.tip: The words "the moment everything began to change" show the opening had huge effects on the town.

sc2.sentence: Most days of fifth grade blur together, but the afternoon I won the state science fair felt _____ because it convinced me to become a scientist.

traps.why: Forgettable fits days that "blur together," but "but" sets this day apart.
Pleasant is too weak for a day that shaped your whole future.
Momentous is not about a passing moment; this day changed a future.

sc2.tip: "But" sets this day apart from days that "blur together," and "convinced me to become a scientist" shows huge effects.

scapegoat.hook: When the whole class talks but one kid gets detention, that kid is the scapegoat, blamed for everyone.

traps.why: The true culprit is really guilty; a scapegoat is blamed unfairly.
Scape looks like escape, but a scapegoat cannot escape the blame.
A critic does the blaming; the scapegoat is the one blamed.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "Don't make me the scapegoat." People say it when they are blamed for something others did.

traps.why: That describes the blamer; the scapegoat is the one getting blamed.
A scapegoat does not deserve the blame; that is the whole point.
It looks like escape plus goat, but it means an unfairly blamed person.

syn2.tip: Think about who gets blamed when a group messes up but one person takes the fall. That person is the scapegoat.

traps.why: Heroes get praise, but the players were "blaming him alone."
Being captain is an honor; the clue shows the rookie was blamed.
A culprit is truly guilty, but the whole team missed shots.

sc1.tip: "Although the whole team had missed" sets up a contrast with "blaming him alone." He took blame others shared.

sc2.sentence: When the cookie jar was found empty, my little brother quickly made our dog the _____, pointing at the crumbs on its nose even though he had eaten most cookies himself.

traps.why: Making the dog the favorite would be praise, not pointing blame.
A witness only sees what happened; the dog was blamed instead.
Guarding the jar is not the point; the brother was shifting blame.

sc2.tip: "Pointing at the crumbs" shows blame, and "even though he had eaten most cookies himself" shows that blame was unfair.

copious.hook: Copious notes fill page after page, so many that your hand cramps from writing so much.

traps.why: Scarce means there is very little, the opposite of copious.
Copied means duplicated; it only looks like copious.
Copious notes are not always careful; copious is about the amount.

syn1.tip: Copious often shows up in "copious notes" or "copious amounts." Both mean a whole lot of something.

traps.why: Small in number is the opposite of copious.
Copious looks like copy, but it means a large amount.
Copious means a lot, not too much; it is not a complaint.

syn2.tip: Think of "copious notes" that fill a whole notebook. The word is about how much of something there is.

traps.why: Sparse fits her classmates' few words, but "unlike" sets Ines apart.
Neat is about tidiness; twelve pages shows how much she wrote.
Excessive means too much; twelve pages just shows she wrote a lot.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her classmates, who jotted down only a few words" sets up a contrast, and "twelve pages" shows a large amount.

sc2.sentence: Our garden produced _____ tomatoes this summer; we had so many that we filled every bowl, gave bags to neighbors, and still made three batches of sauce.

traps.why: Few is the opposite; the sentence says "we had so many."
Neighbors would not want rotten tomatoes; the clue is about how many.
Store tomatoes can be pricey, but the clue is about how many you had.

sc2.tip: "We had so many" restates the blank, and filling bowls, giving bags away, and making sauce all show a large amount.

rebuttal.hook: In a debate, the rebuttal is when you fire back, answering the other side's points one by one.

traps.why: An agreement goes along with an argument; a rebuttal argues against it.
Rebuke means a scolding; it only looks like rebuttal.
A question asks something; a rebuttal answers the other side.

syn1.tip: Debates have a "rebuttal round," when each side answers the other. The re at the start means back, as in answering back.

traps.why: Approval supports an idea; a rebuttal argues against it.
An insult attacks a person; a rebuttal answers an argument with reasons.
A summary repeats points; a rebuttal pushes back against them.

syn2.tip: Think of the rebuttal round in a debate. You answer back, showing why the other side's points are wrong.

traps.why: Kwame explained why their evidence was weak, so he did not approve.
An introduction starts a debate; Kwame is answering the other side.
Kwame was not saying sorry; he was arguing "point by point."

sc1.tip: The other team argued first, then Kwame explained "point by point why their evidence was weak." That is answering back.

sc2.sentence: Instead of simply agreeing with the article claiming video games rot your brain, Leah wrote a _____ for the school paper, citing studies that games improve problem solving.

traps.why: A summary would repeat the article; Leah argued against it.
"Instead of simply agreeing" rules out praising the article.
A headline is just a title; Leah wrote a whole argument with studies.

sc2.tip: "Instead of simply agreeing" signals disagreement, and "citing studies that games improve problem solving" shows she argued back.

scant.hook: A scant spoonful of sugar is barely any at all, just a few grains at the bottom.

traps.why: Plentiful means a lot, the opposite of scant.
Slanted means tilted; it only looks like scant.
Rare things can be precious, but scant is about the small amount.

syn1.tip: Scant sounds a bit like scanty and scarce. All three describe having very little of something.

traps.why: More than enough is the opposite of scant.
Scant means very little, not nothing at all.
Timing is not the point; scant means a very small amount.

syn2.tip: Think of "scant rainfall" in a desert. There is a little, but hardly enough to get by.

traps.why: Ample means plenty, but they had just one short practice.
Time can be valuable, but the clue shows how little they had.
Relaxed prep would not leave them nervous; they had too little time.

sc1.tip: "Only" and "just one short practice the night before" show the team had barely any time to get ready.

sc2.sentence: Last year the creek overflowed every spring, but after months without rain, only a _____ trickle of water now runs over the rocks.

traps.why: Roaring fits last year's flooding, but "but" points to less water now.
Frozen water would not run; the clue is about how little is left.
Months without rain leave only a small trickle, not a generous one.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "overflowed," and "months without rain" plus "only" show that very little water is left.

emphatic.hook: An emphatic no comes with a fist on the table and no room to argue.

traps.why: Hesitant means unsure, the opposite of emphatic.
Empathetic means sharing feelings; it only looks like emphatic.
You can be emphatic without being angry; it means firm and strong.

syn1.tip: Emphatic is related to emphasis. When you put emphasis on words, you say them strongly so people know you mean it.

traps.why: Doubtful words are the opposite of emphatic ones.
That describes empathetic, a lookalike; emphatic means firm and forceful.
Speed does not matter; emphatic means said with force and certainty.

syn2.tip: Look for emphasis inside emphatic. An emphatic answer stresses every word so no one doubts it.

traps.why: "Absolutely not, never" is completely certain, not uncertain.
Slapping the table and declaring loudly is forceful, not polite.
"Absolutely not, never" is perfectly clear, not confusing.

sc1.tip: "She slapped the table and declared, 'Absolutely not, never!'" shows a strong, forceful answer.

sc2.sentence: Usually my grandmother answers questions with a gentle maybe, but when I asked if I could skip my vegetables, her _____ reply left no room for argument.

traps.why: Vague fits her usual "maybe," but this reply left no room for argument.
Empathetic means understanding feelings; this reply was firm, not sympathetic.
A cheerful reply might still allow arguing; "no room" shows force.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with her usual "gentle maybe," and "left no room for argument" shows a firm, forceful reply.

apathetic.hook: Inside apathetic is 'path,' meaning feeling, and 'a' means without, so an apathetic person feels nothing about it.

traps.why: Eager is the opposite of apathetic; eager people care a lot.
Pathetic looks similar but means pitiful, not uninterested.
Apathetic people may seem lazy, but apathetic is about not caring.

syn1.tip: Inside apathetic is 'path,' meaning feeling, as in sympathy. The 'a' in front means without, so it means without feeling or interest.

traps.why: Full of concern is the opposite; apathetic means showing no concern.
'Path' suggests feeling, but the 'a' means without, so no pity.
Not caring can seem rude, but rudeness is about bad manners.

syn2.tip: Picture an apathetic shrug that says 'whatever.' The word is about not caring at all.

traps.why: Thrilled matches the excited class, but 'although' says Kevin was different.
Anxious people care a lot; Kevin said he did not care.
Sympathetic looks similar but means caring about others' feelings.

sc1.tip: 'Although' signals a contrast with the excited class, and 'shrugging' and 'did not care' tell you Kevin had no interest.

sc2.sentence: Because Marcus had already seen the movie five times, he felt _____ about watching it again and spent the whole showing scrolling through his phone.

traps.why: Eager is the opposite; Marcus ignored the movie for his phone.
Nervous is a feeling, but nothing here shows worry, only boredom.
Sympathetic looks like apathetic but means feeling for someone else.

sc2.tip: 'Already seen the movie five times' causes the feeling, and 'scrolling through his phone' shows he had no interest.

wane.hook: Picture the moon after it is full: each night the bright part wanes into a thinner sliver.

traps.why: Grow is the opposite of wane, which means get smaller.
Wander looks a little like wane but means roam around.
Vanish means gone at once; wane means weakening little by little.

syn1.tip: Think of the waning moon, which shrinks a bit each night after it is full. To wane is to fade slowly.

traps.why: Gaining strength is the opposite of waning.
Waning is slow and gradual, not a sudden stop.
That describes wavering; wane means steadily growing smaller.

syn2.tip: Waxing and waning describe the moon growing and shrinking. Wane is the shrinking half, so it means getting weaker or smaller.

traps.why: Grow is the opposite; 'but' shows their excitement shrank.
Excitement can spread, but the chore made it shrink, not spread.
Wander looks like wane but means roam, which excitement cannot do.

sc1.tip: 'At first' and 'but' set up a contrast: they adored the hamster, then their excitement got smaller 'as the weeks passed.'

sc2.sentence: As the sun set and clouds rolled in, the light in the backyard began to _____, so we could barely see the soccer ball by the end of the game.

traps.why: Brighten is the opposite; they could barely see.
Sparkling light is about light, but it would not make seeing hard.
Spreading light would help you see the ball, not hide it.

sc2.tip: 'Sun set,' 'clouds rolled in,' and 'could barely see' all show the light getting weaker little by little.

forlorn.hook: Picture a forlorn puppy sitting alone in the rain, looking left behind and forgotten.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of forlorn, which means sad and alone.
Forward starts like forlorn but means bold or ahead.
Both are unhappy feelings, but forlorn is sad and alone, not mad.

syn1.tip: Say forlorn slowly and it sounds sad. Picture someone left all alone, looking abandoned and lonely.

traps.why: Glad and welcomed is the opposite of sad and left alone.
Forlorn is deep sadness and loneliness, not a small disappointment.
'For' is not 'fore' meaning before; forlorn has nothing to do with planning.

syn2.tip: Forlorn describes someone who feels left behind and alone, like the last kid waiting to be picked up.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite; he was left behind and staring sadly.
Restless people fidget, but Felix sat still for hours.
Forgetful looks similar but means not remembering things.

sc1.tip: 'Left behind when all his friends went away' and 'staring at the empty street for hours' show Felix is lonely and sad.

sc2.sentence: After her best friend moved across the country, Maya looked _____ at lunch, sitting by herself and pushing her food around without eating a bite.

traps.why: Delighted is the opposite; Maya just lost her best friend nearby.
Relieved is a good feeling, but the clues are sad and lonely.
The sentence mentions food, but Maya is not eating it.

sc2.tip: 'Best friend moved across the country' causes the feeling, and 'sitting by herself' shows she is lonely and sad.

gaudy.hook: Picture a gaudy outfit: neon colors, giant sequins, and so much glitter that it hurts to look at.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite of gaudy, which means too showy.
Elegant praises a look; gaudy criticizes it as tacky.
Gaudy things may look expensive, but gaudy is about showiness, not price.

syn1.tip: Gaudy has a negative feeling. Think of clothes so bright and sparkly they look tacky, not pretty.

traps.why: Simple and tasteful is the opposite of gaudy.
Gaudy is bright, but it is a put-down, not a compliment.
Gaudy means way too bright, not just a little colorful.

syn2.tip: Gaudy means too much: too bright, too sparkly, too loud for good taste.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite; the sweater had lights, glitter, and jewels.
Sweaters are cozy, but the clues are about showiness, not warmth.
Elegant is praise, but everyone squinted and giggled at the sweater.

sc1.tip: The list 'blinking lights, glitter, and plastic jewels' and 'squint and giggle' show the sweater was too showy.

sc2.sentence: Mom wanted a calm, simple look for the living room, so she was horrified when Dad hung a _____ purple curtain covered in shiny gold fringe and flashing beads.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite; the curtain had gold fringe and flashing beads.
Tasteful is praise, but Mom was horrified by the curtain.
Faded is about color, but shiny and flashing things are not faded.

sc2.tip: 'Calm, simple look' contrasts with 'horrified,' and 'shiny gold fringe and flashing beads' describe something too showy.

contaminate.hook: When a factory dumps chemicals into a river, it contaminates the water and makes it unsafe to drink.

traps.why: Purify means make clean, the opposite of contaminate.
Contain starts like contaminate but means hold inside.
A spill can cause pollution, but spill just means let liquid fall.

syn1.tip: Think of 'contaminated water' in the news: it has something harmful mixed in, just like polluted water.

traps.why: Cleaning thoroughly is the opposite of contaminating.
Hold inside means contain, a lookalike word, not contaminate.
'Con' can mean together, but contaminate means spoil with something harmful.

syn2.tip: Contaminate is about spoiling something by mixing in dirt, germs, or poison.

traps.why: Germs do not clean things; they make samples dirty and ruin results.
Contain looks similar but means hold, which does not ruin samples.
Lab workers examine samples, but germs cannot examine anything.

sc1.tip: 'Germs from their hands' getting in would 'ruin the results,' so the blank means to make the samples impure.

sc2.sentence: Dad warned us never to let raw chicken juice touch the salad because it can _____ fresh vegetables, filling them with harmful germs that make people sick.

traps.why: Washing makes vegetables cleaner, the opposite of filling them with germs.
Juice can add taste, but the clue is harmful germs.
Softening changes texture, but the sentence is about germs and sickness.

sc2.tip: The phrase 'filling them with harmful germs' restates the blank, so the word means to make something impure.

malleable.hook: Malleable comes from the Latin word for hammer: malleable metal can be hammered into new shapes without breaking.

traps.why: Rigid means stiff, the opposite of easily shaped.
This 'mal' comes from hammer, not the 'mal' meaning bad.
Fragile things break easily; malleable things bend without breaking.

syn1.tip: Think of a mallet, a kind of hammer. Something malleable can be hammered or pressed into a new shape.

traps.why: Hard to change is the opposite of malleable.
The 'mal' here means hammer, not bad, so it is not badly made.
Both describe materials, but malleable things bend instead of breaking.

syn2.tip: The ending -able means 'able to be.' Malleable things are able to be shaped, like clay or soft gold.

traps.why: Brittle things crack; the potters could stretch and mold the clay.
Clay can be heavy, but weight does not explain molding it.
Dry clay is dusty, but warm clay being molded is soft.

sc1.tip: 'Press, stretch, and mold it' describes clay that changes shape easily, and 'before it was hardened' tells you it is still soft.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the stiff plastic ruler that snapped when Leo bent it, the copper wire was _____ enough for him to twist into the shape of a star.

traps.why: Rigid matches the ruler, but 'unlike' says the wire was different.
Copper is shiny, but shine does not let you twist it.
Wire can be sharp, but that is not why it bends.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike the stiff plastic ruler that snapped' signals contrast, and 'twist into the shape of a star' shows the wire bends easily.

raucous.hook: Raucous sounds a lot like ruckus: picture a raucous ruckus of crows squawking outside your window at dawn.

traps.why: Quiet is the opposite of raucous, which means loud and harsh.
Cautious rhymes with raucous but means careful.
Both are about sound, but raucous sounds harsh, not tuneful.

syn1.tip: Say raucous out loud: it sounds harsh and croaky, like a crow. It means loud and harsh, so noisy fits.

traps.why: Soft and gentle is the opposite of raucous.
This describes pleasant sound; raucous sound is grating and unpleasant.
Raucous is very loud and harsh, not a little talkative.

syn2.tip: Raucous sounds like 'ruckus,' a noisy commotion. Picture a crowd yelling or crows cawing.

traps.why: Quiet is the opposite; the cheering was deafening.
Fans can be polite, but polite cheering would not drown out a whistle.
Cautious sounds like raucous but means careful.

sc1.tip: 'Harsh and deafening' and 'could not hear the referee's whistle at all' show the cheering was loud and grating.

sc2.sentence: The librarian, who usually enjoyed a calm afternoon, frowned when a _____ group of teenagers burst in shouting, laughing, and banging their backpacks on the tables.

traps.why: Silent is the opposite; the group was shouting and banging.
Libraries suggest studying, but this group was making noise, not studying.
Sleepy people are calm, but this group burst in shouting.

sc2.tip: 'Calm afternoon' contrasts with what happened, and 'shouting, laughing, and banging' show the group was loud and rough.

aggravate.hook: Aggravate holds 'grav,' as in gravity: it comes from a Latin word meaning make heavier, so problems get worse.

traps.why: Improve is the opposite of aggravate, which means make worse.
Ignoring a problem leaves it alone; aggravating it makes it worse.
Aggravate doesn't start a problem; it makes an existing one worse.

syn1.tip: You've heard 'scratching will aggravate a bite.' Inside is 'grav,' as in gravity: it makes a problem heavier, or worse.

traps.why: Making something less painful is the opposite of aggravating it.
'Grav' suggests weight, but aggravate means making problems worse, not heavier.
Making up for a problem repairs it; aggravating it makes it worse.

syn2.tip: Aggravate is used with problems, injuries, and pain. It means taking something already bad and making it more serious.

traps.why: Healing would get him back sooner, not keep him off longer.
Bandages go on sprains, but basketball cannot bandage an injury.
Doctors inspect injuries, but playing basketball does not inspect anything.

sc1.tip: 'Keep him off the court even longer' shows the result: playing on the sprain would make it worse.

sc2.sentence: Hoping to calm the argument, Sam made a joke, but it only seemed to _____ the situation, and both of his sisters started yelling even louder than before.

traps.why: Ease matches 'hoping to calm,' but 'but' shows the opposite happened.
Jokes often lighten moods, but here the yelling got louder.
A joke can interrupt, but the clue is the fight getting worse.

sc2.tip: 'Hoping to calm' then 'but' signals the joke did the opposite, and 'yelling even louder' shows the argument got worse.

trite.hook: A trite saying like 'every cloud has a silver lining' has been repeated so often that it no longer surprises anyone.

traps.why: Original means new and fresh, the opposite of trite.
Trivial looks similar but means unimportant, not worn out.
A trite line may be true; it is just worn out.

syn1.tip: Think of a phrase you've heard a hundred times, like 'It was all a dream.' Trite means worn out from use.

traps.why: New and fresh is the opposite of trite.
That means trivial, a lookalike word, not trite.
Trite means used so often it is dull, not just a bit familiar.

syn2.tip: Trite has a negative feeling. Ask yourself: is it boring because it has been used too much? Then it is trite.

traps.why: Creative fits 'fresh and surprising,' but the blank is what to avoid.
'Once upon a time' is short; the problem is it's overused.
Stories can open funny, but the clue is about being worn out.

sc1.tip: 'Avoid' plus 'instead' signal contrast: the blank is the opposite of 'fresh and surprising,' like the worn-out 'Once upon a time.'

sc2.sentence: Everyone groaned at the _____ joke about the chicken crossing the road, since they had all heard it at least a hundred times before.

traps.why: Brand-new is the opposite; they had heard it a hundred times.
People groan at rude jokes, but the clue is hearing it often.
Long jokes can bore people, but the clue is repetition, not length.

sc2.tip: 'Heard it at least a hundred times' explains why 'everyone groaned': the joke was worn out from overuse.

bravado.hook: Bravado looks like brave, but it is fake bravery: loud boasting that hides a nervous heart.

traps.why: Shyness is the opposite of showy, boastful bravado.
Bravado looks like brave, but it is fake courage, not real courage.
'Bravo' is a cheer, but bravado means fake boldness, not clapping.

syn1.tip: Bravado has 'brav' like brave, but it is a show, not the real thing. Picture someone strutting and boasting to look tough.

traps.why: Quiet humility is the opposite of loud, showy bravado.
Bravado sounds like brave, but it is only a show of courage.
Bravado can be loud, but it is about acting tough, not anger.

syn2.tip: Bravado is about acting brave, not being brave. When it vanishes the moment danger appears, it was only a show.

traps.why: His fear did not disappear; he ran screaming.
Haunted houses spark curiosity, but the clue is his boasting.
Nothing shows boredom; the clue is boasting that turned to screaming.

sc1.tip: 'Boasted that he wasn't afraid,' then 'but' and 'ran screaming,' show his boldness was just a show that quickly vanished.

sc2.sentence: Ava's _____ before the spelling bee, all that strutting and loud talk about winning easily, was really just a mask for the nervous butterflies in her stomach.

traps.why: Shyness is the opposite of strutting and loud talk.
Spelling bees need preparation, but strutting and boasting are not studying.
Sympathy is caring for others, not strutting and boasting.

sc2.tip: The words 'all that strutting and loud talk' restate the blank, and 'just a mask' tells you the boldness was fake.

obnoxious.hook: Picture a kid kicking your seat for a whole flight while humming loudly. That kid is being obnoxious.

traps.why: Pleasant is the opposite of obnoxious.
Anxious rhymes with obnoxious but means worried.
Obnoxious people are often loud, but obnoxious means annoying, not noisy.

syn1.tip: You hear it in 'stop being so obnoxious.' The word has a sour feeling, so pick the choice that is unpleasant to be around.

traps.why: Very charming is the opposite of obnoxious.
Slightly bothersome is too weak; obnoxious means very annoying.
That describes noxious, which looks similar but means harmful.

syn2.tip: Everyone wants an obnoxious person to stop. That is strong dislike, so look for the strongest unpleasant choice.

traps.why: Courteous means polite, the opposite of his rude behavior.
He was eating popcorn, but the list shows annoying behavior, not hunger.
Anxious sounds like obnoxious but means worried, and he was not worried.

sc1.tip: The list 'talking loudly,' 'kicking our seats,' and 'crunching popcorn right next to our ears' describes behavior that bothers everyone nearby.

sc2.sentence: Although my little brother thought his loud fake burps at dinner were hilarious, the rest of the family found them _____ and asked him to stop.

traps.why: Amusing is how he felt; the family wanted him to stop.
Dinner is food, but burps are not delicious.
Anxious sounds like obnoxious but means worried, which burps cannot be.

sc2.tip: 'Although' signals a contrast: he thought the burps were 'hilarious,' but the family 'asked him to stop,' so they found them very annoying.

anguish.hook: Picture someone sobbing after terrible news, hardly able to breathe. That deep, sharp pain is anguish.

traps.why: Joy is the opposite of anguish.
Anger starts like anguish but means being mad, not suffering.
Worry is much too weak; anguish is terrible pain.

syn1.tip: Anguish shows up in 'cried out in anguish.' It is the deepest kind of pain or sadness, so choose the strongest suffering word.

traps.why: Deep delight is the opposite of anguish.
Mild disappointment is far too weak for anguish.
Others feel sympathy for someone in anguish, but anguish is the suffering itself.

syn2.tip: Anguish is what someone feels after a terrible loss. Look for the choice that is both sad and strong.

traps.why: Relief is a good feeling, but she cannot imagine starting over.
Gratitude is a happy feeling; losing her garden made her miserable.
Annoyance is too mild for losing twenty years of work.

sc1.tip: She 'wept' after losing twenty years of work and was 'unable to imagine starting over.' That points to deep sorrow, not a mild or happy feeling.

sc2.sentence: The runner's _____ was clear to everyone in the stadium: she had twisted her ankle just steps from the finish line and lay crying on the track.

traps.why: She did not win; she got hurt before the finish line.
Speed fits a race, but she lay crying on the track.
Excitement is a happy feeling; she was hurt and crying.

sc2.tip: The colon explains the blank: she 'twisted her ankle' just before finishing and 'lay crying.' Pick the word for terrible pain and sorrow.

conserve.hook: Turn off the faucet while you brush your teeth, and you conserve water so there is more for later.

traps.why: Waste is the opposite of conserve.
Converse looks like conserve but means to talk with someone.
Recycling helps the planet too, but conserve means to use less.

syn1.tip: You've heard 'conserve energy' and 'conserve water.' Both mean using less so it lasts, so pick the word about keeping, not using up.

traps.why: Using up quickly is the opposite of conserving.
That means converse, which looks like conserve.
Cleaning litter helps nature, but conserve means keeping something from being wasted.

syn2.tip: Conservation groups work to keep forests and animals from being lost. To conserve is to guard something so none of it is wasted.

traps.why: Shorter showers save water; they do not waste it.
Purifying cleans water, but shorter showers are about using less.
Use is too general; the examples are about using less.

sc1.tip: 'During the drought' and the examples 'shorter showers' and watering 'only once a week' all show people using less water so it lasts.

sc2.sentence: Instead of letting the laptop's battery drain on games, Maya dimmed the screen and closed extra apps to _____ power for her long bus ride home.

traps.why: Dimming the screen saves power; it does not waste it.
Charging adds power, but dimming and closing apps only keep it.
Closing apps cannot make new power; it only keeps what is left.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of letting the battery drain' signals a contrast. Dimming and closing apps make power last longer for 'her long bus ride.'

exert.hook: Ex means out: when you exert yourself on a steep hike, you push your strength out into every step.

traps.why: Withhold means to hold back, the opposite of exert.
Exit looks a bit like exert but means to leave.
Exerting yourself can exhaust you, but exert means to use effort.

syn1.tip: You hear 'exert force' or 'exert pressure' in science class. Both mean putting strength to work, so choose the word for using something.

traps.why: Holding back is the opposite of exerting.
Ex means out, but exert means to use, not to leave out.
Lightly touching is too weak; exert means putting real effort in.

syn2.tip: Exert goes with force, effort, or influence, things you bring into action. Find the phrase that means using them.

traps.why: Saving strength is the opposite of pushing a piano upstairs.
Strength can be measured, but the movers had to use it.
Praising strength is talking about it; the movers had to use it.

sc1.tip: 'Groaning as they pushed it one step at a time' shows the movers working as hard as they can, putting all their strength to use.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his teammates, who barely moved during practice, Jamal would _____ every ounce of energy in drills, sprinting until he was soaked with sweat.

traps.why: Sprinting until soaked means he used his energy, not saved it.
Hiding energy is what the lazy teammates did, not Jamal.
Coaches may measure energy, but sprinting shows Jamal using it.

sc2.tip: 'Unlike his teammates, who barely moved' sets up a contrast, and 'sprinting until he was soaked with sweat' shows Jamal using all his energy.

conspicuous.hook: Conspicuous contains spic, a form of spect, meaning look: a conspicuous thing is one everybody looks at.

traps.why: Hidden is the opposite of conspicuous.
Suspicious looks similar but means seeming guilty or untrustworthy.
Bright colors can stand out, but conspicuous means easy to notice.

syn1.tip: Think of 'a conspicuous spot,' where everyone can see it. The 'spic' part is like 'spect,' which means look.

traps.why: Hard to find is the opposite of conspicuous.
Beautiful things may get noticed, but conspicuous only means easy to notice.
Barely visible is far too weak; conspicuous things grab attention.

syn2.tip: Picture a kid in a bright costume at a plain event. Choose the phrase that means everyone notices right away.

traps.why: Every head turned toward him, so he was not invisible.
Suspicious looks similar but means distrustful; the clue is about standing out.
Raincoats suggest bad weather, but the clue is about everyone noticing him.

sc1.tip: 'Where everyone wore navy uniforms' contrasts with his 'bright yellow raincoat,' and 'every head turned toward him.' He stood out.

sc2.sentence: The new sign was so _____ that no driver could miss it: it was ten feet tall, bright red, and flashing with lights all night long.

traps.why: A faint sign is easy to miss, the opposite of this one.
A big sign may cost a lot, but cost doesn't make drivers see it.
Flashing lights may seem modern, but the clue is that nobody could miss it.

sc2.tip: 'No driver could miss it' and the description 'ten feet tall, bright red, and flashing' show a sign that is impossible not to notice.

contradict.hook: Contra means against and dict means say, so to contradict is to say against what someone claimed.

traps.why: Confirm means to agree it's true, the opposite of contradict.
Contribute also starts with con but means to give or add.
Insulting is being rude; contradicting just says the opposite.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: 'contra' means against and 'dict' means say. Find the word for speaking against a claim.

traps.why: Agreeing completely is the opposite of contradicting.
Dict means speak, but contradict is about speaking against, not softly.
Questions come up in arguments, but contradict means stating the reverse.

syn2.tip: When the facts contradict a story, they tell a different version. Contradict means stating the reverse of what was said.

traps.why: The video showed her at the mall, so it did not confirm her claim.
Security cameras record things, but the video went against her claim.
Repeating her claim would agree with it; the video showed otherwise.

sc1.tip: 'Seemed believable until' signals a change, and the video shows her 'at the mall' when she claimed to be home. It says the opposite.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa insists the town's old bridge was built in 1920, but Mom won't _____ him, because arguing with Grandpa only makes him louder.

traps.why: Supporting him would not cause an argument, so the reason makes no sense.
Admire is a warm feeling; the clue is about avoiding an argument.
Visiting Grandpa is about family, but the clue is about arguing.

sc2.tip: 'Because arguing with Grandpa only makes him louder' tells you Mom avoids saying the opposite of what he claims about the bridge.

ingenious.hook: Ingenious comes from the same Latin word as engine: an ingenious idea works like a clever little machine.

traps.why: Foolish is the opposite of ingenious.
Genuine looks similar but means real or sincere.
Inventions can be complicated, but ingenious means clever, not complex.

syn1.tip: Ingenious sounds a lot like 'genius.' An ingenious plan is a genius plan, so pick the word for smart and inventive.

traps.why: Dull and ordinary is the opposite of ingenious.
That means genuine or ingenuous, words that look like ingenious.
Slightly unusual is too weak; ingenious means very clever.

syn2.tip: Ingenious inventions solve problems in a new way nobody thought of. Look for the phrase with both 'smart' and 'new.'

traps.why: Hanging dripping bottles is a clever trick, not an ordinary one.
Awkward is negative, but the sentence admires his smart idea.
Bottles are cheap, and the sentence praises his idea, not its cost.

sc1.tip: The colon introduces his solution: upside-down bottles that 'slowly dripped water into each pot.' That is a smart, original idea.

sc2.sentence: Although the cardboard robot costume looked simple, it was actually _____: buttons on the sleeve made its eyes light up and its arms wave.

traps.why: Plain fits 'looked simple,' but 'although' and 'actually' signal the opposite.
Cardboard can be flimsy, but light-up eyes show clever design.
Genuine looks like ingenious but means real, which the buttons don't show.

sc2.tip: 'Although' and 'actually' signal a contrast with 'looked simple,' and the light-up eyes and waving arms show clever invention.

ludicrous.hook: Ludicrous comes from Latin ludus, meaning play: a ludicrous idea, like a fish riding a bike, makes you laugh.

traps.why: Sensible is the opposite of ludicrous.
Luxurious looks similar but means fancy and comfortable.
A ludicrous excuse might be a lie, but ludicrous means laughably silly.

syn1.tip: Picture someone saying 'That's ludicrous' about a crazy plan. The word means so silly it's laughable, just like the word that sounds a bit like it.

traps.why: Perfectly reasonable is the opposite of ludicrous.
Slightly odd is too weak; ludicrous things are absurd enough to laugh at.
Ludicrous things make people laugh, not cry.

syn2.tip: Something ludicrous makes people burst out laughing because it makes no sense. Pick the phrase with both 'funny' and 'foolish.'

traps.why: Geese stealing homework is not believable, and everyone laughed.
Tearful is sad, but everyone laughed at the excuse.
Lucky sounds a bit like ludicrous but means fortunate.

sc1.tip: 'Everyone laughed,' and geese flying off with homework could never happen. The excuse is so silly it is laughable.

sc2.sentence: The movie's plot was meant to be serious, but it was so _____ that the audience giggled when the villain was defeated by a rubber duck.

traps.why: A villain beaten by a rubber duck is not realistic.
Frightening is the wrong feeling; the audience giggled.
Movies can be long, but length doesn't make people giggle.

sc2.tip: 'Meant to be serious, but' signals contrast, and a villain beaten 'by a rubber duck' made people giggle. The plot was silly enough to laugh at.

folly.hook: Folly rhymes with jolly, but there is nothing jolly about the folly of hiking into the desert without water.

traps.why: Wisdom is the opposite of folly.
Foolish acts can be dangerous, but folly means foolishness itself.
Bravery is admirable; folly is foolish, not admirable.

syn1.tip: Folly is close to 'fool.' Think of 'it would be folly to try,' meaning it would be foolish.

traps.why: Careful planning is the opposite of folly.
Folly is not harmless fun; it means acting without sense.
A small error is too mild; folly is a truly foolish act.

syn2.tip: When someone says 'that plan is folly,' they mean it is foolish and likely to fail. Choose the phrase describing a lack of good sense.

traps.why: A straw house in hurricane country is not genius; the architect rejected it.
Beach houses can be luxurious, but this plan was foolish.
Comfort is pleasant, but the architect warned against the plan.

sc1.tip: Straw on a beach where 'hurricanes strike every year' is a terrible idea, and the architect 'recommended concrete instead.' The plan is foolish.

sc2.sentence: Mia's friends warned that skipping sleep to play video games before the big test was _____, and sure enough, she yawned through every question and failed.

traps.why: She failed, so skipping sleep was not wisdom.
Games are fun, but her friends warned her, and she failed.
Tests need practice, but playing games instead of sleeping is not practice.

sc2.tip: 'Warned' and the result, she 'yawned through every question and failed,' show that skipping sleep was a foolish choice.

inhibit.hook: Feeling inhibited is like having a hand on your shoulder holding you back from raising your hand in class.

traps.why: Encourage is the opposite of inhibit.
Inhabit looks almost the same but means to live in.
Destroy is too strong; inhibit means to hold back.

syn1.tip: You might hear 'inhibit growth' in science. To inhibit is to slow something down or keep it from happening, like a brake.

traps.why: Helping along is the opposite of inhibiting.
Stop forever is too strong; inhibit means to slow or restrain.
That means inhabit, which looks like inhibit.

syn2.tip: Something that inhibits growth keeps it from going full speed. Choose the phrase that means keeping something back.

traps.why: If cold sped up growth, gardeners would not need to wait.
Inhabit looks like inhibit but means to live in.
Gardens need water, but nights cannot water growth.

sc1.tip: 'So gardeners often wait' tells you the chilly nights cause a problem. Cold holds back the plants' growth.

sc2.sentence: Loud chatter in the library used to _____ my concentration, but now that I wear earplugs, I can read for an hour without losing my place.

traps.why: Chatter hurt concentration; earplugs were the fix.
Noise does not sharpen focus, and the earplugs solved a problem.
Entertain is pleasant, but the chatter was a problem to block out.

sc2.tip: 'But now that I wear earplugs' signals a contrast: before, the chatter kept the reader from focusing. It held back concentration.

mediate.hook: Mediate comes from a Latin word for middle: a mediator stands between two arguing sides and helps them meet halfway.

traps.why: Provoke means to stir up a fight, the opposite of settling one.
Meditate means to think quietly; it only looks like mediate.
Arguing is what the two sides do, not what the helper does.

syn1.tip: Think of the word middle hiding in mediate. A mediator stands in the middle and helps both sides settle things fairly.

traps.why: Starting a quarrel creates a fight; mediating helps end one.
Medi hints at middle, but mediate is not about measuring anything.
A mediator stays fair to both sides instead of taking one.

syn2.tip: In the news, a mediator is someone called in to help two groups settle a dispute, like a strike between workers and owners.

traps.why: Meditate means to think quietly, which would not settle the partners' disagreement.
The partners were already arguing; they wanted the teacher to help end it.
Punishing is harsh and would not help them find a fair solution.

sc1.tip: The words 'help them find a fair solution' show the teacher acts as a fair helper in the middle of two sides.

sc2.sentence: Instead of taking sides when her twin brothers fought over the video game controller, Mom sat between them and tried to _____ until they agreed to share turns.

traps.why: Quarreling is what the brothers were doing, not how Mom helped.
Retreating means pulling away, but Mom stayed between them to help.
Medicate means to give medicine, which would not end a fight.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of taking sides' and 'sat between them' show Mom acted as a fair go-between who helped both brothers agree.

inept.hook: Inept is in- plus apt: someone not apt for the job, like a juggler who drops every single ball.

traps.why: An expert is highly skilled, the opposite of inept.
Inert means not moving; it only looks like inept.
Nervous people may fumble, but inept means lacking skill.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: in- means not, and -ept is like apt, meaning able or fit. Inept means not able.

traps.why: Graceful means smooth and skillful, the opposite of inept.
A lazy person avoids work; an inept one tries but lacks skill.
In- here means not, not inside, so inept has nothing to do with internal.

syn2.tip: Picture an inept waiter dropping trays of food. Clumsy fits that picture. Inept is the opposite of adept, which means skilled.

traps.why: Handy means good with tools, but the wheel falling off shows Jonah was not.
Adept looks like inept but means skilled, which is the opposite here.
Eagerness is about wanting to help, not about lacking skill.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike his sister, who could fix any bike' sets up a contrast, and the wheel falling off shows Jonah lacked skill.

sc2.sentence: Because the new goalie was so _____, the other team scored six easy goals before halftime, and the coach finally sent in a backup.

traps.why: A talented goalie would block shots, not let in six easy goals.
Being famous has nothing to do with letting in easy goals.
Lucky is a positive word, but six easy goals point to a bad performance.

sc2.tip: 'Because' links the blank to the result: six easy goals and a backup coming in. That points to a goalie who lacked skill.

resolute.hook: Resolute is related to resolution: a New Year's resolution is a firm promise, and only a resolute person keeps it.

traps.why: Hesitant means unsure, the opposite of firmly determined.
Absolute rhymes with resolute but means complete or total.
Stubborn is a negative word; resolute praises firm determination.

syn1.tip: Think of a resolution, a firm decision you resolve to keep. A resolute person sticks to the decision no matter what.

traps.why: Being easily discouraged is the opposite of staying firmly determined.
Re- and solve seem to suggest solving again, but that is not the meaning.
Slightly interested is far too weak; resolute means strongly determined.

syn2.tip: Resolute sounds like resolve. When you resolve to do something, you are firm in purpose and do not back down.

traps.why: A discouraged person gives up, but Isabel signed up again right away.
Reckless means careless, but practicing every day shows careful determination.
Resentful looks a bit like resolute but means bitter, which the sentence doesn't show.

sc1.tip: 'Even after failing' sets up a surprise, and 'signing up for a third attempt the very next morning' shows she stayed firmly determined.

sc2.sentence: Mia was _____ about learning the hard piano piece; no matter how many wrong notes she hit, she refused to quit and kept practicing every single night.

traps.why: Doubtful means unsure, but refusing to quit shows she was firm.
Musical fits the piano topic but not the clue 'refused to quit.'
Interested is too weak; practicing every night without quitting shows firm determination.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon restates the blank: 'refused to quit and kept practicing every single night' describes someone firmly determined.

incite.hook: Picture one angry shout in a quiet crowd that incites a riot, stirring everyone up at once.

traps.why: Calm means to settle people down, the opposite of stirring them up.
Invite means to ask someone to come; it only looks like incite.
Encourage is positive, but incite usually means stirring up something bad.

syn1.tip: Incite usually goes with trouble: you incite a riot, a fight, or panic. Think of stirring up bad feelings.

traps.why: Settling down is the opposite of stirring people up.
Cite means to quote, but incite means to stir up, not to quote.
Push gently is too mild; incite means stirring up strong feelings.

syn2.tip: Picture a speaker who incites a crowd: the people get stirred up, angry, and ready to act.

traps.why: Preventing panic would not send shoppers rushing for the exits.
Explaining panic would not cause people to run for the doors.
Insert means to put something in; it looks like incite but doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: Look at the effect: 'sending shoppers rushing for the exits.' The fake alarm must have stirred up panic.

sc2.sentence: Instead of calming the angry fans after the referee's bad call, the team's mascot waved his arms and booed, which only seemed to _____ them further.

traps.why: Soothe means to calm, but the booing made the fans angrier.
Entertain is pleasant, but booing made the angry fans even angrier.
Invite looks like incite, but inviting fans further makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of calming' signals the opposite of calming, and 'only seemed to... them further' shows the mascot stirred the fans up more.

omen.hook: The word ominous comes from omen: dark storm clouds are an omen, a sign of what is coming.

traps.why: A memory looks back at the past; an omen points ahead.
Amen ends a prayer; it sounds like omen but means something else.
An omen may warn of a disaster, but it is not the disaster itself.

syn1.tip: The word ominous grows from omen. Ominous clouds are a sign that a storm is on the way.

traps.why: An omen looks ahead, not back at the past.
A lucky charm is meant to bring luck; an omen only signals what's coming.
Any message is too general; an omen is a sign about the future.

syn2.tip: People read omens to guess what will happen next, so look for a choice about the future.

traps.why: Storms are a sailing topic, but a storm does not predict calm seas.
An accident just happens; the seagull was read as predicting calm seas.
A rescue saves people; it does not tell what lies ahead.

sc1.tip: The phrase 'meant calm seas lay ahead' shows the seagull was read as a sign of what would happen next.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa laughed when Lucy called the broken mirror a bad _____; he said shattered glass could not predict anything, so she should just sweep it up.

traps.why: A memory looks back, but Grandpa talks about predicting what comes next.
Amen sounds like omen but is a word that ends a prayer.
A lesson teaches from the past; the clue is about predicting the future.

sc2.tip: Grandpa answers that glass 'could not predict anything,' so Lucy must have called the mirror a sign of the future.

relinquish.hook: To relinquish is to let go: picture a kid finally handing the TV remote over to a younger sibling.

traps.why: Holding onto something is the opposite of letting it go.
Re- often means again, but relinquish means give up, not repeat.
Taking turns shares something; relinquish means handing it over completely.

syn1.tip: When you relinquish a prize, a title, or control, you let it go and someone else takes it.

traps.why: Seize means to grab hold of, the opposite of giving up.
Relish means to enjoy; it looks like relinquish but means something else.
Losing happens by accident; relinquishing means choosing to give something up.

syn2.tip: Picture a king who must relinquish his crown: he surrenders it and lets someone else rule.

traps.why: Keeping the role would not let a younger member gain experience.
Performing her role would not open it up for a younger member.
Re- can mean again, but repeating her role would not help anyone else lead.

sc1.tip: 'So that a younger member could gain experience' gives the reason: Hannah had to let go of the job.

sc2.sentence: Although the puppy whined and tugged, Leo refused to _____ his grip on the leash until they had safely crossed the busy street.

traps.why: Tightening is the opposite of letting go, and refusing to tighten makes no sense.
Relish looks like relinquish but means to enjoy, which doesn't fit.
Improving his grip is about the leash, but refusing to improve it makes no sense.

sc2.tip: 'Refused' plus 'until they had safely crossed' tells you Leo would not let go of the leash on the busy street.

dispel.hook: Dis- means apart or away: to dispel a fear is to drive it away, like sunlight burning off morning fog.

traps.why: Strengthen makes a fear bigger; dispel makes it disappear.
Dispel has spell inside, but it is not about spelling words.
Doubts are what get dispelled, not the act of dispelling them.

syn1.tip: You often hear 'dispel a myth' or 'dispel fears.' Both mean driving something away until it is gone.

traps.why: Stir up makes feelings grow, the opposite of making them vanish.
Dispel is not about magic spells; it means to drive something away.
Dispel means making something vanish completely, not just moving it a bit.

syn2.tip: Dis- means apart or away. To dispel something is to drive it away so it no longer exists.

traps.why: Spreading the rumor is the opposite of what showing the kitchen would do.
Dispense means to hand out; it looks like dispel but doesn't fit.
Enjoying a rumor would not make the cook prove it false.

sc1.tip: The cook let students 'watch her prepare lunch' to prove the rumor false, so she wanted the rumor to go away.

sc2.sentence: Though Ava felt nervous about the new school, her friendly locker neighbor helped _____ her worries by inviting her to sit together at lunch.

traps.why: A friendly invitation would shrink her worries, not increase them.
Display means to show off, not to make something disappear.
Noticing her worries would not make them go away.

sc2.tip: 'Though' and 'nervous' set up a change, and a 'friendly' lunch invitation is a kind act that would make worries disappear.

elicit.hook: Elicit starts with e-, meaning out: a good joke elicits laughter, drawing it right out of the audience.

traps.why: Holding back keeps a reaction in, the opposite of drawing it out.
Illicit, which sounds like elicit, means illegal; elicit means draw out.
Answering is the response itself; elicit means drawing that response out.

syn1.tip: The e- at the start means out. A question that elicits answers draws them out of people.

traps.why: Keeping something in is the opposite of bringing a reaction out.
Rip out is far too forceful; elicit gently draws a response.
Saying something aloud is speaking, not drawing a reaction out of someone.

syn2.tip: You often hear 'elicit a response' or 'elicit a smile.' In each, something is brought out of a person.

traps.why: Silencing answers is the opposite of what open-ended questions are for.
Grading comes later; the questions were meant to get answers in the first place.
Punishing thoughtful answers is harsh and makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: Her students 'rarely spoke in class,' so the open-ended questions were meant to draw answers out of them.

sc2.sentence: No matter how many silly faces Dad made, he could not _____ even a tiny smile from the grumpy baby, who kept frowning.

traps.why: Removing a smile is the opposite; Dad wanted to draw one out.
Elect means to choose by voting; it looks like elicit but doesn't fit.
Smiles are seen, not heard, and Dad wanted to bring one out.

sc2.tip: 'No matter how many silly faces' shows Dad tried hard, yet the baby 'kept frowning,' so he failed to draw out a smile.

jeopardize.hook: Jeopardy means danger, so to jeopardize something is to put it in danger, like texting while riding your bike.

traps.why: Protect means to keep safe, the opposite of putting at risk.
Destroy is too strong; jeopardize means put at risk, not ruin completely.
Jeopardy is also a quiz show, but jeopardize means put in danger.

syn1.tip: Inside jeopardize is jeopardy, which means danger. To jeopardize something is to put it in danger.

traps.why: Keeping something safe is the opposite of putting it at risk.
Ruin forever is too strong; jeopardize means something could be lost.
Warning about danger helps; jeopardizing causes the danger.

syn2.tip: You often hear 'jeopardize your chances.' It means doing something that could cost you, putting those chances at risk.

traps.why: Missing practice would hurt his chance, not improve it.
Celebrating is positive, but the coach is giving a warning.
Discussing his chance would not be a result of missing practice.

sc1.tip: Coach 'warned,' and 'missing too many practices' is a bad habit, so the result must be putting Dante's chance at risk.

sc2.sentence: Smart hikers stay on marked trails, but a few careless ones wander off and _____ their own safety by getting lost in the woods.

traps.why: Getting lost does not protect safety; it puts it at risk.
Enjoying safety sounds nice, but getting lost is a danger.
Exploring fits hiking, but you explore woods, not your own safety.

sc2.tip: 'Smart hikers' contrast with 'careless ones,' and 'getting lost in the woods' shows their safety is being put at risk.

whimsical.hook: A whim is a sudden silly idea; whimsical things feel like whims come to life, like a teapot dancing on legs.

traps.why: Serious is the opposite of playful and fanciful.
Wistful means sadly longing; it only looks a bit like whimsical.
Childish is negative; whimsical is a fond word for odd, playful fun.

syn1.tip: Whimsical comes from whim, a sudden silly idea. Whimsical things are playful and full of fancy.

traps.why: Practical means sensible and useful, the opposite of fanciful.
Spooky is odd in a scary way; whimsical is odd in a fun way.
A whim comes suddenly, but whimsical means playfully odd, not sudden.

syn2.tip: Picture a Dr. Seuss book: odd, imaginative, and fun. That fanciful feeling is what whimsical describes.

traps.why: Pigs with butterfly wings are the opposite of realistic.
Dancing teapots are fun, not frightening.
Wishful means hoping; it looks a bit like whimsical but doesn't fit.

sc1.tip: The examples after 'like' tell you: 'pigs with butterfly wings' and 'teapots that danced' are playful, fanciful ideas.

sc2.sentence: Grandma's living room was plain and serious, but her backyard was totally _____, with flamingo statues wearing sunglasses and a birdbath shaped like a giant teacup.

traps.why: Formal matches the living room, but 'but' signals the backyard is different.
Messy is negative; flamingos in sunglasses show playful fun, not disorder.
Wistful means sadly longing; it looks like whimsical but fits nothing here.

sc2.tip: 'But' signals a contrast with 'plain and serious,' and flamingos in sunglasses show the backyard was playful and fanciful.

fraud.hook: A fraud is a trick to grab your money, like a fake prize email asking for your bank password.

traps.why: Honesty is the opposite of fraud, which is dishonest trickery.
A joke can trick people, but it is harmless fun, not stealing money.
Fraud is one kind of crime, but crime is far too general.

syn1.tip: Think of "credit card fraud," where someone tricks a bank to take money. Pick the word for a money trick.

traps.why: An honest deal is the opposite of fraud.
Fraud costs people money, but it is done on purpose, not by mistake.
A joke is playful; fraud is a harmful trick to take money.

syn2.tip: Fraud is always negative and done on purpose. Look for the choice that is both sneaky and deliberate.

traps.why: A real breakthrough would be amazing, but the seller was caught cheating buyers.
A bargain is a good deal; buyers here lost all their money.
A donation gives money away; this seller took money by lying.

sc1.tip: The quote marks around "miracle" and "caught keeping all the money" tell you the pill was fake and the seller was a cheat.

sc2.sentence: The website promised free tickets to the concert, but instead of sending tickets, it stole people's credit card numbers; the whole offer was a _____.

traps.why: A giveaway is what the site promised, but it stole instead of giving.
A treat is a pleasant surprise; stealing card numbers is nothing pleasant.
A mistake is accidental; stealing card numbers on purpose is much worse.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast: the promise of free tickets hid a plan that "stole" numbers. A deliberate money trick is the answer.

legacy.hook: A legacy is what you leave behind, like a grandparent's recipes or a school record that stands for years.

traps.why: A legacy comes from the past, so future points the wrong way.
Legend looks similar but means a famous story, not something handed down.
A will is the paper listing who gets things, not the things themselves.

syn1.tip: Think of "leaving a legacy": it is what someone leaves behind for the people who come later.

traps.why: Something brand new is the opposite of something passed down from the past.
That is a legend, a word that only looks like legacy.
Legacies often follow a death, but legacy is what remains, not the farewell.

syn2.tip: A legacy lasts after the person is gone. Pick the choice about something passed from one generation to the next.

traps.why: Regret is a sad feeling, but this sentence praises what she left behind.
A salary is pay while working, not what lasts after her career.
A failure is the opposite of something beloved and lasting.

sc1.tip: "Thousands of students who went on to share her love of learning" is what she left behind that keeps going. That is her legacy.

sc2.sentence: Because the inventor's company kept making her safety helmets for decades after she retired, her _____ protected millions of bike riders she never met.

traps.why: Retirement is when she stopped working; what kept protecting riders is what she left.
A prediction looks ahead; the helmets are something left behind from her work.
Legend looks like legacy but means a story, and a story cannot protect riders.

sc2.tip: "Kept making her safety helmets for decades after she retired" shows something lasting that she left. Choose the word for what a person leaves behind.

heritage.hook: Your heritage is what your family hands down: the foods, songs, and stories from where your ancestors came from.

traps.why: A trend is new and passes quickly; heritage is old and lasting.
An heirloom is one object passed down; heritage is a whole culture.
Nationality is which country you legally belong to, not your customs.

syn1.tip: Heritage looks like "inherit": it is what you inherit from your family's past, such as customs and celebrations.

traps.why: Recent ideas are the opposite of customs kept for generations.
A will passes on money, but heritage means customs and culture.
A birthplace is one spot; heritage is the whole culture of your ancestors.

syn2.tip: Think of "Heritage Month," which honors the foods, music, and customs a group has kept for generations.

traps.why: A vacation is a short trip, but recipes and dances come from family tradition.
Recipes might suggest a restaurant, but these are her grandmother's, passed down.
A passport is a travel document, not recipes and dances handed down.

sc1.tip: The examples "grandmother's recipes," "folk festival," and "old photographs" are all things handed down in a family. That points to heritage.

sc2.sentence: Although Marco was born in Ohio and had never visited Italy, he treasured his Italian _____, from his great-grandfather's pasta recipe to the songs his family sang at holidays.

traps.why: Marco was born in Ohio, so Italy is not his birthplace.
He never visited Italy, so it cannot be an Italian vacation.
A fashion changes quickly; a great-grandfather's recipe has lasted generations.

sc2.tip: "Although... never visited Italy" tells you the Italian part of him comes from family. The "recipe" and "songs" are handed down.

prominent.hook: Something prominent sticks out, like a famous face on a magazine cover or a tall tower everyone can see.

traps.why: Unknown is the opposite of prominent, which means well known.
Promising means likely to succeed later; prominent means already well known.
Famous people may be rich, but prominent is about importance, not money.

syn1.tip: Prominent people stand out and get noticed. Think of "a prominent leader" whom everyone recognizes.

traps.why: Barely noticed is the opposite of standing out and being well known.
Prominent means widely known and important, much more than slightly popular.
Prominent people may feel proud, but the word means others know them.

syn2.tip: Prominent describes something that stands out so everyone sees it, like "a prominent nose." A prominent person stands out in public life.

traps.why: Discoveries in textbooks worldwide mean she is the opposite of unknown.
An amateur does science as a hobby; worldwide textbook fame shows a top expert.
Careless is negative, but the sentence praises her worldwide discoveries.

sc1.tip: The clue "discoveries appeared in textbooks worldwide" tells you everyone knows her work. Choose the word for important and well known.

sc2.sentence: Because the mayor had led the town for twenty years and appeared on the news almost every week, she was one of the most _____ people in the state.

traps.why: Private people stay out of view; she was on the news every week.
Promising fits someone just starting; she has already led for twenty years.
Being on the news makes you known, not rich.

sc2.tip: "Appeared on the news almost every week" is the cause; the effect is that many people know her. Choose the word meaning well known.

foster.hook: To foster is to help something grow, the way a foster family cares for a child or a gardener tends seedlings.

traps.why: Discourage is the opposite: it holds growth back instead of helping it.
Foster children may be adopted, but here foster means help something grow.
Force pushes hard; foster gently helps something grow over time.

syn1.tip: Picture a foster parent caring for a child so the child can thrive. To foster anything is to nurture it and help it grow.

traps.why: Hold back is the opposite of helping something grow.
Foster sounds like faster, but it has nothing to do with speed.
A helper may watch closely, but foster means actively helping something grow.

syn2.tip: Foster is a gentle, positive word. In "foster a love of reading," it means help that love grow over time.

traps.why: Prevent is the opposite of what a fun hands-on exhibit is built to do.
Measuring checks how much kids like science; the exhibit is built to grow it.
You cannot demand a love; the hands-on exhibit gently grows it.

sc1.tip: The museum "built a hands-on exhibit" so kids could enjoy science. That purpose shows they want the love of science to grow.

sc2.sentence: Strict rules and constant tests can crush a child's curiosity, but a patient teacher who welcomes every question will _____ it instead.

traps.why: Squash means the same as crush, but "but" signals the teacher does the opposite.
Ignoring curiosity does nothing; welcoming questions actively helps it grow.
Punish is harsh; a patient, welcoming teacher helps curiosity grow.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "crush" with what a "patient teacher who welcomes every question" does. You need the opposite of crush: help it grow.

desperate.hook: Desperate is how you feel when hope is nearly gone, like a goalie diving wildly to stop a last-second shot.

traps.why: Confident people feel sure of success, the opposite of desperate.
Separate sounds similar, but it means apart, not hopeless.
Annoyed is mild; desperate means nearly out of hope.

syn1.tip: Desperate is related to "despair," which means losing hope. Think of "desperate times," when people feel hopeless and will try anything.

traps.why: Calm and patient is the opposite of a desperate, frantic person.
Slightly worried is far too weak; desperate people have nearly lost hope.
Eagerness is happy excitement; desperation comes from fear and hopelessness.

syn2.tip: A desperate person has run out of good options, so they grab at any chance. Think of "a desperate attempt."

traps.why: Cautious people avoid risk, but these sailors would try any risky plan.
Being stranded might be boring, but bored people don't risk anything to escape.
Cheerful is happy, but starving sailors willing to risk anything are not.

sc1.tip: "No food left" and "willing to try any plan, no matter how risky" show they had lost hope and would do anything.

sc2.sentence: At first Jamal calmly searched his room for his lost phone, but after an hour with no luck he became _____, tearing apart drawers and digging through the trash.

traps.why: Patient describes how he started; "but" shows he changed.
Curious people explore for fun; tearing through the trash shows panic.
Playful is lighthearted, but tearing apart drawers shows panic.

sc2.tip: "At first... calmly" contrasts with "but after an hour." "Tearing apart drawers" shows he is frantic and ready to try anything.

dynamic.hook: Dynamic shares a Greek root with dynamite: picture a coach so full of energy she seems ready to burst with ideas.

traps.why: Dull is the opposite of dynamic, which means full of energy.
Dynamic shares a root with dynamite, but it doesn't mean likely to blow up.
Energetic people may be loud, but dynamic is about energy, not noise.

syn1.tip: Dynamic is a positive word for people full of energy and fresh ideas. Think of "a dynamic duo" who make exciting things happen.

traps.why: Tired is the opposite of dynamic and full of energy.
Hyper suggests jumpy, too much energy; dynamic is positive, focused energy.
Dynamic people bring new ideas, but modern just means recent.

syn2.tip: Imagine the opposite of a boring, sleepy speaker. Dynamic describes someone who brings action and excitement to a room.

traps.why: "Unlike the dull speaker" means she was the opposite of boring.
Nervous speakers don't stride confidently or get crowds cheering.
Strict suggests sternness, but she told lively stories that made people cheer.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the dull speaker" signals a contrast, and "striding," "lively stories," and "cheer" show she was full of energy.

sc2.sentence: Because the new art teacher was so _____, always bursting with fresh project ideas and bouncing between tables, even students who hated drawing started looking forward to class.

traps.why: Gloomy is the opposite of a teacher bursting with ideas and bouncing around.
Art class can be messy, but the clue is about energy and ideas.
Dynamic shares dynamite's root, but an explosive temper would scare students away.

sc2.tip: "Bursting with fresh project ideas" and "bouncing between tables" describe someone full of energy. That energy is why students began looking forward to class.

controversy.hook: Controversy starts with contra, meaning "against": picture a town split in two, each side arguing against the other.

traps.why: Agreement is the opposite of controversy, where people argue.
Conversation looks similar, but a chat is friendly, not a heated public argument.
A riot is violent disorder, much stronger than a public argument.

syn1.tip: Contro- comes from contra, meaning "against." A controversy is when people line up against each other on a question.

traps.why: Peaceful harmony is the opposite of people arguing in public.
Rumors spread around, but controversy means people argue over an issue.
A complaint is one person's gripe; a controversy divides many people.

syn2.tip: Think of a news story that "stirs up controversy." Many people take sides and argue openly.

traps.why: Celebrations are happy; residents arguing loudly is not.
Residents arguing loudly shows the opposite of agreement.
Heated here means angry, not hot weather, and a drought involves no arguing.

sc1.tip: "Residents arguing loudly at every council meeting" shows many people publicly disagreeing. "Heated" here means angry, which fits a big argument.

sc2.sentence: Most new school rules pass quietly, but the ban on phones at lunch sparked a _____ that filled the newspaper with angry letters for weeks.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with rules that pass quietly, so silence is the opposite.
Sparked here means started; angry letters show an argument, not a fire.
A celebration is happy, but the letters were angry.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with rules that "pass quietly," and "angry letters for weeks" shows many people arguing in public.

diverse.hook: A diverse garden has roses, cacti, and sunflowers side by side: lots of different kinds in one place.

traps.why: Identical means all the same, the opposite of diverse.
Divided means split apart; diverse means made of many different kinds.
A crowd can be large without having different kinds in it.

syn1.tip: Think of "diversity" in a school: many backgrounds together. Diverse things differ from each other.

traps.why: All the same is the opposite of diverse.
Size isn't the point; even a small group can be diverse.
That is reverse, which only looks like diverse.

syn2.tip: Diverse is close to "different." A diverse menu offers many different dishes, not just one kind.

traps.why: Uniform means all alike, but the members range widely in age and birthplace.
Chess clubs can be competitive, but the examples show variety, not rivalry.
Chess players may be quiet, but the clue lists many different kinds of members.

sc1.tip: "Ranging from sixth graders to teachers" and "from Brazil to Korea" are examples of very different members. That variety is the clue.

sc2.sentence: Ten years ago every student in our small town had the same background, but today the school is far more _____, with families from twelve different countries.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with "the same background," so similar is backward.
Families from twelve countries show the school is connected to the world, not isolated.
Boring is negative; the sentence describes a school with many backgrounds.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "the same background" with today. "Families from twelve different countries" shows the school now has great variety.

integrity.hook: Integrity comes from the same root as integer, a whole number: a person of integrity is whole and honest everywhere.

traps.why: Deceit means lying and tricking, the opposite of integrity.
Intelligence looks similar but means being smart, not being honest.
Polite people have good manners, but integrity means honest and principled.

syn1.tip: Integrity is a positive word for character. Think of "a person of integrity" who does the right thing even when no one is watching.

traps.why: Sneaky habits are the opposite of honest, principled behavior.
Manners are about politeness; integrity is about honesty and doing right.
Stubbornness is negative; integrity is sticking to what is right.

syn2.tip: People with integrity stick to their principles. You can hear it in "she has too much integrity to cheat."

traps.why: Greed would mean keeping the money; she gave it back.
Intelligence looks like integrity, but returning money shows honesty, not smarts.
"Right away" is about timing, but returning money no one would miss shows honesty.

sc1.tip: "Even though no one would have known" is the key. Doing the honest thing when you could get away with it shows integrity.

sc2.sentence: Several players on the other team cheated to win, but our captain refused to bend the rules, and her _____ earned her respect from both teams.

traps.why: Trickery is what the cheaters used; the captain refused to bend rules.
Stubbornness is negative, but refusing to cheat earned her respect.
Jealousy might come from losing, but it wouldn't earn respect from both teams.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cheaters with the captain who "refused to bend the rules." Sticking to what is right is integrity.

wily.hook: Think of Wile E. Coyote, whose name plays on wily, always scheming tricky plans to catch the Road Runner.

traps.why: Honest is the opposite of wily, which means clever with tricks.
Wild looks like wily but means untamed, not tricky.
Wise is clever in a good way; wily cleverness is sneaky.

syn1.tip: Wily is about tricks. Picture a fox in a story who fools everyone with a sneaky plan.

traps.why: Innocent people don't scheme, so innocent is the opposite of wily.
Wiry looks like wily but means thin and strong.
Gifted praises talent; wily points to sneaky tricks.

syn2.tip: Wily things outsmart others with tricks, so think of a word meaning sneaky and clever, like a fox's plan.

traps.why: A gullible rabbit gets fooled; this rabbit did the fooling.
Rabbits are fast, but this one won by a trick, not speed.
Willing looks like wily but means ready to help, not tricky.

sc1.tip: The rabbit "outsmarted" the fox "by tricking him." You need a word meaning clever and tricky.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his honest older brother, who always admitted his mistakes, Jake was _____ enough to blame the broken lamp on the cat and get away with it.

traps.why: Truthful matches the brother, but the sentence contrasts Jake with him.
Clumsiness might break a lamp, but blaming the cat takes trickery.
Brave is positive; sneakily blaming the cat is not brave.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his honest older brother" signals contrast, and blaming the cat and "getting away with it" shows tricky cleverness.

rancid.hook: Sniff milk left out on the counter for a week: that sour, nasty stink is rancid.

traps.why: Fresh is the opposite of rancid.
Rapid looks a bit like rancid but means fast.
Frozen is about storing food, but rancid means it has gone bad.

syn1.tip: Rancid is almost always used about food, like butter or oil, that has gone bad and smells sour.

traps.why: Wholesome food is good for you, the opposite of rancid.
Random starts like rancid but means without a pattern.
Spicy describes taste, but rancid means spoiled, not hot.

syn2.tip: If you pictured food in a trash can, you were close. Rancid food has turned bad and stinks.

traps.why: Pure oil wouldn't give off a sour, nasty smell.
Oil is often golden, but color doesn't explain a nasty smell.
Sweet is pleasant, but the smell is sour and nasty.

sc1.tip: "Sat open in the hot garage for a year" causes the "sour, nasty smell." The word must mean spoiled.

sc2.sentence: Although the cheese looked perfectly fine on the outside, one sniff told Mom it was _____, so she threw the whole block into the trash.

traps.why: Fresh fits how it looked, but "although" means the sniff said otherwise.
Delicious food doesn't get thrown into the trash.
Melted cheese can still be eaten; the sniff showed it had spoiled.

sc2.tip: "Although" it looked fine, "one sniff" and throwing it "into the trash" show it smelled spoiled.

obliterate.hook: It comes from Latin for striking out letters: picture a giant eraser wiping a page until nothing is left.

traps.why: Create means make something, the opposite of obliterate.
Oblige looks like obliterate but means do someone a favor.
Damage is too weak; obliterate means destroy completely.

syn1.tip: Obliterate means wipe out completely. Picture a storm leaving nothing behind, not just a few dents.

traps.why: Building up is the opposite of wiping out.
A slight dent is far too weak; obliterate leaves nothing.
Obliterate has letters like litter, but it means wipe out.

syn2.tip: Think of a rocket that obliterates a target: afterward, nothing is left. That is wiping something out.

traps.why: The tide left no trace, so it destroyed rather than built.
Dampening is too weak; the castles left no trace at all.
Water surrounds sandcastles, but surrounding them wouldn't leave no trace.

sc1.tip: "Leaving no trace of the morning's work" tells you every sandcastle was destroyed completely.

sc2.sentence: Lena thought the rain would only smudge her chalk mural a little, but the downpour went on to _____ it completely, washing every color down the drain.

traps.why: Brighten is positive, but the colors washed down the drain.
