Dampen is too weak for washing every color away.
Preserve means keep safe, the opposite of destroying the mural.

sc2.tip: "Only smudge... a little, but" signals contrast. "Completely" and "washing every color down the drain" mean total destruction.

allot.hook: Inside allot is lot, an old word for a share, so to allot is to hand out shares.

traps.why: Withhold means keep back, the opposite of giving out shares.
Allow looks like allot but means let something happen.
Earning is getting something; allotting is handing it out.

syn1.tip: Find "lot" inside allot. A lot is a share, so to allot is to give each one its share.

traps.why: Taking back is the opposite of handing out shares.
Dividing shares can involve math, but allot means give them out.
Let happen means allow, which only looks like allot.

syn2.tip: When you allot something, you deal it out in portions, the way a teacher hands out minutes or supplies.

traps.why: Deny means refuse to give, but each group gets five minutes.
You can lose time, but Mr. Lee is planning how to share it.
Selling involves payment; Mr. Lee is simply dividing up time.

sc1.tip: "Only thirty minutes" and "exactly five minutes to each of the six groups" show him dividing time into shares.

sc2.sentence: The art club had only twenty paintbrushes, so Ms. Ortiz had to _____ them carefully, giving exactly two to each table so that no group ran short.

traps.why: Hoarding means keeping them all, but she gave two to each table.
Brushes need cleaning, but the sentence is about giving them out.
Alter starts like allot but means change.

sc2.tip: The phrase after the blank, "giving exactly two to each table," restates the missing word. It means handing out shares.

flounder.hook: Picture a fish flopping helplessly on a dock: that is how a nervous speaker looks when they flounder.

traps.why: Excel means do very well, the opposite of flounder.
A flounder is a fish, but the verb means struggle clumsily.
Float looks a bit like flounder but means rest on water.

syn1.tip: Think of a fish out of water, flopping around helplessly. A person who flounders is struggling and confused.

traps.why: Thrive means do well, the opposite of flounder.
Flourish looks like flounder but means grow and succeed.
Pausing is too mild; floundering is clumsy, confused struggling.

syn2.tip: If someone flounders in a speech, they stumble and lose their way. It's a clumsy, confused kind of struggle.

traps.why: Stammering and flipping pages show stress, not relaxing.
Flourish looks like flounder but means succeed, which Diego did not.
Boasting is confident; Diego was stammering because he wasn't ready.

sc1.tip: "Stammering and flipping through pages" and "had not read the chapter" show he was struggling in confusion.

sc2.sentence: Maya glided smoothly across the ice, but her little brother, wearing skates for the first time, could only _____ and grab the wall to stay upright.

traps.why: Glide describes Maya, but "but" shows her brother did the opposite.
Skaters spin, but a beginner grabbing the wall is struggling.
Wander rhymes with flounder but means roam around.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts him with Maya, who "glided smoothly." Grabbing the wall "to stay upright" shows clumsy struggling.

vagabond.hook: The vag in vagabond comes from a Latin word for wandering, the same root found in vague.

traps.why: A resident lives in one place, the opposite of a vagabond.
Tourists travel, but they have homes to return to.
A villain is wicked; a vagabond is simply homeless and wandering.

syn1.tip: Vagabond starts like vague, from a Latin word for wandering. Picture someone drifting town to town with no home.

traps.why: A settler stays put, the opposite of a vagabond.
Vandal starts like vagabond but means someone who damages property.
Hikers walk far, but they have homes; vagabonds don't.

syn2.tip: Vagabonds drift from place to place with no home, so drifter fits. Settlers do the opposite.

traps.why: A landlord owns property; this person had no home at all.
Vandal looks like vagabond, but nothing here is destroyed.
Merchants trade, but they have jobs, and this person had none.

sc1.tip: "No home and no job" plus "drifted from village to village" describe someone who wanders without a home.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his cousins, who had lived in the same house their whole lives, Uncle Ray had been a _____ in his youth, sleeping in barns and hitchhiking across the country.

traps.why: A homebody stays home, like the cousins, not Uncle Ray.
Farmers have barns, but they don't hitchhike around the country.
Champion is praise for winning, which has nothing to do with wandering.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his cousins" who stayed in "the same house" signals contrast. Sleeping in barns and hitchhiking show a homeless wanderer.

decrepit.hook: Decrepit comes from a Latin word for creaking: picture a creaky old shack with a sagging roof.

traps.why: Brand-new is the opposite of decrepit.
Decent starts like decrepit but means good enough.
Old places can be dirty, but decrepit means falling apart.

syn1.tip: Decrepit things are falling apart from age. Think of a creaky old barn or a car held together with tape.

traps.why: Freshly painted means cared for, the opposite of decrepit.
A little dust is far too mild; decrepit means breaking down.
An old house might be small, but decrepit is about condition.

syn2.tip: Something decrepit is so old and worn that it is breaking down, like rotten stairs or a sagging roof.

traps.why: A sturdy house wouldn't have rotten stairs and a sagging roof.
Charming is positive, but every detail here is broken or rotten.
Spacious describes size, but the clues describe bad condition.

sc1.tip: The examples "sagging roof," "broken windows," and "stairs so rotten" all show a house in terrible condition.

sc2.sentence: The neighbors had replaced their old bikes with sleek new ones, but Sam still rode his _____ bicycle with its rusty chain and wobbly, bent front wheel.

traps.why: Shiny fits the neighbors' bikes, but "but" shows Sam's is different.
Bikes can be speedy, but a bent wheel and rusty chain aren't.
Decent looks like decrepit, but a bent, rusty bike isn't decent.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Sam's bike with the "sleek new ones," and the "rusty chain" and "bent front wheel" show it is worn-out.

haphazard.hook: Hap means luck, as in happen and mishap, so haphazard means left to luck with no plan.

traps.why: Orderly means neatly arranged, the opposite of haphazard.
Haphazard contains hazard, but it means random, not dangerous.
Happy starts like haphazard but is about feelings.

syn1.tip: Think of a haphazard pile of shoes by the door: tossed anywhere, with no plan or order.

traps.why: Carefully arranged is the opposite of haphazard.
Hazard is inside the word, but haphazard means unplanned, not dangerous.
Haphazard starts like happy, but it has nothing to do with mood.

syn2.tip: Haphazard things happen by chance, with no planning, like books tossed anywhere on a shelf.

traps.why: Careful fits if you miss "instead of," but they skipped sorting.
Hazard is in the word, but the books weren't dangerous, just disordered.
Helpful is positive, but finding titles took ages.

sc1.tip: "Instead of sorting" signals contrast, and "finding any title took ages" shows they were shelved with no order at all.

sc2.sentence: Because the class planned the field trip in a rush, the schedule was _____: buses arrived late, lunch was forgotten, and nobody knew which group went where.

traps.why: Organized is the opposite; late buses and forgotten lunch show disorder.
Exciting is positive, but every detail shows a mess.
Field trips cost money, but the clues are about poor planning.

sc2.tip: "Planned... in a rush" causes the mess that follows: late buses, forgotten lunch, confused groups. The schedule had no real order.

amass.hook: Amass hides the word mass: you keep gathering until you have a huge mass of something.

traps.why: Scatter means spread out, the opposite of amass.
Amaze sounds like amass but means surprise greatly.
You might count a collection, but amass means gather it.

syn1.tip: Look inside amass and you'll find mass, a big heap. To amass is to collect until the pile is large.

traps.why: Giving away is the opposite of piling up.
Collectors may show off, but amass means gather a lot.
Picking up one thing is too small; amass means gather a large amount.

syn2.tip: People amass fortunes, collections, or points. The idea is gathering more and more until there is a heap.

traps.why: Spending is the opposite of what saving does.
Borrowing is about money too, but Keisha saved her own.
Donating is kind, but saving builds money up rather than giving it.

sc1.tip: "Saving a little from every birthday and allowance" over years causes a big pile of money, so the word means gather up.

sc2.sentence: Most kids lose interest in rock hunting after a week, but Theo kept going for years and managed to _____ more than five hundred stones from beaches and riverbanks.

traps.why: Scatter means spread out, the opposite of building a big pile.
Rock hunters polish stones, but the clue is about gathering for years.
Theo kept going, so he gained stones instead of losing them.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Theo with kids who quit, and "kept going for years" shows him gathering a large pile.

reclusive.hook: A recluse shuts the door on the world; the word comes from Latin for shut away.

traps.why: Sociable means enjoying company, the opposite of reclusive.
Exclusive looks like reclusive but means open to only a few.
Reclusive people avoid others, but that doesn't make them rude.

syn1.tip: A recluse hides away from people. Think "closed off": reclusive people keep to themselves and live alone.

traps.why: Seeking company is the opposite of avoiding people.
Re- can mean again, but reclusive means shut away from people.
Reclusive people want to be alone; they aren't necessarily unfriendly.

syn2.tip: Reclusive people withdraw from others and stay hidden away, like a hermit in a cabin.

traps.why: An outgoing artist wouldn't refuse every interview for twenty years.
Exclusive looks like reclusive but describes a club, not a hermit.
An island sounds adventurous, but the clues show avoiding people.

sc1.tip: "Lived alone," "refused every interview," and no public event "in over twenty years" all show someone who avoids people.

sc2.sentence: Her twin brother loved crowded parties and chatted with everyone, but Nora was so _____ that she spent weekends alone in her room with a book.

traps.why: Talkative describes her brother, but "but" shows Nora is different.
Popular people have friends around; Nora chose to be alone.
Generous is kind, but it doesn't explain spending weekends alone.

sc2.tip: "But" sets Nora against a brother who "loved crowded parties." Spending weekends "alone" shows she avoids people.

discern.hook: To discern is to pick something out with effort, like spotting your friend's face in a crowded, noisy hallway.

traps.why: Ignore means to pay no attention, the opposite of noticing.
Discard starts like discern but means to throw away.
Searching is looking for something; discern means actually noticing it.

syn1.tip: Discern is about noticing. If you can barely discern a lighthouse in fog, you can just detect it.

traps.why: Mixing things up is the opposite of telling them apart.
Discern sounds like concern, which means worry about.
Looking for something is the search; discern means spotting the difference.

syn2.tip: Think of a discerning shopper who can tell a real brand from a fake. Discern means to see the difference.

traps.why: Overlook means to miss something, the opposite of what the expert does.
Disguise looks similar, but the expert is finding differences, not hiding them.
Copying goes with paintings, but the expert is noticing differences, not making them.

sc1.tip: The clue is "so alike that only an expert could." Only a trained eye notices differences that tiny, so you need a noticing word.

sc2.sentence: Through my scratched old glasses, I could barely _____ the words on the board, but with my new pair every letter looks sharp and clear.

traps.why: Ignore means not paying attention; the problem was seeing, not attention.
Discard looks like discern but means throw away, which makes no sense here.
Erasing goes with a board, but glasses help you see, not erase.

sc2.tip: Look at the contrast after "but": with new glasses "every letter looks sharp and clear." So with old glasses you could barely make them out.

frivolous.hook: Frivolous things are fluff: glitter, party hats, and silly jokes when it is time to be serious.

traps.why: Serious is the opposite of frivolous.
Furious looks a bit like frivolous but means very angry.
Frivolous purchases can cost a lot, but frivolous means silly, not costly.

syn1.tip: A frivolous lawsuit might be over a missing french fry. Look for the choice that means not serious.

traps.why: Deeply serious is the opposite of frivolous.
The -ous ending can mean full of, but frivolous isn't about energy.
Silly things may cost money, but frivolous is about mattering little.

syn2.tip: Picture someone asking about snack flavors during a fire drill. The question is frivolous because it has little importance right then.

traps.why: Practical means useful, which is what Mr. Kim wants instead of these items.
Microscopes are scientific; glitter stickers and party hats are not.
Stickers and hats aren't dangerous, just silly, so harmful is far too strong.

sc1.tip: The signal is "rather than." Useful microscopes are set against stickers and party hats, so the blank means silly and unimportant.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa called my plan to buy a light-up hat with my birthday money _____, saying it was a waste spent on something that didn't really matter.

traps.why: Sensible means wise, but Grandpa calls the plan a waste.
Spending on yourself isn't his point; he says the hat didn't matter.
Furious looks a bit like frivolous, but a plan can't be angry.

sc2.tip: After the comma, Grandpa restates his view: "a waste spent on something that didn't really matter." That describes something silly and unimportant.

misconception.hook: Misconception splits into mis, meaning wrong, and conception, meaning idea: a wrong idea, like thinking bats are blind.

traps.why: A fact is true; a misconception is a belief that is wrong.
Deception ends the same way but means tricking someone on purpose.
People may argue about beliefs, but a misconception is simply a wrong one.

syn1.tip: Split it: mis means wrong, and a conception is an idea. A wrong idea is an error in thinking.

traps.why: A proven fact is true, the opposite of a mistaken belief.
Mis means wrong here, not missing.
A lie is told on purpose; a misconception is believed honestly.

syn2.tip: The prefix mis means wrong, as in misspell and misunderstand. A misconception is a belief that turns out to be wrong.

traps.why: Studies prove the belief wrong, so it can't be a fact.
The studies made a discovery, but the popular belief itself was wrong.
Experiments go with studies, but the blank names the wrong belief.

sc1.tip: Look at "but" and "studies show." The popular belief is proven wrong, so the blank names a wrong belief.

sc2.sentence: Many people hold the _____ that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space, a mistaken idea that astronauts have shown to be false.

traps.why: Astronauts showed it is false, so it is not a fact.
Proof shows something is true; this idea was shown false.
A deception is a trick played on purpose; nobody is tricking anyone here.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank right after the comma: "a mistaken idea that astronauts have shown to be false." That is a wrong belief.

ferocious.hook: Ferocious and fierce both come from a Latin word for wild: picture a lion roaring with its claws out.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of ferocious.
A ferocious animal may frighten you, but it isn't frightened itself.
Grumpy is only mildly cross, far too weak for ferocious.

syn1.tip: Ferocious sounds a bit like fierce, and they share a root. Think of a ferocious dog snarling behind a fence.

traps.why: Tame means gentle and calm, the opposite of ferocious.
Ferocious predators may be hungry, but ferocious means fierce and wild.
Precious rhymes with ferocious but means very valuable.

syn2.tip: The -ous ending means full of, and the start links to fierce. Something full of fierceness is savage.

traps.why: Calm fits "usually gentle," but the river changed and began tearing out trees.
Heavy rain makes rivers deeper, and shallow water can't tear out trees.
Choppy water is a little rough; tearing out trees needs something much fiercer.

sc1.tip: "Usually gentle" sets up a change, and "roaring" water "tearing whole trees" shows how wild it became. You need a word for extremely fierce.

sc2.sentence: The storm was so _____ that its winds knocked down power lines across town and kept everyone indoors for two days.

traps.why: A mild storm wouldn't knock down power lines.
Brief is about time, and this storm kept people inside for days.
Breezy means gently windy, far too weak to knock down power lines.

sc2.tip: The words "so" and "that" show cause and effect. A storm that knocks down power lines must be extremely fierce.

prolong.hook: Prolong has long right inside it: to prolong a visit is to make it last longer.

traps.why: Shorten is the opposite of prolong.
Belong rhymes with prolong but means to be part of something.
Postpone means move to a later time, not make something last longer.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: prolong contains long. To prolong something is to make it longer, or extend it.

traps.why: Cutting something short is the opposite of prolonging it.
Putting something off delays its start; prolong makes it last longer.
Prolong contains long, but it has nothing to do with wishing.

syn2.tip: Think of a referee who prolongs a game with extra time. The game lasts longer than planned.

traps.why: Staying three more nights makes the visit longer, not shorter.
They are already visiting; staying longer doesn't push the visit later.
Repeating means coming back another time; they want to stay longer now.

sc1.tip: The family asks to "stay three more nights." Staying more nights makes the visit last longer, so the blank means make longer.

sc2.sentence: Most of us wanted the boring assembly to end quickly, but the speaker seemed determined to _____ it with one long story after another.

traps.why: Long stories make the assembly longer, not shorter.
Telling one long story after another is the opposite of hurrying.
Speakers describe things, but the stories made the assembly last longer.

sc2.tip: "But" sets the speaker against students who wanted it "to end quickly." With "one long story after another," he makes it last longer.

aptitude.hook: Aptitude starts with apt, as in apt to learn: an aptitude for drawing means it comes naturally to you.

traps.why: A weakness is something you're bad at, the opposite of aptitude.
Attitude looks like aptitude but means how you feel about something.
You can be interested in something without being naturally good at it.

syn1.tip: Aptitude tests measure what you're naturally good at. If you have an aptitude for math, you have a talent for it.

traps.why: Total inability is the opposite of aptitude.
Altitude looks like aptitude but means height above the ground.
Hard work is effort you put in; aptitude is ability you have naturally.

syn2.tip: Hear "apt" at the start, as in "apt to learn quickly." An aptitude is an ability that comes naturally.

traps.why: Playing songs on his own shows a gift for music, not a dislike.
Attitude looks like aptitude, but the clue is about natural ability.
Nobody had taught him, so he didn't have a teacher.

sc1.tip: He played songs "before anyone had taught him a single note." Doing something with no lessons shows a natural ability.

sc2.sentence: Although my brother practiced soccer every single day, he never showed much _____ for it, while his little sister scored three goals in her very first game.

traps.why: Practicing every day shows effort; what he lacked was natural ability.
The sentence says he lacked something good his sister had, not weakness.
Altitude looks like aptitude but means height, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets daily practice against the result, and his sister scores in "her very first game." The blank is the natural ability he lacked.

deprive.hook: To deprive someone is to take away what they need, like a power outage depriving a whole town of light.

traps.why: Provide means to give, the opposite of deprive.
Derive looks like deprive but means to get something from a source.
Taking things away can be a punishment, but deprive just means withhold.

syn1.tip: You've heard of sleep deprivation, when people don't get the sleep they need. To deprive is to deny someone something.

traps.why: Giving back is the opposite of taking away.
Deprive contains priv like private, but it doesn't mean keep secret.
Losing something can make you sad, but deprive means taking it away.

syn2.tip: Think of a phone being taken as punishment. Your parents deprive you of it, which means they take it away from you.

traps.why: Reminding brings something to mind; the lot would actually take the park away.
Relieve means freeing someone from a burden, but losing a park is bad.
Informing just tells them something; the children would lose their park.

sc1.tip: The lot leaves children with "nowhere safe to play." Something is taken from them, so the blank means take away.

sc2.sentence: The long drought would _____ the farm's thirsty crops of water, taking away the one thing they needed most to grow.

traps.why: Relieve sounds like freeing them of a burden, but water helps crops.
A drought can't remind crops of anything; it takes their water.
To assure crops of water would promise it, the reverse of taking it.

sc2.tip: The words after the comma restate the blank: "taking away the one thing they needed most." That is what the missing word means.

ornate.hook: Ornate and ornament are related: picture a frame so covered in carved ornaments that hardly any plain wood shows.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite of ornate.
Old buildings are often ornate, but ornate is about decoration, not age.
Tasteless is an insult; ornate just describes lots of decoration.

syn1.tip: Ornate is related to ornament, like the decorations you hang on a tree. Something ornate is fancy and covered in decoration.

traps.why: Simply designed is the opposite of ornate.
Fresh paint can look nice, but ornate means full of fancy detail.
Ornate things can cost a lot, but ornate is about decoration.

syn2.tip: Think of ornaments covering every branch of a holiday tree. Ornate describes something richly decorated with detail.

traps.why: The theater is unlike the plain buildings, so it can't be simple.
The theater is old, but the clue lists decorations, not damage.
Theaters can be big, but angels and gold trim describe decoration, not size.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the plain modern buildings" signals a contrast, and the angels, swirls, and gold trim describe heavy decoration. The blank means fancy and detailed.

sc2.sentence: The jewelry box was so _____ that it took the woodcarver three months to finish all the tiny flowers, vines, and birds on its lid.

traps.why: A plain box wouldn't have tiny flowers, vines, and birds.
Weight doesn't explain months of carving tiny details.
The woodcarver is still making it, so it can't be ancient.

sc2.tip: "So _____ that it took three months" shows cause and effect. Months of carving "tiny flowers, vines, and birds" means it was full of fancy detail.

finesse.hook: Finesse shares its start with fine: picture a cake decorator shaping sugar petals with a light, graceful, sure touch.

traps.why: Clumsiness is the opposite of finesse.
Fitness looks and sounds like finesse but means being physically healthy.
Skilled people may work fast, but finesse is about grace, not speed.

syn1.tip: Finesse comes from the French word for fine. Doing something with finesse means doing it with fine, graceful skill.

traps.why: Awkward fumbling is the opposite of finesse.
Finesse looks like finish, but it has nothing to do with ending.
Planning happens beforehand; finesse is the graceful skill shown while doing something.

syn2.tip: Picture a dancer or chef with a light, sure touch. Finesse is not just skill, but skill with grace and delicacy.

traps.why: Clumsy work wouldn't make the flowers look delicate and real.
Working fast doesn't make sugar flowers look delicate and real.
Fitness looks like finesse but means physical health, which doesn't fit here.

sc1.tip: The result is the clue: each flower "looked delicate and real." Work that delicate takes graceful, refined skill.

sc2.sentence: While the younger players just kicked the ball as hard as they could, the team captain dribbled past defenders with _____, gently guiding the ball wherever she wanted.

traps.why: The younger players used force; the captain is gentle and controlled.
She guides the ball wherever she wants, so she isn't awkward.
Anger is the wrong feeling for someone gently guiding the ball.

sc2.tip: "While" contrasts kicking "as hard as they could" with the captain "gently guiding the ball." The blank means gentle, controlled skill.

arduous.hook: Arduous comes from a Latin word meaning steep: picture an exhausting climb up a mountain that takes all day.

traps.why: Easy is the opposite of arduous.
Arduous tasks may be risky, but arduous means hard work, not danger.
Arduous jobs often take long, but arduous is about effort, not time.

syn1.tip: Arduous comes from a Latin word for steep. Think of an arduous climb up a steep hill: it is very difficult.

traps.why: Needing no effort is the opposite of arduous.
Hard tasks can be dangerous, but arduous is about effort.
Arduous looks like ardor, which means passion, but arduous means hard work.

syn2.tip: Arduous tasks make you sweat, like carrying furniture up three flights of stairs. The word means needing great effort.

traps.why: Deep snow and weeks of exhaustion show the trip was anything but effortless.
Thrilling is a happy, exciting word; the clues describe misery and exhaustion.
The trip lasted weeks, and the clue is about effort, not length.

sc1.tip: The semicolon leads to examples: "deep snow, steep trails, and weeks of exhaustion." All that shows the trip took huge effort.

sc2.sentence: My older sister said the science project would be quick and simple, but it turned out to be _____, keeping us up late gluing and measuring for five nights.

traps.why: Easy matches the sister's prediction, but "but" says the opposite happened.
A tiny project wouldn't keep you up late for five nights.
Relaxing is a pleasant word; five late nights of work is exhausting.

sc2.tip: "But" flips the sister's prediction of "quick and simple." Five late nights of gluing and measuring shows the project took great effort.

impasse.hook: An impasse is like a dead-end street: im- means not, so there is no way to pass through.

traps.why: A breakthrough is sudden progress, the opposite of being stuck.
Arguments can cause an impasse, but impasse means the stuck situation itself.
Impact looks similar but means a hit or a strong effect.

syn1.tip: The im- means not, so an impasse is a place you cannot pass. Picture a dead-end street where everything stops.

traps.why: A clear way forward means progress, the opposite of an impasse.
Quarrels may lead to an impasse, but impasse means being stuck.
A pause is short and ends easily; an impasse means no progress at all.

syn2.tip: Talks are said to "reach an impasse." Picture two cars nose to nose on a narrow road, neither able to move.

traps.why: Neither group gave in, so they never reached an agreement.
A compromise means each side gives a little; here neither side did.
Nobody won the room; both groups stayed stuck.

sc1.tip: "Neither... would give up" and "after an hour of arguing" show no side moved, so they were stuck with no progress.

sc2.sentence: The class could not agree on a field trip: half wanted the zoo, half wanted the science museum, and every new vote ended in the same tie, a frustrating _____.

traps.why: A decision would end the tie, but every vote stayed tied.
"Frustrating" shows bad feelings, not a happy celebration.
The trip is the topic, but the class never even chose one.

sc2.tip: "Every new vote ended in the same tie" tells you nothing moved forward. The blank renames that stuck situation.

taunt.hook: Taunt rhymes with haunt: a bully's taunts can haunt you long after the teasing stops.

traps.why: Praise means saying nice things, the opposite of mean teasing.
Haunt rhymes with taunt but means to visit like a ghost.
Bullies may dare people, but taunt means making fun of them.

syn1.tip: Taunting is something bullies do with mean words on the playground. Pick the choice that means making fun of someone.

traps.why: Cheering someone on is kind support, the opposite of taunting.
Joking with friends is friendly; taunting is mean.
Bullies may scare people, but taunting means mocking them.

syn2.tip: Taunting is teasing with a sting. Friendly teasing doesn't count, so look for the choice that is both teasing and mean.

traps.why: Mean mimicking is not a compliment; it is the reverse.
Asking questions isn't mean, and a teacher wouldn't need to stop it.
The kids weren't teaching about accents; they were copying him to be mean.

sc1.tip: "Mimicking the way he spoke until the teacher stepped in" shows mean behavior a teacher must stop, so the blank means tease cruelly.

sc2.sentence: Most fans clapped kindly for Leo even after he missed the final shot, but a few rude ones in the stands began to _____ him about his clumsy throw.

traps.why: Encouraging is what the kind fans did; "but" points to the opposite.
Coaching helps a player improve; rude fans were not trying to help.
Consoling is kind comfort, the wrong feeling for rude fans.

sc2.tip: "But a few rude ones" contrasts with the kind fans, so the blank is something mean, like making fun of him.

chasm.hook: The ch in chasm sounds like k: picture a canyon so deep and wide you would need a bridge to cross.

traps.why: A summit is the top of a mountain, not a deep crack.
Bridges cross chasms, but a bridge is not the gap itself.
Charm starts like chasm but means pleasing appeal.

syn1.tip: Chasm usually comes with "deep" or "wide." Picture a huge crack in the ground, like a canyon you cannot jump across.

traps.why: A high peak rises up; a chasm drops far down.
A rope bridge may cross a chasm, but it isn't the gap.
A dent is tiny; a chasm is huge and deep.

syn2.tip: Chasms are big. Think of the Grand Canyon: a deep, wide opening in the earth, much bigger than a hole or a ditch.

traps.why: A summit is the top, but this place had a bottom far below.
A tunnel goes through a mountain; it doesn't split it open to the sky.
A ditch is shallow, but this bottom was almost too far to see.

sc1.tip: "Split the mountain in two" and a bottom "so far below that they could barely see the river" describe a huge, deep gap.

sc2.sentence: Most of the hiking trail was an easy stroll, but near the end it stopped at a rocky _____ so wide that only a swaying rope bridge could carry hikers across.

traps.why: A hilltop is high ground; you don't need a bridge to cross it.
A ledge is a narrow shelf on a cliff, not a gap to cross.
A pothole is far too small to need a rope bridge.

sc2.tip: Only "a swaying rope bridge" could carry hikers "across," so the blank must be a wide, deep gap in the land.

disarray.hook: An array is a neat arrangement; add dis- and the neat rows fall apart into a jumble.

traps.why: Order means everything is neat, the opposite of disarray.
Dismay looks similar but means a feeling of alarm or worry.
Messy places can be noisy, but disarray is about things being jumbled.

syn1.tip: Spot the parts: dis- means not, and an array is a neat arrangement. Disarray is the state of not being neat.

traps.why: Tidiness means neat and in place, the opposite of disarray.
Display also starts with dis but means a show or exhibit.
Messy things aren't necessarily broken; disarray means mixed up.

syn2.tip: You often hear "in disarray" about a messy room or a team that lost its plan. Pick the choice meaning things are mixed up.

traps.why: Scattered toys and cushions show the room was not in order.
The room may be quiet after the kids leave, but the details describe mess.
Dismay is a feeling, and a living room can't feel anything.

sc1.tip: The colon brings examples: toys "covered the floor," cushions "scattered," crayons "everywhere." Those details describe a very messy state.

sc2.sentence: Our coach expected the team to be ready for the big game, but when the bus broke down and three players got lost, the whole morning fell into _____.

traps.why: "Fell into place" means things worked out, the opposite of this morning.
A routine is normal and expected; this morning was anything but.
"Fall into line" means to obey, but this morning became chaotic.

sc2.tip: "But" signals things went against the coach's plan, and a broken bus plus lost players means everything got chaotic.

brash.hook: Picture a brash rookie strutting into the locker room, bragging loudly before he has played a single game.

traps.why: Modest people don't brag, the opposite of brash.
Brave is boldness praised; brash is boldness that is rude.
Brisk looks similar but means quick and lively.

syn1.tip: Brash people brag and push themselves forward, often rudely. It has a negative feeling, so look for a word for annoying overconfidence.

traps.why: Shy people hold back, the opposite of loud, brash ones.
Confident is a positive word; brash means too confident and rude.
Brutal looks similar but means cruel and violent.

syn2.tip: Brash is boldness gone too far. Plain confidence is fine; brash adds rudeness and bragging, so pick the choice with a negative feel.

traps.why: A humble player would never announce he was the best.
He claimed skill, but the clue is his rude bragging, not ability.
First days can be nerve-racking, but he was boasting, not worried.

sc1.tip: He "announced that he was the best" and told the captain to "hand him the ball" on his "very first day." That's rude overconfidence.

sc2.sentence: Unlike her quiet, polite older sister, Mia was so _____ that she told the principal his new lunch rules were silly and that she could do his job better.

traps.why: Timid people are fearful and wouldn't talk to the principal that way.
Honest is a kind word, but bragging she could do his job is rude.
Lunch is the topic, but hunger doesn't explain bragging about his job.

sc2.tip: "Unlike her quiet, polite older sister" tells you Mia is loud and rude, bragging she could do the principal's job better.

monotonous.hook: Mono means one and tone is sound: a monotonous voice stays on one note until everyone dozes off.

traps.why: Exciting is full of thrills, the opposite of monotonous.
Monstrous looks similar but means huge or horrible.
Mono means one, but monotonous is about sameness, not being alone.

syn1.tip: Mono means one, as in monorail. Monotonous means one tone over and over, so it gets boring.

traps.why: Varied means full of changes, the opposite of monotonous.
A monotonous voice can be loud; the problem is sameness, not volume.
Tone suggests music, but monotonous means boringly the same.

syn2.tip: Something monotonous keeps doing the same thing again and again. Look for the choice about repeating, not about volume or music.

traps.why: Thrilling things keep you awake, but Marco fell asleep.
Long drives can be risky, but the clue is fields that look the same.
Colorful means full of variety, but every mile looked exactly the same.

sc1.tip: "Mile after mile" of fields that "looked exactly the same" and Marco falling asleep point to something boring because it never changes.

sc2.sentence: Jaden loved the first few levels of the video game, but after the hundredth round of jumping over the same barrels, it became _____ and he switched it off.

traps.why: Exciting fits the first levels, but "but" shows his feelings changed.
Games can cost money, but the clue is jumping the same barrels.
Monstrous looks similar but means huge or horrible.

sc2.tip: "But" shows his feelings changed, and "the same barrels" after a "hundredth round" shows the game got boring from repeating.

empathetic.hook: Path means feeling, as in sympathy: an empathetic friend feels your worries right along with you.

traps.why: Uncaring means not caring about others, the opposite of empathetic.
Energetic looks similar but means full of energy.
Polite is about good manners, not sharing someone's feelings.

syn1.tip: Look for path, meaning feeling, inside the word. An empathetic person can feel what someone else feels.

traps.why: Ignoring pain is the opposite of feeling it with someone.
That describes energetic, a word that only looks like empathetic.
Advice is helpful, but empathy means feeling what others feel.

syn2.tip: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else's shoes. Empathetic people feel along with others, so pick the choice about sharing feelings.

traps.why: Knowing how lonely it feels would make her warm, not cold.
Being interested in new kids isn't the same as feeling their loneliness.
Suspicious is a distrustful feeling, the wrong tone for her kindness.

sc1.tip: "Because she knew exactly how lonely the first week could feel" shows she shares new students' feelings from her own moves.

sc2.sentence: My brother usually laughs when I trip, but when I lost my dog, he was surprisingly _____, sitting with me quietly and saying he felt sad too.

traps.why: Amused fits his usual laughing, but "but" shows he changed.
Energetic looks similar, but he was sitting quietly.
Nosy is a negative word, but he was kind and shared your sadness.

sc2.tip: "But" shows a change from his usual laughing, and "saying he felt sad too" tells you he shared your feelings.

ratify.hook: The U.S. Constitution became law only after enough states voted to ratify it, giving their official yes.

traps.why: Reject means to say no, the opposite of ratify.
Ration looks similar but means to hand out in small amounts.
Groups debate before voting, but ratify means the final yes.

syn1.tip: You may have heard that states had to ratify the Constitution. Ratify is what a group does when it votes yes to make something official.

traps.why: Formally rejecting is saying an official no, the opposite of ratify.
Discussion comes before ratifying; ratify is the final approval.
Suggesting is much weaker than giving official approval.

syn2.tip: Ratify sounds official: votes, treaties, signed rules. Pick the choice meaning a group gives its final, formal yes.

traps.why: Rejecting it would stop the code, not let it take effect.
Discussing doesn't make a rule official; only approval does.
The council already wrote and proposed it; the vote makes it official.

sc1.tip: "Could not take effect until" the vote shows the vote is what makes it official, so the blank means formally approve.

sc2.sentence: The team captains agreed on the new practice schedule in the hallway, but it was not final until the coach signed the form to _____ it.

traps.why: Canceling would end the schedule, not make it final.
Ration looks similar but means to hand out in small amounts.
Questioning a plan doesn't make it final; signing gives approval.

sc2.tip: "Not final until the coach signed the form" shows the signature makes the schedule official, so the blank means approve formally.

reproach.hook: A look of reproach is the raised eyebrow a teacher gives that silently says, "I expected better from you."

traps.why: Praise shows approval, the opposite of reproach.
Approach looks similar but means coming closer.
Punishment is a penalty; reproach is only a look or word of disapproval.

syn1.tip: Reproach often comes as "a look of reproach," the disappointed glance that makes you feel guilty. Pick the choice about disapproval.

traps.why: Admiration is approval and respect, the opposite of reproach.
Confusion can show on a face too, but reproach shows disapproval.
Fury is wild anger, much stronger than quiet reproach.

syn2.tip: A look of reproach says "you let me down." It is quiet disappointment, not rage, so choose the calm word for disapproval.

traps.why: Approval wouldn't make a student apologize.
A bored look wouldn't make someone fall silent and apologize.
Amusement is a happy feeling, the wrong tone for a look causing apology.

sc1.tip: The look made the student "fall silent and apologize," so it must show disapproval. People apologize when they feel blamed.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa did not need to scold me for breaking the window; the quiet _____ in his eyes told me how disappointed he was.

traps.why: Pride shows he is pleased, but he was disappointed.
A sparkle is a happy look, the wrong feeling for disappointment.
Approach looks similar but means coming closer.

sc2.tip: "Told me how disappointed he was" restates the blank: the look in his eyes showed disapproval instead of scolding.

impair.hook: You've seen signs for the hearing impaired: impair means to weaken something so it works less well.

traps.why: Improve means make better, the opposite of impair.
Repair rhymes with impair but means to fix.
Destroy is too strong; impair means weaken, not wreck completely.

syn1.tip: You've probably seen "hearing impaired" or "vision impaired." To impair something is to weaken it or make it work less well.

traps.why: Strengthen is the opposite of weakening something.
Impair seems to mean "not a pair," but it means to weaken.
Doctors test hearing, but impair means damage it.

syn2.tip: Impair is not about pairs. Think of "impaired vision": eyes that work, just not fully. Look for the choice meaning make weaker.

traps.why: Sharpening memory would be good, but staying up "was a mistake."
Repair rhymes with impair but means to fix.
Tests measure memory, but lack of sleep damages it.

sc1.tip: "Was a mistake" and "lack of sleep" tell you the effect is bad, so the blank must mean weaken or damage.

sc2.sentence: A cracked helmet may look fine, but even a small break can _____ its ability to absorb a hard fall, leaving your head less protected.

traps.why: Boosting would make it safer, but your head ends up less protected.
Repair rhymes with impair, but a break doesn't fix anything.
A break doesn't prove safety; it leaves your head less protected.

sc2.tip: "But" warns that looking fine isn't the whole story, and "leaving your head less protected" shows the break weakens the helmet.

grueling.hook: Picture a grueling boot camp: hours of push-ups that leave you too tired to lift your arms.

traps.why: Relaxing is the opposite of grueling.
Gruesome looks similar but means horrible or gory, not tiring.
Grueling things are often long, but grueling means draining, not long.

syn1.tip: Think of a grueling workout or a grueling race. The word always describes something that wears you out.

traps.why: Easy and pleasant is the opposite of grueling.
Slightly difficult is far too weak; grueling means extremely demanding.
The word contains gruel, but grueling describes hard, tiring effort.

syn2.tip: Grueling describes something that takes all your energy, like a long race. Look for the choice about being worn out.

traps.why: A leisurely hike would not make the scouts collapse.
Hikes can be scenic, but pretty views don't explain the collapsing.
Gruesome looks similar but means horrible or gory, not tiring.

sc1.tip: The scouts "collapsed in their tents" and "slept until noon." That result tells you the hike wore them out.

sc2.sentence: Coach Ramirez promised an easy warm-up, but practice turned out to be _____, with two hours of sprints that left the whole team gasping on the grass.

traps.why: Relaxing fits the easy warm-up, but "but" signals the opposite happened.
Mild is too weak for two hours of sprints that left players gasping.
Optional is about practice rules, not how tiring it was.

sc2.tip: The word "but" flips "an easy warm-up" around, and "gasping on the grass" shows practice was extremely tiring.

congregate.hook: Con means together and greg comes from the Latin for flock, so people congregate like a flock of sheep.

traps.why: Scatter is the opposite of congregate.
Congratulate looks similar but means to praise someone's success.
A church congregation worships, but congregate just means to gather.

syn1.tip: Con means together, as in connect. People who congregate come together in one spot.

traps.why: Spread apart is the opposite of congregate.
Congregations pray, but congregate means gathering anywhere for any reason.
Crowds may talk loudly, but congregate is about gathering, not noise.

syn2.tip: Think of a congregation, a group that has gathered. The verb congregate means forming that group.

traps.why: Students who scatter would not stand in clusters together.
Whisper is about talking, and the clusters are described as noisy.
Wandering means moving around, not standing together in clusters.

sc1.tip: The students are "standing in noisy clusters" in one place. Forming clusters means they gather together.

sc2.sentence: During class the students sit quietly at separate desks, but at lunch they _____ around the same table, crowding together to share snacks and stories.

traps.why: Scattering is the opposite of crowding together around one table.
Study fits class, but lunch is about sharing snacks and stories.
Nothing in the sentence is about a contest; they are crowding together.

sc2.tip: "But" sets "separate desks" against lunch, and "crowding together" tells you they gather around one table.

noxious.hook: Noxious shares a Latin root meaning harm with obnoxious, so noxious fumes are the kind that hurt you.

traps.why: Healthy is the opposite of noxious.
Anxious rhymes with noxious but means worried.
Noxious gases may be cloudy, but noxious means harmful.

syn1.tip: You often hear about noxious fumes or noxious weeds. Both are things that can hurt you.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite of noxious.
Obnoxious looks similar but means annoying, not poisonous.
Many gases are invisible, but noxious is about harm.

syn2.tip: Noxious fumes from a factory make people sick. Pick the choice that means something can poison you.

traps.why: Harmless gases would not make people dizzy or sick.
Fragrant means pleasant smelling, the wrong feeling for gases that make people sick.
Color doesn't explain why the gases make people sick.

sc1.tip: The gases "can make people dizzy or sick," which is why students need a vent hood. That points to harmful gases.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa used to spray _____ chemicals on his garden, but now he uses only safe, natural sprays that will not hurt the bees or the neighbor's dog.

traps.why: Gentle chemicals would be safe, but "but" shows the old ones weren't.
Cost isn't the contrast; the sentence contrasts harmful with safe.
Organic matches the new natural sprays, not the old ones Grandpa stopped using.

sc2.tip: "But now he uses only safe" sprays that "will not hurt" animals. The old chemicals must be the opposite: harmful.

overbearing.hook: Picture someone looming over you, bearing down and telling you exactly how to do everything: that's overbearing.

traps.why: Meek means quiet and easily led, the opposite of overbearing.
Over and bearing suggest carrying too much, but the word means bossy.
Confident is a positive word; overbearing is negative and means controlling.

syn1.tip: Imagine someone standing over you, pressing their will on you. An overbearing person bosses everyone around.

traps.why: Very relaxed is the opposite of overbearing.
Over and bear hint at a heavy load, but the word means controlling.
Slightly firm is too weak; overbearing people control everything.

syn2.tip: An overbearing parent or coach decides every detail for others. Look for the choice about controlling people.

traps.why: An easygoing person would let others speak and decide.
A timid person would not insist on making every decision.
Organized is positive, but the project went badly because of her.

sc1.tip: She "insisted on making every decision" and "never let the rest of us speak." That describes someone bossy.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his _____ older brother, who orders everyone around and controls the TV remote, Leo lets his friends choose the games and listens to their ideas.

traps.why: A patient brother wouldn't order everyone around.
A shy person doesn't order everyone around.
Being athletic has nothing to do with ordering people around.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets the brother against Leo, who "listens." The brother "orders everyone around," so he is bossy.

interrogate.hook: Picture a detective in a small room firing question after question at a nervous suspect.

traps.why: Answering is the opposite of asking questions.
Interrupt looks similar but means to cut in while someone talks.
Police may accuse suspects, but interrogate means to ask questions.

syn1.tip: You hear interrogate in detective stories: police interrogate a suspect. Notice the word interrogation contains the idea of asking.

traps.why: Ask casually is too weak; interrogating is close, pointed questioning.
Answering is the opposite of interrogating.
Punishment may come later, but interrogate only means questioning.

syn2.tip: Think of an interrogation room on a TV show, where detectives ask question after question. That is the meaning.

traps.why: Ignoring her is the opposite of asking her many questions.
Interrupt looks similar but means cutting in, not questioning.
The list after the colon is questions, not compliments.

sc1.tip: After the colon comes a list: "where exactly," "who would be there," "when she would return." Those are pointed questions.

sc2.sentence: Because Dad wanted to know every detail about the broken window, he began to _____ my little brother, asking what time it happened and who threw the ball.

traps.why: Comfort is kind, but Dad is demanding details, not soothing him.
Punishment might follow, but asking questions is what Dad does here.
Ignoring him is the opposite of asking him questions.

sc2.tip: "Because Dad wanted to know every detail," he starts "asking what time" and "who threw." That is close questioning.

hapless.hook: Hap is an old word for luck, found in happen and perhaps, so hapless means without luck.

traps.why: Fortunate means lucky, the opposite of hapless.
Hap looks like happy, but hapless means without luck.
Hapless people may trip, but hapless is about bad luck, not skill.

syn1.tip: Split it: hap plus less. Hap is an old word for luck, as in happen, so hapless is without luck.

traps.why: Blessed with luck is the opposite of hapless.
Hap is not short for happy; it is an old word for luck.
Hapless people suffer bad luck; it isn't their carelessness.

syn2.tip: The ending less means without, as in hopeless. Hap meant luck, so the word means without luck.

traps.why: Slipping and losing a glove in one minute is not lucky.
Talent is about skill, and the sentence lists only mishaps.
Hap looks like happy, but nothing in this minute is happy.

sc1.tip: Look at the list: he "slipped in the mud, lost his glove," and gave up a goal "all in one minute." That's bad luck.

sc2.sentence: Everyone expected the _____ team to lose again after a season of injuries and bad bounces, but this time the ball finally rolled their way and they won.

traps.why: A season of injuries and bad bounces is not fortunate.
An undefeated team wouldn't be expected to lose again.
Popularity has nothing to do with injuries and bad bounces.

sc2.tip: "Lose again" and "injuries and bad bounces" show bad luck, and "finally rolled their way" confirms luck had been against them.

reprieve.hook: In old movies, a prisoner gets a last-minute reprieve, a call that delays the punishment just in time.

traps.why: A burden weighs you down; a reprieve lifts the weight for a while.
Reprimand looks similar but means a scolding.
A reprieve feels good, but it's a break, not a prize you earned.

syn1.tip: Think of a snow day giving you a reprieve from a test. A reprieve is a welcome pause from something bad.

traps.why: A new punishment is the opposite of a reprieve.
A reprieve is usually temporary; the unpleasant thing often comes back.
Re can mean again, but reprieve doesn't mean another attempt.

syn2.tip: A prisoner's reprieve delays the punishment. Picture a pause before something unpleasant returns.

traps.why: A cool, rainy afternoon is a drop in heat, not an increase.
A forecast predicts weather; the rain actually interrupted the heat.
A rainy afternoon is the opposite of a drought.

sc1.tip: The heat was "interrupted" for "a brief" time "before temperatures climbed again." That is a short break from something unpleasant.

sc2.sentence: The coach had planned laps all afternoon, but a sudden thunderstorm gave the tired team a _____, so they rested inside until the sky cleared and practice resumed.

traps.why: The storm stopped the workout; the team rested instead.
Resting inside is a relief, not a punishment.
Trophies come from winning; the storm only paused practice.

sc2.tip: The storm caused the team to rest, "so they rested inside," and then "practice resumed." That is a short break.

shrill.hook: Think of a teakettle screaming on the stove or a referee's whistle: that thin, ear-stabbing sound is shrill.

traps.why: Muffled means soft and dull, the opposite of shrill.
Thrilling looks like shrill but means exciting.
Booming is a loud sound too, but it's deep, not high.

syn1.tip: Say shrill out loud with a sharp, thin voice. It names a high sound that stabs your ears, like a whistle.

traps.why: Low-pitched is the opposite of shrill.
A sound can be shrill and perfectly in tune.
Shrill is about how high a sound is, not how long it lasts.

syn2.tip: A shrill whistle makes you cover your ears. Look for the choice about how high the sound is.

traps.why: A gentle beep wouldn't make the dog howl and hide.
The beep is "so high," so it can't be deep.
Faint is far too weak for a sound that sends the dog running.

sc1.tip: The beep was "so high and sharp" that the dog "howled and ran under the bed." That describes a piercing sound.

sc2.sentence: Mom's singing voice is usually warm and low, but when she spotted a spider in the bathtub, she let out a _____ scream that rattled the windows.

traps.why: Deep matches her usual voice, but "but" signals a change.
A silent scream could not rattle the windows.
Spotting a spider brings fright, not cheer.

sc2.tip: "Usually warm and low, but" tells you the scream was the opposite of low: a high, sharp sound.

prim.hook: Prim is short and tight, like pursed lips and a buttoned collar on someone who never relaxes the rules.

traps.why: Sloppy is the opposite of prim.
Prime looks similar but means first or best.
Prim people are often pictured as old, but prim is about stiff neatness.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "prim and proper." The two words go together because they mean nearly the same thing.

traps.why: Very easygoing is the opposite of prim.
That is what prime means; prim is a different word.
Slightly tidy is too weak; prim means stiffly proper.

syn2.tip: Picture someone sitting straight with hands folded, frowning at giggles. Prim means stiff and overly proper.

traps.why: A carefree person wouldn't frown at children forgetting please.
A tight bun and straight posture are not sloppy.
She frowns at the children, so cheerful has the wrong feeling.

sc1.tip: She "sat perfectly straight," wore "a tight bun," and "frowned" at forgotten manners. All of that shows stiff properness.

sc2.sentence: At the messy pizza party, my _____ cousin refused to eat with her fingers, using a fork and napkin while everyone else licked sauce off their hands.

traps.why: Sloppy fits the party, but she is the neat one using a fork.
Hunger doesn't explain why she refused to eat with her fingers.
Rowdy means wild; she is the calm, careful one.

sc2.tip: "While everyone else" sets her apart from the messy crowd. A fork and napkin at a pizza party show she is fussily proper.

tirade.hook: Picture a coach pacing the locker room, yelling for ten straight minutes about dropped passes: that's a tirade.

traps.why: Praise is kind words, the opposite of an angry tirade.
Parade rhymes with tirade but means a procession.
An argument has two sides; a tirade is one person's angry speech.

syn1.tip: People "launch into a tirade" or "go on a tirade." Both phrases describe someone ranting angrily for a long time.

traps.why: A gentle reminder is the opposite of a tirade.
Too weak; a tirade is long and furious.
That's a parade, which only rhymes with tirade.

syn2.tip: A tirade goes on and on, full of anger, like a coach yelling about sloppy passing. Look for long and angry.

traps.why: He is angry at the children, not saying sorry.
Parade rhymes with tirade, but he is angrily listing rules.
He might clean later, but here he is "angrily listing" rules.

sc1.tip: He went on for "ten minutes," "angrily listing every rule." A long, angry speech is the answer.

sc2.sentence: Instead of calmly explaining why we were late, Coach Lee launched into a _____, shouting about responsibility until his face turned red and the whole team stared at their shoes.

traps.why: "Instead of calmly explaining" rules out a calm explanation.
A joke is lighthearted, but he is shouting and red-faced.
He is shouting angrily, the opposite of a compliment.

sc2.tip: "Instead of calmly" signals the opposite, and "shouting" until "his face turned red" shows a long, angry speech.

receptive.hook: A receptive mind works like a radio receiver: tuned in and ready to take in new signals.

traps.why: Stubborn is the opposite: a stubborn person refuses new ideas.
A polite person can still reject every idea. Receptive means willing to accept them.
Gullible means too easily fooled, a negative idea. Receptive is a good quality.

syn1.tip: Receptive belongs to the same family as receive. A receptive person is ready to receive ideas, like an open door.

traps.why: Unwilling to change is the opposite of being open to new ideas.
This is about talking. Receptive is about taking in what others say.
Receptive people consider ideas fairly. They don't automatically agree with everything.

syn2.tip: Think of a receptionist who greets and takes in visitors. Receptive people welcome and consider what others offer.

traps.why: Hostile is the opposite. A hostile principal would not adopt student plans.
Obedient means doing whatever you're told. The principal chose to adopt one plan.
Accustomed means used to something. Nothing says she was used to student ideas.

sc1.tip: Look at "listening carefully to every suggestion" and "adopting the plan." Those actions show a principal open to ideas.

sc2.sentence: My grandfather usually grumbles about new gadgets, but when I showed him how video calls work, he was surprisingly _____ and asked me to teach him more.

traps.why: Skeptical fits his usual grumbling, but "but" and "surprisingly" signal a change.
Learning new technology can be confusing, but he eagerly asked to learn more.
Forgetful has nothing to do with welcoming a new idea.

sc2.tip: "Usually grumbles" plus "but" signals a switch, and "asked me to teach him more" shows he welcomed the new idea.

illustrious.hook: Illustrious is related to luster: picture a famous name glowing brightly because of great deeds.

traps.why: Unknown is the opposite. Illustrious people are famous.
Illustrated looks similar but means having pictures.
Notorious means famous for something bad. Illustrious is famous for something great.

syn1.tip: Illustrious sounds like "luster," a bright shine. An illustrious person's name shines with fame earned through great work.

traps.why: Forgotten and ignored is the opposite of famous and admired.
It looks like illustration, but illustrious has nothing to do with pictures.
Famous people may be rich, but illustrious means admired for great achievements.

syn2.tip: Think of "an illustrious career," the kind full of awards and honors. The word carries strong praise.

traps.why: Obscure means little known. Winning two Nobel Prizes made her famous.
Controversial adds argument and doubt. The sentence praises her achievement.
Lucky suggests chance, but Nobel Prizes come from hard-earned achievement.

sc1.tip: After the colon, "the first person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences" describes a career of huge, admired achievement.

sc2.sentence: The violinist had played for presidents and kings for fifty years, so when she visited our small music school, every student lined up to meet the _____ performer.

traps.why: Amateur means not professional. She played for presidents and kings for decades.
Notorious means famous for bad things. Students lined up out of admiration.
Performers can be nervous, but that wouldn't make every student line up.

sc2.tip: Playing "for presidents and kings for fifty years" caused "every student" to line up, so she must be famous and admired.

pious.hook: Pious goes with piety: picture a pilgrim kneeling in prayer at every chapel along a long road.

traps.why: Sinful is the opposite of deeply religious.
Curious ends the same way but means eager to know things.
Ceremonies can be religious, but ceremonial means formal, not deeply faithful.

syn1.tip: Pious is the adjective for "piety," devotion to religion. Picture someone praying often and faithfully.

traps.why: Doubting all religion is the opposite of a pious person's strong faith.
Mildly is too weak. Pious means deeply religious.
You can study religions without believing. Pious is about personal faith.

syn2.tip: Pious people pray, worship, and follow their faith closely. The word is about how strongly someone believes, not what they know.

traps.why: Skeptical means doubting. Doubters would not pray at every church.
Long walks make people weary, but weariness didn't cause the journey.
Money has nothing to do with praying and visiting a holy shrine.

sc1.tip: Walking "hundreds of miles to visit a holy shrine" and "praying at every church" show faith strong enough to drive the journey.

sc2.sentence: Though her older brother rarely thought about religion, Ana was _____, attending services every week and reading her prayer book each night before bed.

traps.why: Indifferent describes her brother. "Though" tells you Ana is different.
Studious is about schoolwork. Her activities are about faith.
Superstitious means believing in luck and omens, a less respectful idea than faith.

sc2.tip: "Though" sets Ana against a brother who "rarely thought about religion," and weekly services and nightly prayer show her deep faith.

attentive.hook: An attentive student pays attention: eyes forward, ears open, pencil ready.

traps.why: Distracted is the opposite. An attentive person is focused.
Attractive looks similar but means good-looking.
Obsessed is far too strong. Attentive just means carefully noticing.

syn1.tip: Attentive is built like "attention." Someone attentive is paying attention, alert to what is going on around them.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite. Attentive people notice details.
Nosy is a negative kind of noticing. Attentive is a good quality.
Being awake is not enough. Attentive means actively watching and noticing.

syn2.tip: Hear "attention" inside attentive. Picture a waiter who notices your empty glass before you ask.

traps.why: Bored fits the doodlers, but "unlike" tells you Marco is different.
Doodling is drawing, but Marco was the one taking notes, not drawing.
Marco asked questions, so he wasn't silent. The clue is about focus.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the students who doodled" sets up a contrast, and "careful notes" plus "thoughtful questions" show Marco was paying close attention.

sc2.sentence: The lifeguard stayed _____ all afternoon; she never looked at her phone and kept her eyes on every swimmer in the crowded pool.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite. She kept her eyes on every swimmer.
Lifeguards sit in the sun, but the clue is about watching swimmers.
Anxious adds worry. The clue shows calm, careful watching, not fear.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "never looked at her phone" and "kept her eyes on every swimmer" restate the blank: she was carefully watching.

feral.hook: Feral cats come from tame pets but grow up outdoors, wild and wary of every human hand.

traps.why: Tame is the opposite. Feral animals avoid people.
Federal looks similar but means having to do with the national government.
Feral animals may be hungry, but feral means wild, not underfed.

syn1.tip: You often hear "feral cats," ones living outdoors away from people. Think wild, not tame.

traps.why: Domestic means living with people as pets. Feral is the opposite.
Vicious means cruel and violent. Feral animals are wild but usually avoid people.
A lost pet is missing, but feral means it has become wild.

syn2.tip: Feral describes animals that live like wild ones, even if their ancestors were pets. Picture a cat that hisses and runs from you.

traps.why: Friendly is the opposite. These kittens hissed and fled from people.
Kittens are cute, but the sentence describes hissing and fleeing, not charm.
Orphaned means without parents. The clue is about avoiding people.

sc1.tip: "Never handled by people" leads to "so," and "hissing and fleeing from anyone" shows the kittens are wild, not used to humans.

sc2.sentence: Our dog Biscuit sleeps on the couch and loves belly rubs, but the _____ dogs roaming the abandoned farm snarled and bolted whenever a person came near.

traps.why: Pampered describes Biscuit. "But" tells you the farm dogs are the opposite.
Playful is a happy word. These dogs snarled and ran from people.
Purebred is about a dog's family line, not whether it is wild.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the couch dog with these dogs, which "snarled and bolted whenever a person came near." They are wild, not tame.

grotesque.hook: Picture a grotesque gargoyle on a cathedral: bulging eyes, twisted snout, ugly in a strange way.

traps.why: Beautiful is the opposite of grotesque.
Picturesque has the same ending but means pretty as a picture.
Monsters are often gigantic, but grotesque is about ugliness, not size.

syn1.tip: Grotesque begins like "gross," and gargoyles on old buildings are a classic example: ugly in a twisted, strange way.

traps.why: Pleasant to look at is the opposite of grotesque.
Grotesque things can be big, but the word is about ugliness.
A bit untidy is far too mild. Grotesque is shockingly, weirdly ugly.

syn2.tip: Grotesque things are bent out of shape: twisted faces, odd bulges. Think of a gargoyle or a scary mask.

traps.why: Adorable is the opposite. A twisted nose and bulging eye aren't cute.
Masks can be colorful, but the details describe ugly shapes, not colors.
Picturesque looks similar but means pretty and charming.

sc1.tip: The examples after "with": "a twisted nose, one bulging eye, and a mouth stretched crookedly" all describe features that are ugly and bent out of shape.

sc2.sentence: In the fairy tale, the princess expected a handsome prince to arrive, but instead a _____ troll with warty skin and a lopsided jaw lumbered out of the forest.

traps.why: Charming fits the prince she expected, but "but instead" signals the opposite.
Royal fits a fairy tale, but warts and a lopsided jaw describe ugliness.
Tiny is about size, and "lumbered" suggests something big and heavy anyway.

sc2.tip: "But instead" contrasts the troll with a "handsome prince," and "warty skin and a lopsided jaw" show it was strangely ugly.

predominant.hook: Predominant contains dominant: the color, sound, or idea that dominates by outnumbering all the others.

traps.why: Minor means small or less important, the opposite of predominant.
Predicted also starts with pred but means expected ahead of time.
Dominant can suggest bossy people, but predominant means most common.

syn1.tip: Find "dominant" inside predominant. The predominant thing dominates by being the strongest or most common, like the main color in a painting.

traps.why: Least common is the exact opposite.
Predominant is about how much there is, not about cost.
Pre can mean before, but predominant isn't about arriving first.

syn2.tip: If blue is "the predominant color," you see more blue than anything else. Predominant means there is more of it.

traps.why: Rarest is the opposite. Pine makes up nearly three-quarters of the trees.
Tallest is about height, but the clue is about how many trees.
Greenest is about color, but the clue counts trunks.

sc1.tip: "Making up nearly three-quarters of all the trunks" tells you pine outnumbers the others, so it is the most common tree.

sc2.sentence: Because nearly every student in our class speaks Spanish at home, Spanish is the _____ language you hear in the hallway during lunch and recess.

traps.why: Unusual is the opposite. Nearly every student speaks Spanish.
Only is too strong. "Nearly every" means some students speak other languages.
Official means chosen by a government or school, not most commonly heard.

sc2.tip: "Because nearly every student" speaks Spanish, it causes Spanish to be heard more than any other language: the most common one.

lucid.hook: Lucid comes from the Latin word for light: a lucid explanation lets light into a confusing idea.

traps.why: Confusing is the opposite of lucid.
Lucky starts with luc but means having good fortune.
Clear explanations are often short, but lucid means easy to understand.

syn1.tip: Lucid shares a light root with "translucent." A lucid idea is clear, like light shining through glass.

traps.why: Hard to follow is the opposite of lucid.
Detailed writing can still be confusing. Lucid means easy to understand.
Childish is an insult. Lucid is praise for clear thinking.

syn2.tip: Lucid is a compliment for explanations and writing. If the idea "finally makes sense," the explanation was lucid.

traps.why: Confusing describes the textbook. "Even though" tells you her explanation was different.
Technical explanations are often hard. Hers made the idea easy.
Lengthy is about length, but the clue says it was easy to grasp.

sc1.tip: "Even though" the textbook "confused everyone," the explanation "made the idea easy to grasp." The blank must mean clear and understandable.

sc2.sentence: Mr. Ortiz's directions for the science project were _____; every step was numbered, explained in plain words, and simple enough for a third grader to follow.

traps.why: Vague means unclear, the opposite of numbered steps in plain words.
Strict is about rules, not about how easy directions are to understand.
Optional means you don't have to do it. The clue is about clarity.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "numbered," "plain words," and "simple enough for a third grader to follow" restate the blank. The directions were clear.

revoke.hook: Revoke breaks into re (back) and voke (call): to revoke a permission is to call it back.

traps.why: Grant means to give permission, the opposite of revoke.
Provoke looks similar but means to make someone angry.
Re can mean again, but revoke means take back, not say again.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: re means back and voc means call. To revoke something is to call it back, cancelling it.

traps.why: Give out is the opposite of taking back.
The parts suggest calling again, but revoke means officially taking something back.
Pausing is too weak. Revoking takes something away completely.

syn2.tip: You hear it in "revoke a license" or "revoke a card." Something that was given is officially taken back.

traps.why: Extend is the opposite. Reckless driving wouldn't earn more permission.
Explaining the rules is related, but the effect lasts "for the rest of the summer."
Provoke looks similar but means to stir up anger.

sc1.tip: "Caught driving the golf cart recklessly" is the cause, and "for the rest of the summer" shows the effect: his permission was taken away.

sc2.sentence: Last year the city gave the food truck a permit to park downtown, but after dozens of complaints about litter, officials voted to _____ it.

traps.why: Renew means extend it. "But after dozens of complaints" signals taking it away.
Revive looks similar but means bring back to life.
Honor is positive. Complaints about litter lead to a negative action.

sc2.tip: "Gave the food truck a permit" followed by "but after dozens of complaints" signals a reversal. The officials took the permit back.

fictitious.hook: Fictitious is a cousin of fiction: a fictitious town, like a novel's characters, exists only on the page.

traps.why: Actual means real, the opposite of fictitious.
Suspicious rhymes with fictitious but means seeming dishonest.
Made-up things can seem mysterious, but fictitious just means not real.

syn1.tip: Fictitious is in the same family as "fiction," stories that are made up. Something fictitious is imaginary, not real.

traps.why: Based on fact is the opposite of fictitious.
Some true things are hard to believe. Fictitious means not real at all.
Slightly exaggerated is too weak. Fictitious means completely invented.

syn2.tip: Think of the fiction section of the library. A fictitious person or place was invented by someone's imagination.

traps.why: Authentic means real, which is what readers wrongly believed.
Historical means really existed in the past. Holmes was created by an author.
Suspicious sounds like fictitious but means seeming dishonest.

sc1.tip: "Although many readers believed" he was real, he was "created by author Arthur Conan Doyle." That contrast tells you he is made up.

sc2.sentence: Because the reporter used a _____ name to protect the student's privacy, nobody at school could figure out who had given the interview.

traps.why: A genuine name would reveal who the student was.
A famous name wouldn't protect privacy. It would draw attention.
An official name is the real one, so everyone would know.

sc2.tip: The name was used "to protect the student's privacy," and as a result "nobody could figure out who" it was. So the name was made up.

sustain.hook: A singer sustains a long note by holding it, and a piano's sustain pedal keeps the sound ringing.

traps.why: Abandon means to give up, the opposite of keeping something going.
Obtain also ends in -tain, but it means to get something.
Starting something is different from keeping it going over time.

syn1.tip: Think of a singer who sustains a note: she keeps it going. Maintain also means to keep something going.

traps.why: Bringing something to a halt stops it, the opposite of sustaining it.
Getting underway is beginning, not keeping something going.
The parts may suggest holding under, but sustain means keep going.

syn2.tip: Picture a runner who sustains her speed for the whole race. She keeps going at that pace.

traps.why: She did slow down, so reducing her pace is what she actually did.
Runners record their times, but slowing down shows she couldn't keep the pace.
Obtain looks similar but means to get, and she already had the speed.

sc1.tip: The word "but" signals a contrast: a "blistering speed" at first, then "slowed to a jog." She could not keep that pace going.

sc2.sentence: Our campfire kept dying out, so Dad added dry logs every few minutes to _____ the flames until the marshmallows were finally golden brown.

traps.why: Extinguish means to put out, but Dad was adding logs to feed the fire.
Contain looks similar, but adding logs keeps flames going rather than holding them in.
You might inspect a fire, but adding logs is about keeping it burning.

sc2.tip: The fire "kept dying out," so Dad "added dry logs every few minutes." That is the cause and effect of keeping something going.

impose.hook: Impose comes from Latin words for put on: you impose a rule by putting it on people who didn't ask.

traps.why: Lifting a rule takes it away, the opposite of imposing one.
Expose looks similar but means to uncover or reveal.
Suggesting is far too gentle; imposing forces something on people.

syn1.tip: Think of a library that imposes a fine. You have no choice; it is forced on you.

traps.why: Doing away with a rule removes it, the opposite of imposing it.
Impose has pose inside, but it has nothing to do with posing.
A polite request is much too weak; imposing gives people no choice.

syn2.tip: People complain when someone imposes on them. It means pushing something on others that they did not want.

traps.why: The principal wanted less noise, so he was adding a rule, not canceling one.
Oppose looks similar, but the principal created the rule rather than fighting it.
Students "did not welcome" the rule, so nobody was celebrating it.

sc1.tip: The rule is "new" and students "did not welcome" it. The principal is forcing an unwanted rule on them.

sc2.sentence: Ms. Lee usually let us choose our own reading books, but this month she decided to _____ a strict list of required titles, giving us no choice at all.

traps.why: A suggestion leaves you a choice, but the sentence says "no choice at all."
Dropping the list would give students choice again, but they had none.
Expose looks similar but means to reveal, not to force on people.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "let us choose" with "no choice at all." She forced a list on the class.

surplus.hook: Sur- means over, as in surface, so a surplus is the amount over what you need, plus some extra.

traps.why: A shortage is not enough, the opposite of a surplus.
Surprise starts the same way but means something unexpected.
Extra things may go into storage, but surplus means the extra amount itself.

syn1.tip: You can see "plus" inside surplus. A surplus is extra, more than what you need.

traps.why: A missing amount means too little, the opposite of a surplus.
Plus is inside the word, but surplus means leftover, not a sum.
The full amount is all you need; a surplus goes beyond that.

syn2.tip: Think of a farm selling its surplus apples. Those are the ones left over after the farm has enough.

traps.why: They ordered "far more" than needed, so there was no shortage.
Ordering pizza gives a receipt, but you can't donate a receipt to feed people.
Surprise looks similar, but the clue is about leftover food.

sc1.tip: The class "ordered far more pizza than the students could possibly eat." What's left over is the extra amount.

sc2.sentence: Last winter our town ran out of road salt, but this year the crews bought so much that they now have a _____ piled high in the garage.

traps.why: A shortage was last winter; "but" shows this year they have too much.
A sample is a tiny amount, not something "piled high."
Surface looks similar but means the outside layer of something.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "ran out" with "bought so much" and "piled high." They now have more than they need.

lethal.hook: Think of the movie title Lethal Weapon: a lethal weapon is one that can kill.

traps.why: Harmless means causing no harm, the opposite of lethal.
Legal looks a bit like lethal but means allowed by law.
Painful is too weak; lethal means something can actually kill.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of a "lethal dose" of poison. That is enough to cause death.

traps.why: Something safe to handle is harmless, the opposite of lethal.
Mildly harmful is much too weak; lethal things can cause death.
Lethal things are scary, but lethal means they can kill.

syn2.tip: Lethal has a dark, serious feeling. Some mushrooms contain a lethal poison, meaning eating them could kill you.

traps.why: A gentle sting would not "kill a person within minutes."
Itchy is far too weak for a sting that can kill.
Jellyfish can be colorful, but color has nothing to do with killing.
