sc1.tip: The sting is strong "enough to kill a person within minutes." A sting that can kill is deadly.

sc2.sentence: Most spiders in our backyard are harmless, but the black widow's bite can be _____, so Mom told us never to touch one.

traps.why: "But" contrasts with harmless, so the bite must be dangerous, not mild.
Itchy is too weak; Mom wouldn't ban touching a spider for an itch.
The bite may be tiny, but the contrast is about danger, not size.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the black widow against spiders that are "harmless." Its bite must be the opposite: deadly.

exploit.hook: Gamers exploit a glitch when they use a bug in the game to get an unfair edge.

traps.why: Ignoring something means paying no attention, the opposite of using it.
Explore looks similar but means to travel through and discover.
Exploiting a weakness uses it; repairing a weakness fixes it.

syn1.tip: A team exploits the other side's weak defense by using it to score. Exploit means to use something to your advantage.

traps.why: Passing up a chance means not using it, the opposite of exploiting it.
Exploit looks like explode, but it means to take advantage of.
An exploit can be a daring deed, but the verb means take advantage.

syn2.tip: Hackers exploit a weak spot in a program. When you exploit something, you take advantage of it.

traps.why: Priya aimed every kick at the weak side, so she didn't ignore it.
Fixing the goalie's weakness would help the other team, not Priya.
Explain looks similar, but Priya used the weakness instead of describing it.

sc1.tip: Priya spots a weakness and aims "every penalty kick at the right corner" because of it. She is taking advantage of it.

sc2.sentence: Instead of letting the rainy weekend go to waste, Jamal decided to _____ the free time by finally finishing the model rocket he had started months ago.

traps.why: "Instead of" letting it go to waste, he did the opposite of wasting it.
Dread is a gloomy feeling, but Jamal happily got something done.
You can measure time, but Jamal made full use of it.

sc2.tip: The words "instead of letting the rainy weekend go to waste" set up a contrast. Jamal made full use of his time.

predecessor.hook: Pre- means before and the rest comes from a Latin word for going away: your predecessor held the job before you.

traps.why: A successor comes after you, the opposite of a predecessor.
Predator starts the same way but means an animal that hunts.
An assistant helps you in a job but didn't hold it before you.

syn1.tip: Pre- means before. Your predecessor is the person who had your role before you did.

traps.why: Someone who comes after is a successor, the opposite of a predecessor.
Pre- means before, but a predecessor doesn't tell the future.
A coworker works with you; a predecessor held the job earlier.

syn2.tip: Think of a new principal who keeps rules from her predecessor. The predecessor was the principal before her.

traps.why: Her successor comes after her, but this person led the squad before.
An opponent is on another team and wouldn't start this squad's traditions.
Predator looks similar but means a hunting animal.

sc1.tip: The person "had led the squad for three seasons before graduating." That is the captain who came before her.

sc2.sentence: Our new mayor loves building bike lanes, unlike her _____, who spent eight years in office paving wider roads for cars instead.

traps.why: A new mayor's successor hasn't served yet, so couldn't have spent eight years.
Voters choose mayors but don't spend years in office.
A supporter backs a mayor but doesn't hold the office.

sc2.tip: The word "unlike" contrasts the "new mayor" with someone who already "spent eight years in office." That person came before her.

premise.hook: Every sitcom has a premise, like a family of aliens moving to the suburbs: the setup the whole show rests on.

traps.why: A conclusion comes at the end; a premise is where an idea starts.
Promise looks similar but means a pledge to do something.
Premises can mean a building, but a premise is a basic idea.

syn1.tip: The premise of a movie is the idea it is built on, like toys coming alive at night. It is the basis.

traps.why: A final result comes at the end, not at the start.
A plot twist is a surprise later in a story, not its basic idea.
Pre- might suggest a preview, but a premise is the idea a story rests on.

syn2.tip: When a friend asks what a show's premise is, you tell them the basic setup the story starts from.

traps.why: The idea comes first and "the whole plot grows from" it, so it's not the ending.
A novel has a cover, but a cover isn't an idea the plot grows from.
Promise looks similar, but the clue describes the story's starting idea.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "the whole plot grows from that idea." The missing word names the basic idea a story starts from.

sc2.sentence: Because the whole debate depended on the idea that homework helps students learn, Maya won by proving that _____ false.

traps.why: The idea everything depended on comes first, not at the end.
Debates have audiences, but you can't prove an audience false.
Promise looks similar, but the clue is the idea the debate depended on.

sc2.tip: The debate "depended on the idea that homework helps," so knocking down that idea made Maya win. That base idea is the missing word.

decree.hook: Picture a herald unrolling a scroll in the town square and shouting, "By royal decree."

traps.why: Degree looks and sounds similar but means a unit or a diploma.
A suggestion is too weak; a decree must be obeyed.
A rumor spreads among people, but a decree is an official command.

syn1.tip: Think of a king who issued a decree declaring a holiday. A decree is an order from someone in charge.

traps.why: A polite request is too weak; a decree is a command.
People may protest a decree, but a decree is the order itself.
Decree sounds like degree, which can mean a diploma.

syn2.tip: Kings, queens and emperors issue decrees. Picture a royal scroll: it carries a command everyone must follow.

traps.why: A request can be refused, but "no one dared disobey" this command.
A rumor isn't official, but the sentence calls it "the official command."
Degree sounds like decree but means a unit or a diploma.

sc1.tip: The end of the sentence restates the blank: "the official command." A royal official command is a decree.

sc2.sentence: After the emperor issued a _____ banning swords in the city, guards began taking weapons from every traveler who passed through the gates.

traps.why: A warning doesn't ban anything, but guards began enforcing a real ban.
A complaint wouldn't make guards start taking weapons.
Decrease looks similar but means getting smaller.

sc2.tip: Because of what the emperor issued, "guards began taking weapons." Only an official order would cause guards to act like that.

epidemic.hook: Epi- means upon and dem means people, as in democracy: an epidemic is a disease falling upon many people.

traps.why: A cure ends a disease; an epidemic is the disease spreading.
Epic starts the same way but means a long heroic story.
An infection can hit one person; an epidemic spreads to many.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of a flu epidemic that closes schools. It is a disease breaking out among many people.

traps.why: A minor cold in one person is far too small for an epidemic.
A full recovery means people got well, the opposite of an epidemic.
Epidemic starts like epic, a heroic poem, but means spreading disease.

syn2.tip: The "dem" in epidemic is the same as in democracy, meaning people. An epidemic is a disease that spreads among many people.

traps.why: Officials were describing the spread itself, not something that stops it.
Allergies don't spread from person to person like this virus did.
Epic looks similar but means a long heroic story.

sc1.tip: Look at "nearly half the students" and "rapid spread." A virus spreading that fast to so many people is an outbreak.

sc2.sentence: Doctors expected only a few flu cases this winter, but the virus spread so quickly that the city faced a true _____ within a month.

traps.why: A cure would stop the flu, but the virus was spreading quickly.
A sniffle fits "a few cases," but "but" signals something much bigger.
A vaccine prevents disease; the sentence describes the virus spreading.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "only a few flu cases" with a virus that "spread so quickly." The city faced a widespread disease.

precedent.hook: Pre-cede means go before: a precedent is something that went before and shows what to do next time.

traps.why: President sounds similar but means a leader of a country or group.
An exception is a one-time break from the pattern; a precedent sets one.
Courts look at precedents, but a precedent is an earlier example.

syn1.tip: When something "sets a precedent," it becomes an example that people point to later. Pre- means before.

traps.why: A later copy comes after; a precedent comes before.
Precedent sounds like president, a head of state, but means an earlier example.
The parts suggest going before, but precedent isn't about standing in line.

syn2.tip: Pre- means before. A precedent is something that happened before and guides what people decide later.

traps.why: You can set a record, but a record isn't a privilege others demand.
A limit holds things back, but here other classes wanted the same thing.
President sounds similar but means a leader, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: Because one class got pajama day, "soon every other class demanded the same privilege." The first event became an example others used.

sc2.sentence: Lena's request to bring her hamster was denied because there was no _____: no student had ever brought a pet to school before.

traps.why: President sounds similar but means a leader, not an earlier example.
Precaution looks similar but means a step taken to stay safe.
Punishment isn't the issue; the clue says no one had done it before.

sc2.tip: After the colon, the sentence restates the blank: "no student had ever brought a pet to school before." There was no earlier example.

rudimentary.hook: Rudimentary comes from Latin rudis, meaning rough or untaught, like a beginner's first rough sketch.

traps.why: Advanced is the opposite of rudimentary; it means far along, not simple.
Rude looks like the start of rudimentary, but it means impolite.
Early stages may not last, but rudimentary means simple, not short-lived.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a rudimentary knowledge of Spanish." That means only the simplest beginner's level.

traps.why: Fully grown and complete is the opposite of rudimentary.
That describes rude, which only looks like rudimentary.
Basic skills are often useful, but rudimentary means simple, not useful.

syn2.tip: Rudimentary describes something at its first, simplest stage, like a toddler's first words.

traps.why: Fluent is the opposite; she could not yet hold a real conversation.
Her Japanese wasn't forgotten; she could still say hello and count.
Impressive is too positive for someone who can only greet and count.

sc1.tip: The clue is "she could say hello and count to ten, but... not yet hold a real conversation." That describes a simple beginner's level.

sc2.sentence: My little brother's drawings of our dog are still _____, just circles and sticks, but my older sister's sketches are so detailed they look like photographs.

traps.why: Realistic describes the sister's sketches, not drawings of just circles and sticks.
Drawings can be colorful, but the clue is about how simple they are.
Rude looks like rudimentary, but stick drawings are not impolite.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with the sister's "so detailed" sketches. "Just circles and sticks" shows the drawings are simple.

vendetta.hook: Vendetta is an Italian word for revenge; picture two families trading payback for a hundred years.

traps.why: Friendship is the opposite of a bitter vendetta.
A vendor sells things; the word only looks like vendetta.
An argument can be short; a vendetta lasts a long, bitter time.

syn1.tip: Picture the phrase "a family vendetta" in a movie: two sides angry at each other for years.

traps.why: A peace treaty ends fighting, the opposite of a vendetta.
That is a vendor, which only looks like vendetta.
Friendly competition is too positive; a vendetta is bitter and hostile.

syn2.tip: A vendetta is negative and long lasting. Look for a choice that is both angry and long.

traps.why: A partnership is friendly, but the families refused to shop on each other's street.
Bakeries use recipes, but the sentence describes a bitter, long fight.
Celebration is too happy for a rivalry described as bitter.

sc1.tip: Look at "bitter," "lasted three generations," and "refusing even to shop on the other's street." That describes a long, angry feud.

sc2.sentence: Most playground arguments end by lunchtime, but the _____ between Max and Leo lasted all through middle school, with neither boy willing to forgive the other.

traps.why: Friends forgive each other, but neither boy was willing to forgive.
Games happen on playgrounds, but this lasted years without forgiveness.
A joke is lighthearted; refusing to forgive for years is bitter.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with arguments that "end by lunchtime." This one "lasted all through middle school" and nobody would "forgive," so it is a long feud.

procure.hook: Picture a detective calling every store in town until she finally procures the very last ticket.

traps.why: Lose is the opposite of procure, which means to get.
Procure contains cure, but it has nothing to do with healing.
You may want something, but procure means actually getting it.

syn1.tip: Think of "the museum procured a rare dinosaur egg." The museum got it, probably with some effort.

traps.why: Give away is the opposite of getting something.
The cure inside procure doesn't mean healing here.
You look for something before you procure it; procure means getting it.

syn2.tip: Procure is a fancier way to say get, usually after some searching or effort.

traps.why: Discard means throw away, but they were searching to collect costumes.
Neighbors donated; the club collected costumes rather than giving them away.
Actors wear costumes, but searching stores shows the club needed to get them.

sc1.tip: The clue is "spent weeks searching thrift stores and asking neighbors for donations." That effort is how they got the costumes.

sc2.sentence: Getting regular tickets was easy, but it took Mia's mom weeks of phone calls to _____ front-row seats; she cheered when the tickets finally arrived in the mail.

traps.why: She cheered when tickets arrived, so she did not refuse them.
Cure looks like procure but means to heal, which makes no sense here.
Advertising involves tickets too, but these tickets arrived for her to keep.

sc2.tip: "Weeks of phone calls" and "the tickets finally arrived" show she worked hard and then got them.

propel.hook: A propeller propels: its spinning blades push a boat or plane forward.

traps.why: Stop is the opposite of propel, which means drive forward.
Propose looks similar but means to suggest an idea.
Boats float, but propel is about driving them forward.

syn1.tip: Propel is inside propeller, the spinning part that pushes a plane or boat forward.

traps.why: Hold back is the opposite of driving something forward.
Nudge gently is too weak; propel means a strong forward push.
That means propose, which only looks like propel.

syn2.tip: Think of a rocket engine that propels a spaceship. It drives the ship forward with force.

traps.why: Anchoring keeps a boat still, but this boat "glides forward quickly."
Rowers keep boats steady, but the clue is about moving forward.
Nudge is too weak; the boat "glides forward quickly."

sc1.tip: "Pulling together in rhythm so it glides forward quickly" shows the oars drive the boat ahead.

sc2.sentence: The bike had no motor, so the only thing that could _____ it up the steep hill was Jamal's legs pumping hard on the pedals.

traps.why: Braking slows a bike, but pumping pedals moves it up the hill.
His legs weren't fixing the bike; they were moving it uphill.
Riders lock bikes, but pumping pedals moves the bike instead of securing it.

sc2.tip: "No motor, so" points to the cause: Jamal's legs "pumping hard on the pedals" are what drive the bike forward.

proponent.hook: Proponent comes from Latin for "put forward": a proponent puts an idea forward and argues for it.

traps.why: An opponent is against an idea, the opposite of a proponent.
Component looks similar but means a part of something.
Inventors create ideas; a proponent backs an idea, whoever invented it.

syn1.tip: Proponent and opponent are a pair. Pro means for, so a proponent is for an idea.

traps.why: That describes an opponent, the opposite of a proponent.
A judge stays neutral; a proponent takes one side.
Mentioning is too weak; a proponent actively argues for an idea.

syn2.tip: Think of "a strong proponent of outdoor learning." That person speaks up for the idea and wants it to happen.

traps.why: He argued that extra sleep helps, so he was for the idea.
Victim makes later start times sound harmful, but he says they help.
An observer only watches; Dr. Haddad "argued at every board meeting."

sc1.tip: Dr. Haddad "argued at every board meeting that extra sleep improves students' grades." Someone who argues for an idea supports it.

sc2.sentence: While most of the class wanted a pizza party, Ava was the only _____ of a class garden, and she spoke up for it until a few friends agreed.

traps.why: Ava "spoke up for" the garden, so she was not against it.
A skeptic doubts an idea, but Ava argued for the garden.
A visitor just stops by; Ava "spoke up for" the garden idea.

sc2.tip: "While most of the class wanted a pizza party" sets up a contrast, and "she spoke up for it" shows Ava supported the garden idea.

distraught.hook: Distraught is related to distracted: picture someone so upset their mind feels pulled in every direction.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of distraught.
Distracted looks similar but means not paying attention, not deeply upset.
Annoyed is too weak; distraught means extremely upset and worried.

syn1.tip: Picture "the distraught boy searched everywhere for his lost puppy." He is not a little bothered; he is wildly worried.

traps.why: Perfectly calm is the opposite of distraught.
Upset people can be tired, but distraught is about worry, not sleepiness.
Distracted only looks like distraught; it means not focusing.

syn2.tip: Distraught is a strong, negative feeling. Look for the choice that means very upset, not just a little.

traps.why: Someone calm wouldn't be crying and searching until midnight.
She might be excited for a pet show, but crying shows she was upset.
She stayed up late, but crying and searching show worry, not sleepiness.

sc1.tip: Look at "crying and searching every corner of the house until midnight." Those actions show she was extremely upset and worried.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa stayed perfectly calm when the car got a flat tire, but Grandma was _____, pacing the roadside and calling every tow company she could find.

traps.why: Relaxed describes Grandpa; the "but" shows Grandma was different.
Cheerful is too positive for someone pacing and calling in a panic.
Waiting by the road can be boring, but pacing and calling show worry.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Grandma with Grandpa, who "stayed perfectly calm." Her "pacing" and "calling every tow company" show she was very upset.

sever.hook: Picture scissors snipping a kite string in one clean cut: to sever is to cut something completely apart.

traps.why: Join is the opposite of sever, which means cut apart.
Serve looks similar but means to bring food or help someone.
Scratch is too weak; sever means cutting all the way through.

syn1.tip: Think of "the storm severed the power lines." The lines were cut completely, so the power went out.

traps.why: Tie together is the opposite of severing something.
Bend slightly is far too weak; sever means a complete break.
That means being severe, a word that only looks like sever.

syn2.tip: You may know the phrase "sever ties," meaning to cut off a connection completely.

traps.why: Tightening would hold the balloon down, but "the line was cut."
Balloons get inflated, but the blank is about the rope, which "was cut."
Loosening isn't enough; the sentence says "the line was cut."

sc1.tip: The sentence says "the moment the line was cut, the balloon rose." So the workers had to cut the rope completely.

sc2.sentence: Instead of simply pausing their friendship after the argument, the two boys decided to _____ all ties, deleting each other's numbers and never speaking again.

traps.why: Strengthening ties doesn't fit "never speaking again."
Loosen is too weak; "never speaking again" is a complete break.
They might discuss things, but "never speaking again" means cutting ties completely.

sc2.tip: "Instead of simply pausing" signals something stronger, and "never speaking again" shows they cut off the friendship completely.

decipher.hook: A cipher is a secret code, so to decipher is to undo the code and read the hidden message.

traps.why: Encode is the opposite: it hides a message in code.
Decide looks a bit similar but means to make a choice.
You might copy a message, but decipher means figure out what it says.

syn1.tip: Find cipher, meaning secret code, inside decipher. Taking the code away lets you read the message.

traps.why: Hiding a message in code is the opposite of deciphering it.
Neat writing is easy to read, but decipher means working out hard writing.
Glancing is too weak; deciphering takes effort to understand.

syn2.tip: Think of trying to decipher a doctor's messy handwriting. You have to work to figure out what it says.

traps.why: Egyptians carved hieroglyphs, but scholars needed "a key" to read them.
Scholars worked for years on the symbols, so they did not ignore them.
Museums display hieroglyphs, but the Rosetta Stone helped scholars read them.

sc1.tip: "Gave them a key to the mysterious symbols" is the clue. You need a key to decode something hard to read.

sc2.sentence: My little sister's note looked like scribbles to everyone else, but I could _____ it easily because I know her backward letters and funny spelling.

traps.why: Knowing her letters helps you read it correctly, not misread it.
Erasing has nothing to do with knowing her backward letters and spelling.
You might fold a note, but the clue is about understanding it.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "looked like scribbles to everyone else." Knowing "her backward letters and funny spelling" lets you figure out what it says.

reiterate.hook: Re means again and iterate means repeat, so reiterate is saying something again so it sinks in.

traps.why: Skip means leave out, the opposite of saying again.
Irritate looks similar but means to annoy.
Interrupting is about talking, but it means cutting in, not saying again.

syn1.tip: Reiterate starts with re, meaning again. Think of a coach who reiterates the rules so nobody forgets.

traps.why: Keeping silent is the opposite of saying something again.
Taking back words means un-saying them, not repeating them.
That means irritate, which only looks like reiterate.

syn2.tip: The prefix re means again, as in redo and replay. Reiterate means saying something again.

traps.why: Confused students need the rules again, so skipping them makes no sense.
Canceling rules wouldn't help confused students understand them.
She already explained these rules yesterday, so she isn't creating new ones.

sc1.tip: "Had explained... yesterday" plus "students still seemed confused" means she needed to say the rules again.

sc2.sentence: Coach Rivera likes to _____ her most important rule, saying it at the start, middle, and end of every practice: never skip your warm-up.

traps.why: She says the rule three times each practice, so she isn't ignoring it.
Players might break rules, but the coach keeps saying hers aloud.
Saying it "at the start, middle, and end" means the rule stays the same.

sc2.tip: "Saying it at the start, middle, and end of every practice" restates the blank: she says the rule again and again.

upheaval.hook: Picture the ground heaving up in an earthquake: an upheaval is any change that shakes life up like that.

traps.why: Stability means staying steady, the opposite of an upheaval.
Upheaval sounds like heaving something up, but it means a major disturbance.
Inconvenience is too weak; an upheaval is a sudden, major change.

syn1.tip: Think of "moving to a new country caused a huge upheaval." Everything in their lives was shaken up at once.

traps.why: A peaceful routine is the opposite of an upheaval.
The parts up and heave suggest lifting, but upheaval means major disturbance.
A small adjustment is too weak for an upheaval.

syn2.tip: Picture life being turned upside down. Upheaval is a negative word for a big, sudden shake-up.

traps.why: Changing school, city, and language at once is the opposite of stability.
Travel can be part of moving, but this is a lasting life change.
Celebration is too happy for so many sudden changes at once.

sc1.tip: The list "a new school, a new city, and a new language all in one month" shows a sudden, major change.

sc2.sentence: Our town had been quiet and unchanged for fifty years, so the new highway cutting through Main Street caused a real _____, closing shops and rerouting every bus.

traps.why: Closing shops and rerouting buses is the opposite of calm.
Celebration is too positive; closing shops is a painful disturbance.
Delay is too weak; closing shops and rerouting buses is a huge change.

sc2.tip: The town was "quiet and unchanged for fifty years," and then shops closed and buses moved. That sharp contrast points to a major disturbance.

animosity.hook: Animosity is the glare two rivals shoot across the field, a dislike that can burn for years.

traps.why: Friendship is a warm feeling, the opposite of animosity.
Animation looks similar but means liveliness or cartoons, not dislike.
Annoyance is too weak; animosity is strong, lasting dislike.

syn1.tip: Think of the feeling between bitter rivals. Animosity is a strong, negative feeling aimed at someone.

traps.why: Warm affection is the opposite of animosity.
Mild irritation is too weak; animosity is strong dislike.
Anim looks like animated, but animosity means hostility, not liveliness.

syn2.tip: Picture two rivals who refuse to shake hands. Animosity names that bitter, unfriendly feeling between people.

traps.why: Glaring and refusing to speak show the opposite of friendship.
Shy people may stay quiet, but glaring shows dislike, not shyness.
Loneliness is about being alone, not about feelings toward a neighbor.

sc1.tip: The neighbors 'glared at each other and refused to speak.' That behavior shows strong dislike between them.

sc2.sentence: Although the two soccer captains had been best friends in third grade, a bitter argument over the championship left nothing but _____ between them by eighth grade.

traps.why: A bitter argument destroys admiration; it leaves the opposite behind.
Loyalty fits their old friendship, but the bitter argument changed that.
Captains need teamwork, but a bitter argument leaves dislike instead.

sc2.tip: 'Although' they 'had been best friends,' a 'bitter argument' changed things. Look for a word that means the opposite of friendship.

rapport.hook: Rapport is that easy click you feel with someone who just gets you, like a favorite coach.

traps.why: Hostility is unfriendly, the opposite of a warm rapport.
Report looks similar but means an account of facts.
You talk with people you have rapport with, but rapport is the connection itself.

syn1.tip: Rapport is something you 'build' or 'have' with people, like a coach with players. Think of a friendly connection.

traps.why: Bitter conflict is the opposite of a friendly rapport.
Report only looks like rapport; it means a written account.
Meeting someone comes first, but rapport is the friendship that grows later.

syn2.tip: People say two friends 'have great rapport' when they understand each other easily. It names a warm, trusting relationship.

traps.why: Learning names and hobbies brings people closer, not farther apart.
Classes have routines, but asking about hobbies builds a relationship.
Kind attention creates friendship, the opposite of a rivalry.

sc1.tip: He 'learned every student's name and asked about their hobbies.' Those kind actions build a friendly connection.

sc2.sentence: On the first day the new lab partners barely spoke, but by October they shared jokes and finished each other's sentences, showing a strong _____.

traps.why: Sharing jokes shows friendship, the opposite of dislike.
Shyness fits the first day, but 'but by October' signals a change.
Lab partners might compete, but jokes and finished sentences show friendship.

sc2.tip: 'But by October' signals a change from barely speaking. Sharing jokes and finishing each other's sentences shows a close, friendly connection.

infer.hook: A detective spots muddy boots and infers you were outside; to infer is to read the clues.

traps.why: Ignoring evidence is the opposite of using it to infer.
Inform looks similar but means to tell someone facts.
A speaker implies a hint; the listener infers, or figures it out.

syn1.tip: Infer is what readers do with clues: you use evidence to figure something out, the way a detective infers who did it.

traps.why: Looking past clues is the opposite of using them to infer.
Hinting at means suggesting, which is implying, not inferring.
Making something up uses no clues; inferring depends on evidence.

syn2.tip: Teachers ask you to infer what a character feels from clues in the story. You figure it out instead of being told.

traps.why: The clues made Mom sure, not doubtful.
Mom wasn't pretending; real clues showed her what happened.
Mom read the clues herself; implying means hinting to someone else.

sc1.tip: Mom used 'muddy paw prints' and 'an empty dog bed' as evidence. Reaching a conclusion from clues is what the blank needs.

sc2.sentence: Nobody told Priya about any surprise, but the whispering friends and the cake hidden in the closet let her _____ that a party was coming.

traps.why: The clues pointed to a party, so they would not make her doubt it.
Clues don't let you announce; they let you work something out.
Priya wasn't planning the party, so she couldn't promise it.

sc2.tip: 'Nobody told' her, 'but' whispers and a hidden cake gave it away. She worked it out herself from clues.

cumbersome.hook: Picture wrestling a giant mattress up narrow stairs; that heavy, awkward struggle is cumbersome.

traps.why: Light things are easy to carry, the opposite of cumbersome.
Awesome rhymes with the end of cumbersome but means amazing.
Big items can be valuable, but cumbersome means hard to carry.

syn1.tip: Cumbersome sounds clunky, and it means clunky: big, heavy, and awkward to carry, like an overstuffed suitcase.

traps.why: Easy to handle is the opposite of cumbersome.
Price has nothing to do with being heavy and awkward.
Fragile things break easily; cumbersome things are heavy and clumsy to move.

syn2.tip: Think of a cumbersome suitcase that won't fit in the car. The word means big, heavy, and hard to move or use.

traps.why: A light tent wouldn't need two people to carry it.
Cozy is a pleasant tent word, but the clue is about weight.
A flimsy tent is weak and thin, not heavy enough for two carriers.

sc1.tip: It 'took two people to carry it,' and the family replaced it with a 'lightweight one.' The blank must mean heavy and hard to carry.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa's old laptop was _____; it weighed nearly ten pounds and was so thick that it would not fit in my backpack.

traps.why: Portable means easy to carry, the opposite of a ten pound laptop.
Speed is about computers, but the clue describes weight and size.
Delicate means easily broken, not heavy and thick.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon explains the blank: it 'weighed nearly ten pounds' and wouldn't 'fit in my backpack.' That means heavy and awkward.

entice.hook: The smell of warm cookies drifting from a bakery door entices you inside before you even decide.

traps.why: Repel means to push away, the opposite of entice.
Entertain looks similar but means to amuse, not to attract.
Forcing makes people act; enticing makes them want to.

syn1.tip: Think of a store offering free samples to entice customers. Entice means drawing someone in with something they want.

traps.why: Drive away is the opposite of entice.
Ordering people uses commands; enticing uses something pleasant.
Trapping holds someone against their will; enticing makes them want to come.

syn2.tip: Bait on a fishing hook entices a fish. To entice is to pull someone toward you with something appealing.

traps.why: Free hot chocolate invites people; it doesn't force them.
Treats and colorful books attract shoppers; they don't scare them.
Ordering is too pushy; free hot chocolate gently draws people in.

sc1.tip: The owner 'offered free hot chocolate' and set out 'colorful books by the door.' Offering pleasant things is how you draw people in.

sc2.sentence: The zookeeper tried shouting and clapping, but nothing worked until she held out a ripe banana to _____ the stubborn monkey down from the tree.

traps.why: A banana attracts a monkey; shouting was the frightening part that failed.
Holding out a banana isn't chasing; it invites the monkey to come.
Scolding is harsh; offering a treat is a pleasant way to attract.

sc2.tip: Shouting failed, 'but' a 'ripe banana' worked. Holding out a treat to draw an animal toward you is what the blank describes.

grievance.hook: Grievance is in the same word family as grief: it's an unfair hurt you speak up about.

traps.why: A compliment is praise, the opposite of a complaint.
Grievance looks like grief, but it means a complaint, not sadness.
Grievances are about unfair treatment, but a punishment is not a complaint.

syn1.tip: People 'file a grievance' when something feels unfair. It sits close to 'grieve,' but it means a complaint you speak up about.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite of a grievance.
Grievance sounds like grieving, but it means a complaint, not mourning.
Revenge strikes back; a grievance just states what is unfair.

syn2.tip: Workers bring grievances to their boss when they feel treated unfairly. Think 'complaint about something unfair.'

traps.why: Calling a rule unfair is complaining, the opposite of praise.
Students carry homework, but they were explaining an unfair rule.
Apologies admit your own fault; the students were pointing out an unfair rule.

sc1.tip: The students were 'explaining that it was unfair.' Telling someone in charge that a rule is unfair is making a complaint.

sc2.sentence: Instead of grumbling in the hallway, the eighth graders wrote down their _____ about the short lunch period and politely asked the student council for a fix.

traps.why: Nobody asks for a fix to something they compliment.
Excuses explain your own mistakes, not a problem you want fixed.
Jokes are lighthearted; asking for a fix means they had a real complaint.

sc2.tip: They wrote about 'the short lunch period' and 'asked for a fix.' People only want a fix when they have a complaint.

impede.hook: Impede hides ped, meaning foot: imagine your feet tangled in rope, every step slowed and blocked.

traps.why: Assist means to help, the opposite of impede.
Impress looks similar but means to make people admire you.
Ped means foot, but impede means to block, not to walk.

syn1.tip: Think of things that impede traffic, like road work or snow. They get in the way and slow everything down.

traps.why: Speed up is the opposite of impede.
The ped part means foot, but impede isn't about stepping.
Impede means slow or block for now, not end forever.

syn2.tip: Imagine a fallen tree on a bike path; it impedes riders. Impede means to get in the way and slow progress.

traps.why: A lack of money hurts progress; it doesn't boost it.
Builders measure progress, but the clue shows progress being stopped.
A half-built library is nothing to celebrate; the tone is negative.

sc1.tip: A 'lack of money' left the library 'half-built for more than a year.' Something held up progress, so the blank means slow or block.

sc2.sentence: The new hallway rule was meant to speed up class changes, but instead the crowded single staircase seemed to _____ every student trying to reach class on time.

traps.why: Hurrying is what the rule wanted; 'but instead' signals the opposite happened.
A crowded staircase doesn't guide students; it blocks them.
Welcome is friendly, but a crowded staircase is a problem here.

sc2.tip: The rule was meant to 'speed up' class changes, 'but instead' things got worse. The blank must mean the opposite of speeding up.

steadfast.hook: Steadfast is steady plus fast in its old sense of firmly fixed, as in 'hold fast.'

traps.why: Unreliable means you can't count on someone, the opposite of steadfast.
Fast here means firmly fixed, as in 'hold fast,' not quick.
Stubborn sounds negative; steadfast praises someone for staying true.

syn1.tip: Break it up: steady plus fast, as in 'hold fast.' Someone steadfast stays firmly fixed in their loyalty.

traps.why: Wavering means going back and forth, the opposite of steadfast.
The fast in steadfast means firm, not quick.
Stationary means not moving physically; steadfast means firm in loyalty.

syn2.tip: Picture a dog waiting at the station every single day. Steadfast describes someone who stays true and never gives up.

traps.why: Occasional fans come sometimes; these fans 'never stopped' coming.
Buying tickets takes money, but the clue is that they never stopped.
Fast in steadfast means firm, and speed has nothing to do with fans.

sc1.tip: The fans 'never stopped' coming 'through every losing season,' even 'in the rain.' Sticking with a team in bad times is loyalty.

sc2.sentence: Most of the kids quit the robotics club after their robot broke twice, but Lena remained _____, staying late every Friday until it finally worked.

traps.why: The other kids were discouraged; 'but' shows Lena was different.
Skill helps with robots, but the clue is that she kept coming back.
Bored people quit; Lena stayed late every Friday.

sc2.tip: 'Most of the kids quit,' 'but' Lena kept 'staying late every Friday.' The blank describes someone who refuses to give up.

refute.hook: When you refute a rumor, you bring the proof that knocks it flat: here's why that's wrong.

traps.why: Confirm means to show something is true, the opposite of refute.
Refuse looks similar but means to say no to something.
Re- often means again, but refute does not mean say again.

syn1.tip: You refute a claim by bringing evidence against it. Debaters refute arguments by showing they're false.

traps.why: Prove right is the opposite of refute.
Turn down means refuse, a word that only looks like refute.
Disagreeing is weaker; refuting means showing with proof that it's false.

syn2.tip: Scientists refute old ideas with new evidence. Refute means you don't just disagree; you prove the idea wrong.

traps.why: Malik's study goes against Ava's claim, so it doesn't support it.
Malik didn't ignore the claim; he answered it with a study.
Malik wasn't admiring Ava's claim; his study showed it was false.

sc1.tip: Malik had 'a study showing goldfish recalled a feeding signal for months,' which shows Ava was wrong. Using evidence to prove a claim false fits the blank.

sc2.sentence: Because the scientist's new photos clearly showed ice on the planet's surface, other researchers could no longer _____ her claim that water existed there.

traps.why: The photos made her claim stronger, so others could support it more, not less.
Re- suggests again, but the photos wouldn't stop anyone from repeating her claim.
The photos made the claim clearer, so understanding it got easier.

sc2.tip: 'Because' the photos 'clearly showed ice,' her claim was proven. Once proof is that strong, no one can show it is wrong.

sedentary.hook: Sedentary comes from the Latin word for 'to sit'; picture a whole Saturday spent on the couch.

traps.why: Energetic means full of activity, the opposite of sedentary.
Lazy is an insult; sedentary just describes a lot of sitting.
Sedimentary describes rock formed in layers, not a sitting lifestyle.

syn1.tip: Doctors warn about a 'sedentary lifestyle,' meaning lots of sitting. Picture desk jobs and long hours of screen time.

traps.why: Always moving is the opposite of sedentary.
Sedentary means sitting a lot, not unable to move at all.
Too much sitting can affect health, but sedentary means sitting, not illness.

syn2.tip: A sedentary job keeps you in a chair all day. If you picture someone seated for hours, you have the meaning.

traps.why: Sofa gaming is the opposite of athletic habits.
Theo wants to change his habits, so they weren't healthy ones.
Cross-country is competitive, but he's changing habits of sitting on the sofa.

sc1.tip: Theo spent the summer 'mostly playing video games on the sofa' and wants to change that by running. The blank describes habits with little movement.

sc2.sentence: Because her new job kept her at a desk for eight hours each day, Aunt Rosa's routine became _____, so she started taking evening walks.

traps.why: Sitting at a desk all day is the opposite of athletic.
Sedimentary describes layered rock, not a daily routine.
Nothing about eight desk hours is adventurous; the clue is the sitting.

sc2.tip: 'Because' her job 'kept her at a desk for eight hours,' her days involved lots of sitting. That's why she started walking.

hoax.hook: Picture a toy submarine wearing a fake monster head and fooling the whole world: that famous Loch Ness photo was a hoax.

traps.why: Truth is the opposite of a hoax, which is meant to fool you.
Hoard looks like hoax, but it means a hidden pile of things.
Hoaxes can seem mysterious, but a hoax is a trick, not an unsolved puzzle.

syn1.tip: Think of headlines like "the moon landing hoax" or "a hoax phone call." Each one is about someone trying to fool people on purpose.

traps.why: A real discovery is true, the opposite of a fake meant to fool you.
Mistakes also spread wrong ideas, but a hoax is done on purpose.
Hoaxes often involve monsters, but the hoax is the trick itself.

syn2.tip: A hoax is never an accident. Look for the choice that shows someone fooling people on purpose.

traps.why: A toy with a fake head is the opposite of a real discovery.
The photo showed a creature, but the clue says it was really a toy.
Once it was revealed as a toy, it was no longer a mystery.

sc1.tip: The clue is "actually a toy submarine with a fake head attached." Something faked to fool people is a hoax.

sc2.sentence: Everyone believed the news that school was canceled for a week, but the message turned out to be a _____ sent by an older student as an April Fools' prank.

traps.why: A fact is true, but this message was a prank.
A promise is a kind of message, but it is not meant to fool people.
Secrets are hidden, but this message was shared to trick everyone.

sc2.tip: The word "but" shows the news was not real, and "April Fools' prank" tells you it was a trick meant to fool people.

alleviate.hook: Picture an ice pack on a twisted ankle: it does not cure the injury, but it alleviates the pain.

traps.why: Worsen is the opposite: it makes pain or a problem worse.
Elevate looks similar, but it means to lift something higher.
Cure is too strong; alleviate only makes a problem less severe.

syn1.tip: Think of medicine ads that "alleviate headache pain." The medicine makes the pain smaller, so alleviate means to ease.

traps.why: Intensify means to make stronger, the opposite of alleviate.
Eliminate means to remove completely; alleviate just makes it lighter.
Doctors diagnose problems, but that means finding them, not easing them.

syn2.tip: Alleviate is about making a heavy problem lighter. Pick the word for taking some of the pain or weight away.

traps.why: A second lunch period makes crowding smaller, not bigger.
The principal did more than watch; he took action to fix it.
Elevate looks like alleviate but means to raise up.

sc1.tip: Look at "so fewer students would be eating at the same time." The new lunch period makes the crowding problem less severe.

sc2.sentence: The medicine did not cure Leo's cold, but it did _____ his stuffy nose and sore throat enough for him to sleep through the night.

traps.why: The sentence says the medicine did not cure the cold.
A worse sore throat would not help Leo sleep.
Trigger means to start symptoms, but the medicine helped him.

sc2.tip: The contrast "did not cure... but it did" points to something less than a cure. "Enough for him to sleep" shows it eased his symptoms.

mediocre.hook: A mediocre pizza is the one you eat and never mention again: not bad, not good, just plain okay.

traps.why: Excellent means very good, the opposite of mediocre.
Terrible is too strong; mediocre is ordinary, not awful.
Medical starts the same way but is about doctors and health.

syn1.tip: Mediocre is what you call something that is just okay. Its feeling is a little disappointed, like a C grade.

traps.why: Truly outstanding is the opposite of mediocre.
That is too strong; mediocre things are only ordinary.
Medi- hints at middle, but mediocre describes quality, not location.

syn2.tip: People say "mediocre at best" about a show or meal that let them down. It means ordinary and nothing special.

traps.why: The "but" shows the film did not live up to the amazing trailer.
The sentence says it was "not terrible," so dreadful is too strong.
Animated describes the kind of movie, not how good it was.

sc1.tip: The words after the colon restate the blank: "not terrible, but not good enough to recommend." That describes something merely average.

sc2.sentence: Everyone raved about the new pizza place, but Leah found its pizza _____, no better than the frozen kind her family buys at the grocery store.

traps.why: The "but" shows Leah disagreed with everyone who raved.
Too strong; it was just no better than ordinary frozen pizza.
Price is a different topic; the clue compares how good it tasted.

sc2.tip: "Everyone raved... but Leah" signals she did not agree, and "no better than the frozen kind" means only ordinary.

relentless.hook: To relent is to ease up, and -less means without, so relentless rain falls without ever easing up.

traps.why: Occasional means happening only now and then, the opposite of relentless.
Restless rhymes with relentless, but it means unable to sit still.
Relentless things can be powerful, but relentless is about never stopping.

syn1.tip: Split it: relent plus -less. To relent is to give up or ease off, so relentless means without ever easing off.

traps.why: Stopping now and then is the opposite of relentless.
That describes restless, a word that looks like relentless.
Relentless things may be loud, but the word means they never stop.

syn2.tip: Think of a relentless defender in basketball who guards you every second of the game. The word is about never stopping.

traps.why: Wind that lasts nine days is not brief.
The plain is frozen, and the clue is about never pausing.
Sudden is about how it starts, not lasting nine days.

sc1.tip: The clue is "blew for nine days without a single pause." Wind that never stops is relentless.

sc2.sentence: Most players would have given up after falling behind by twenty points, but Mia was _____, chasing every loose ball until the final buzzer.

traps.why: The "but" shows Mia did not give up like most players.
Mia may be talented, but the clue is about never stopping.
A lazy player would not chase every ball until the end.

sc2.tip: "Most players would have given up... but Mia" sets up a contrast, and "until the final buzzer" shows she never let up.

benign.hook: Benign comes from Latin bene, meaning well, so a benign bump is one the doctor says will leave you well.

traps.why: Dangerous is the opposite of benign.
Bene- means good, but benign means harmless, not actively helpful.
Benign bumps are often small, but benign is about being safe.

syn1.tip: Doctors say a lump is "benign" when it is nothing to worry about. The bene- start has a good, safe feeling.

traps.why: Likely to cause harm is the opposite of benign.
Size is a different idea; benign things can be big but safe.
Pain is related to injuries, but benign means it will not harm you.

syn2.tip: A benign bump is the good news at the doctor. Look for the choice meaning safe, nothing to worry about.

traps.why: The beetle "would not hurt anyone," so it is not poisonous.
The beetle is bright red, but the clue is about being safe.
Rare is about how often you see it, not whether it hurts.

sc1.tip: "Though... looked dangerous" sets up a contrast, and "would not hurt anyone" tells you the beetle is harmless.

sc2.sentence: Because the snake in the garden turned out to be _____, Dad let it slither away instead of calling animal control to remove it.

traps.why: Dad would call for help if the snake were deadly.
Hunger has nothing to do with whether Dad needed help.
A huge snake would more likely make Dad call animal control.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals cause and effect. Dad let the snake go "instead of calling animal control," so it must be safe.

bland.hook: Picture a bowl of plain white rice with no butter, no salt, and no sauce: that is bland.

traps.why: Spicy food is full of flavor, the opposite of bland.
Rotten food tastes bad, but bland food has little taste at all.
Blond looks like bland but describes light yellow hair.

syn1.tip: Think of a "bland diet" for an upset stomach: plain toast and rice with no spices. Bland means lacking flavor.

traps.why: Exciting is the opposite of bland, which means dull.
Cold food can be unpleasant, but bland is about lacking flavor or interest.
Salt adds flavor, which bland food is missing.

syn2.tip: Bland works for food and for other things: a bland speech or bland colors. Either way, nothing about it stands out.

traps.why: The cook forgot the spices, so the stew could not be spicy.
Burnt is a cooking problem, but the clue is about missing spices.
Hot sauce was added "to give it some flavor," not warmth.

sc1.tip: The cook "forgot to add any spices," so campers wanted "to give it some flavor." The stew had no flavor.

sc2.sentence: The speaker's talk was so _____ that even the teachers struggled to stay awake; he never changed his tone or told a single joke.

traps.why: A lively talk would keep the teachers awake.
Loudness is about volume, and a loud talk would keep people awake.
Nothing shows anger; the clue says he never changed his tone.

sc2.tip: After the semicolon, "never changed his tone or told a single joke" explains the blank. A talk like that is dull.

avid.hook: An avid fan never misses a game, wears the jersey every Saturday, and knows every player's name by heart.

traps.why: Uninterested is the opposite of avid.
Vivid looks like avid but means bright and clear.
Avid people often get skilled, but avid means eager, not talented.

syn1.tip: You hear the phrase "avid reader" for someone who can't put books down. Avid has a happy, excited feeling.

traps.why: Unwilling is the opposite of avid, which means very eager.
Greedy is negative, but avid is a positive word for eagerness.
Experience comes from doing something a lot, but avid means eager.

syn2.tip: Think of an "avid fan" or "avid gardener." It describes someone who loves doing something and does it as often as possible.

traps.why: A reluctant reader would not read everywhere he goes.
Reading late might make him sleepy, but the clue shows his eagerness.
Vivid looks like avid but means bright, which does not describe a reader.

sc1.tip: The examples "at breakfast, on the bus, and under his blanket with a flashlight" show Jun is very eager to read.

sc2.sentence: Lily used to complain about every family hike, but after one trip to the mountains she became so _____ about hiking that she now plans a new trail every weekend.

traps.why: The "but" shows Lily stopped complaining and started loving hikes.
Hiking can make people nervous, but she plans trails eagerly.
Nothing suggests confusion; planning hikes weekly shows excitement.

sc2.tip: "Used to complain... but" signals a change, and "plans a new trail every weekend" shows she is now very eager.

dubious.hook: Dubious and doubt come from the same Latin family, so a dubious claim is one that fills you with doubt.

traps.why: Certain means sure, the opposite of doubtful.
Curious people ask questions, but dubious means you don't believe something.
Studious ends the same way but means hardworking at school.

syn1.tip: The -ous ending means full of, and dubious is full of doubt. Think of a "dubious excuse" that nobody believes.

traps.why: Completely convinced is the opposite of dubious.
An easily fooled person believes everything, the opposite of a dubious one.
Confused means not understanding; dubious means not believing.

syn2.tip: Say it slowly: dubious sounds a bit like doubt. Its feeling is suspicious, like when an ad seems too good to be true.

traps.why: A convinced buyer would not stop to read reviews first.
Too strong; Grandpa is just unsure, so he checks the reviews.
Delighted is a happy feeling, but Grandpa does not trust the promise.

sc1.tip: "Promised... overnight, but Grandpa" signals a contrast. He "decided to read reviews before spending any money," so he doubts the claim.

sc2.sentence: Since the website had no contact address and dozens of spelling mistakes, Maria felt _____ about its promise of a free phone and closed the page.

traps.why: A confident person would not close the page right away.
Grateful is a warm feeling, but Maria does not trust the site.
Studious looks similar but means hardworking, which does not fit.

sc2.tip: "Since" signals a cause: "no contact address" and "spelling mistakes" are warning signs, so Maria doubted the offer and "closed the page."

concede.hook: On election night the losing candidate concedes, stepping to the microphone to admit that the other person won.

traps.why: Deny means to say something is not true, the opposite of concede.
Conceal looks like concede but means to hide.
People argue before they concede, but arguing is not admitting.

syn1.tip: Think of "conceding defeat" in a game or election. You admit the other side was right or won, even if you don't want to.

traps.why: Insisting something is false is the opposite of conceding it.
That means conceal, a word that looks like concede.
Arguing comes before conceding; conceding means you finally accept the point.

syn2.tip: When you concede a point in an argument, you stop fighting it. Look for the choice that means agreeing something is true.

traps.why: "Finally" shows she stopped arguing, so she did not deny it.
Conceal looks like concede but means hide, which does not fit.
She doubted the answer before; "finally" shows she now accepts it.

sc1.tip: "Although she had argued for an hour" sets up a contrast, and "finally had to" shows she unwillingly admitted her classmate was right.

sc2.sentence: When the scoreboard showed his team losing by thirty points with one minute left, the coach decided to _____ defeat, knowing a comeback was impossible.

traps.why: He knew "a comeback was impossible," so he would not deny losing.
Celebrate is a happy word, but losing by thirty is not cheerful.
He knew he could not prevent the loss, since a comeback was impossible.

sc2.tip: "Losing by thirty points" and "knowing a comeback was impossible" cause the coach to admit his team had lost.

ordeal.hook: Long ago an ordeal was a painful test, like walking on hot coals; now it means any terrible experience you must endure.

traps.why: A delight is a happy experience, the opposite of an ordeal.
Order looks like the start of ordeal but means a command or arrangement.
Journeys can be hard, but a journey is a trip, not a painful experience.

syn1.tip: Here trial means a hard test you must get through, as in "trials and troubles." An ordeal is a long, painful experience.

traps.why: A pleasant adventure is the opposite of an ordeal.
Too weak; an ordeal is very painful or difficult, not a minor bother.
Some ordeals happen on trips, but a long trip isn't necessarily painful.

syn2.tip: People say "what an ordeal" after something miserable, like a long hospital stay. The word has a heavy, unhappy feeling.

traps.why: Two days stuck on hard chairs with no food is not a success.
Too weak; two miserable days is much worse than an inconvenience.
Bargains are about cost, but the clue describes suffering.

sc1.tip: The details "stuck for two days," "sleeping on hard chairs," and "almost no food" describe a long, painful experience.

sc2.sentence: The dentist visit Max had dreaded for weeks turned out to be quick and painless, not the long _____ he had imagined.

traps.why: Max "dreaded" the visit, so he did not imagine a reward.
Celebration is happy, but Max expected something he dreaded.
Order looks like ordeal but means a command, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Quick and painless, not the long" sets up a contrast. The blank is the opposite of painless, something Max "dreaded."

agitated.hook: A washing machine's agitator churns clothes back and forth; an agitated person feels that same churning inside.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of agitated.
Agile looks similar but means quick and nimble.
Cheerful is lively but happy; agitated is lively in a nervous, upset way.

syn1.tip: Picture a washing machine churning clothes. An agitated person feels churned up inside, nervous and unable to settle.

traps.why: Calm and steady is the opposite of agitated.
Busy people move a lot too, but happily, not nervously.
Quick and nimble describes agile, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Agitated people can't sit still because they are worried. Look for a choice showing both nerves and movement.

traps.why: Peaceful is the opposite; stamping and pacing show the horses were not peaceful.
Barn horses get hungry, but nervous pacing during thunder points to fear.
Agile looks similar but means nimble, not nervous.

sc1.tip: The clue is "stamping their hooves and pacing nervously." Those actions show animals that are upset and can't calm down.

sc2.sentence: Although my little brother usually sleeps calmly through the night, he was _____ before his first day of school, tossing, turning, and asking questions until midnight.

traps.why: Peaceful is the opposite; tossing and turning shows he couldn't settle.
Sleep is the topic, but he stayed up until midnight worrying.
Cheerful is too happy; tossing and turning shows nerves.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a change from "calmly," and "tossing, turning" shows a nervous, restless boy.

outspoken.hook: Break it apart: an outspoken person speaks out, saying exactly what they think for everyone to hear.

traps.why: Shy is the opposite of outspoken.
Rude is negative; outspoken just means openly honest, not mean.
Talkative means talking a lot; outspoken means boldly sharing opinions.

syn1.tip: Think of "speaking out" about something you believe. An outspoken person says what they think openly.

traps.why: Quiet and private is the opposite of outspoken.
Outspoken isn't about words already spoken; it describes a bold speaker.
Outspoken people are honest, not necessarily mean.

syn2.tip: Outspoken describes a person, not words. It means someone who boldly speaks out with their views.

traps.why: Timid fits her shy brother, but "unlike" means Nadia is different.
Gloomy is about mood; the clue is about sharing opinions freely.
Outnumbered starts the same way but means having fewer people on your side.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her shy brother, who rarely shares his views" sets up a contrast. Nadia must boldly share hers.

sc2.sentence: Because Marcus is so _____ about fairness, he stood up in the cafeteria and told the principal that the new lunch rules punished everyone for one person's mistake.

traps.why: Quiet is the opposite; he spoke up to the principal.
Rude is too negative; he spoke honestly about fairness, not to insult.
Unsure people hesitate; standing up to the principal shows boldness.

sc2.tip: "Because" links cause and effect. He "stood up" and "told the principal," so he speaks out boldly.

nemesis.hook: In Greek myth, Nemesis was the goddess of payback; today your nemesis is the rival who always stands in your way.

traps.why: An ally is on your side, the opposite of a nemesis.
A coach is part of competition but helps you instead of opposing you.
A champion is a winner; a nemesis is the opponent you keep facing.

syn1.tip: Think of a superhero's nemesis, the villain who keeps coming back. It names the opponent you can't seem to beat.

traps.why: A loyal partner helps you, the opposite of a nemesis.
A first-time challenger is new; a nemesis battles you again and again.
A minor annoyance is too weak; a nemesis is a serious, lasting foe.

syn2.tip: A nemesis keeps showing up to beat you, like Batman's Joker. Look for an opponent you face again and again.

traps.why: A partner plays beside you; Claire kept losing to this player.
Coaches are in tennis, but Claire lost the final to another player.
Claire is a player, not a teacher; the clue describes a repeat opponent.

sc1.tip: "For three straight years" she "lost... to the same player." That repeated, tough opponent is her long-time rival.

sc2.sentence: Although the two chess players smile and shake hands before every match, each considers the other a _____, since they have battled for the school title five years in a row.

traps.why: Teammates play together; these two battle against each other.
They have met for five years, so they are hardly strangers.
Players who've battled for the title five years are not beginners.

sc2.tip: "Although" tells you the smiles hide something. "Battled for the school title five years in a row" shows long-time rivals.

inflict.hook: Bullies inflict pain and storms inflict damage; the word always arrives carrying something harmful.

traps.why: Prevent means stop something from happening, the opposite of inflict.
Infect looks similar but means spread germs or disease.
The victim suffers harm; inflicting means doing the harm to someone.

syn1.tip: You "inflict pain" or "inflict damage." Something that inflicts harm makes it happen to someone else.

traps.why: Healing fixes harm, the opposite of inflicting it.
Spreading germs is infect, a lookalike word.
Feeling pain is what happens to the victim, not the one inflicting it.

syn2.tip: Inflict always comes with something bad: wounds, damage, punishment. Choose the phrase about making harm happen.

traps.why: Repair is the opposite; the storm made the damage.
People measure damage, but dented cars show the storm caused it.
Prevent means stop; the dents and bare trees prove damage happened.

sc1.tip: Look at "denting parked cars and stripping nearly every apple." The storm did the harm, so the verb must mean cause.

sc2.sentence: The coach warned that a single careless tackle could _____ a serious injury on a teammate, so she made everyone practice safe blocking for a whole week.

traps.why: A careless tackle can't heal anyone; it causes harm.
The teammate would suffer the injury; the tackle causes it.
A careless tackle causes injuries rather than preventing them.

sc2.tip: "Careless tackle" and "serious injury" point to harm, and "so" shows the coach wants to stop the tackle from causing it.

slander.hook: Slander throws mud: false words tossed at someone to stain their good name.

traps.why: Praise means say good things, the opposite of slander.
Slumber looks similar but means sleep.
Teasing is often playful; slander is lying to ruin someone's name.

syn1.tip: Slander means spreading lies to damage someone's good name. Picture mud smeared on a clean reputation.

traps.why: Speaking well of someone is the opposite of slander.
Fair criticism is true; slander is false and hurtful.
Joking around is friendly; slander is meant to harm.

syn2.tip: The key to slander is that the words are false and hurtful. Pick the choice that includes lying.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite; a jealous rival spreading rumors wants to hurt her.
Copying recipes isn't spreading lies; "false rumors" points to damaging talk.
Defend means protect, but false rumors attack her.

sc1.tip: "Jealous" and "spreading false rumors" tell you the baker wanted to hurt her reputation with lies.

sc2.sentence: Instead of praising the new mayor for fixing the park, the angry letter tried to _____ her, claiming falsely that she had stolen money from the town budget.

traps.why: Thanking is kind; the letter made false claims to hurt her.
Electing is about mayors, but false claims of stealing attack her name.
Flattering means praising too much, the opposite of what the letter did.

sc2.tip: "Instead of praising" signals a contrast, and "claiming falsely" shows the letter spread lies to hurt her name.

regal.hook: Regal comes from the Latin word for king, the same root found in "reign" and "royal."

traps.why: Humble means modest and plain, the opposite of regal.
Legal looks and sounds similar but means allowed by law.
Kings are often rich, but regal means fit for royalty, not rich.

syn1.tip: Regal shares a root with "reign" and "royal." Think of crowns and thrones.

traps.why: Poor and plain is the opposite of regal grandeur.
Allowed by law means legal, a lookalike word.
Boastful is negative; regal is a positive, dignified word.

syn2.tip: Picture a queen on her throne. Regal describes anything grand enough to belong to royalty.

traps.why: Shabby means worn out, the opposite of a jeweled crown.
Legal looks similar but means allowed by law.
Actors can be nervous, but she "swept grandly," showing royal dignity.

sc1.tip: "Velvet cape," "jeweled crown," and "swept grandly" all paint a picture of royalty, so the blank needs a royal word.

sc2.sentence: Our scruffy mutt usually looks silly, but after his bath and haircut he sat on the porch with his head held high, looking almost _____.

traps.why: Ridiculous matches "silly," but "but" signals a change.
Dogs on porches nap, but a head held high shows pride.
Legal looks like regal but means allowed by law.

sc2.tip: "But" flips "silly" around, and "head held high" shows a proud, dignified look, like a king.

sleek.hook: Picture a wet seal gliding through water, its fur smooth and shining: that is sleek.

traps.why: Rough is the opposite of sleek.
Sleepy looks similar but means tired.
Sleek things often look fast, but sleek describes a smooth shape.

syn1.tip: Picture a seal's wet, shiny fur or a race car's curves. Sleek means smooth and glossy.

traps.why: Bumpy and dull is the opposite of sleek.
Sleek things may be fast, but sleek is about looks, not power.
Drowsy describes sleepy, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Sleek shapes have no bumps or rough edges, like a dolphin's body. Choose the phrase about a smooth, glossy look.

traps.why: Clunky means bulky and awkward, the opposite of a glossy, rounded nose.
Trains can be noisy, but the clue describes shape and shine.
Sleepy looks similar but means tired.

sc1.tip: A "glossy, rounded nose" that can "slice through the air" describes a smooth, streamlined shape.

sc2.sentence: My old bike was rusty and covered in scratches, but my new one is _____, with glossy black paint and curved lines that gleam in the sunlight.

traps.why: Battered fits the old bike, but "but" means the new one is different.
Weight is about bikes, but glossy, gleaming paint describes a shiny look.
Squeaky is a sound; the clue describes glossy, gleaming paint.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the new bike with the "rusty" old one, and "glossy black paint" points to a smooth, shiny look.

devout.hook: Devout sounds like devoted; a devout person stays loyal to their faith or cause, year after year.

traps.why: Disloyal is the opposite of devout.
Devious looks similar but means sneaky and tricky.
Fanatical is extreme and negative; devout is sincere, steady faith.

syn1.tip: Devout is close to "devoted." A devout person gives steady, sincere loyalty to a faith or a cause.

traps.why: Barely interested is the opposite of devout.
Sneaky and sly describes devious, a lookalike word.
Fans can be loud, but devout means steady, deep loyalty.

syn2.tip: Picture someone who never misses a service or a game. Devout describes loyalty that runs deep and lasts.

traps.why: A casual fan wouldn't attend every game for fifty years.
Devious looks similar but means sneaky.
Famous is about being known; the clue shows loyalty.

sc1.tip: "For fifty years" and "never missed a home game, even during the coldest snowstorms" show deep, lasting loyalty.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa is a _____ gardener; while the rest of us stay indoors on rainy mornings, he is outside at dawn caring for his roses, just as he has for forty years.

traps.why: A lazy gardener wouldn't work at dawn in the rain.
He has gardened for forty years, so he isn't new.
Part-time is too weak; he gardens every rainy dawn for forty years.

sc2.tip: The contrast "while the rest of us stay indoors" and "for forty years" show Grandpa's steady, deep devotion.

temperate.hook: Temperate weather keeps the temperature in the comfortable middle, never blazing hot or freezing cold.

traps.why: Extreme is the opposite of temperate.
Temporary looks similar but means lasting a short time.
Tropical is a climate word, but it means hot and humid.

syn1.tip: Temperate starts like "temperature." A temperate climate keeps its temperature in a comfortable middle range.

traps.why: Very harsh is the opposite of temperate.
Lasting a short time means temporary, a lookalike word.
Rain is weather, but temperate is about mild temperatures.

syn2.tip: Temperate places avoid both blazing heat and bitter cold. Look for the choice meaning balanced, in the middle.

traps.why: Harsh is the opposite; gentle summers show a mild climate.
Dry is about rain, but the clue is about heat and cold.
Temporary looks similar but means lasting a short time.

sc1.tip: "Unlike scorching deserts and freezing poles" rules out both extremes, and "gentle summers" confirms a mild climate.

sc2.sentence: Grandma moved to the coast because its _____ weather, never too hot in July and never too cold in January, let her garden almost all year.

traps.why: Fierce weather is extreme; this weather is never too hot or cold.
Storms are weather, but the clue is about gentle temperatures.
Humid is about dampness; the clue describes mild temperatures.

sc2.tip: The phrase right after the blank, "never too hot... and never too cold," restates the missing word. It means mild.

perish.hook: Perishable food goes bad fast; to perish is to die or be destroyed.

traps.why: Survive is the opposite of perish.
Punish looks similar but means make someone pay for wrongdoing.
Sicken is too weak; perish means actually die.

syn1.tip: Food labeled "perishable" can spoil and go bad. To perish is to die or be destroyed.

traps.why: Being rescued is the opposite of perishing.
Lost things may be forgotten, but perish means die or be destroyed.
Weakened is too mild; perish means gone for good.

syn2.tip: People "perish in a shipwreck" and plants "perish in a frost." Pick the choice meaning gone for good.

traps.why: Flourish means grow well, the opposite of what drought does.
Sprouting is about plants, but these are already growing and lack water.
Perch looks similar but means sit up high, like a bird.

sc1.tip: "Without enough water during the long drought" is the cause. What happens to plants with no water? They die.

sc2.sentence: While the sturdy oak survived the forest fire, the young pine trees nearby were not so lucky and began to _____ in the flames.

traps.why: Thrive matches the oak, but "not so lucky" shows the pines did worse.
Swaying is just moving; "not so lucky" and "flames" show destruction.
Sprouting is plant growth, which doesn't happen in flames.

sc2.tip: "While the sturdy oak survived" sets up a contrast, and "not so lucky" tells you the pines were destroyed.

hypothetical.hook: Hypothetical questions start with "what if": what if dogs could talk? They imagine things rather than report facts.

traps.why: Proven means shown to be true, the opposite of something only imagined.
Hypnotic starts like hypothetical but means putting someone into a trance.
Scientists use hypothetical cases, but scientific means based on science, not imagined.

syn1.tip: Think of "a hypothetical situation" that begins with "what if." It is supposed or pretend, not real.

traps.why: Factual means based on facts, the opposite of imagined.
Hysterical looks similar but means wildly emotional or very funny.
Hypothetical questions can be hard, but hypothetical means imagined, not hard.

syn2.tip: Hypothetical goes with "what if." Anything you answer with "what if" is imagined, not something that really happened.

traps.why: No one has visited such a planet, so the question cannot be about facts.
Historical means about the past, but this trip has never happened.
Hysterical looks similar but means wildly emotional, which makes no sense here.

sc1.tip: Look at "no one has ever visited" and "what would you pack if you could." The question is about something imagined.

sc2.sentence: Although the robot invasion in our debate was only _____, the class argued about it as seriously as if real robots were marching down Main Street.

traps.why: "As if real robots" shows the invasion was not actual.
The class was serious, but "although" says the invasion itself was not real.
Hypnotic looks similar but means causing a trance, not imagined.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with "as if real robots." The invasion must be the opposite of real: imagined.

homage.hook: When a band plays a famous song to honor the person who wrote it, they pay homage: a public bow of respect.

traps.why: An insult shows disrespect, the opposite of homage.
Hostage ends like homage but means a captured person.
A monument can honor someone, but homage is the respect itself.

syn1.tip: You "pay homage" the way you "pay tribute": both mean showing public honor to someone.

traps.why: Mockery makes fun of someone, the opposite of showing respect.
Homage starts with "hom" but has nothing to do with home.
People "pay" homage, but they pay it with respect, not money.

syn2.tip: Homage usually follows "pay," as in "pay homage to a hero." Think honor and respect shown openly.

traps.why: You can pay money, but recreating his scene honors him rather than pays him.
Scorn is disrespect, but she copied the scene of her favorite director.
Postage ends like homage but is the cost of mailing something.

sc1.tip: She copied a scene by her "favorite director," "shot for shot." That is a way of honoring him.

sc2.sentence: Instead of mocking the old cartoon, the animators paid _____ to it, hiding tiny drawings of its characters throughout their new movie as a respectful thank-you.

traps.why: "Instead of mocking" tells you they did the opposite of mockery.
Damages are money paid for harm, but this was a thank-you.
Mileage ends like homage but means distance traveled.

sc2.tip: "Instead of mocking" signals the opposite, and "respectful thank-you" restates it. They showed honor.

spectacle.hook: Spect means look: a spectacle is so dazzling everyone stares, like fireworks bursting over a dark lake.

traps.why: "Spectacles" can mean glasses, but one spectacle is an impressive sight.
Speck starts the same but means a tiny spot, nothing impressive.
An audience watches a spectacle, but the spectacle is the thing seen.

syn1.tip: Spect means look, as in spectator. A spectacle is something to look at, a remarkable sight.

traps.why: A spectacle is impressive, the opposite of dull.
Spect means look, but a spectacle is what you see, not careful looking.
Crowds gather at a spectacle, but they are not the spectacle.

syn2.tip: Think of "quite a spectacle" at a parade or fireworks show. It names a big, eye-catching display.

traps.why: Spectators are the people staring; the lights are what they stare at.
The lights were "amazing" and "painting the sky," not disappointing.
A forecast predicts the sky; the lights were actually filling it.

sc1.tip: "Amazing," "waves of green and purple," and "the whole campground staring upward" describe an impressive sight.

sc2.sentence: The tiny town's Fourth of July parade was usually just three tractors and a fire truck, but this year's hot air balloons made it a real _____.

traps.why: "But" contrasts the usual small parade, so this year was impressive, not a letdown.
A spectator watches; the parade itself cannot be one.
The parade was a tradition already; the balloons made it impressive, not traditional.

sc2.tip: "Usually just three tractors" plus "but" means this year was the opposite of plain. Look for an impressive sight.

unrest.hook: Un + rest: when a crowd cannot rest easy because it is angry and stirred up, there is unrest.

traps.why: Calm is peace and quiet, the opposite of unrest.
Un + rest might suggest tiredness, but unrest means angry disturbance.
A riot is a violent outburst; unrest is widespread anger, often milder.

syn1.tip: You often hear "political unrest" or "unrest in the streets." It means people are upset and things are stirred up.

traps.why: Peaceful order is the opposite of an angry, stirred-up situation.
Unrest is stronger than worry; people are angry and disturbed.
A celebration can be noisy, but it is happy, and unrest is angry.

syn2.tip: Split it: un + rest. A group that cannot settle down because people are angry is in unrest.

traps.why: Excitement is happy, but students were complaining about losing recess.
Contentment means satisfied, the opposite of complaining loudly.
No recess might be boring, but petitions show anger, not boredom.

sc1.tip: Recess was "canceled" and students "complained loudly and started petitions." That shows anger spreading.

sc2.sentence: Although the cafeteria had been peaceful all year, _____ broke out when the new menu replaced pizza Friday with boiled spinach, and students began chanting in protest.

traps.why: "Although" contrasts the peaceful past, and chanting in protest is not calm.
Applause is approval, but students were protesting the spinach.
The topic is food, but "chanting in protest" shows anger, not hunger.

sc2.tip: "Although... peaceful" signals a change to the opposite, and "chanting in protest" shows angry disturbance.

utmost.hook: Utmost care means the most care you possibly can give, like carrying a full fishbowl across a crowded room.

traps.why: Least means the smallest amount, the opposite of utmost.
Average is ordinary; utmost is the highest possible.
Utmost often comes before "care," but it means greatest, not careful.

syn1.tip: Utmost has "most" inside it. Think of "the utmost care": the most care possible.

traps.why: Lowest possible is the opposite of highest possible.
Fairly large is too weak; utmost means the very greatest.
Utmost has "most" in it but has nothing to do with time.

syn2.tip: Look for "most" at the end of utmost. It means the greatest amount there can be.

traps.why: Gloves and a full hour show huge care, not the least.
An hour to cross one room is far beyond usual care.
Quickest clashes with taking a full hour to cross a single room.

sc1.tip: "Fragile," "soft gloves," and "a full hour to cross a single room" show the greatest care possible.

sc2.sentence: Mateo usually rushed through chores, but when babysitting his baby sister, he showed the _____ patience, reading her the same picture book eleven times without complaining.

traps.why: "But" turns away from rushing; eleven readings show great patience.
