His usual habit is rushing, so this patience was far beyond usual.
Eleven readings without complaining show long patience, not brief.

sc2.tip: "Usually rushed" plus "but" signals a change, and "eleven times without complaining" shows the greatest patience possible.

prolific.hook: A prolific apple tree drops more apples than you can pick; a prolific author fills whole shelves with books.

traps.why: Idle means doing nothing, the opposite of producing lots of work.
Professional also starts with "pro" but means doing something as a job.
Prolific people may become famous, but prolific means producing a lot.

syn1.tip: You often see "a prolific writer" or "a prolific scorer." Both produce a lot: many books or many goals.

traps.why: Producing little is the opposite of prolific.
Prolific is about how much someone makes, not how good it is.
Fairly busy is too weak; prolific means a great amount of work.

syn2.tip: Prolific is about quantity. Think of a garden or author that keeps turning out more and more.

traps.why: Sixty novels plus stories and plays is the opposite of slow.
She wrote mysteries, but the clue counts how many works she produced.
An occasional writer writes now and then, not sixty novels.

sc1.tip: "More than sixty mystery novels in addition to dozens of short stories and plays" is a huge amount of work.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his brother, who has finished only one painting in three years, Leo is so _____ that his bedroom walls are covered with dozens of new canvases.

traps.why: "Unlike" means Leo is the reverse of his slow brother.
Covered walls might look messy, but the clue is how much he paints.
Professional starts like prolific but means working as a job.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his brother" who finished "only one painting" signals the opposite: Leo produces "dozens."

restless.hook: Rest + less: without rest, a restless kid squirms, taps a pencil, and checks the clock every minute.

traps.why: Calm means still and relaxed, the opposite of restless.
Without rest sounds like tired, but restless means unable to stay still.
Careless also ends in -less but means not paying attention.

syn1.tip: Think of "restless legs" that keep bouncing. Restless means you cannot settle down or sit still.

traps.why: Calm and peaceful is the opposite of restless.
Rest can mean a break, but restless means fidgety, not hardworking.
Restless people may be uneasy, but they are not necessarily angry.

syn2.tip: Rest + less means without rest. A restless person cannot relax, so they keep moving and fidgeting.

traps.why: Tapping pencils and bouncing knees is the opposite of relaxed.
Without rest might sound sleepy, but bouncing knees shows too much energy.
Careless also ends in -less but means sloppy, not unable to sit still.

sc1.tip: "Tapped their pencils, bounced their knees, and stared out the windows" all show kids who cannot keep still.

sc2.sentence: After a long car ride, the puppy was anything but calm; she was so _____ that she ran circles around the yard and wouldn't stop jumping on everyone.

traps.why: "Anything but calm" rules out peaceful.
Long rides can make you sleepy, but she ran circles and kept jumping.
The car ride is the topic, but running and jumping show energy, not sickness.

sc2.tip: "Anything but calm" tells you the answer means the opposite of calm, and "ran circles" proves it.

rugged.hook: Picture a rugged mountain trail: jagged rocks and bumps that shake your jeep like a paint mixer.

traps.why: Smooth is even and flat, the opposite of rugged.
Rigid looks similar but means stiff and unbending.
Rugged mountains may be steep, but rugged means rough and uneven.

syn1.tip: Think of "rugged mountains" or "rugged terrain": land full of rocks and bumps, the rough kind.

traps.why: Flat and even is the opposite of rugged.
Rugged contains "rug" but has nothing to do with rugs.
Rugged land is often in mountains, but rugged means rough, not tall.

syn2.tip: Rugged describes ground you stumble on: rocks, ridges, and bumps. Think of a jeep bouncing on a rough trail.

traps.why: "Steep, uneven ground" is the opposite of flat.
Paved trails are smooth, but this one had jagged rocks and logs.
Rigid looks similar but means stiff, which does not describe a trail.

sc1.tip: "Jagged rocks, fallen logs, and steep, uneven ground" describe rough land. That is why they needed sturdy boots.

sc2.sentence: Our old pickup truck is so _____ that it has survived twenty winters, three floods, and my sister learning to drive without a single breakdown.

traps.why: A fragile truck would break; this one never broke down.
Old trucks can be rusty, but rust does not explain surviving everything.
Ragged looks similar but means torn and worn out, not tough.

sc2.tip: "Survived twenty winters, three floods" and "without a single breakdown" show the truck is tough. Rugged can mean sturdy.

cynical.hook: A cynical person hears "free gift" and immediately asks, "What's the catch?"

traps.why: Trusting means believing in people, the opposite of cynical.
Clinical sounds similar but means having to do with medical care.
A cynic doubts people's motives but is not necessarily mean to them.

syn1.tip: A cynical person always asks "What's the catch?" They distrust others and expect selfish reasons.

traps.why: Believing the best of people is the opposite of cynical.
Cynics may be gloomy, but cynical is about distrusting people's reasons.
Cynical is a firm belief that people are selfish, not mild doubt.

syn2.tip: Picture someone who thinks every kind act hides a selfish reason. That suspicion of motives is being cynical.

traps.why: A grateful uncle would thank her, not suspect she wanted something.
Cookies are involved, but the clue is about refusing to believe in kindness.
A trusting person would believe she was simply being kind.

sc1.tip: He "assumed she must want something in return" and refused "to believe anyone would be kind for no reason."

sc2.sentence: While her little brother still believes every toy commercial, Priya has grown _____ and assumes advertisers will say anything just to get her money.

traps.why: "While" contrasts her with her believing brother, so she is not trusting.
Money is mentioned, but Priya suspects advertisers; she is not greedy herself.
Clinical sounds similar but means medical or coldly scientific.

sc2.tip: "While" sets her against a brother who "still believes." She "assumes advertisers will say anything," so she distrusts them.

redundant.hook: "Free gift" and "tiny little" are redundant: the second word just repeats what the first already said.

traps.why: Essential means truly needed, the opposite of redundant.
Abundant rhymes with redundant but means plentiful.
Repeated words may sound clumsy, but redundant means needless, not confusing.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "free gift." Gifts are already free, so the word repeats itself. That is redundant.

traps.why: Absolutely necessary is the opposite of something you do not need.
Redundant is a criticism of writing, not praise.
Redundant words are easy to follow; the problem is that they repeat.

syn2.tip: Redundant things could be removed without losing anything, because they just say or do the same thing again.

traps.why: The editor crossed it out, so the phrase was not necessary.
Contradictory words disagree, but these "mean the same thing."
Abundant sounds like redundant but means plentiful.

sc1.tip: The editor crossed it out "because they mean the same thing." Using both words repeats the idea for no reason.

sc2.sentence: Coach bought three more boxes of bandages, but they were _____, simply duplicating the full boxes already sitting in our team's first-aid kit.

traps.why: The kit was already full, so the extra boxes were not essential.
Cost is not the point; "simply duplicating" tells you they repeated supplies.
Coach bought the boxes, so they were not missing, just extra.

sc2.tip: "Simply duplicating the full boxes already sitting in" the kit restates the answer: the new boxes repeat what was there.

supple.hook: A supple gymnast bends like a willow branch in the wind, curving easily without ever snapping.

traps.why: Rigid means stiff and unbending, the opposite of supple.
Subtle sounds a bit like supple but means slight or hard to notice.
Gymnasts are strong, but supple is about bending, not power.

syn1.tip: Picture a gymnast's supple muscles stretching into a split. The word describes something that bends easily.

traps.why: Hard to bend is the exact opposite of supple.
Supple looks like supply, but it has nothing to do with having plenty.
Quick movement is speed; supple is about bending without breaking.

syn2.tip: Think of fresh leather or a stretched muscle. Supple things bend and fold easily.

traps.why: Brittle describes the sun-baked leather that cracks, not the fresh leather.
Leather can be shiny, but the clue is about folding and bending.
Subtle sounds like supple but means slight, which does not fit folding.

sc1.tip: The word "but" sets fresh leather against leather that "turns stiff and cracks," so the blank means soft and easy to bend.

sc2.sentence: Because the yoga teacher had practiced stretching every morning for twenty years, her body was still _____ enough to touch her toes without bending her knees.

traps.why: A rigid body could not reach the toes; years of stretching cause bendiness.
Simple looks a little like supple but means plain or easy to understand.
Stretching can make you sore, but soreness does not help you touch your toes.

sc2.tip: "Stretching every morning for twenty years" is the cause; touching her toes easily is the effect, so the blank means able to bend.

paltry.hook: A paltry tip is so small it feels almost like an insult, like one penny for an hour of work.

traps.why: Huge is the opposite of paltry, which means pitifully small.
Salty rhymes with paltry but describes taste, not amount.
Paltry pay may feel unfair, but the word is about how little there is.

syn1.tip: You often hear "a paltry sum" for a disappointing amount of money. The word carries a feeling of being let down by smallness.

traps.why: More than enough is plenty, the opposite of paltry.
Poultry means chickens and turkeys; it only sounds like paltry.
Paltry money may be hard earned, but paltry describes its tiny size.

syn2.tip: Paltry amounts leave you wishing for more. Think of a paltry two dollars for a whole day of chores.

traps.why: Whopping means huge, but "hardly enough" for one ball shows the amount was tiny.
Fifteen dollars is exact, but the clue is about the amount being too small.
Respectable sounds pleased; the club is disappointed it was "hardly enough."

sc1.tip: "Hardly enough to buy even one new soccer ball" after "weeks of washing cars" tells you the amount was disappointingly small.

sc2.sentence: Although the movie star earned millions for every film, she left the waiter a _____ tip of only a few coins, which surprised everyone at the table.

traps.why: Lavish means very generous, but "only a few coins" is tiny.
Polite sounds kind, but the tip surprised everyone by being so small.
Tips are customary, but a usual tip would not surprise everyone.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets her millions against the tip, and "only a few coins" tells you the tip was pitifully small.

precocious.hook: Precocious comes from Latin for ripened early, like one fruit turning ripe long before the rest of the tree.

traps.why: Slow means behind others, the opposite of a precocious child's early talent.
Precious looks similar but means dear or valuable, not advanced early.
Pre- means before, but precocious means skilled early, not ready ahead of time.

syn1.tip: Pre- means before. A precocious child shows grown-up skills before most kids that age, like reading chapter books at four.

traps.why: Behind for age is the opposite of a precocious child's early skill.
Precocious kids have adult abilities, but they are young, not old.
Precious, which looks like precocious, can mean cute; precocious means advanced early.

syn2.tip: The pre- at the start means before. A precocious kid is ahead of schedule, doing things before others their age.

traps.why: Composing at five "when most children are just learning their letters" is not typical.
Precious looks like precocious but means dear, not early talented.
Music can be noisy, but the clue is about talent arriving early.

sc1.tip: "Composing his first pieces of music at age five, when most children are just learning their letters" shows talent far ahead of his age.

sc2.sentence: My little cousin is so _____ that at just six years old she beats adults at chess and reads her dad's science magazines for fun.

traps.why: Childish means immature, but she beats adults and reads grown-up magazines.
Precious looks similar but means dear, which would not explain beating adults.
She reads for fun, but being playful would not let her beat adults at chess.

sc2.tip: "So ... that" links the blank to its result: a six-year-old beating adults at chess is far ahead of her age.

apparition.hook: An apparition suddenly appears, pale and floating, then vanishes; the word is related to appear.

traps.why: Ghost costumes exist, but an apparition is the ghostly figure itself.
Partition looks similar but means a dividing wall.
Ghosts may haunt graveyards, but an apparition is the figure, not the place.

syn1.tip: Apparition is related to appear. It is something that suddenly appears, like a pale figure floating near a lake at night.

traps.why: Apparel looks similar but means clothing.
Monsters are scary too, but they have solid bodies; an apparition is ghostly.
Skeletons are spooky bones, but an apparition is a floating ghostly figure.

syn2.tip: Look for appear inside apparition. It names a ghostly figure that seems to appear out of nowhere.

traps.why: Castles have statues, but statues do not float.
Partition looks like apparition but means a dividing wall.
Castles have dungeons, but a dungeon cannot be pale and floating.

sc1.tip: "Pale, floating," "fog," and "old castle" set a spooky scene, and "turned out to be a curtain" means they mistook it for a ghost.

sc2.sentence: The shape drifting through the graveyard vanished straight through a stone wall, so the frightened campers decided it must have been an _____ rather than a person.

traps.why: Owls fly at night, but no owl can pass through a stone wall.
Apparatus looks similar but means a piece of equipment.
An intruder is a living person, and the campers decided it was not.

sc2.tip: "Vanished straight through a stone wall" causes their decision, and "rather than a person" tells you it was ghostly, not alive.

coerce.hook: To coerce is to squeeze someone with threats until they give in, like a bully demanding your lunch money.

traps.why: Allow means letting someone choose, the opposite of forcing them.
Persuade is the gentle, friendly version; coerce uses threats.
Curse sounds a bit like coerce but means to swear or cast a spell.

syn1.tip: You may hear that a confession was "coerced," meaning pressured out by threats. The word feels harsh and bullying.

traps.why: Letting someone choose is the opposite of forcing them.
Gently talking someone into something is friendly; coercing uses threats.
Co- often means together, but coerce means to force, not cooperate.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "coerced into it," said when someone had no real choice because they were threatened.

traps.why: Coaxing is gentle sweet talk, but the villain uses threats.
Bribing offers rewards, but the villain threatens to switch off electricity.
Curse sounds like coerce, but threats force obedience; they do not cast spells.

sc1.tip: "By threatening to switch off its electricity" shows the villain using threats, so the blank means force, not gentle persuasion.

sc2.sentence: Instead of kindly asking the younger kids to share the swings, the bully tried to _____ them into leaving by warning that he would break their bikes.

traps.why: Encourage is kind and supportive, but he is threatening to break bikes.
Charming wins people over nicely, which is the opposite of "instead of kindly asking."
A bribe offers a reward, but the bully only gives a threat.

sc2.tip: "Instead of kindly asking" signals a contrast, and "warning that he would break their bikes" is a threat, so the bully forces them.

wry.hook: A wry smile is crooked and knowing, the face you make when your umbrella breaks the moment it starts raining.

traps.why: Wiry looks like wry but means thin and tough.
Wry mockery is gentle; cruel is far too harsh.
Goofy humor is loud and silly; wry humor is quiet and dry.

syn1.tip: Think of "dry humor": a joke told with a straight face. A wry smile is a small, knowing grin at bad luck.

traps.why: Wry always has a bit of humor, so it is never completely serious.
Wry teasing is gentle, not cruel.
Rye bread is made from grain; wry only sounds like rye.

syn2.tip: Picture Dad's "wry smile" when the waterproof tent leaked. He is quietly amused at the irony, not angry or silly.

traps.why: The coach is not truly happy about the rain; he is joking dryly.
His joke is gentle and harmless, so cruel is far too strong.
Wiry looks like wry but describes a thin, tough body, not a grin.

sc1.tip: After a downpour, the coach jokes "at least the field won't need watering," a dry, ironic joke about bad luck.

sc2.sentence: Instead of complaining when the power went out during her birthday party, Mom made a _____ joke about finally getting a candlelit dinner, and everyone laughed.

traps.why: A nasty joke would be mean, but everyone laughed at her gentle humor.
Wiry looks like wry but means thin and tough, not dryly funny.
Tearful is sad, but "instead of complaining" Mom made everyone laugh.

sc2.tip: "Instead of complaining" tells you Mom chose humor, and joking about a "candlelit dinner" in a blackout is dry and ironic.

tarnish.hook: Silver left in damp air tarnishes, turning dark and dull, just as one lie can darken a good name.

traps.why: Polishing makes something shine, the opposite of tarnishing it.
Varnish looks and rhymes with tarnish but means coating wood with shiny finish.
Tarnish dulls or damages; destroy is far too strong.

syn1.tip: You hear of a "tarnished reputation" or tarnished silver. Both mean something once shiny or clean is now marked and dulled.

traps.why: Making something sparkle is the opposite of tarnishing it.
Tarnish only dulls a surface; smashing is much too strong.
Paint covers a surface, but tarnish is darkening that comes from damage.

syn2.tip: Picture an old silver spoon gone dark and spotty. That dark film is tarnish, and it dulls the shine.

traps.why: An angry outburst would hurt the reputation, not make it shine.
Varnish looks like tarnish but means coating wood, which makes no sense here.
They already earned the reputation; they fear the outburst would damage it.

sc1.tip: The reputation is "spotless" and they "worried" about an "angry outburst," so the blank means damage or stain it.

sc2.sentence: After a year in Grandma's damp basement, the silver trophy had begun to _____, its once gleaming surface now dull and covered in dark spots.

traps.why: Sparkle is the opposite of "dull and covered in dark spots."
Vanish rhymes with tarnish, but the trophy is still there with dark spots.
Cracking is damage, but the clue describes dullness and spots, not breaks.

sc2.tip: "Once gleaming" but "now dull and covered in dark spots" restates what the blank means: losing its shine.

meddle.hook: Meddle sounds like medal, but nobody wins a prize for meddling in a fight that is not theirs.

traps.why: Ignoring means staying out, the opposite of meddling.
Pedal rhymes with meddle but means pushing bike pedals.
Assist is welcome help; meddling is unwanted butting in.

syn1.tip: People say "stop meddling" or "don't meddle in my business." The word has a negative feeling of unwanted interference.

traps.why: Staying out of things is the opposite of meddling.
Medal sounds like meddle but is a prize, not interfering.
Lending a hand is welcome help; meddling is unwelcome.

syn2.tip: Think of a "meddling" neighbor who pokes into everyone's affairs. Meddling means getting involved where you aren't wanted.

traps.why: His advice was "unwanted" and made them angrier, so it was not help.
Listening quietly would not involve offering advice that made them angrier.
Tattling is telling an adult; Max is giving unwanted advice to his sisters.

sc1.tip: "Offering unwanted advice" in an argument that isn't his, which "only made both of them angrier," shows Max butting in.

sc2.sentence: Our neighbor means well, but she loves to _____ in everyone's business, rearranging our garden gnomes and telling my parents how to raise us.

traps.why: Investing in a business means putting in money, not rearranging gnomes.
"Means well, but" warns her actions are unwelcome, not real help.
Pedal rhymes with meddle but means pushing bike pedals.

sc2.tip: "Means well, but" signals something annoying, and moving our gnomes and telling parents how to raise us is interfering.

smother.hook: Smother has mother hidden inside: picture a mother bear hugging her cub so tightly it can hardly breathe.

traps.why: Smolder looks similar but means to burn slowly with smoke.
Igniting starts a fire; smothering puts it out by blocking air.
Smother contains mother, but it means cutting off air, not caring for.

syn1.tip: Think of smothering a fire with a blanket or lid. Covering it blocks the air, so it can't breathe.

traps.why: Fanning gives a fire more air, the opposite of smothering.
That is smolder, which only looks like smother.
Mother is inside smother, but the word means blocking air.

syn2.tip: Picture Grandma putting a heavy lid on a pan fire. Smother means covering something so no air gets in.

traps.why: Fanning adds air, but the lid is "cutting off their air."
Spraying water can fight fire, but a lid works by blocking air.
Feeding flames makes them grow, but these flames "went out."

sc1.tip: "Grabbed a metal lid" and "cutting off their air until they went out" tell you the blank means covering the fire so it can't breathe.

sc2.sentence: Instead of letting the campfire burn all night, the ranger piled thick dirt over it to _____ the last glowing coals.

traps.why: Relighting would keep the fire going, but the ranger is stopping it.
Campfires roast marshmallows, but dirt piled on coals is meant to put them out.
People poke campfire coals, but piled dirt covers them instead.

sc2.tip: "Instead of letting the campfire burn," the ranger "piled thick dirt over it," burying the coals and cutting off their air.

surly.hook: A surly person answers with a grunt and a scowl, like a bear woken too early from its nap.

traps.why: Polite is the opposite of surly.
Early looks like surly but is about time, not mood.
Surly is grumpy and rude; furious is much stronger anger.

syn1.tip: Picture a "surly clerk" who grunts and won't look up. Surly is a grumpy, unfriendly rudeness.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of surly.
Curly looks like surly but describes hair.
Tired people can be grumpy, but surly is about rudeness, not tiredness.

syn2.tip: Surly has a sour feeling. Think of someone grunting and snapping at you instead of saying hello.

traps.why: That fits a usually friendly driver, but he was grunting and snapping.
Early looks like surly, but grunting and snapping describe a mood, not time.
Being late is about time, but the clue describes rude behavior.

sc1.tip: "Usually friendly" signals a change, and "grunting instead of saying hello" and "snapping" describe a rude, grumpy mood.

sc2.sentence: Because the waiter was so _____ with every table, sighing loudly and rolling his eyes at questions, the restaurant manager finally asked him to work in the kitchen.

traps.why: A patient waiter would not sigh and roll his eyes at questions.
Clumsy waiters spill things, but sighing and eye rolling show rudeness.
Sighing and eye rolling are grumpy, not raging, so furious is too strong.

sc2.tip: "Sighing loudly and rolling his eyes at questions" shows rudeness, and that behavior causes the manager to move him away from customers.

reputable.hook: Reputable is built on reputation: a reputable brand has spent years earning people's trust.

traps.why: Unreliable is the opposite of reputable.
Repeatable looks similar but means able to be done again.
Popular means liked by many people, not necessarily trusted.

syn1.tip: Think of "reputation." A reputable business has a good reputation, so people respect it.

traps.why: Shady means dishonest, the opposite of reputable.
Refundable looks similar but means you can get your money back.
Trusted brands may cost more, but reputable is about trust, not price.

syn2.tip: Inside reputable is "repute," the root of "reputation." Someone with a good reputation is someone people trust.

traps.why: Doubtful sources are the random blogs she avoided.
Long sources might help a report, but the clue is about trust.
Repeatable only looks like reputable and means able to be repeated.

sc1.tip: "Such as university websites and well-known encyclopedias" versus "instead of random blogs" shows she chose trusted sources.

sc2.sentence: Because the repair shop had fixed cars honestly for forty years and earned glowing reviews, Mom called it the most _____ garage in town.

traps.why: Dishonest is the opposite of fixing cars honestly.
Forty years is long, but the clue is honest work and good reviews.
Reportable looks similar but means worth reporting.

sc2.tip: "Fixed cars honestly" and "earned glowing reviews" are the cause. The effect is a garage people trust.

artifact.hook: Picture a museum glass case full of clay pots and arrowheads: every one is an artifact made by human hands.

traps.why: A fossil is natural remains, not an object people made.
Artist looks similar but means a person who makes art.
An invention is newly created; an artifact comes from long ago.

syn1.tip: Artifact contains "art," meaning skill in making things. Think of objects people made long ago that end up in museums.

traps.why: Rocks form in nature; artifacts are made by people.
A modern machine is new, the opposite of an old artifact.
Artifact contains "fact," but it is an object, not information.

syn2.tip: Picture a museum display of old tools and pots. Artifacts are things people made and used long ago.

traps.why: Archaeologists dig up fossils too, but a carved pot was made by people.
Artist looks similar, but a pot is not a person.
Farmers grow crops, but the pot was something they made.

sc1.tip: "A carved clay pot" made by people and "the archaeologists uncovered" point to an old human-made object.

sc2.sentence: Jayden thought the rusty spoon he dug up was just junk, but the museum guide explained it was a real _____ used by settlers three hundred years ago.

traps.why: A replica is a copy, the opposite of a real old object.
Fossils are dug up, but a spoon is made by people.
Minerals are found in the ground naturally; settlers made the spoon.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "just junk," and "used by settlers three hundred years ago" shows an old object people made.

culprit.hook: Every mystery ends by naming the culprit: the one whose sticky fingerprints are on the empty cookie jar.

traps.why: A victim is the one harmed, the opposite of the culprit.
A witness sees the wrongdoing but did not do it.
A detective finds the culprit; the detective is not to blame.

syn1.tip: Culprit shows up in mysteries: "Who is the culprit?" means who did the bad thing.

traps.why: The one harmed is the victim, the opposite of the culprit.
That describes a detective, who catches the culprit.
A tattletale reports the problem but did not cause it.

syn2.tip: When something goes wrong and people ask who did it, the culprit is the answer: the one to blame.

traps.why: The rabbit was taking lettuce, not being harmed.
Hero is too positive for a rabbit eating Ming's lettuce.
Rabbits can be pets, but this one was causing the problem.

sc1.tip: "Lettuce kept disappearing" and the rabbit "squeezing under the fence" show the rabbit caused the problem.

sc2.sentence: The muddy paw prints leading from the spilled trash can straight to the dog's bed made it obvious that Biscuit was the _____ behind the mess.

traps.why: Biscuit made the mess; he was not harmed by it.
A detective solves the mess; the paw prints point to the one who caused it.
A witness only sees the mess; the prints show Biscuit made it.

sc2.tip: The "muddy paw prints" lead "straight to the dog's bed," evidence pointing to the one who caused "the mess."

stamina.hook: Stamina is what keeps a marathon runner jogging at mile twenty-five when everyone else has stopped to walk.

traps.why: Fatigue means tiredness, the opposite of stamina.
Speed is about how fast, not how long you can keep going.
Stammer looks similar but means a stumble in speech.

syn1.tip: Coaches say runners need stamina to finish long races. Think of lasting a long time without tiring.

traps.why: A burst is quick and short; stamina lasts a long time.
Constant tiredness is the opposite of having stamina.
Big muscles mean strength, not the energy to keep going.

syn2.tip: Stamina is what keeps you going in the last lap. It is about lasting, not about being fast or big.

traps.why: Speed helps racing, but going far without rest takes lasting energy.
Fatigue is tiredness, which would make runners stop.
Balance is a sports skill, but the clue is about going a long way.

sc1.tip: "Keep moving for more than twenty-six miles without stopping" tells you runners need energy that lasts a long time.

sc2.sentence: Although Ava was the fastest sprinter on the team, she lacked _____ and was always gasping for air halfway through the long cross-country races.

traps.why: She is the fastest, so speed is the one thing she has.
Gasping for air shows she has plenty of tiredness.
Talent is too general; gasping halfway shows she runs out of energy.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts her speed with a weakness, and "gasping for air halfway through the long" races shows she lacks lasting energy.

resent.hook: Resent is the verb behind resentment, the bitter feeling of getting blamed for your little sister's mess.

traps.why: Appreciate means value, the opposite of resent.
Resent is not "re" plus "sent"; it is about bitter feelings.
Ignoring means not paying attention; resenting means feeling bitter.

syn1.tip: Resent is the verb behind "resentment," the bitter feeling of being treated unfairly. Don't read it as "re-sent."

traps.why: Feeling thankful is the opposite of resenting.
Resent looks like "re" plus "sent," but it means feeling bitter.
Feeling sorry is pity; resenting is bitterness about unfairness.

syn2.tip: You resent something when it seems unfair, like being blamed for what someone else did. The feeling is bitterness.

traps.why: Unfair treatment would not make Sofia admire her brother.
Pity is feeling sorry for someone, but he got the better deal.
Thank is too positive for someone who keeps taking her turn.

sc1.tip: "Because their parents always gave him the front seat, even when it was clearly her turn" shows unfair treatment, which causes bitter feelings.

sc2.sentence: Instead of feeling grateful for the extra chores his coach assigned, Marcus started to _____ them, grumbling that the other players never had to stay late.

traps.why: "Instead of feeling grateful" rules out appreciating.
Finishing chores is an action; the clue is about his bitter grumbling.
He was grumbling about the chores, so he had not forgotten them.

sc2.tip: "Instead of feeling grateful" signals the opposite feeling, and "grumbling that the other players never had to" shows he felt unfairly treated.

exemplary.hook: Exemplary sounds like example: exemplary work is the paper a teacher holds up and says, "Do it like this."

traps.why: Shameful is the opposite of exemplary.
Exempt looks similar but means free from a rule.
Average is too weak; exemplary means good enough to copy.

syn1.tip: Exemplary is related to "example." Something exemplary is so good it is an example for others to follow.

traps.why: Work full of mistakes is the opposite of exemplary.
That means exempt, a different word that looks similar.
Barely good enough is much too weak for exemplary.

syn2.tip: Think of a teacher saying, "Do it like this." An exemplary piece of work is the model worth copying.

traps.why: The notebook has neat diagrams, the opposite of messy.
Ordinary is too weak; he wanted everyone to copy it.
The praise is about neat work, not what the notebook cost.

sc1.tip: Mr. Ito "praised" it and held it up as notes "he hoped everyone would copy," so the notebook is a model for others.

sc2.sentence: Coach Rivera was frustrated by the team's sloppy passing, but she pointed to Dante's _____ footwork and told everyone to study exactly how he moved.

traps.why: Clumsy fits only if you miss the "but" after sloppy passing.
Decent is too weak for footwork everyone should study.
Exempt looks similar but means free from a rule.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Dante with the team's "sloppy passing," and "study exactly how he moved" shows his footwork is a model to copy.

hefty.hook: To heft a box is to lift it and feel its weight, so a hefty box makes you grunt.

traps.why: Light is the opposite of hefty.
Hearty looks similar but means warm and cheerful or filling.
A hefty price is large, but hefty itself does not mean costly.

syn1.tip: Heft means weight. If you heft a box, you lift it to feel how heavy it is.

traps.why: Small and light is the opposite of hefty.
Tall and thin describes size, but not heaviness.
Soft and fluffy describes feel, not weight.

syn2.tip: Picture a hefty bag of dog food that needs two hands to lift. Hefty means it has a lot of size and weight.

traps.why: A tiny piano would not make movers groan and rest.
Pianos can break, but the groaning shows the piano is heavy.
Shiny describes looks, but the clue is about how hard it was to carry.

sc1.tip: The movers "groaned" and stopped "every few steps to catch their breath," so the piano must be large and heavy.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa's old dictionary was so _____ that it made Lily's backpack sag, while her new e-reader weighed less than a sandwich.

traps.why: A flimsy book would not make a backpack sag.
Old books get dusty, but dust does not make a backpack sag.
Hearty looks similar but means cheerful or filling.

sc2.tip: "Made Lily's backpack sag" is the effect of weight, and "while" contrasts it with something that "weighed less than a sandwich."

censor.hook: When a TV show bleeps a rude word, someone has decided to censor it.

traps.why: Censor looks like census, a count, but it means remove unacceptable parts.
A sensor detects things; censor only sounds the same.
Printing shares words; censoring removes them first.

syn1.tip: Censored movies have bleeped or blacked-out words. To censor is to edit out what someone thinks is unacceptable.

traps.why: Sharing without changes is the opposite of censoring.
That is what a sensor does; censor only sounds the same.
That is a census, which looks similar but means counting.

syn2.tip: Think of a bleep over a rude word on TV. Someone censored it, taking out the part they judged unacceptable.

traps.why: Approving would let the rude words stay, not black them out.
Praise is too positive for articles she found inappropriate.
Sense sounds like censor but means notice or feel.

sc1.tip: "Blacking out words she considered inappropriate" tells you the advisor removes unacceptable content before printing.

sc2.sentence: The library's old policy let leaders _____ books they disliked, but now readers can see every page exactly as the author wrote it.

traps.why: Leaders would not recommend books they disliked.
Borrowing happens at libraries, but the contrast is about pages being changed.
Censor looks like census, a count, but counting does not hide pages.

sc2.tip: "But now readers can see every page exactly as the author wrote it" contrasts with the old way, when parts were removed.

plentiful.hook: Plentiful starts with plenty: picture an orchard in fall with more apples than you could ever pick.

traps.why: Scarce is the opposite of plentiful.
Pitiful looks similar but means sad or poor.
Plentiful food is about amount, not taste.

syn1.tip: Plentiful starts with "plenty." If something is plentiful, there is plenty of it.

traps.why: Barely any is the opposite of plentiful.
The -ful means full, but plentiful is about amount, not taste.
Price is a different idea from how much there is.

syn2.tip: Hear "plenty" at the start. Plentiful things come in large amounts, like apples piled high at a fall orchard.

traps.why: Rare fits only if you miss "unlike" before the scarce desert.
Sour describes taste; the clue is about how much fruit there is.
Poisonous fruit would not give monkeys easy meals.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the dry desert, where food is scarce" signals a contrast, and "rarely have to travel far" means fruit comes in large amounts.

sc2.sentence: After weeks of warm sun and steady rain, tomatoes were so _____ in our garden that we gave bags of them to every neighbor on the street.

traps.why: If tomatoes were scarce, there would be none to give away.
Rain can rot crops, but nobody gives neighbors bags of rotten tomatoes.
Pitiful looks similar but means sad or poor.

sc2.tip: "Warm sun and steady rain" caused a big harvest, and giving "bags of them to every neighbor" shows there were large amounts.

rebellious.hook: Rebellious holds the word rebel: picture a kid crossing his arms and saying, "You can't make me."

traps.why: Obedient is the opposite of rebellious.
Rebels may be angry, but rebellious means resisting rules.
Skipping rules on purpose is different from not wanting to work.

syn1.tip: A rebel fights against those in charge. Rebellious means acting like a rebel, refusing to follow rules.

traps.why: Following orders is the opposite of being rebellious.
That is too strong; rebellious usually means resisting rules, not fighting battles.
Rebels can be loud, but noise is not resisting authority.

syn2.tip: Rebellious holds "rebel." Picture someone saying, "You can't make me." That is resisting the rules.

traps.why: "Unlike his obedient sister" means Theo is the opposite of obedient.
Lights-out is about sleep, but Theo stayed up breaking the rule.
Helpful is too positive for sneaking out against camp rules.

sc1.tip: "Unlike his obedient sister" sets up a contrast, and "ignoring the camp's lights-out rule" shows Theo resists rules.

sc2.sentence: After the principal banned hats, a few _____ students wore them anyway, and some even started a petition arguing that the rule was unfair.

traps.why: Obedient students would not wear banned hats.
Starting a petition shows they knew the rule and resisted it.
Hats are about style, but the clue is about defying the ban.

sc2.tip: "Wore them anyway" after a ban, plus a petition calling "the rule" unfair, shows students resisting authority.

reprimand.hook: A reprimand is the stern talking-to a referee or principal gives you right after you break the rules.

traps.why: Praise is the opposite of reprimand; it means saying someone did well.
Reminding is too gentle; a reprimand is a stern scolding.
Reprint starts like reprimand but means to print again.

syn1.tip: Think of a referee reprimanding a player for arguing. The word has a stern, negative feeling, like getting in trouble.

traps.why: Cheering someone on encourages them, the opposite of a reprimand.
Telling on someone reports the wrongdoing; reprimanding is scolding them for it.
A gentle warning is too mild; a reprimand is a sharp scolding.

syn2.tip: A reprimand happens after someone does wrong, so look for the choice that means scolding them sharply.

traps.why: Nobody gets praised sternly for leaving a burner on.
Comforting is kind; the teacher is stern because the students broke a safety rule.
Excusing them lets them off, but the teacher acts sternly about safety.

sc1.tip: The word "sternly" and the danger of leaving a gas burner on tell you the teacher is scolding the partners.

sc2.sentence: Instead of praising the team for winning, the coach chose to _____ them for their poor sportsmanship, listing every rude comment they had made.

traps.why: "Instead of praising" rules out congratulating; the coach is unhappy with them.
Nobody is rewarded for poor sportsmanship and rude comments.
Coaches train teams, but listing rude comments is scolding, not training.

sc2.tip: "Instead of praising" signals the opposite of praise, and "poor sportsmanship" and "rude comment" show the coach is scolding them.

fabricate.hook: Fabricate shares a Latin root with fabric; picture someone weaving a fake excuse out of nothing.

traps.why: Confessing means telling the truth; fabricating means making up something false.
Discovering finds something real; fabricating makes up something that isn't real.
Exaggerating stretches the truth; fabricating makes the whole thing up.

syn1.tip: Think of someone who fabricates an excuse for being late. The excuse did not happen; it was made up.

traps.why: Owning up means admitting the truth, the opposite of fabricating.
Finding out learns real facts; fabricating creates false ones.
Adding to a story is weaker; fabricating invents the whole thing.

syn2.tip: A fabricated story is a false one. Pick the phrase that means creating something untrue.

traps.why: Confirming shows something is true, but her story was a lie.
The teacher would be the one believing; Tessa is creating the story.
Editing fixes a story; the clue is that she made up a lie.

sc1.tip: "Rather than admit" and "saw through the lie" show Tessa was making up a false story.

sc2.sentence: The reporter was fired after editors learned she would _____ quotes, writing words that no real person had ever actually said to her.

traps.why: Recording quotes captures real words, but these words were never said.
Checking quotes is good reporting and would not get her fired.
Shortening real quotes is much weaker than writing words nobody said.

sc2.tip: The phrase "words that no real person had ever actually said" restates the blank: she made the quotes up.

indignant.hook: You feel indignant when you get blamed for a mess your little brother made: angry because it's unfair.

traps.why: Pleased is the opposite of indignant, which means angry about unfairness.
Being blamed might embarrass you, but indignant means angry, not ashamed.
Indulgent looks similar but means giving in to wishes, not angry.

syn1.tip: Picture being blamed for something you didn't do. That hot, unfair feeling is being indignant.

traps.why: Calmly accepting things is the opposite of being indignant.
Guilt fits someone who did wrong; indignant people feel wrongly blamed.
Being puzzled is far too mild; indignant means truly angry.

syn2.tip: Indignant people feel they were treated unfairly, and it makes them angry.

traps.why: Nobody is grateful for being blamed for something they didn't do.
She was at the dentist, so she has nothing to feel guilty about.
Amused is too lighthearted; unfair blame makes people angry.

sc1.tip: "Since she had been at the dentist" shows she was blamed unfairly, and unfair blame makes someone angry.

sc2.sentence: Although Marcus had cleaned the kitchen all by himself, his sister got the credit, so he felt _____ rather than proud of his hard work.

traps.why: Satisfied fits if you miss that his sister unfairly got the credit.
Thankful is a happy feeling; losing credit unfairly makes him angry.
Marcus did nothing wrong, so guilt doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: "His sister got the credit" for work he did alone is unfair, and "rather than proud" points to an angry feeling.

plummet.hook: Plummet comes from plumb, a lead weight on a string that drops straight down.

traps.why: Soar means rise high, the opposite of plummet.
Drifting down is slow and gentle; plummeting is a fast, steep fall.
Falling things may shatter, but plummet means the fall itself.

syn1.tip: Think of temperatures or a rock plummeting. The word always means a sudden, fast drop downward.

traps.why: Rising quickly is the opposite of plummeting.
A slow slide is too gentle; plummeting is fast and steep.
A fall can break things, but plummet means falling, not breaking.

syn2.tip: Plummet is about direction and speed: straight down, very fast.

traps.why: Climbing means going up, but the temperatures dropped forty degrees.
Fluctuate means go up and down; these temperatures only fell.
Holding steady can't explain a forty-degree drop.

sc1.tip: "Dropping forty degrees in just a few hours" describes a fast, steep fall.

sc2.sentence: The kite floated gently for an hour, but when the wind suddenly died, it began to _____ toward the lake and hit the water with a loud splash.

traps.why: Drift fits the gentle floating, but "but" and "loud splash" show a fast fall.
Soaring goes up, but the kite hit the water.
Hovering stays in one place, yet the kite crashed into the lake.

sc2.tip: "But when the wind suddenly died" signals a change, and "a loud splash" shows the kite fell fast.

incredulous.hook: In- means not and cred means believe, so incredulous means not believing what you just heard.

traps.why: Convinced means fully believing, the opposite of incredulous.
Ridiculous has a similar ending but means silly.
Dishonest is about telling lies; incredulous is about not believing.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: in- (not) and cred (believe), as in credit. Incredulous means not believing.

traps.why: Trusting quickly is the opposite of being incredulous.
Shocked people may go quiet, but incredulous is about believing, not speaking.
Slightly unsure is too weak; incredulous means you can't believe it at all.

syn2.tip: The cred inside incredulous is the same as in credible, meaning believable. Add in- for not.

traps.why: The crowd was sure they misheard, so they weren't confident in the news.
Respectful silence is quiet, but the clue is that they couldn't believe it.
A record-breaking surprise wouldn't make a crowd bored.

sc1.tip: "Sure they had misheard" shows the crowd could not believe what the announcer said.

sc2.sentence: Everyone else believed Leo's story about meeting a famous singer, but his best friend just raised one eyebrow, looking completely _____.

traps.why: The "but" means the friend did not believe like everyone else.
Thrilled is excited; a raised eyebrow shows doubt, not excitement.
Starstruck fits the famous singer, but the friend doubts the story.

sc2.tip: "Everyone else believed" followed by "but" means the friend didn't, and a raised eyebrow shows doubt.

irate.hook: Irate is related to ire, an old word for anger; picture a customer slamming a broken toaster on the counter.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of irate, which means very angry.
Bothered is much too mild; irate means extremely angry.
Angry people may be loud, but irate means the anger itself.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "an irate customer" demanding a refund. The word is close to ire, which means anger.

traps.why: Slightly upset is too weak; irate is very strong anger.
Being content is the opposite of being irate.
Confusing situations can annoy people, but irate means angry, not confused.

syn2.tip: Irate is a strong word. Pick the choice that shows anger at its highest level.

traps.why: Shouting and demanding answers is not patient behavior.
A long wait can tire people, but sleepy people don't shout.
Polite people don't crowd a desk shouting.

sc1.tip: "Shouting and demanding answers" after a three-hour wait and a cancellation shows the passengers were very angry.

sc2.sentence: Mr. Lee is usually calm when students forget their homework, but when someone spilled juice on his laptop, he became _____ and shouted for ten minutes.

traps.why: Relaxed fits "usually calm," but "but" signals a change to anger.
He might worry about his laptop, but shouting shows anger.
Someone else spilled the juice, so he has no reason to feel embarrassed.

sc2.tip: "Usually calm" plus "but" signals a change, and "shouted for ten minutes" shows extreme anger.

scoff.hook: When people scoff, they make a little "pfft" sound at your big idea, as if it could never work.

traps.why: Admiring is the opposite of scoffing at something.
Cough rhymes with scoff but just means clearing your throat.
Scolding is angry criticism; scoffing is laughing at something as foolish.

syn1.tip: Think of critics who scoffed at flying machines. They laughed at the idea as silly.

traps.why: Cheering for an idea is the opposite of scoffing at it.
Laughing with someone is friendly; scoffing is laughing at them unkindly.
Frowning shows disapproval, but scoffing means mocking laughter.

syn2.tip: Scoffing has a mean, mocking feeling. Look for the choice that treats something as a joke.

traps.why: "Stopped laughing" shows they had been mocking, not cheering.
Helping fits a project, but the cousins were laughing at it.
Gasping shows surprise, but the clue says they had been laughing.

sc1.tip: "They stopped laughing when it actually walked" tells you the cousins had been laughing at Aiden's plan.

sc2.sentence: Because the idea of a fifth grader starting a lemonade empire sounded so silly, Maya's classmates would _____ whenever she talked about her business plans.

traps.why: People don't applaud an idea they think sounds silly.
Investing fits business plans, but the classmates thought the idea was silly.
Listening is neutral; the clue "so silly" points to mocking.

sc2.tip: "Because" the idea "sounded so silly," the classmates' reaction must be to make fun of it.

voracious.hook: A voracious reader devours books the way a starving wolf devours dinner.

traps.why: Full means you've had enough to eat, the opposite of voracious.
Vicious sounds similar but means cruel or violent.
Picky is about what you eat; voracious means wanting huge amounts.

syn1.tip: Think of the voracious caterpillar eating every leaf. The word means a huge appetite.

traps.why: Barely interested is the opposite of a voracious appetite.
Slightly curious is too weak; voracious means extremely eager.
Voracious eaters may eat fast, but the word means eager, not quick.

syn2.tip: A voracious reader can never get enough books. The word means a huge, eager appetite for something.

traps.why: A reluctant reader wouldn't beg for more books.
Careful describes how she reads, but the clue is how much she wants.
Three novels a week is far more than occasional reading.

sc1.tip: "Three novels every week" and "always begged the librarian for more" show a huge appetite for books.

sc2.sentence: My little brother usually picks at his vegetables, but after soccer practice he is so _____ that he eats two full plates of pasta and asks for dessert.

traps.why: Picky fits his usual habit, but "but" signals the opposite.
Practice can make him tired, but eating two plates shows a huge appetite.
A satisfied eater wouldn't keep asking for dessert after two plates.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts his usual picking, and "two full plates" plus "asks for dessert" show a huge appetite.

instigate.hook: The kid who instigates a food fight throws the first meatball and then watches the chaos spread.

traps.why: Stopping something is the opposite of instigating it.
Investigate looks similar but means look into something carefully.
Joining a fight means taking part after someone else instigated it.

syn1.tip: Think of the principal asking who instigated the food fight. She wants the person who got it going.

traps.why: Calming things down is the opposite of instigating trouble.
Taking part is joining in; instigating is causing it to begin.
Putting something off delays it; instigating makes it begin.

syn2.tip: Instigate usually goes with trouble, like fights or arguments. Pick the phrase that means deliberately causing it.

traps.why: Throwing the first snowball begins a fight; it doesn't end one.
Noah threw a snowball on purpose, so he wasn't avoiding a fight.
Noah wasn't just watching; he threw the first snowball himself.

sc1.tip: "Tossing the first snowball" and "soon the whole playground had joined in" show Noah got the fight going.

sc2.sentence: The coach benched the two players who had tried to _____ an argument with the referee, since the coach blames whoever stirs up trouble, not those who get dragged in.

traps.why: Settling an argument is good, and the coach wouldn't bench them for it.
Joining is getting "dragged in," which the coach does not blame.
Players who avoid an argument wouldn't be benched for it.

sc2.tip: The coach "blames whoever stirs up trouble, not those who get dragged in," so these players began the argument.

nonchalant.hook: A nonchalant kid shrugs and yawns before a big test, as if nothing in the world could worry him.

traps.why: Anxious means worried, the opposite of nonchalant.
Seeming not to care isn't the same as being impolite.
Nonstop also starts with non but means without stopping.

syn1.tip: Picture a nonchalant shrug after losing a game. The word means calm and acting like it's no big deal.

traps.why: Nervous and tense is the opposite of nonchalant.
Nonchalant people may yawn, but the word means unworried, not tired.
Cold and cruel is harsh; nonchalant is just relaxed and unbothered.

syn2.tip: A nonchalant person acts like nothing is a big deal. Look for calm plus not worried.

traps.why: Terrified fits the trembling contestants, but "while" sets Jada apart.
She yawns, but "no big deal" shows calm, not tiredness.
She chats, but the clue "no big deal" is about being unworried.

sc1.tip: "While the other contestants trembled" sets up a contrast, and "as if the spelling bee final were no big deal" shows calm.

sc2.sentence: Ben had practiced his piano piece so many times that he walked onstage looking _____, with his hands in his pockets and a relaxed grin.

traps.why: Jittery means nervous, but he had a relaxed grin.
Lots of practice can tire you, but a relaxed grin shows calm.
Embarrassed people don't stroll onstage with a relaxed grin.

sc2.tip: "Practiced so many times" causes confidence, and "hands in his pockets and a relaxed grin" shows he was calm.

adamant.hook: Adamant comes from a Greek word for an unbreakable stone; an adamant person will not crack or budge.

traps.why: Flexible means willing to bend or change, the opposite of adamant.
People who insist may sound angry, but adamant is about not budging.
Abundant looks a bit like adamant but means plentiful.

syn1.tip: Picture someone who digs in their heels and won't budge. Adamant people stand firm no matter how hard others push.

traps.why: Giving in is exactly what an adamant person refuses to do.
Adamant people may argue, but the word means they won't change their minds.
Adamant people are already sure; they are not slow or unsure.

syn2.tip: Picture someone saying, "No, and that's final." Adamant describes that unbending attitude, not anger or loudness.

traps.why: Lena is sure she won't miss practice, so she is not doubtful.
Worried is about fear; the clue shows her standing firm against pressure.
Sorry suggests regret; Lena is not apologizing, she is refusing to change.

sc1.tip: "Although her friends begged" sets up a contrast: they pushed, but she didn't give in. You need a word for firmly refusing to change.

sc2.sentence: Dad was _____ about bedtime; no amount of begging, bargaining, or whining could get him to let us stay up past nine.

traps.why: A relaxed dad might give in, but no begging worked on him.
A forgetful dad might let you stay up; this dad never did.
Happy is about mood; the clue is about refusing to give in.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon explains the blank: "no amount of begging" could change his mind. That means he was completely firm.

ardent.hook: Ardent comes from a Latin word meaning "burning," so an ardent fan burns with enthusiasm.

traps.why: Indifferent means not caring at all, the opposite of ardent.
Arid looks a little like ardent but means very dry.
Interested is too mild; ardent means burning with devotion.

syn1.tip: Picture an "ardent fan" who never misses a game. Ardent means deeply devoted and passionate, not just mildly interested.

traps.why: Bored means not excited at all, the opposite of ardent.
Ardent fans may cheer loudly, but ardent is about deep devotion.
Ardent comes from "burning," but it describes strong feelings, not fire.

syn2.tip: Ardent feelings "burn" strongly. Think of an ardent supporter who cheers, gives, and shows up every single time.

traps.why: An indifferent person wouldn't volunteer every weekend and adopt three dogs.
Occasional is too weak; he helped every weekend and gave much of his salary.
He volunteered on his own, so he was clearly not unwilling.

sc1.tip: Look at the list: he "volunteered every weekend, donated much of his salary, and adopted three dogs." Only a deeply devoted supporter does all that.

sc2.sentence: Though Kim had once found science boring, she became so _____ about astronomy that she saved her allowance for a telescope and stayed up nightly stargazing.

traps.why: That fits her old feelings, but "Though" signals she changed.
Confusion wouldn't make her save for a telescope and stargaze every night.
Nervous is a worried feeling; her actions show eager excitement.

sc2.tip: "Though" signals a change: science used to be "boring," but now she saves her allowance and stargazes nightly. You need a word for passionately enthusiastic.

evoke.hook: Evoke breaks into e (out) and voke (call): a song can call old memories out of your mind.

traps.why: Suppress means to hold back, the opposite of calling up.
Evade looks similar but means to escape or avoid.
Voke comes from "call," but evoke is not about talking aloud.

syn1.tip: Evoke contains "voc," meaning call, as in "voice." To evoke a memory is to call it up into your mind.

traps.why: Pushing a memory away is the opposite of evoking it.
Evoke sounds a bit like "awoke," but it means calling up feelings.
Explaining describes things in words; evoking calls up a feeling or memory.

syn2.tip: Think of a song that "evokes memories" of summer. The song doesn't explain anything; it simply brings feelings back to mind.

traps.why: The scent brings memories back; it doesn't wipe them out.
Recording saves something for later; the scent calls old memories up.
Evade looks like evoke but means to escape or avoid.

sc1.tip: The scent is the cause; "memories of Grandma's kitchen" are the effect. You need a verb meaning to bring those memories back to mind.

sc2.sentence: Although the movie was only a cartoon about a lost puppy, its sad ending managed to _____ deep sadness in nearly everyone in the theater.

traps.why: "Although" means the cartoon surprised people by stirring feelings, not stopping them.
Hiding keeps a feeling in; the sad ending drew sadness out.
Describing tells about a feeling; the ending actually stirred it up.

sc2.tip: "Although... only a cartoon" sets up a surprise: it still stirred real feeling. The "sad ending" brought out emotion in the audience.

precarious.hook: Picture a Jenga tower wobbling as one more block is pulled; that tower is in a precarious state.

traps.why: Secure means safe and steady, the opposite of precarious.
Precious looks similar but means very valuable.
Precarious seems to have "care" inside, but it means unsafe.

syn1.tip: Think of a "precarious position," like a glass on a table's edge. Precarious things are shaky and could fall at any moment.

traps.why: Something firmly in place is safe, the opposite of precarious.
Pre- often means before, but precarious has nothing to do with planning.
Precarious things might fall; they have not broken yet.

syn2.tip: Precarious describes danger that hasn't happened yet, like a ladder on uneven ground or a vase at the shelf's edge.

traps.why: A steady stack would not be ready to topple.
Right angle is a math phrase; the clue says the stack might fall.
A gentle lean is too mild; this stack was ready to topple.

sc1.tip: "Ready to topple at the slightest bump" tells you the angle was dangerous and unsteady. Choose the word that means likely to fall.

sc2.sentence: Because the rope bridge had several snapped boards and frayed cables, the hikers decided the crossing was too _____ to risk and turned back.

traps.why: Snapped boards and frayed cables make a bridge weak, not sturdy.
Scenic is a positive word; the broken boards make the crossing dangerous.
Precious looks like precarious but means valuable.

sc2.tip: The cause comes first: "snapped boards and frayed cables." The effect is that the hikers "turned back," so the crossing must have been dangerously unsteady.

expel.hook: Expel splits into ex (out) and pel (drive): to expel is to drive something out, like air from your lungs.

traps.why: Absorb means to take in, the opposite of forcing out.
Expand looks similar but means to grow larger.
Excel rhymes with expel but means to do very well.

syn1.tip: Expel starts with "ex," meaning out, as in "exit." Your lungs expel air when you breathe out, pushing it away from your body.

traps.why: Letting something in is the opposite of forcing it out.
Schools expel students as punishment, but expel itself means forcing out.
A gentle nudge is too weak; expel means forcing something out.

syn2.tip: Think of the "ex" in exit. Whether it's air from lungs or a student from school, expel means making something leave by force.

traps.why: A sneeze sends germs out; it doesn't keep them inside.
Your body doesn't study germs during a sneeze; it pushes them out.
Expand looks like expel but means to make bigger.

sc1.tip: "A powerful burst of air" is the cause. A burst of air pushes dust and germs out of your nose, so you need a verb meaning force out.

sc2.sentence: Most cats happily swallow their dinner, but whenever Whiskers finds a pill hidden in her food, she manages to _____ it, leaving the soggy tablet on the floor.

traps.why: Gulping means swallowing, but the pill ends up on the floor.
Enjoy is positive; the "but" shows Whiskers rejects the pill.
Expand looks like expel but means to make bigger.

sc2.tip: "But" signals that Whiskers does the opposite of swallowing. The pill ends up "on the floor," so she must push it out of her mouth.

hamper.hook: A hamper is also a laundry basket; picture tripping over one in the hallway, and it hampers your path.

traps.why: Assist means to help, the opposite of getting in the way.
A hamper basket stores laundry, but the verb means to get in the way.
Hammer looks similar but means to pound with a tool.

syn1.tip: Picture a heavy backpack that "hampers your climb." Anything that slows you down or gets in your way hampers you.

traps.why: Clearing the way helps progress, the opposite of hampering it.
Hamper only slows something down; destroying ends it entirely.
A picnic hamper is a basket, but the verb means to slow down.

syn2.tip: Hamper means slowing something down or making it harder, not stopping it completely. Think of mud hampering a runner.

traps.why: Stopping every few hundred feet means the snow slowed them, not sped them.
Tracking follows progress; the snow is physically getting in the way.
Reward is positive; the snow forced them to keep stopping.

sc1.tip: "Forcing them to stop every few hundred feet" shows the snow kept slowing the team down. You need a verb meaning to get in the way of.

sc2.sentence: Wearing a cast on her right wrist did not stop Ava from finishing the art project, but it did _____ her, so she needed twice as long to draw each line.

traps.why: Needing twice as long shows the cast made things harder, not easier.
Defeat is too strong; she still finished, just more slowly.
Inspire is positive; the cast slowed her down.

sc2.tip: "Did not stop... but" tells you the cast was a problem without ending the project. "Twice as long" shows it slowed her down.

impeccable.hook: Impeccable comes from Latin for "not sinning": picture a kitchen so spotless you couldn't find a single crumb.

traps.why: Sloppy means full of mistakes, the opposite of impeccable.
Impossible looks similar but means cannot happen.
Fancy things can be pricey, but impeccable means without a flaw.

syn1.tip: Im- often means not, as in "imperfect." Impeccable means not faulty; think of "impeccable manners," with nothing wrong at all.

traps.why: Full of errors is the opposite of impeccable.
Mostly correct is too weak; impeccable means perfect.
Impeccable can describe clothes, but it means perfect in any way.

syn2.tip: Impeccable leaves no room for even one flaw. "Mostly correct" isn't enough; the word means perfect.

traps.why: A sloppy routine would have wobbles, but the judges found none.
Decent is too weak for a routine that earned perfect tens.
Impossible looks like impeccable but means cannot happen.

sc1.tip: Everything after the semicolon restates the blank: "not a single wobble or misstep" and "a perfect ten." The routine had no flaws at all.

sc2.sentence: Although Marcus usually rushed through his chores, the day before his grandparents' visit he left his bedroom _____, with every shirt folded and not a speck of dust anywhere.

traps.why: That fits his usual rushing, but "Although" signals a change.
Decorations aren't mentioned; folded shirts and no dust mean perfectly clean.
Crowded is about how full a room is; the clue is about cleanliness.

sc2.tip: "Although... usually rushed" signals a change. "Every shirt folded" and "not a speck of dust" show the room was perfect this time.

prodigy.hook: Mozart was a famous prodigy: he was writing music at age five, when most kids are learning to tie shoes.

traps.why: A beginner is just starting out, the opposite of a gifted expert.
Product looks similar but means something that is made.
A teacher may train a prodigy, but the prodigy is the gifted youngster.

syn1.tip: A prodigy is usually young, as in "child prodigy" or "chess prodigy." Think of a kid whose talent amazes adults.

traps.why: A slow learner struggles, the opposite of a prodigy.
Spoiled is negative; prodigy praises a child's amazing talent.
A prodigy is young; a talented adult misses that key part.

syn2.tip: You often hear "child prodigy." The word fits a young person with talent far beyond their age, like a nine-year-old beating chess champions.

traps.why: A beginner couldn't play sonatas that adult pianists struggle with.
A critic judges music; Mei is the one amazingly performing it.
Failure is negative; Mei is succeeding far beyond her age.

sc1.tip: "By age seven" and playing music "many adult pianists struggled with" point to a child with amazing talent.

sc2.sentence: Though he was only ten and still needed a booster seat in the car, Ethan was a math _____ who solved college problems that stumped his older cousins.

traps.why: A beginner couldn't solve college problems that stump older students.
Ethan is ten, so he isn't a teacher; he is an amazing student.
Disaster is negative; Ethan is solving problems others can't.

sc2.tip: "Though he was only ten" sets up a surprise. A child solving "college problems that stumped his older cousins" is extraordinarily talented for his age.

conscientious.hook: Conscientious has "conscience" inside: a conscientious worker listens to the little voice saying, "Do it right."

traps.why: Careless means not paying attention, the opposite of conscientious.
Conscious looks similar but means awake and aware.
Smart students may be careful too, but conscientious is about effort.

syn1.tip: Find "conscience" inside conscientious. A person who listens to their conscience does work carefully and correctly, checking every answer twice.

traps.why: Sloppy work is messy and careless, the opposite of conscientious.
Fussy is negative; conscientious is a compliment for careful work.
Busy people do a lot, but not always carefully.

syn2.tip: Picture a student who "checks every answer twice." Conscientious is a compliment for someone who does careful, complete work.

traps.why: Hasty means rushed, but Priya double-checks everything.
Conscious looks like conscientious but just means awake and aware.
Bored students rush; Priya carefully records each result.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her careless lab partner" signals a contrast, so Priya is the opposite of careless. "Double-checking every measurement" confirms it.

sc2.sentence: Because Jonah was so _____ about his paper route, wrapping every newspaper in plastic whenever rain was forecast, his customers never once found a soggy paper on their porch.

traps.why: A careless carrier wouldn't bother wrapping papers before rain.
Conscious looks like conscientious but means awake and aware.
Bored workers cut corners; Jonah's extra plastic shows care.

sc2.tip: This is cause and effect: Jonah wrapped "every newspaper in plastic," so customers "never once found a soggy paper." That shows careful, responsible work.

cryptic.hook: Cryptic is related to "crypt," a hidden underground room; cryptic messages keep their meaning hidden.

traps.why: Obvious means easy to understand, the opposite of cryptic.
Cryptic comes from "hidden," not scary; it means puzzling.
Critical looks similar but means finding fault or very important.

syn1.tip: Think of a "cryptic message" or "cryptic clue" in a puzzle. Cryptic words hide their meaning, so you have to work to figure them out.

traps.why: Clear means easy to understand, the opposite of cryptic.
Cryptic notes are often short, but cryptic means hard to understand.
Dishonest means lying; a cryptic message can be true, just hard to read.

syn2.tip: If you have to puzzle over what something means, it's cryptic. A "cryptic note" with strange symbols leaves you guessing.

traps.why: A simple clue wouldn't take an hour of arguing to figure out.
Funny is about laughing; the campers were arguing over the meaning.
Spookiness isn't the point; nobody could work out what it meant.

sc1.tip: The campers "spent an hour arguing" about what the clue "could possibly mean." A clue nobody can figure out is mysterious and hard to understand.

sc2.sentence: Most of Grandpa's text messages are long and clear, but last night he sent a _____ one that said only "Owl. Blue door. Noon?" leaving everyone confused.

traps.why: That fits his usual texts, but "but" signals this one was different.
Cheerful is about mood; the message left everyone confused.
Critical looks like cryptic but means finding fault.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "long and clear," and the strange message left everyone "confused." You need a word meaning mysterious and hard to understand.

solicit.hook: Those 'No Soliciting' signs on doors mean: do not knock here to ask for money or sell things.

traps.why: Decline means to say no, the opposite of asking for something.
Donating is giving what someone asks for, not doing the asking.
Solidify starts like solicit but means to make something solid.

syn1.tip: Think of 'No Soliciting' signs on doors. They tell people not to knock and ask for money.

traps.why: Giving away is the opposite of asking someone to give to you.
Paying back is about money too, but solicit means asking for it.
Speak with is too general; solicit means asking for something specific.

syn2.tip: Picture someone at your door asking for donations. That person is soliciting, asking for money or help.

traps.why: Refusing donations would not help pay for the class trip.
Money gets spent later, but going door to door is for asking.
Solidify looks like solicit but means to make solid.

sc1.tip: 'To pay for the class trip' and 'went door to door' tell you the students were asking people for money.

sc2.sentence: Rather than demand that classmates help clean the park, Jada decided to politely _____ volunteers by posting friendly sign-up sheets around school.

traps.why: Ordering is bossy, but 'rather than demand' and 'politely' rule that out.
Dismissing volunteers sends them away instead of asking them to come.
Volunteers might be rewarded later, but sign-up sheets ask for help.

sc2.tip: 'Rather than demand' and 'politely' show Jada asked people for help instead of ordering them to help.

flamboyant.hook: Flamboyant comes from a French word meaning flaming; picture an outfit so bright it seems to blaze.

traps.why: Plain is the opposite of flamboyant, which means bold and eye-catching.
Buoyant ends like flamboyant but means able to float or cheerful.
Flamboyant people may get noticed, but the word describes style, not fame.

syn1.tip: Flamboyant starts like flame. Something flamboyant blazes with color and grabs attention.

traps.why: Quiet and modest is the opposite of flashy, bold style.
Flam looks like flame, but flamboyant means showy, not on fire.
Stars can be flamboyant, but the word is about showy style.

syn2.tip: Picture a parade costume full of feathers and sequins. That eye-catching style is flamboyant.

traps.why: Modest fits the plain guests, not a suit covered in sequins and feathers.
Buoyant looks similar but means able to float, which suits do not.
Drab means dull, but sequins and feathers are anything but dull.

sc1.tip: 'While most guests wore plain dark clothing' sets up a contrast, and 'sequins, feathers, and a glittering bow tie' show showy style.

sc2.sentence: Because the new mascot costume was so _____, with neon feathers and flashing lights, every fan in the stadium turned to stare at it.

traps.why: A dull costume would not make every fan turn and stare.
Costumes can be comfortable, but comfort does not make crowds stare.
Flammable looks similar but means easy to burn, not eye-catching.

sc2.tip: 'Neon feathers and flashing lights' caused 'every fan' to stare, so the costume was bold and showy.

deluge.hook: Picture a sudden deluge of rain turning your whole street into a rushing river.

traps.why: A drought is a long time with no rain, the opposite of a flood.
A puddle is far too small; a deluge is a huge flood.
Delay starts like deluge but means a wait, not a flood.

syn1.tip: Think of a storm so heavy the streets fill with water. A deluge is a flood of rain or of anything.

traps.why: A tiny trickle is a small amount, the opposite of a deluge.
A drizzle is too light; a deluge overwhelms everything.
De can mean down, but deluge means a flood, not a drop.

syn2.tip: Deluge can mean more than water. 'A deluge of emails' means so many arrive that you are buried in them.

traps.why: A trickle is a few, but sorting took the staff a whole week.
A handful is far too few to need a week of sorting.
A shortage means too few, but the applications 'poured' in.

sc1.tip: 'Poured into the office' and 'so many that the staff needed a week' tell you a huge flood arrived.

sc2.sentence: The school expected only a few complaints about the new lunch menu, but instead a _____ of angry notes filled the principal's mailbox by Friday.

traps.why: A handful matches 'a few,' but 'but instead' means many more came.
A trickle is small, but the notes filled the whole mailbox.
Someone might summarize complaints, but a summary would not fill a mailbox.

sc2.tip: 'Expected only a few' and 'but instead' signal the opposite happened: so many notes came that they 'filled' the mailbox.

belligerent.hook: Belligerent comes from Latin bellum, war; a belligerent goose acts like it is going to war over its pond.

traps.why: Peaceful is the opposite of belligerent, which means eager to fight.
Belligerent people may be loud, but the word means ready to fight.
Intelligent ends with a similar sound but means smart.

syn1.tip: The Latin root bell means war, as in rebellion. A belligerent person is ready for battle.

traps.why: Eager to please is friendly, the opposite of looking for a fight.
Slightly grumpy is too weak; belligerent means ready to fight.
Belligerent starts with bell, but it has nothing to do with bells.

syn2.tip: Picture an angry goose charging at you. Belligerent describes someone looking for a fight or an argument.

traps.why: Gentle fits 'normally friendly,' but growling and lunging are not gentle.
Obedience is about dog training, but lunging at the fence is not obeying.
Intelligent sounds similar but means smart, not ready to fight.

sc1.tip: 'Normally friendly' signals a change, and 'growling, barking, and lunging' show the dog became ready to fight.

sc2.sentence: After losing the game, the _____ player shoved his opponent and shouted insults until the referee sent him off the field.

traps.why: A gracious player would shake hands, not shove and shout insults.
Players are often tired after games, but shoving shows a fight.
Intelligent sounds similar but means smart, not eager to fight.

sc2.tip: 'Shoved his opponent' and 'shouted insults' show the player was looking for a fight.

insatiable.hook: In- means not and sate means fill up; an insatiable hunger is a hunger that can never be filled.

traps.why: Easily satisfied is the exact opposite of never satisfied.
Very hungry is too weak; insatiable means no amount is ever enough.
Insanitary looks similar and means dirty, not impossible to satisfy.

syn1.tip: Break it up: in (not) + sati (as in satisfied) + able. Insatiable means not able to be satisfied.

traps.why: Already full is the opposite of a want that never fills up.
Slightly eager is far too weak for a want that never ends.
Picky eaters want little, but insatiable means wanting more and more.

syn2.tip: The word satisfy hides inside insatiable, and in- means not. So it describes a want that never gets filled.

traps.why: A tiny appetite would stop long before three bowls of cereal.
Picky eaters refuse food, but he kept eating everything.
Invisible looks similar but means unable to be seen.

sc1.tip: 'Even after three bowls of cereal and two bananas' he wanted 'more.' Nothing could fill him up.

sc2.sentence: Most kids lose interest in dinosaurs after a few years, but Leo's hunger for fossil facts stayed _____; he read every book the library had and begged for more.

traps.why: Faint fits kids who lose interest, but Leo begged for more.
Fossils are science, but the clue is that his hunger never ended.
Insincere looks similar but means fake, and Leo truly wanted more.

sc2.tip: 'Most kids lose interest ... but' sets up a contrast, and 'begged for more' shows his hunger was never filled.

convene.hook: Con- means together and ven means come, as in convention: when people convene, they come together to meet.

traps.why: Scatter means to spread apart, the opposite of coming together.
Convince starts like convene but means to persuade someone.
You might invite people to a meeting, but convene means actually gathering.

syn1.tip: Think of a convention, a big gathering of people. Convene means to gather for a meeting.

traps.why: Split up means to go separate ways, the opposite of convene.
This is about meetings too, but convene means holding one, not canceling.
Con- can mean with, but convene is about meeting, not agreeing.

syn2.tip: Con- means together, as in connect. People who convene come together, usually for an official meeting.

traps.why: Judges who scatter could not hold an official meeting together.
Convince looks similar but means to persuade, not to meet.
Artists compete in a contest, but judges meet to choose winners.

sc1.tip: 'For an official meeting' tells you the judges are coming together as a group.

sc2.sentence: Every Monday the student council members _____ in Room 12, so the room fills with people arriving for the meeting right after lunch.

traps.why: If members scattered, the room would empty instead of filling up.
Intervene ends like convene but means to step in and interfere.
A room could be for relaxing, but 'arriving for the meeting' points to gathering.

sc2.tip: 'The room fills with people arriving for the meeting' shows the members come together.

retract.hook: Re means back and tract means pull, as in tractor; a cat retracts its claws by pulling them back in.
