traps.why: Extend means to stretch out, the opposite of pulling back.
React looks like retract but means to respond to something.
Re- can mean again, but retract means pull back, not do again.

syn1.tip: Re means back and tract means pull, as in tractor. To retract is to pull back.

traps.why: Stick out is the opposite of pulling or taking something back.
Retract looks like re plus track, but it means take back.
People often apologize after retracting words, but retract means taking them back.

syn2.tip: Think of a cat pulling its claws back in, or a person taking back something they said. Both retract.

traps.why: You would not defend a statement whose facts were wrong.
Newspapers publish, but the apology shows he took the statement back.
React looks similar but means respond, which does not fit 'his statement.'

sc1.tip: 'His facts were wrong' and 'print an apology' show he had to take back what he said.

sc2.sentence: Our turtle happily stretches its neck out to munch lettuce, but whenever the dog barks, it will quickly _____ its head into its shell.

traps.why: Extend means stretch out, but 'but' and 'into its shell' mean pulling in.
Attract looks similar but means to draw something toward you.
Turtles can shake their heads, but 'into its shell' means pulling back.

sc2.tip: 'Stretches its neck out ... but' sets up a contrast, and 'into its shell' shows the head gets pulled back in.

improvise.hook: Improvise means acting on the spot, like jazz players inventing a tune or actors making up a scene with no script.

traps.why: Rehearsing is practicing ahead, the opposite of making it up on the spot.
Improve starts like improvise but means to make something better.
Speeches are often memorized, but improvising means not working from memory.

syn1.tip: Think of improv comedy, where actors make up scenes on the spot. To improvise is to invent as you go.

traps.why: Following a script is planned, the opposite of improvising.
That means improve, which looks similar but is a different word.
Vis means see, but im- means not, so improvise means not planned ahead.

syn2.tip: Im- means not, and the rest is related to provide, to see ahead. Improvising is acting without seeing ahead or planning.

traps.why: Rehearsing happens before a speech, not on the spot in the middle.
Improve looks similar but means make better, not make up.
Forgetting words might cause a pause, but he kept making up new lines.

sc1.tip: 'Forgot the words' and 'making up new lines on the spot' show Kai had to invent without planning.

sc2.sentence: Usually Mom follows recipes exactly, but tonight we had no eggs or butter, so she had to _____ and toss in whatever she found in the pantry.

traps.why: Tossing in whatever she found is the opposite of careful planning.
Improve looks similar but means make better, not make up as you go.
Recipes involve measuring, but 'whatever she found' means no exact plan.

sc2.tip: 'Follows recipes exactly, but' signals a contrast, and 'toss in whatever she found' shows she cooked without a plan.

methodical.hook: Methodical holds the word method: a methodical person has a step-by-step method, like a detective checking every clue twice.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite of methodical, which means careful and orderly.
Melodic looks a bit like methodical but means tuneful.
Methodical work can take time, but the word means orderly, not slow.

syn1.tip: The word method is inside methodical. Someone methodical follows a method, step by step.

traps.why: Here and there means randomly, the opposite of methodical.
Careful work may be slow, but methodical means in order.
Fussy and picky sound negative, but methodical is a compliment.

syn2.tip: Picture a detective checking each clue in order. Methodical describes careful work done step by step.

traps.why: Careless fits the random brother, but 'Unlike her brother' means Aisha was different.
Losing a key can make you frantic, but she checked calmly room by room.
Melodic looks similar but means tuneful, which has nothing to do with searching.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike her brother, who searched randomly' sets up a contrast, and 'one by one from top to bottom' shows careful order.

sc2.sentence: Because Dev was so _____ about his science project, writing each step in a notebook and testing every sample three times, his results had no mistakes.

traps.why: Sloppy work would cause mistakes, not results with none.
Metallic starts like methodical but means made of metal.
Projects can feel boring, but testing three times shows great care.

sc2.tip: 'Writing each step' and 'testing every sample three times' led to 'no mistakes,' so Dev worked in a careful, orderly way.

sumptuous.hook: Sumptuous comes from a Latin word for expense, so think of a sumptuous feast costing a huge sum.

traps.why: Shabby means worn and cheap, the opposite of sumptuous.
Scrumptious sounds similar but means delicious, not rich and splendid.
Huge is about size, but sumptuous means rich and costly-looking.

syn1.tip: Think of a palace feast with gold plates. Sumptuous describes rich, splendid things that look costly.

traps.why: Plain and simple is the opposite of rich and splendid.
A sumptuous meal may be tasty, but the word means splendid and costly.
This sounds negative, but sumptuous is an admiring word.

syn2.tip: Sumptuous comes from a Latin word for expense. It describes things so rich and splendid they look costly.

traps.why: Humble means simple, but golden plates and silk are not simple.
Banquets can be crowded, but the clues describe rich splendor, not people.
Presumptuous looks similar but means too bold or rude.

sc1.tip: 'Golden plates, silk tablecloths, and dozens of rich dishes' are examples of rich splendor.

sc2.sentence: Our campsite dinner was just beans from a can, but the wedding reception the next night was _____, with crystal glasses, silk napkins, and a towering cake.

traps.why: Modest fits the canned beans, but 'but' signals the reception was different.
Weddings can be noisy, but the clues describe costly, splendid things.
Suspicious looks a bit similar but means doubtful or untrustworthy.

sc2.tip: 'Just beans from a can, but' signals a contrast, and 'crystal glasses, silk napkins' show the reception was rich and splendid.

rigorous.hook: Rigorous has rigor inside it, an old word for stiffness: rigorous rules are strict and never bend.

traps.why: Easy is the opposite of rigorous.
Vigorous looks similar but means full of energy, not strict and thorough.
Hard training can be risky, but rigorous means strict and demanding.

syn1.tip: Think of rigorous training or a rigorous test: it asks a lot of you. The ending -ous means full of, so full of rigor, or strictness.

traps.why: Loose and careless is the opposite of rigorous.
Rigor once meant stiffness, but rigorous describes strict standards, not frozen things.
Rigorous work is hard, but it is not cruel or mean.

syn2.tip: A rigorous check leaves nothing out, and a rigorous coach accepts no shortcuts. Look for the choice that means strict and complete.

traps.why: Relaxed is the opposite; tests only a few pass are not relaxed.
Lenient means going easy, the opposite of a program few can pass.
Brief is about length, and "years of study" shows it is long.

sc1.tip: The examples "years of study," "hours of daily exercise," and tests "only a few candidates pass" all describe a very hard, strict program.

sc2.sentence: Ms. Lee's art class was relaxed and easygoing, but her math class was far more _____, with daily quizzes, strict deadlines, and no excuses for late homework.

traps.why: Casual fits the art class; "but" signals the math class is the opposite.
Crowded is about class size; quizzes and deadlines show how demanding it is.
Enjoyable is a happy feeling word; strict deadlines point to a tough class.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the math class against the "relaxed and easygoing" art class. Then "daily quizzes, strict deadlines" tells you it is tough.

imminent.hook: Imminent sounds a bit like "in a minute": something imminent could happen any minute now.

traps.why: Eminent sounds similar but means famous and respected.
Distant means far off, the opposite of imminent.
An imminent storm may be dangerous, but imminent only means coming soon.

syn1.tip: Picture dark clouds just before rain: the storm is imminent. Ask yourself whether the choice means coming very soon.

traps.why: Far in the future is the opposite of about to happen.
Finished means it already happened; imminent means it has not happened yet.
Someday is too weak; imminent means very soon.

syn2.tip: Imminent describes something right around the corner, like a launch at the end of a countdown. Pick the choice that means very soon.

traps.why: Postponed means pushed later, but the countdown shows only ten seconds left.
Eminent sounds similar but means famous, which makes no sense for a launch.
With "ten seconds left," the launch has not happened yet.

sc1.tip: The clue is "only ten seconds left" on the countdown and the crowd holding "its breath." The launch is about to happen.

sc2.sentence: The weather forecasters said the hurricane was still a week away, but by Friday morning its arrival was _____, and families rushed to board up their windows before it hit.

traps.why: Distant fits "a week away," but "but" shows things changed.
If it were delayed, families would not rush to board up windows.
Harmless is the wrong feeling; families rushing to prepare shows worry.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "still a week away," and families "rushed to board up their windows." The storm was about to hit.

protagonist.hook: Protagonist comes from Greek words meaning first actor: the character who takes center stage in the story.

traps.why: The villain usually works against the protagonist.
The author writes the story; the protagonist is a character in it.
Pro can mean for, but a protagonist is not a supporter or fan.

syn1.tip: In English class you hear protagonist and antagonist: the protagonist is the main character the story follows.

traps.why: The chief enemy is the antagonist, who opposes the protagonist.
A minor character has a small part; the protagonist has the biggest one.
The setting is where the story happens, not who it follows.

syn2.tip: Proto means first, so the protagonist is the first, or most important, character in a story.

traps.why: A sidekick helps the hero, but Zara's adventures "drive every chapter."
The reader reads the novel; Zara is a character inside it.
An illustrator draws pictures; Zara is a young inventor in the story.

sc1.tip: The clue is "whose adventures drive every chapter." The character at the center of every chapter is the main character.

sc2.sentence: Our teacher asked us to describe the story's _____, or main character, explaining what she wants most and how she changes by the final chapter.

traps.why: The villain opposes the hero; the sentence says "or main character."
A setting is a place, and a place cannot want things or change.
A theme is the story's message, not a character who wants something.

sc2.tip: The words "or main character" restate the blank right after it. Pick the word that means main character.

morale.hook: Morale is a group's mood meter: a winning streak sends it soaring, while three losses in a row sink it.

traps.why: Moral looks similar but means a story's lesson or right and wrong.
Teamwork is working together; morale is how confident the group feels.
Gloom is a dark, hopeless mood, the opposite of good morale.

syn1.tip: You often hear "boost morale" or "team morale." Notice the extra e: morale is about a group's mood, not a lesson.

traps.why: A story's lesson is its moral, a different word without the final e.
Ranking is a team's place in the standings, not its spirit.
Shared gloom is the opposite of high morale.

syn2.tip: Think of "the team's morale was high": it describes how confident and hopeful a group feels.

traps.why: Moral looks similar but means a lesson; a pep talk lifts spirits.
A pep talk cannot fix a low budget; it lifts a group's spirit.
Encouraging words do not repair equipment; they lift a team's confidence.

sc1.tip: The clues are "three straight losses" and "an encouraging pep talk." Encouragement fixes low spirits, so the blank is the team's spirit.

sc2.sentence: Although the hikers were cold, hungry, and soaked from the storm, their _____ stayed high because they sang silly songs and joked about the adventure all the way down.

traps.why: They were cold, and "although" shows something else stayed high.
They were hungry, so supplies were low, and songs do not add food.
Singing and joking show they felt cheerful, not afraid.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with being "cold, hungry, and soaked," and "sang silly songs and joked" shows their spirits stayed up.

formidable.hook: Formidable comes from a Latin word for fear: a formidable opponent is one you would be nervous to face.

traps.why: Weak is the opposite of formidable.
Formal looks similar but means proper and dressed up.
A strong rival may be famous, but formidable means hard to beat.

syn1.tip: You hear "a formidable opponent" in sports. Ask which choice describes a rival that makes you nervous.

traps.why: Easy to defeat is the opposite of formidable.
Formidable has nothing to do with forming things, despite its look.
Slightly tricky is too weak; formidable means very hard to beat.

syn2.tip: Picture an undefeated champion. Formidable describes someone or something so strong it seems frightening to take on.

traps.why: Feeble means weak, but an undefeated team is strong.
Friendly is the wrong feeling; weeks of preparing shows they were worried.
Formal looks similar but means proper, which explains nothing about preparing.

sc1.tip: The clue is "undefeated" and "so Amara's team spent weeks preparing." You only prepare that long for a rival that is hard to beat.

sc2.sentence: The tiny kitten looked harmless, but when the big dog wandered too close, she hissed and swatted so fiercely that she became a _____ enemy.

traps.why: Gentle fits "harmless," but "but" and "so fiercely" show the change.
Cuddly has a sweet feeling, but hissing and swatting are fierce.
Forgivable looks similar but means easy to forgive, not hard to beat.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "looked harmless," and "hissed and swatted so fiercely" shows the kitten became a scary enemy.

ruthless.hook: Ruth is an old word for pity, so ruthless literally means without pity.

traps.why: Kind is the opposite of ruthless.
Restless looks similar but means unable to sit still.
Strict is too mild; ruthless means showing no mercy at all.

syn1.tip: The ending -less means without. Ruth is an old word for pity, so ruthless means without pity.

traps.why: Full of mercy is the opposite of ruthless.
Ruth here is not a name; it is an old word for pity.
A bit stern is too weak; ruthless means completely without mercy.

syn2.tip: Split it: ruth plus -less. Ruth meant pity, and -less means without, so the word means without pity.

traps.why: Firing workers without warning is not generous.
Hesitant means slow to act, but he fired workers "without warning."
Frugal is a positive word for saving money, but this owner was cruel.

sc1.tip: The clues are "without warning" and "showing no concern for how they would pay their bills." That describes someone with no mercy.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the forgiving referee from last week, today's referee was _____, handing out penalties for even the tiniest mistakes and ignoring every player's plea for a second chance.

traps.why: Lenient fits the forgiving referee, but "unlike" shows today's was different.
A distracted referee would miss mistakes, not punish the tiniest ones.
Cheerful is the wrong feeling for ignoring every plea.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the forgiving referee" signals the opposite of forgiving, and "ignoring every player's plea for a second chance" shows no mercy.

obsolete.hook: Floppy disks and pay phones are obsolete: they still exist in museums, but newer things replaced them.

traps.why: Modern is the opposite of obsolete.
Absolute looks similar but means complete or total.
Obsolete things may still work; nobody uses them because newer ones exist.

syn1.tip: Think of floppy disks or VCRs. Something obsolete has been replaced by something newer, so people stopped using it.

traps.why: Brand new is the opposite of obsolete.
A little old is too weak; obsolete means replaced and out of use.
Some old things are collected, but obsolete just means nobody uses them.

syn2.tip: Obsolete is about being replaced. Ask which choice describes something people have stopped using because something better came along.

traps.why: Essential means necessary, but the digital catalogs replaced the drawers.
Absolute looks similar but means total, which makes no sense here.
New computers would not break the drawers; they just made them unneeded.

sc1.tip: The clue is "Once the library installed digital catalogs." The new system replaced the drawers, so they were no longer used.

sc2.sentence: My grandfather's typewriter was once the best tool for writing letters, but now that everyone uses laptops and phones, it is _____ and sits unused in the attic.

traps.why: Useful fits "once the best tool," but "but now" shows that changed.
Popular things get used; this one "sits unused in the attic."
Price is not the point; laptops and phones replaced the typewriter.

sc2.tip: "But now that everyone uses laptops and phones" contrasts with "once the best tool," and it "sits unused." Newer things replaced it.

deficiency.hook: Old sailors without fruit got scurvy from a vitamin C deficiency: their bodies were short on something needed.

traps.why: Surplus means more than enough, the opposite of deficiency.
Efficiency looks similar but means working without waste.
A deficiency can cause illness, but it means a shortage.

syn1.tip: You hear "vitamin deficiency" from doctors. It is related to deficit, which means being short, like a deficit in a budget.

traps.why: Abundance means plenty, the opposite of deficiency.
Defiance looks similar but means refusing to obey.
You can have a vitamin deficiency, but a vitamin is not a shortage.

syn2.tip: A deficiency means you do not have enough of something you need. Look for the choice about not having enough.

traps.why: With too much iron, the doctor would not say eat more iron.
With an allergy, she would tell him to avoid those foods, not eat more.
Efficiency looks similar but means working well, not a shortage.

sc1.tip: The doctor told him to "eat more spinach, beans, and red meat," foods full of iron. You add more when you have too little.

sc2.sentence: The new school library had plenty of computers and comfy chairs, but it had a serious _____ of books, since half the shelves sat completely empty.

traps.why: Abundance fits "plenty," but "but" and the empty shelves show the opposite.
A serious collection would fill shelves, but half sat empty.
Efficiency looks similar but means working without waste, not a shortage.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "plenty of computers," and "half the shelves sat completely empty" shows there were not enough books.

endorse.hook: When a star athlete appears in a sneaker ad, she endorses the shoes by publicly saying they are great.

traps.why: Oppose is the opposite of endorse.
Enforce looks similar but means to make people obey a rule.
People may buy endorsed products, but endorse means to publicly approve.

syn1.tip: Think of a celebrity endorsement in a commercial: the star publicly backs a product or idea.

traps.why: Criticizing is the opposite of endorsing.
Quietly tolerate is too weak; endorsing is open, active approval.
Enforce looks like endorse but means making people follow rules.

syn2.tip: Candidates hope famous people will endorse them. To endorse is to put your name behind something in public.

traps.why: She later appeared in ads recommending it, so she did not criticize it.
A doctor recommending a drink in ads is not the company making it.
Enforce looks similar but means to make people obey rules.

sc1.tip: The clue is "appeared in ads recommending it to athletes." Recommending something in public means approving and supporting it.

sc2.sentence: Mayor Diaz first opposed the plan for a new skate park, but after kids packed the meeting with petitions, she changed her mind and decided to _____ it.

traps.why: Reject matches her first view, but she "changed her mind."
Ignoring the plan is not changing her mind from opposing it.
Endure looks similar but means to put up with something hard.

sc2.tip: "First opposed" plus "but" and "changed her mind" tells you she flipped to the opposite of opposing: she supported it.

paradox.hook: "Less is more" is a paradox: it sounds like nonsense, yet it often turns out to be true.

traps.why: Agreement is the opposite of a contradiction.
Para looks like pair, but a paradox is not a pair of anything.
A paradox seems false but is true; a lie is simply false.

syn1.tip: Phrases like "less is more" seem to argue with themselves. A paradox is a statement that sounds self-contradictory but holds true.

traps.why: A paradox seems impossible, not obvious.
Despite the joke "pair of docs," paradox has nothing to do with doctors.
A paradox may seem wrong, but it is not a mistake.

syn2.tip: A paradox sounds impossible at first, yet it turns out to be true. Look for the choice that combines puzzling and true.

traps.why: "Sounds like a fact, but it is true" makes no sense with "but."
Parade looks similar but means a march down a street.
A solution answers a problem; this statement seems impossible yet is true.

sc1.tip: "It sounds like a _____, but it is true" means the blank sounds false. Pulling harder makes the trap hold "more tightly," which seems backward.

sc2.sentence: Because the statement "I always lie" contradicts itself no matter how you read it, our class spent the whole period arguing about this puzzling _____.

traps.why: The statement "contradicts itself," which is the opposite of agreement.
Paragraph also starts with para, but this is one short statement.
Homework is schoolwork; the clue is a statement that contradicts itself.

sc2.tip: The cause is "contradicts itself no matter how you read it," and the effect is a class arguing about it. A self-contradicting puzzle is a paradox.

hierarchy.hook: Picture a ladder where everyone stands on a rung above or below someone else: that is a hierarchy.

traps.why: Equality means everyone is level, the opposite of a ranked system.
A monarchy is rule by a king or queen, not any system of ranks.
Hierarchy may look like it contains "higher," but it isn't about how tall something is.

syn1.tip: Think of a "pecking order" or "chain of command." A hierarchy lines people up from top to bottom.

traps.why: Equal standing means no one outranks anyone, the opposite of a hierarchy.
A hierarchy involves a group, but this misses the ranking from top to bottom.
Kings may top some hierarchies, but hierarchy means any system of levels.

syn2.tip: Ask yourself who is on top and who is below. A hierarchy is about levels, like a boss, managers, and workers.

traps.why: Chaos means no order at all, but every bee knows its exact place.
A honeycomb is part of a beehive, but it doesn't rank bees by level.
A routine is a daily habit; the sentence describes ranks from top to bottom.

sc1.tip: "Sits at the top," "rank below her," and "exact place" all describe levels from highest to lowest.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the strict _____ at her old school, where seniors bossed everyone, the new art club treated every member as an equal, from beginners to experts.

traps.why: "Unlike" means the old school was the opposite of treating everyone equally.
Teamwork is working together; seniors bossing everyone shows ranks instead.
A tradition is a custom; the clue is about who outranks whom.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts the blank with "treated every member as an equal," so the blank is a system where some, like seniors, outrank others.

prevalent.hook: Prevalent comes from the same Latin word as prevail: something prevalent has won out and shows up everywhere.

traps.why: Rare is the opposite of prevalent; rare things are hard to find.
Relevant looks similar but means connected to the topic at hand.
Diseases can be prevalent, but prevalent means common, not dangerous.

syn1.tip: Think of "prevail": something prevalent has spread and won out, so you see it everywhere.

traps.why: Scarce means there is very little, the opposite of prevalent.
Popular means liked; prevalent just means found often, liked or not.
Previous starts the same way but means coming before.

syn2.tip: You often hear "prevalent in winter" about colds. If something is prevalent, it is found almost everywhere.

traps.why: If almost everyone carries one, smartphones are the opposite of rare.
Phones can cost a lot, but the clue is about how many students have one.
Relevant looks like prevalent but means connected to the topic.

sc1.tip: "Hard to find a student ... who does not carry one" means nearly everyone has one, so they are very common.

sc2.sentence: Although wild wolves were once _____ across the state, roaming nearly every forest, today only a few small packs survive in the northern mountains.

traps.why: Wolves roamed "nearly every forest," so they were once plentiful, not scarce.
Wolves can be dangerous, but the clue is about how widespread they were.
Protection is about wildlife, but the clue describes wolves being everywhere.

sc2.tip: "Although" contrasts the past with "only a few small packs" today, and "roaming nearly every forest" tells you wolves were once everywhere.

compensate.hook: Break a friend's pencil and hand them a new one, and you compensate them for their loss.

traps.why: To charge is to make someone pay you, the opposite of repaying them.
Compete starts the same way but means trying to win.
Spending is too general; compensate means paying someone back for a loss.

syn1.tip: Think of "compensate for a loss": you give something back to balance out what someone lost.

traps.why: Taking away makes a loss bigger; compensating makes up for it.
Apologizing is saying sorry; compensating means actually giving something back.
Compensate has nothing to do with pens; it means making up for a loss.

syn2.tip: Picture a scale: when one side loses weight, you compensate by adding something back to even it out.

traps.why: Charging takes money from people; refunds give money back.
A theater might warn people, but refunds are a way to pay them back.
Compliment looks a bit similar but means to praise someone.

sc1.tip: "Canceled at the last minute" is the cause; "full refunds and free passes" is the effect: the theater pays people back for their loss.

sc2.sentence: Lena's sister offered to _____ her for the broken headphones; in other words, she would save her allowance and buy Lena a brand-new pair.

traps.why: Blame fits the topic of broken things, but the sister is paying Lena back.
Charging would make Lena pay, but the sister is the one buying.
Forgiving lets a wrong go; buying a new pair makes up for it.

sc2.tip: "In other words" signals a restatement: saving up to "buy Lena a brand-new pair" means paying her back for her loss.

infamous.hook: Infamous isn't "not famous": it means famous for the wrong reasons, like a villain everyone has heard of.

traps.why: The "in" seems to mean not famous, but infamous means badly famous.
Celebrated means famous for good things; infamous is famous for bad things.
Infinite looks similar but means endless.

syn1.tip: Infamous contains "famous," but the "in" doesn't mean "not." It describes someone well known for something bad, like an infamous pirate.

traps.why: Infamous people are known for bad deeds, the opposite of good ones.
Infamous people are very well known, just for bad reasons.
Slightly disliked is too weak; infamous means widely known for wrongdoing.

syn2.tip: Think of "the infamous Blackbeard." Everyone knew his name, and it made them shiver.

traps.why: "Everyone knew it," so the intersection was famous, not unknown.
Praised is positive, but traffic jams and "worst spot" are negative.
Drivers avoided it because everyone knew about it, not because they ignored it.

sc1.tip: "Everyone knew it as the worst spot" tells you the intersection was well known for something bad.

sc2.sentence: Though the old pirate ship looks harmless now in the museum, it was once _____ for raiding villages, and sailors trembled at the mere sight of its black flag.

traps.why: Sailors trembled at the sight of it, so the ship was well known.
Trembling sailors show fear, the opposite of admiration.
Forgiven fits the topic of wrongdoing, but sailors still trembled at the ship.

sc2.tip: "Though" contrasts "harmless now" with the past, and "sailors trembled" shows the ship was widely known and feared.

milestone.hook: Old roads had stones marking each mile; a milestone in your life marks how far you have come.

traps.why: A setback moves you backward; a milestone marks progress forward.
Milestone contains "stone," but it means an important stage, not a big rock.
Milestones once marked distance, but now the word means an important event.

syn1.tip: Think of a baby's first steps, a "big milestone." It is a key point that shows how far someone has come.

traps.why: A setback is a step backward, the opposite of a milestone.
The "stone" in milestone doesn't make it an actual rock.
A milestone is one point along the journey, not the whole trip.

syn2.tip: Picture a mile marker on a road: each one shows you have reached a new point. Life milestones mark big steps forward.

traps.why: Reading a whole book alone is progress, not a step backward.
She struggled before; reading the book herself is the achievement after it.
Milestone once meant a stone marking miles, but this isn't about distance.

sc1.tip: Reading "a whole chapter book by herself" after she "had struggled" is a big achievement, an important step in her progress.

sc2.sentence: After months of falling off, Jamal finally rode his bike all the way around the block without help, a _____ his whole family celebrated with pizza that night.

traps.why: Riding without help is progress, not a step backward.
He fell off before, but this time he succeeded, which is no accident.
A chore is a dull task, not an exciting achievement worth celebrating.

sc2.tip: "Finally" after "months of falling off," plus a family celebration, signals a big step forward in his progress.

wrath.hook: Wrath is anger so huge it feels like a storm, like "the wrath of the gods" in Greek myths.

traps.why: Calm is peaceful, the opposite of wrath.
Wreath looks similar but is a ring of leaves or flowers.
Annoyance is mild; wrath is extreme anger.

syn1.tip: You may know "the wrath of the gods" from myths: anger strong enough to bring down storms.

traps.why: Patience means staying calm, the opposite of wrath.
Irritation is too weak; wrath is extreme anger.
Sorrow is a strong feeling too, but it is sadness, not anger.

syn2.tip: Wrath is a heavy, angry word. Picture a giant roaring after someone wrecked his castle.

traps.why: Nobody dreads praise, and ruining her roses would not earn it.
She was proud of the roses, but the twins dreaded her anger, not pride.
Wreath looks like wrath but is a ring of flowers.

sc1.tip: "Dreaded" and "flattened every bloom" of her "prize roses" tell you the twins expected a very angry reaction.

sc2.sentence: Usually the gentle librarian only whispered, but when someone spilled juice on a rare map, her _____ echoed through the building and sent kids scrambling for the exits.

traps.why: "But" shows she was not gentle this time; kids fled from her.
She usually whispered, but "but" signals something loud and angry instead.
Laughter wouldn't send kids scrambling after juice ruined a rare map.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts her usual "gentle" whispering with what came next, and kids "scrambling for the exits" shows huge anger.

chronicle.hook: Chronicle holds "chron," meaning time, as in chronological: a chronicle tells events in the order they happened.

traps.why: A prediction is about the future; a chronicle records the past.
Chron means time, but a chronicle records events, not tells the time.
A novel is a made-up story; a chronicle records real events.

syn1.tip: Spot "chron," meaning time, as in "chronological order." A chronicle records events in the order they happened.

traps.why: A forecast tells what will happen; a chronicle tells what did happen.
A fantasy is made up; a chronicle sticks to real events.
A calendar is about time too, but it plans days rather than recording events.

syn2.tip: Newspapers named "Chronicle" report what happened, day after day. A chronicle is a time-ordered account of events.

traps.why: He wrote down what already happened, not what would happen.
Expeditions need budgets, but he was writing down daily events in order.
A sketch is a drawing; he was writing down each day's events.

sc1.tip: "Writing down each day's" weather and discoveries "in the order they happened" describes a record kept in time order.

sc2.sentence: Instead of jumping around in time like her last book, Maya's new graphic novel is a _____ of one summer, told day by day from June to August.

traps.why: "Instead of jumping around" means this book is orderly, not a jumble.
A souvenir is an object from a trip, not a day-by-day account.
The book tells about a summer day by day, not what will happen.

sc2.tip: "Instead of jumping around in time" sets up a contrast, and "told day by day from June to August" describes events in time order.

stigma.hook: Long ago a stigma was a mark burned onto skin; today it is an invisible mark of shame.

traps.why: Honor is respect, the opposite of the shame a stigma brings.
Stamina looks a bit similar but means the energy to keep going.
Some illnesses carry a stigma, but stigma means the shame itself.

syn1.tip: You hear "the stigma of" something people unfairly look down on. It is a negative word for a mark of disgrace.

traps.why: A badge of honor brings pride, the opposite of a stigma.
In science class, a stigma is a flower part, but not in this sense.
People may fear a stigma, but the word means the shame attached to something.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "remove the stigma": people say it when they want something to stop being seen as shameful.

traps.why: The counselor wants to remove embarrassment, not pride.
Tutoring may cost money, but the clue is about feeling embarrassed.
Stamina looks a bit like stigma but means energy to keep going.

sc1.tip: "Nothing to be embarrassed about" tells you the counselor is fighting a feeling of shame attached to getting help.

sc2.sentence: Wearing glasses once carried a _____ at Ella's school, but now so many popular kids wear stylish frames that nobody thinks twice about it.

traps.why: A prize is positive, but "but now" shows glasses used to be looked down on.
Glasses have lenses, but the clue is about how people judged them.
Stamina looks a bit like stigma but means energy to keep going.

sc2.tip: "But now" signals a change: since popular kids wear glasses and "nobody thinks twice," glasses must once have brought shame.

susceptible.hook: If you are susceptible to colds, every sneeze in the classroom seems to find you first.

traps.why: Immune means protected, the opposite of susceptible.
Suspicious looks similar but means not trusting someone.
Contagious means able to spread to others, not easily caught.

syn1.tip: You hear "susceptible to colds" or "susceptible to injury." It means easily affected, an easy target for germs or harm.

traps.why: Fully protected is the opposite of easily affected.
Easily spread describes germs; susceptible describes who catches them.
Always sick is too strong; susceptible means likely to be harmed.

syn2.tip: Notice the "-ible" ending, like "able to be." Someone susceptible is able to be affected easily.

traps.why: Thin, delicate skin makes babies less able to resist sunburn, not more.
Babies aren't used to sunburn; their delicate skin burns easily.
Suspicious looks like susceptible but means not trusting.

sc1.tip: "Thin and delicate" skin is the cause; the effect is that babies burn easily, so they "should be kept in the shade."

sc2.sentence: Unlike the sturdy oak trees, which survived the ice storm without a scratch, the young maples were _____ to damage, and many lost branches overnight.

traps.why: "Unlike" the oaks, the maples were harmed, so they were not immune.
Young trees weren't used to damage; they were easily hurt by it.
Suspicious looks like susceptible but means not trusting.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts oaks that survived "without a scratch" with maples that "lost branches," so the maples were easily harmed.

accelerate.hook: A car's gas pedal is called the accelerator because pressing it makes the car accelerate, or speed up.

traps.why: Slowing down is the opposite of accelerating.
Moving along is too general; accelerate means going faster and faster.
Fast cars can crash, but accelerate only means gaining speed.

syn1.tip: Think of a car's "accelerator," the gas pedal: pressing it makes the car speed up.

traps.why: Delaying makes things slower, the opposite of accelerating.
Accept starts the same way but means to take or agree to something.
Travel is too general; accelerate means picking up speed.

syn2.tip: Picture a runner near the finish line pushing to go faster. That burst of speed is accelerating.

traps.why: Braking slows you down, but the cyclist passed other riders.
Cyclists steer, but pedaling harder and passing riders is about speed.
Celebrate sounds a bit like accelerate but means to have a party.

sc1.tip: "Pedaled harder" and "passing two other riders" show the cyclist gaining speed near the finish line.

sc2.sentence: The roller coaster creeps slowly up the first hill, but once it tips over the top, the cars _____ so fast that everyone's stomach drops.

traps.why: "But" shows a change from creeping slowly, so the cars don't crawl.
The cars climb before the top; after the top they race downward.
Celebrate sounds a bit like accelerate but means to have a party.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the slow "creeps" up the hill with what happens after the top, and "so fast" tells you the cars speed up.

irritable.hook: Like skin that itches at the lightest touch, an irritable person gets annoyed by the smallest thing.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of irritable.
Furious is far too strong; irritable means easily annoyed, not raging.
Tired people can get cranky, but sleepy is about needing rest.

syn1.tip: Think of something that irritates your skin. An irritable person gets annoyed as easily as skin gets itchy.

traps.why: Patient and calm is the opposite of irritable.
Both describe being easily upset, but irritable means annoyed, not scared.
Openly violent is much too strong; irritable people just snap or grumble.

syn2.tip: Look inside the word: irritable means able to be irritated. Someone irritable is quick to feel annoyed.

traps.why: Cheerful people don't snap at their friends; that's the opposite.
Irresistible looks similar but means too appealing to refuse.
She was talking to friends, but snapping shows annoyance, not chattiness.

sc1.tip: The clue is "snapping at her friends over the smallest things." Someone who snaps over tiny things is easily annoyed.

sc2.sentence: Usually Marcus is relaxed and friendly, but after the long bus ride with no air conditioning he was so _____ that even his little sister's humming bothered him.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite; a calm person wouldn't be bothered by humming.
The hot bus might make him sweaty, but sweat doesn't explain being bothered.
Delighted is a happy feeling, but the sentence describes annoyance.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change from "relaxed and friendly," and "even his little sister's humming bothered him" shows he was easily annoyed.

outcast.hook: Break it apart: an outcast has been cast out, pushed outside the circle by the group.

traps.why: A favorite is loved by the group, the opposite of an outcast.
Outlaw looks similar but means a criminal on the run.
Outcasts may wander, but a traveler hasn't been rejected by anyone.

syn1.tip: Split it: out plus cast. An outcast has been cast, or thrown, out of a group.

traps.why: A popular person is welcomed, the opposite of an outcast.
Cast can mean throwing a fishing line, but that's not this word.
A newcomer may feel left out, but hasn't been pushed away.

syn2.tip: Think of the ugly duckling, whom the other birds pushed away. An outcast is someone a group has rejected.

traps.why: A leader heads the pack; this wolf was driven away from it.
Outburst looks similar but means a sudden explosion of feeling.
Wolves may guard a pack, but he was driven out of it.

sc1.tip: "Because the other wolves drove him away from the pack" tells you he was rejected by the group.

sc2.sentence: Priya had been the most popular girl in class, but after everyone learned she was spreading rumors, she became a social _____ whom no one would sit with at lunch.

traps.why: A social butterfly is popular, the opposite of what Priya became.
A social worker helps people; it has nothing to do with rejection.
Outcome looks similar but means a result, not a person.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change from "most popular," and "no one would sit with" her shows the group rejected her.

inert.hook: Picture a lizard lying inert on a warm rock, so still it looks like part of the stone.

traps.why: Lively is the opposite of inert.
Inner looks similar but means on the inside.
Tired creatures may lie still, but inert means not moving, not worn out.

syn1.tip: In science, helium is an inert gas because it does nothing. Inert things just sit there, not moving or reacting.

traps.why: Explosive things react wildly, the opposite of inert.
Fragile means easily broken; inert is about not moving or reacting.
Alert rhymes with inert but means watchful and ready to act.

syn2.tip: Picture the lizard lying inert on a rock. It isn't moving at all.

traps.why: Reactive is the opposite; the sentence says helium does not react.
Helium is invisible, but that isn't why it doesn't react.
The sentence says helium is safe, so dangerous is backward.

sc1.tip: The clue is "because it does not react with other substances." A gas that never reacts is chemically inactive.

sc2.sentence: After the race, my brother collapsed on the couch and lay _____ for an hour, not even lifting a finger when his favorite show came on.

traps.why: Restless means unable to keep still, the opposite of what he did.
Inept looks similar but means clumsy or unskilled.
Busy means doing things, but he didn't even lift a finger.

sc2.tip: "Not even lifting a finger" restates the blank. Someone who doesn't move at all is lying still.

venomous.hook: Venom plus -ous, full of: a venomous snake is full of venom it injects with a bite.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite of venomous.
Many venomous snakes are scaly, but scaly describes skin, not poison.
Ravenous sounds similar but means extremely hungry.

syn1.tip: Find "venom" inside the word, and -ous means full of. A venomous creature is full of poison.

traps.why: Safe is the opposite of venomous.
Venomous animals may have fangs, but sharp teeth don't mean poison.
Contagious means a sickness spreads between people, not a poison bite.

syn2.tip: Think of venom, the poison a snake or spider injects. Venomous animals can poison you.

traps.why: Harmless snakes couldn't deliver a dangerous bite.
Some desert snakes are active at night, but that doesn't make bites dangerous.
Timid means shy, which wouldn't make hikers need to watch their step.

sc1.tip: "Watch where they step" and "a dangerous bite" tell you these snakes can hurt you by biting, so they carry poison.

sc2.sentence: Although the tiny blue-ringed octopus looks cute enough to pick up, it is actually _____, and a single bite can make a swimmer seriously ill.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite; its bite makes swimmers seriously ill.
The octopus has blue rings, but color doesn't explain a harmful bite.
Adorable is a warm word, but the sentence warns of danger.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with "looks cute," and "a single bite can make a swimmer seriously ill" points to poison.

dexterity.hook: Dexter is Latin for right hand, so dexterity means having handy, skillful hands.

traps.why: Clumsiness is the opposite of dexterity.
Hands can be strong, but dexterity is about skill, not power.
Sincerity ends the same way but means honesty.

syn1.tip: Picture someone doing quick magic tricks or knitting tiny sweaters. Dexterity is skill, especially with your hands.

traps.why: Awkwardness is the opposite of dexterity.
Dexter once meant right hand, but dexterity means skill, not which hand.
Toughness is about being strong; dexterity is about being skillful.

syn2.tip: Think of a surgeon or a juggler. Dexterity is the clever, quick handling of things with your hands.

traps.why: Carelessness would ruin delicate work; it's the opposite of what's needed.
Tiny parts with tweezers need careful hands, not strong ones.
The sentence stresses delicate placement, not doing it quickly.

sc1.tip: "Every tiny mast and sail must be placed with tweezers" describes delicate handwork, which takes skillful hands.

sc2.sentence: My little brother usually drops everything he holds, but juggling lessons gave him such _____ that he can now keep four balls in the air.

traps.why: Clumsiness is the opposite; he can now keep four balls up.
Boredom is a negative feeling, but the sentence describes success.
Juggling takes skillful hands, not strong ones.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "drops everything," and keeping "four balls in the air" shows his hands became very skillful.

outlandish.hook: Something outlandish seems to come from an outland, a far foreign place, because it is so strange.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of outlandish.
Outlandish isn't about being outside on land; it means very strange.
Outlandish outfits may be colorful, but colorful doesn't mean bizarre.

syn1.tip: Think of an outlandish hat shaped like a giant fish. It means so strange it seems from another land.

traps.why: Sensible is the opposite of outlandish.
Land might suggest countryside, but outlandish means weird, not rural.
Fashionable is approving; outlandish suggests something oddly strange.

syn2.tip: You may hear "an outlandish story" or "an outlandish costume." Both are wildly strange, hard to believe.

traps.why: Scientists wouldn't dismiss an obvious idea; it was called bizarre-sounding.
Brilliant is praise, but dismissed shows scientists rejected the idea.
The topic is science, but dismissed as scientific makes no sense.

sc1.tip: "Dismissed" and "bizarre-sounding" tell you scientists thought the idea was too strange, even though "but" shows it proved true.

sc2.sentence: Leo's outfit was so _____ that everyone in the cafeteria stared: he wore a purple cape, swim goggles, and a single rain boot.

traps.why: A plain outfit wouldn't make everyone stare; it's the opposite.
Clothes can be comfortable, but that wouldn't make people stare.
Outspoken looks similar but means saying your opinions boldly.

sc2.tip: The list after "stared" (a cape, swim goggles, one rain boot) shows the outfit was extremely strange.

subdue.hook: Sub means under: to subdue a bucking horse is to bring it under your control.

traps.why: Release means let go, the opposite of subdue.
Subtract looks similar but means take away numbers.
Destroy is too strong; subdue means bring under control, not wipe out.

syn1.tip: Sub means under, as in submarine. When you subdue something, you bring it under your control.

traps.why: Unleash means set free, the opposite of subdue.
Sub means under, but subdue isn't about guessing too low.
Animals may be examined after being subdued, but examine means inspect.

syn2.tip: Firefighters subdue a fire and police subdue a suspect. In both cases, they overpower it and get it under control.

traps.why: Releasing the alligator wouldn't let the vet examine it.
Zookeepers feed animals, but feeding doesn't stop thrashing for an exam.
Provoke means stir up, the opposite of calming a thrashing animal.

sc1.tip: The alligator was "frightened" and "thrashing," and the vet needed to examine it "safely." The keepers had to bring it under control.

sc2.sentence: The rowdy crowd cheered louder and louder, but the principal managed to _____ them with just one stern look, and the gym fell silent.

traps.why: Exciting the crowd would make it louder, not silent.
Entertain is a fun word, but a stern look isn't entertaining.
Subtract looks similar but means take away numbers.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the loud crowd with the result, "the gym fell silent." The principal brought them under control.

succumb.hook: Picture a tired kid trying to stay up on New Year's Eve, then finally succumbing to sleep on the couch.

traps.why: Hold out means keep resisting, the opposite of succumb.
Give away looks close to give in but means hand something over.
Succumb comes from words meaning lie under, but it means give in.

syn1.tip: You often hear "succumb to temptation" or "succumb to sleep." Either way, the person stops resisting and gives in.

traps.why: Resist is the opposite of succumb.
Succeed looks similar but means do well, nearly the reverse.
People struggle before they succumb, but struggling means still fighting.

syn2.tip: Think of eating the last cookie after promising not to. When you succumb, you yield to a pressure you were fighting.

traps.why: Objecting to temptation means fighting it, but yet signals she might fail.
Her friends were texting, but you reply to messages, not to temptation.
You rise to a challenge, but temptation is something you give in to.

sc1.tip: "Had sworn to study" followed by "yet" signals she might break her promise and give in to temptation.

sc2.sentence: After running the marathon in blazing heat, the exhausted runner began to _____ to dizziness and had to be helped off the course by medics.

traps.why: Adjusting means coping well, but the runner needed medics to help.
Runners may wave to medics, but you can't wave to dizziness.
Objecting means fighting back, but the runner could no longer resist.

sc2.tip: "Exhausted" and "had to be helped off the course" show cause and effect: the runner couldn't fight the dizziness and gave in.

thwart.hook: Picture a goalie diving to thwart a penalty kick, stopping the shooter's plan cold.

traps.why: Assist means help, the opposite of thwart.
Bad plans may get punished, but thwart means stop them happening.
Delay is too weak; thwart means stop the plan, not just slow it.

syn1.tip: Picture a goalie blocking a shot. To thwart someone is to stop their plan so it never succeeds.

traps.why: Encourage means cheer someone on, the opposite of thwart.
A warning tells about danger, but thwart means actually stop the plan.
Thaw looks similar but means melt.

syn2.tip: A tall fence thwarted the raccoons. It blocked them from reaching the trash, so their plan failed.

traps.why: Supporting their plans would help the squirrels steal more seed.
Grandma already knew about the raids; the wire was meant to stop them.
Admire is a warm word, but Grandma was annoyed by the stealing.

sc1.tip: The squirrels "kept stealing," so Grandma used a "slippery wire." Her goal was to stop their plans.

sc2.sentence: The robbers had planned the heist for months, but an alert security guard managed to _____ them before they even reached the vault.

traps.why: Help is the opposite; a guard stops robbers, not helps them.
Applaud means praise, but the guard was against the robbers.
Guards are hired, but hiring robbers wouldn't stop them.

sc2.tip: "Planned for months, but" signals the plan failed, and "before they even reached the vault" shows the guard stopped them.

deviate.hook: De means away and via means road, so to deviate is to go off the road.

traps.why: Follow means stick to the path, the opposite of deviate.
Devote looks similar but means give your time or love to something.
Travelers may hurry, but deviate is about leaving the route, not speed.

syn1.tip: De means away and via means road, as in "via the highway." To deviate is to wander away from the planned route.

traps.why: Stay on course is the opposite of deviate.
Speed is about how fast you go, not leaving the path.
De can mean down, but deviate means turn away, not go down.

syn2.tip: The pilot deviated from the flight path to avoid a storm. He turned aside from the usual route.

traps.why: Returning means coming back, but the warning is about wandering off.
Benefiting is good, but the guide is warning about something dangerous.
Hikers take photos, but photographing wouldn't get them lost.

sc1.tip: The guide warns about "unstable" cliffs and getting "lost," so the danger is leaving the "marked trail," or straying from it.

sc2.sentence: Mom usually follows recipes exactly, but tonight she decided to _____ from the instructions and added cinnamon to the spaghetti sauce.

traps.why: Copying the instructions is what she usually does; but signals a change.
She was cooking, but cooking from instructions doesn't explain the surprise cinnamon.
Quoting means repeating words, not changing what she does.

sc2.tip: "Usually follows recipes exactly, but" signals she did something different, turning away from the instructions.

ethical.hook: An ethical person does what is morally right, even when nobody is watching.

traps.why: Dishonest is the opposite of ethical.
Legal means allowed by law, and some legal things are still unfair.
Ethnic looks similar but describes a people or culture, not right behavior.

syn1.tip: Ethics are ideas about right and wrong, so an ethical choice is the morally right one.","x":""}

traps.why: Wrong and unfair is the opposite of ethical.
Laws and ethics overlap, but legal does not always mean morally right.
That describes ethnic, a lookalike word, not ethical.

syn2.tip: If you have heard of a "code of ethics," it lists the right and fair ways to behave.

traps.why: Telling his teacher was honest, so dishonest is the opposite.
Copying was the convenient choice; Kwame chose the harder, right one.
Telling the teacher is the opposite of sneaky.

sc1.tip: "Though" sets up a contrast: copying was "easy," but Kwame did the right thing and "told his teacher."

sc2.sentence: Maya refused to share the embarrassing photo of her classmate, because she believed that spreading hurtful pictures for laughs was never the _____ thing to do.

traps.why: The photo was shared for laughs, but Maya cared about what was right.
Popularity is not the point; Maya refused because it was hurtful.
Cruel is the opposite; Maya avoided the photo because it was wrong.

sc2.tip: "Refused" and "because... hurtful" show Maya was choosing what is morally right.

threshold.hook: A threshold is the strip under a doorway; step over it and something new begins.

traps.why: The center is the middle, the opposite of the edge where something starts.
A ceiling is part of a room, but a threshold is at the doorway's bottom.
Threshold seems to contain hold, but it has nothing to do with gripping.

syn1.tip: Picture a doorway: the threshold is the edge you step across to go inside.

traps.why: A final stage is the end, the opposite of a starting point.
A porch is near the door, but a threshold is the doorway itself.
The hold in threshold does not mean holding on to something.

syn2.tip: "On the threshold of" something means just about to begin it.

traps.why: The discovery would happen soon, so they were at its start, not its end.
Results come after a discovery, which had not happened yet.
Middle means partway in, but the discovery had not begun.

sc1.tip: "Would soon change medicine" tells you the discovery had not happened yet, so they were at its beginning.

sc2.sentence: Nervous about her first day, Lena lingered at the _____ of the classroom, but once she spotted her best friend inside, she walked straight in.

traps.why: She had not gone in yet, so she could not be at the center.
A window is part of a room, but she walked in through the door.
The back is inside the room, and she had not entered yet.

sc2.tip: She "walked straight in" afterward, so before that she was standing at the doorway.

sentiment.hook: Sentiment comes from the same Latin word as sense and sentimental: it is all about what you feel.

traps.why: A fact can be proved, while a sentiment is a feeling.
Sentence looks similar but means a group of words.
Cards hold greetings, but a sentiment is the feeling behind the words.

syn1.tip: Think of "sentimental," which describes someone full of feelings.

traps.why: Proof shows something is true; a sentiment is just what someone feels or thinks.
A speech may share a sentiment, but it is the talk, not the feeling.
Scent sounds like the start of sentiment but means a smell.

syn2.tip: "I share your sentiment" means "I agree with what you think or feel."

traps.why: Calling the trip the best day is praise, not a complaint.
Dev said it out loud to everyone, so it was no secret.
Everyone nodded in agreement, the opposite of doubt.

sc1.tip: Dev "said" something and everyone "nodded," so the blank names the opinion they all shared.

sc2.sentence: Although most of the town wanted the old library torn down, Mrs. Ortiz's _____ was the opposite: she believed the building should be saved and repaired.

traps.why: She believed something, which is an opinion, not proof.
A rumor is gossip passed around, but this is what she herself believed.
Repairs cost money, but the sentence is about what she believed.

sc2.tip: "Was the opposite: she believed" shows the blank is what she thought, an opinion against the town's.

bizarre.hook: Bizarre sounds like bazaar, a market, but means wildly strange, like a cat wearing a tuxedo.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of bizarre.
Strange things can be scary, but bizarre only means very odd.
Costumes can be fancy, but bizarre means weird, not elegant.

syn1.tip: Bizarre things make you stare and say, "That is so weird."

traps.why: Plain and normal is the opposite of bizarre.
Something bizarre can be loud, but bizarre means strange.
Bizarre is much stronger than slightly different.

syn2.tip: Bizarre is stronger than odd; it means so strange it is hard to believe.

traps.why: A glowing lure and huge teeth are not ordinary at all.
The details describe something strange and creepy, not lovely.
Needle teeth and a dangling lure describe an odd look, not a graceful one.

sc1.tip: The details after the comma, a "glowing lure dangling from its head" and teeth "too long for its mouth," describe something very strange.

sc2.sentence: Most of the science fair projects were ordinary volcanoes and plant studies, but Jamal's was _____: a robot hamster that played the harmonica while reciting poems.

traps.why: The word but sets Jamal's project apart from the typical ones.
A singing robot hamster is the opposite of a simple project.
Nothing says it was unfinished; the clue is how strange it was.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Jamal's project with the "ordinary" ones, and a harmonica-playing robot hamster is wildly strange.

voluntary.hook: Volunteers do voluntary work: they choose to help, and no one makes them.

traps.why: Required is the opposite of voluntary.
Volunteers are helpful, but voluntary means done by choice.
Many people may join, but voluntary is about choosing, not popularity.

syn1.tip: Think of a "volunteer," someone who chooses to help; voluntary means done by choice.

traps.why: Being forced is the opposite of choosing.
Volunteers often help others, but voluntary just means chosen.
Volunteers may work in groups, but voluntary means by choice.

syn2.tip: "Involuntary" describes a sneeze you cannot stop; take away "in" and voluntary means something you chose.

traps.why: No one is required to come, so the session is not necessary.
The sentence says nothing about crowds, only about choosing to attend.
Those who come do better, and the clue is about choice, not dullness.

sc1.tip: The words after the semicolon, "no one is required to attend," explain the blank: going is your choice.

sc2.sentence: Because the art club is _____, Priya only goes on weeks when she feels like painting, and nobody marks her absent when she skips.

traps.why: If it were required, someone would mark her absent.
Popularity would not explain why nobody marks her absent.
Painting is messy, but that does not explain skipping freely.

sc2.tip: "Only goes... when she feels like" and "nobody marks her absent" show attending is her choice.

evident.hook: Evident contains vid, meaning see, as in video: when something is evident, anyone can see it.

traps.why: Hidden is the opposite of evident.
Evil starts like evident but means very wicked.
Evident things are easy to see, not necessarily important.

syn1.tip: Inside evident is "vid," meaning see, as in "video." Evident things are easy to see.

traps.why: Hard to notice is the opposite of evident.
Evidence is used in court, but evident just means clearly seen.
Vid means see, but evident means obvious, not pretty.

syn2.tip: Think of "self-evident": something so clear it needs no explaining.

traps.why: The paw prints and empty bowl remove any doubt.
Muddy floors are not lucky; the clues just make the answer clear.
The clues were all over the floor, the opposite of secret.

sc1.tip: The "muddy paw prints" and "empty food bowl" are clues that make the answer plain to see.

sc2.sentence: Leo tried to hide his disappointment about losing the spelling bee, but his slumped shoulders and quiet voice made his sadness _____ to everyone.

traps.why: The word but shows his attempt to hide his sadness failed.
Losing may embarrass him, but the clue is that others could see his sadness.
Slumped shoulders show sadness that others noticed, nothing funny.

sc2.tip: "Tried to hide... but" signals the opposite happened: his shoulders and voice let everyone see his sadness.

irrelevant.hook: Ir- means not, so irrelevant means not relevant: off topic, like talking about pizza in math class.

traps.why: Connected is the opposite of irrelevant.
Irritating looks similar but means annoying.
An irrelevant point can be true; it is just off topic.

syn1.tip: Ir- means not, as in "irregular." Irrelevant means not relevant, not connected to the point.

traps.why: Right on point is the opposite of irrelevant.
Irrelevant is about being off topic, not about being false.
Volume has nothing to do with whether a point fits the topic.

syn2.tip: Ask yourself, "Does it relate?" If not, it is irrelevant.

traps.why: Movies have nothing to do with recycling, so they were not related.
Her points wasted everyone's time, so they were not helpful.
Movies can entertain, but the clue is that they were off topic.

sc1.tip: "Favorite movies" in a debate "about recycling" that "wasted everyone's time" had nothing to do with the topic.

sc2.sentence: Mr. Chen said our book reports should focus only on the story's plot and characters, so details about the author's pet cat were _____ and should be left out.

traps.why: Essential details would be kept, but these should be left out.
The cat may be cute, but the clue is that it is off topic.
True facts can still be left out if they do not fit the topic.

sc2.tip: "Focus only on... plot and characters, so" explains why cat details get left out: they do not connect to the report.

compatible.hook: Com- means together: compatible things go together, like a charger that actually fits your phone.

traps.why: Mismatched is the opposite of compatible.
Comfortable looks similar but means relaxed and at ease.
A charger can be portable, but compatible means it works with your device.

syn1.tip: Game boxes say "compatible with your console," meaning the two work together.

traps.why: Unable to connect is the opposite of compatible.
That describes portable gadgets, not ones that work together.
That describes competitive, a lookalike word.

syn2.tip: Com means together, as in "combine"; compatible things can go together without problems.

traps.why: Machines are not comfortable; the problem is they cannot work together.
Systems are not familiar with each other; the game simply would not run.
Competitive looks similar, but the issue is working together, not competing.

sc1.tip: The game "would not run" "because" of the blank, so the two systems could not work together.

sc2.sentence: Mia and Jada argue about everything from music to pizza toppings, yet their friendship has lasted because their personalities are surprisingly _____ where it truly matters.

traps.why: The word yet shows their personalities fit despite the arguing.
Arguing might seem stubborn, but the friendship lasted because they fit together.
Competitive looks similar, but a lasting friendship needs people who get along.

sc2.tip: "Yet" and "has lasted" signal that despite the arguing, their personalities fit together well.

explicit.hook: Explicit instructions spell out every single step, leaving nothing for you to guess.

traps.why: Vague is the opposite of explicit.
Explosive starts the same way but means likely to blow up.
Clear directions can be short; explicit is about clarity, not length.

syn1.tip: Explicit is the opposite of "implicit," which means hinted. Explicit means stated clearly.

traps.why: Hinting is the opposite of stating something clearly.
Shouting is about volume; explicit is about being clear and detailed.
Explain looks like explicit, but explicit means already stated clearly.

syn2.tip: Being explicit means you "spell it out," leaving no doubt about what you mean.

traps.why: The word unlike shows today's directions were not vague.
Exact page counts and sources leave nothing mysterious.
The clue is about how clear the directions were, not whether they were required.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the vague hint" sets up a contrast, and "exactly two pages" shows the directions were clear and detailed.

sc2.sentence: Because the sign at the pool was _____ about the rules, listing 'no running, no diving, and no food on the deck,' nobody could claim they didn't know.

traps.why: An unclear sign would let people claim they did not know.
A faded sign would be hard to read, but this one was clear.
Nothing suggests the sign was silly; it listed rules plainly.

sc2.tip: The sign was "listing" each rule, so "nobody could claim they didn't know": it stated the rules clearly.

virtue.hook: "Patience is a virtue" means waiting calmly is one of the good qualities a person can have.

traps.why: Evil is the opposite of virtue.
Virus looks similar but is a germ that makes you sick.
A talent is a skill; a virtue is a good quality of character.

syn1.tip: You have heard "patience is a virtue": it means patience is a good quality to have.

traps.why: A bad habit is the opposite of a virtue.
Skills are abilities; virtues are good parts of your character.
Virtue is a lasting quality in a person, not a passing feeling.

syn2.tip: Kindness, honesty, and courage are all virtues: good qualities in someone's character.

traps.why: Grandpa praised honesty, so it is not a fault.
The sentence says honesty is more valuable than talent, so it is something else.
Honesty is a quality a person has, not a prize they receive.

sc1.tip: Honesty is part of character, and "more valuable than talent, wealth, or good looks" tells you it is a good quality.

sc2.sentence: Marcus is not the fastest runner or the best shooter on the team, but his greatest _____ is loyalty: he never gives up on a teammate.

traps.why: Never giving up on a teammate is a strength, not a weakness.
Speed and shooting are skills; loyalty is a quality of character.
Loyalty is part of who Marcus is, not a prize he won.

sc2.tip: "Not the fastest... but" turns from sports skills to "loyalty," a good quality of his character.

terse.hook: A terse text is just "k." with a period: so short it feels a little cold.

traps.why: Wordy means using too many words, the opposite of terse.
Tense looks like terse but means nervous or stiff.
Loud is about volume; terse is about using very few words.

syn1.tip: Think of a terse reply like "No." or "Fine." Terse answers are short and a bit rude, just like curt ones.

traps.why: Long and rambling is the opposite of terse.
Terse is short but cold, not friendly.
That describes tense, which only looks like terse.

syn2.tip: Picture someone answering every question with one flat word. That clipped, cool feeling is what terse means.

traps.why: A single word is the opposite of a lengthy reply.
"Grumbled" and a shut door show he was not cheerful.
Booming is about volume, and a grumble is low and short.

sc1.tip: Look at "just a single grumbled 'Fine'." One grumbled word is a short, cold answer.

sc2.sentence: Usually Grandpa tells long stories at dinner, but tonight his answers were _____, just a nod or a quick "Yep" before he went back to eating.

traps.why: Rambling fits his usual long stories, but "but" signals the opposite tonight.
A nod and a quick "Yep" show no extra thought or care.
Funny stories fit Grandpa, but the clue is how few words he used.

sc2.tip: "But tonight" contrasts with "long stories," and "just a nod or a quick 'Yep'" shows his answers were very short.

zany.hook: Zany is pure cartoon energy: a rubber chicken, a pie in the face, and nonstop goofy chaos.

traps.why: Serious is the opposite of zany.
Lazy looks and rhymes like zany but means not wanting to work.
Zany scenes can be noisy, but zany means wildly silly.

syn1.tip: Think of zany cartoons, where characters bounce off walls and act goofy. Zany means wildly silly.

traps.why: Solemn means grave and serious, the opposite of zany.
Brainy rhymes with zany but means very smart.
Witty humor is clever wordplay; zany humor is wild silliness.

syn2.tip: Zany and wacky even sound alike in feeling. Both describe goofy, over-the-top fun.

traps.why: A rubber-chicken hat is the opposite of boring.
A catapult sounds risky, but marshmallows and chicken hats show silliness.
Lazy looks like zany, and building a catapult takes effort.

sc1.tip: The examples after "like" are the clue: "a rubber-chicken hat" and launching marshmallows are wildly silly.

sc2.sentence: My older cousin acts calm and serious at work, but at family parties he turns _____, juggling dinner rolls and dancing like a chicken.

traps.why: Quiet matches "calm and serious," but "but" signals a change.
Grumpy is a bad mood; juggling rolls and chicken dancing are playful fun.
Dinner rolls are food, but he is juggling them, not eating them.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "calm and serious," and "juggling dinner rolls and dancing like a chicken" shows wild silliness.

shirk.hook: To shirk is to sneak away from a job, like a cat slipping out the door at bath time.

traps.why: To tackle a job is to face it, the opposite of shirking.
Shriek looks like shirk but means scream.
You might complain about a chore, but shirking means avoiding it.

syn1.tip: You often hear "shirk your duties" or "shirk responsibility." It means slipping out of work you should do.

traps.why: Carrying out a duty is the opposite of shirking it.
Assigning gives a job to someone; shirking is escaping your own job.
That is what shrink means, and shrink only looks like shirk.

syn2.tip: Shirk is always about duties and chores. Someone who shirks finds a way out of the work.

traps.why: Faking a stomachache is a way to escape the job, not finish it.
Sharing means doing part of it; Owen wanted to skip it entirely.
Scheduling plans a chore; a fake stomachache is a way to get out of it.

sc1.tip: "Suddenly claiming he had a stomachache" is a fake excuse. Excuses are used to avoid a duty.

sc2.sentence: Unlike her twin, who always finds an excuse to _____ his chores, Mia finishes hers right after school without being asked.

traps.why: Mia completes chores; "unlike" tells you her twin does the opposite.
People don't need excuses to enjoy something; excuses help you escape it.
Organizing chores is still doing them; the twin is avoiding them.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets the twin against Mia, who "finishes hers." And "finds an excuse" means he gets out of his chores.

abhor.hook: Abhor shares a Latin root with horror: you abhor the things that make you shudder.

traps.why: Adore means love deeply, the opposite of abhor.
Dislike is too weak; abhor means hate strongly.
Absorb looks like abhor but means soak up.

syn1.tip: Hear the "hor" in abhor and think of horror. You abhor something that fills you with disgust.

traps.why: Admiring something is the opposite of abhorring it.
Abhor is strong hatred, not a slight dislike.
You might avoid what you fear, but abhor is about hating, not fearing.

syn2.tip: Abhor is related to abhorrent, meaning disgusting. It is one of the strongest ways to say you hate something.

traps.why: She loves broccoli, but "but" and gagging show she hates sprouts.
Tolerating means putting up with it; gagging at the smell is much stronger.
Cooking is mentioned, but gagging shows how she feels about sprouts.

sc1.tip: "Happily eats broccoli... but" sets up a contrast, and "gagging at even the smell" shows strong hatred.

sc2.sentence: Because my parents _____ loud alarm clocks, they wake up to soft music instead of the harsh beeping that used to make them jump.

traps.why: If they adored loud alarms, they wouldn't switch to soft music.
Owning alarm clocks would not explain switching away from the beeping.
Designing clocks has nothing to do with why they chose soft music.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals a reason. They dropped the "harsh beeping that used to make them jump," so they must hate it.

unkempt.hook: Kempt is an old word for combed, so unkempt hair has never met a comb.

traps.why: Neat is the opposite of unkempt.
Unkind looks like unkempt but means mean.
Tired people may look unkempt, but unkempt is about a messy appearance.

syn1.tip: Un- means not, and kempt is an old word for combed. Unkempt hair or clothes look uncombed and messy.

traps.why: Groomed means neat and cared for, the opposite of unkempt.
Unkempt is not "un-kept" meaning thrown away; it means uncombed and messy.
Smell is a different problem; unkempt describes how something looks.

syn2.tip: You often hear "unkempt hair" or "an unkempt lawn." Both look scraggly and not cared for.

traps.why: Tangled hair and wrinkled clothes are the opposite of polished.
Camping can be relaxing, but the clue describes how messy he looked.
Unkind looks like unkempt, but the clue describes hair and clothes.

sc1.tip: The examples after "with" settle it: "tangled hair, a scruffy face, and wrinkled clothes" all describe a messy look.

sc2.sentence: Grandma's garden was always neatly trimmed, but after she moved away, the yard grew _____, with weeds and overgrown bushes everywhere.

traps.why: Tidy matches "neatly trimmed," but "but" signals the yard changed.
Colorful sounds pleasant, but weeds and overgrown bushes show neglect.
An empty house may be quiet, but the clue describes weeds and bushes.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "neatly trimmed," and "weeds and overgrown bushes everywhere" shows a yard nobody cared for.

pliable.hook: Pliable things bend like a pipe cleaner: twist them, fold them, shape them however you like.

traps.why: Rigid means stiff and unbending, the opposite of pliable.
Reliable looks like pliable but means trustworthy.
Clay can be sticky, but pliable is about bending easily.

syn1.tip: The ending -able means able to be. Pliable is related to pliers and ply: able to be bent or folded.

traps.why: Hard to bend is the opposite of pliable.
That means reliable, which only looks like pliable.
That means fragile; pliable things bend without breaking.

syn2.tip: Think of warm clay or a pipe cleaner. If you can shape it with your hands, it is pliable.

traps.why: Stiff wire couldn't be twisted into shapes with bare hands.
Wire may be shiny, but the clue is about twisting it by hand.
Fragile wire would snap, yet this wire holds its form.

sc1.tip: "Twist into animal shapes with bare hands" tells you the wire bends easily.

sc2.sentence: Dry modeling clay cracks when you press it, but after a few minutes in your warm hands it becomes soft and _____ enough to shape into a dragon.

traps.why: Brittle fits dry clay that cracks, but "but" signals the clay changes.
Clay can be colorful, but warming it doesn't change its color.
Reliable looks like pliable but means trustworthy, not easy to shape.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "cracks," and "soft and... enough to shape into a dragon" means easy to bend and mold.

mirth.hook: Mirth and merry come from the same old English word, so mirth is merry laughter.

traps.why: Gloom is sadness, the opposite of mirth.
Myth looks like mirth but means an old legend.
Audiences clap and laugh, but mirth is the laughing, not clapping.

syn1.tip: Mirth is related to merry. Picture a room full of merry people laughing together.

traps.why: Deep sorrow is the opposite of mirth.
A quiet smile is too weak; mirth means laughing fun.
Cheering supports a team; mirth is laughter at something funny.

syn2.tip: You may hear "filled with mirth" in stories about holidays or parties. It means joyful laughter and fun.

traps.why: Sadness matches "gloomy," but "but" and giggling show the mood changed.
Assemblies may have music, but the clue is giggling at a comedian.
Tension is a nervous feeling; giggling students are having fun.

sc1.tip: "Gloomy all week, but" signals a change, and "still giggling at lunch" shows the room filled with laughter.

sc2.sentence: When my baby sister sneezed so hard that spaghetti flew onto Dad's glasses, the whole table was full of _____, and we laughed until our stomachs hurt.

traps.why: Laughing until your stomach hurts is the opposite of sorrow.
Spaghetti on glasses could annoy Dad, but everyone laughed.
Manners belong at dinner, but the clue is the laughter.

sc2.tip: The funny sneeze causes the reaction: "we laughed until our stomachs hurt." The table was full of laughter.

gloat.hook: Picture a winner doing a victory dance right in the loser's face: that's gloating.

traps.why: Sulking is what a sad loser does, not a bragging winner.
Float looks like gloat but means rest on water.
Celebrating can be kind; gloating is mean bragging that rubs it in.

syn1.tip: Gloating has a mean feeling. You gloat over a win when you brag about it to make others feel bad.

traps.why: Acting humble is the opposite of gloating.
That is what float means, and float only looks like gloat.
Winning comes before gloating; gloating is bragging about it afterward.

syn2.tip: Think of "no gloating" after a game. It means don't rub your win in the losers' faces.

traps.why: Winners have no reason to worry about a score they won.
Float looks like gloat but makes no sense with the score.
Think is too general; the coach means bragging in front of the losers.

sc1.tip: "Rather than" sets up a contrast with shaking hands "politely." The opposite of polite winning is bragging about the score.

sc2.sentence: Max began to _____ about his spelling bee win, so by Friday none of his classmates wanted to sit with him at lunch.

traps.why: A smile is too mild to make classmates avoid him.
Studying fits a spelling bee but wouldn't drive classmates away.
Float looks like gloat but means drift on water.

sc2.tip: "So" shows a result: nobody wanted to sit with him. Something about how he talked about "his win" annoyed everyone.

vehement.hook: A vehement speaker pounds the table and leans in, so every word comes out with full force.

traps.why: Mild means gentle and weak, the opposite of vehement.
Violent is too strong; vehement means forceful feeling, not hurting anyone.
