sc2.tip: Look at cause and effect: she faced "so much" trouble "that a failed test barely worried her." Hard times that make you tough are adversity.

intrepid.hook: Intrepid holds trepid, as in trepidation, meaning fear; in- means not, so intrepid means not afraid.

traps.why: Timid means easily scared, the opposite of intrepid.
Reckless is careless risk taking; intrepid praises real courage.
Trepid does suggest trembling, but in- flips it to mean not afraid.

syn1.tip: Think of trepidation, which means fear. The in- at the front means not, so intrepid means without fear.

traps.why: Cowardly means lacking courage, the opposite of intrepid.
Explorers may be fit, but intrepid is about courage, not muscles.
Tepid means lukewarm; it only looks like the end of intrepid.

syn2.tip: Picture the intrepid explorer crossing a frozen sea alone. What word describes someone who dares to do that?

traps.why: A timid captain would stay away like the other sailors.
The sentence says she steered toward danger without hesitation.
Sailors can get seasick, but nothing here is about feeling ill.

sc1.tip: "Though most sailors refused" sets up a contrast. She did the opposite of them, heading in "without hesitation," so she must be fearless.

sc2.sentence: Nothing seemed to scare the _____ young diver; she leaped from the highest platform at the pool and swam into the deep end without a second thought.

traps.why: An anxious diver would be scared, but nothing scared her.
A cautious diver thinks twice; she acted without a second thought.
Divers can be graceful, but the clue is that nothing scared her.

sc2.tip: The first part, "Nothing seemed to scare," tells you the meaning, and the leaps "without a second thought" repeat it.

tenacious.hook: Tenacious comes from Latin tenere, to hold, like tenant: picture a terrier that holds on and never lets go.

traps.why: Wavering means unsure and ready to give in, the opposite of tenacious.
Tense means tight or nervous; it only looks like the start of tenacious.
Spacious means roomy; it just rhymes with tenacious.

syn1.tip: Tenacious shares a root with tenant, from a Latin word meaning to hold. A tenacious person holds on and keeps going.

traps.why: Discouraged people give up; tenacious people refuse to.
Pushy is a rude kind of insisting; tenacious praises someone who won't quit.
Talent helps people succeed, but tenacious is about refusing to give up.

syn2.tip: Think of a tenacious reporter who keeps asking questions. The word describes someone with a firm grip who will not give up.

traps.why: A fickle dog would drop the toy quickly; this one hung on.
A timid dog would let go, not dangle off the ground by its teeth.
A lazy dog would rest, not fight to keep the toy.

sc1.tip: Look at "refused to let go" and "hanging on with its teeth even when" lifted. The blank describes a dog with a grip that won't quit.

sc2.sentence: Most of the class quit the hard puzzle after ten minutes, but _____ Lena kept working on it all weekend until she finally solved it.

traps.why: Bored students quit; the word "but" says Lena was different.
Impatient people give up quickly, and Lena worked all weekend.
Luck didn't solve it; she kept working all weekend.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts Lena with classmates who "quit." She "kept working on it all weekend," so she refused to give up.

fervent.hook: Fervent comes from Latin for boiling, so picture feelings bubbling over like a pot on high heat.

traps.why: Indifferent means not caring, the opposite of fervent.
Interested is too weak; fervent means very strong feeling.
Frequent means happening often; it only looks a bit like fervent.

syn1.tip: Hear it in the phrase "a fervent plea." Someone begging with all their heart is full of strong, sincere feeling.

traps.why: Showing no emotion is the opposite of fervent.
Fervent comes from boiling, but it describes feelings, not temperature.
Anger is strong, but fervent means sincere, eager feeling, not a temper.

syn2.tip: Fervent comes from a word for boiling. Think of feelings so strong they bubble over, like a fervent fan or a fervent wish.

traps.why: A dull speech has no feeling, but her voice trembled with emotion.
Despite her nervousness means her speech was strong, not shy.
Mild is too weak for a voice trembling with emotion.

sc1.tip: "Despite her nervousness" tells you the speech was not shy, and "trembling with emotion" shows how strongly she felt.

sc2.sentence: Grandpa usually shows little interest in sports, but he is a _____ fan of the town's Little League team and never misses a single game.

traps.why: Casual fans care a little; never missing a game shows much stronger feeling.
A reluctant fan wouldn't come to every game; "but" signals a change.
A former fan stopped caring, yet he never misses a game.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts his "little interest" in most sports with this team. "Never misses a single game" shows very strong feeling.

replenish.hook: Replenish is re- (again) plus a root meaning full, as in plenty: you make something full again.

traps.why: Drain means empty out, the opposite of replenish.
Relish means enjoy; it only looks like replenish.
Re- does mean again, but replenish means fill again, not do again.

syn1.tip: Find plen inside, as in plenty. Re- means again, so replenish means making something full again.

traps.why: Consume means use up, the opposite of filling back up.
You might buy supplies, but replenish means filling back up.
Punish means make someone suffer; it just sounds like the end of replenish.

syn2.tip: Picture hikers who replenish their water bottles at a stream. The bottles were used up, and now they are full again.

traps.why: The bake sale already emptied the cabinet; it needs filling.
Bake sales sell things, but the cabinet is empty and needs supplies.
Re- can mean back, but there's nothing left to give back.

sc1.tip: The cabinet was "emptied," and the council needs supplies "before the next event." What do you do to an empty cabinet?

sc2.sentence: The bird feeder in our yard was full on Monday, but by Friday the hungry squirrels had eaten everything, so Dad went out to _____ it with fresh seed.

traps.why: The squirrels already emptied it; Dad added fresh seed.
Nothing was broken, and you can't fix a feeder with seed.
Feeders need cleaning, but "with fresh seed" means filling it.

sc2.tip: The feeder went from "full" to eaten up, and Dad came "with fresh seed." He is making it full again.

devious.hook: Devious comes from Latin for off the main road: a devious person takes a crooked, sneaky path.

traps.why: Honest means truthful, the opposite of devious.
Devoted means loyal; it only looks like devious.
Obvious means easy to see; it just rhymes with devious.

syn1.tip: Think of the devious fox that tricked the crow. Devious describes someone who gets what they want by secret tricks.

traps.why: Sincere means honest and real, the opposite of devious.
Clever is praise; devious means tricky in a dishonest way.
Villains may be violent, but devious is about sneaky tricks.

syn2.tip: Devious has a negative feeling and comes from a word for off the road. A devious person goes around the honest path.

traps.why: Pretending to be a friend while stealing is not truthful.
The hero is mentioned, but the villain's plan is not heroic.
Stealing the map is harmful, and the plan is meant to trick.

sc1.tip: "Pretending to be the hero's friend while secretly stealing" describes a plan full of lies and tricks.

sc2.sentence: Everyone thought the quiet new student was shy and sweet, but she was actually quite _____, secretly switching name tags so others would be blamed for her pranks.

traps.why: Letting others be blamed is the opposite of innocent.
Everyone thought she was shy, but "but" says the truth was different.
She acted "secretly," so she was not obvious.

sc2.tip: "But she was actually" sets up a contrast with "shy and sweet." Switching tags "secretly" so "others would be blamed" is sneaky and dishonest.

quell.hook: Firefighters quell a blaze and teachers quell giggles: picture a loud uproar being pressed down into silence.

traps.why: Worsen means make bigger or worse, the opposite of quell.
Dwell means live somewhere; it just rhymes with quell.
You notice trouble before you quell it; quell means stop it.

syn1.tip: Hear it in "quell the panic" or "quell a riot." You quell something that is getting out of hand.

traps.why: Stirring up trouble is the opposite of quelling it.
Putting up with panic means tolerating it; quell means stopping it.
Quell is stronger than a slight change; it means stopping completely.

syn2.tip: Picture a coach whose steady voice quelled the team's rising panic. The panic didn't just shrink; it ended.

traps.why: Fueling panic would make it grow, not end it.
Inviting a tour is taking action, not ignoring the panic.
Describing panic won't stop it; the tour is meant to end it.

sc1.tip: The principal acted "by inviting everyone to tour the room in daylight," which shows there is no ghost. That would end the panic.

sc2.sentence: At first the crowd's anger only grew louder, but the referee managed to _____ it with a clear explanation, and the stadium soon fell quiet again.

traps.why: The stadium fell quiet, so the anger did not increase.
Applauding the anger would praise it; the referee wanted it gone.
Referees keep records, but recording anger wouldn't quiet a stadium.

sc2.tip: "At first" the anger "grew louder, but" then the stadium "fell quiet again." The blank is what the referee did to stop the anger.

camaraderie.hook: Camaraderie comes from comrade, which first meant roommate: picture teammates bunking together at camp and becoming close.

traps.why: Rivalry means competing against each other, the opposite of camaraderie.
Camouflage means hiding by blending in; it only looks like camaraderie.
Popular kids have many fans, but camaraderie is trust within a group.

syn1.tip: Find comrade inside camaraderie. A comrade is a friend you stick with, so camaraderie is the friendly bond in a group.

traps.why: Hostility means unfriendliness, the opposite of camaraderie.
Groups have leaders, but camaraderie is about friendship among members.
An acquaintance is someone you barely know; camaraderie is a close bond.

syn2.tip: Think of "the camaraderie on the team made every practice fun." It names the warm, trusting feeling teammates share.

traps.why: Rivals compete; this crew cheered for one another.
Early practices are a routine, but joking and cheering show friendship.
Jealousy is a bitter feeling; the crew was warm and supportive.

sc1.tip: Look at "joking together and cheering for one another even off the water." That describes a warm friendship within the group.

sc2.sentence: On the first day of camp the cabinmates barely spoke, but by the last night their _____ was so strong that they cried while hugging goodbye.

traps.why: They were shy at first, but "but" signals that changed.
Rivals wouldn't cry while hugging goodbye.
Barely knowing someone is too weak for crying while hugging goodbye.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts "barely spoke" with the last night. Crying "while hugging goodbye" shows they became close friends.

fluctuate.hook: Fluctuate comes from Latin for wave: picture prices bobbing up and down like waves on the sea.

traps.why: Stabilize means stay steady, the opposite of fluctuate.
Flutter means flap quickly, like wings; it only looks like fluctuate.
Rise is only half of it; fluctuate means going up and down.

syn1.tip: Hear it in "prices fluctuate." Picture a line on a chart that keeps going up, then down, then up again.

traps.why: Staying the same is the opposite of fluctuating.
Flu looks like flow, but fluctuate means changing up and down.
That only goes up; fluctuate means moving both up and down.

syn2.tip: Fluctuate comes from a Latin word for wave. Waves go up and down over and over.

traps.why: Rise covers the soaring part but not the dropping at night.
Settle means become steady, but these temperatures change wildly.
Deserts are hot, but the temperatures also drop near freezing.

sc1.tip: The temperatures are "soaring" in the day and "dropping" at night. The blank must cover both going up and coming down.

sc2.sentence: Unlike the steady hum of the refrigerator, the noise from the old washing machine would _____ constantly, growing quiet for a moment and then suddenly roaring.

traps.why: Humming is what the steady fridge does; "unlike" says the washer differs.
Fade covers getting quiet but not the sudden roaring.
Flutter means flap quickly; it doesn't mean getting louder and softer.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the steady hum" tells you the washer's noise is not steady. "Growing quiet" then "roaring" means going up and down.

inquisitive.hook: Inquisitive shares a root with inquire and question: an inquisitive kid always has another question ready.

traps.why: Uninterested means not caring to know, the opposite of inquisitive.
Exquisite means very beautiful; it only looks like inquisitive.
Talkative people talk a lot; inquisitive people want to learn.

syn1.tip: Inquisitive is related to inquire, which means to ask. Picture the child asking why the sky is blue.

traps.why: Lacking interest is the opposite of inquisitive.
Slightly is too weak; inquisitive means full of questions.
Arguers ask questions too, but inquisitive means wanting to learn.

syn2.tip: Look for inquire inside inquisitive. Someone who keeps asking questions really wants to find things out.

traps.why: An idle boy wouldn't take apart a toaster or ask endless questions.
Taking things apart might look destructive, but asking questions shows curiosity.
Exquisite means very beautiful; it only looks like inquisitive.

sc1.tip: He took the toaster apart "to see how it worked" and asked "question after question." Both examples show a boy who wants to know things.

sc2.sentence: While her older brother found bugs boring, Priya was _____ about them, and she spent hours peering through a magnifying glass and reading library books to learn more.

traps.why: Indifferent matches the bored brother, but "while" says Priya is different.
Some people fear bugs, but she studied them for hours.
Confused people ask questions too, but hours of eager study show curiosity.

sc2.tip: "While her older brother found bugs boring" sets up a contrast. She spent hours studying "to learn more," so she is eager to learn.

vindictive.hook: Vindictive shares a root with vengeance: a vindictive person keeps score and waits to get even.

traps.why: Forgiving means letting go of hurt, the opposite of vindictive.
Victorious means winning; it only looks a bit like vindictive.
Angry is too general; vindictive means wanting payback.

syn1.tip: Vindictive sounds like vengeance, which means revenge. Think of someone who wants to get even.

traps.why: Quick to forgive is the opposite of vindictive.
Slightly annoyed is too weak; vindictive people actively plan payback.
Winning and losing come up, but vindictive is about getting even.

syn2.tip: Picture the girl who erased her rival's name from the sign-up sheet. She was trying to hurt someone to get back at them.

traps.why: A gracious loser congratulates the winner instead of spreading rumors.
Elections involve popularity, but Kyle lost and wanted payback.
Kyle lost the election, so he was not victorious.

sc1.tip: Kyle spent weeks "trying to get back at him." Getting back at someone is revenge, so the blank means wanting revenge.

sc2.sentence: Ella is not the type to hold a grudge; even when her friends tease her, she laughs it off instead of being _____.

traps.why: Laughing it off is forgiving; "instead of" needs the opposite.
Victorious means winning, which has nothing to do with grudges.
She laughs, but the blank is what she avoids being.

sc2.tip: "Not the type to hold a grudge" and "instead of" tell you the blank is the grudge-holding, get-even attitude she avoids.

rotund.hook: Rotund and round both come from Latin rotundus; picture a rotund snowman built from three big snowballs.

traps.why: Skinny is the opposite of rotund, which means round and plump.
Rotund looks like rotate, but it describes a round body, not spinning.
Muscular describes strong bodies; rotund is about being round and plump.

syn1.tip: Rotund sounds like round. Think of a rotund pumpkin: round and plump.

traps.why: Slender means thin, the opposite of rotund.
Rotten looks a bit like rotund, but it means spoiled.
Huge is about size; rotund is about a round, plump shape.

syn2.tip: Hear the word round inside rotund. A rotund body is round and chubby.

traps.why: Slim is the opposite; a barrel shape is round, not thin.
Nimble means quick and light, but this walrus flopped heavily.
Frozen fits the ice, but the barrel shape describes a round, plump body.

sc1.tip: Look at "shaped like a giant barrel" and "nearly two tons." You need a word for a round, heavy body.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his skinny brother, who could slip through any gap in the fence, Marco was so _____ that his round belly got stuck halfway.

traps.why: Lanky means tall and thin, like the brother, not Marco.
Clumsy is about movement; a round belly is about body shape.
Rotten looks like rotund but means spoiled, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Unlike his skinny brother" sets up a contrast, and "round belly" confirms Marco is round and plump.

writhe.hook: Writhe is related to wreath, a ring of twisted branches; picture a worm twisting itself into a little wreath.

traps.why: Freezing means holding still, the opposite of twisting and squirming.
Write sounds a bit like writhe, but it means putting words on paper.
Someone in pain might scream, but writhe means twisting the body.

syn1.tip: Picture a worm on a hot sidewalk. The way it twists and wiggles is how things writhe.

traps.why: Straighten is the opposite of twist.
Wither looks like writhe, but it means to dry up and shrink.
Worms crawl, but writhe means twisting and squirming in place.

syn2.tip: Writhe is related to wreath, a ring of twisted branches. Writhing is twisting your body.

traps.why: Relaxing is the opposite of twisting and curling.
Stretching makes a worm long and straight, not twisting and curling.
The worm wants soil, but on dry paper it can only twist.

sc1.tip: The words "twisting and curling its body" describe the missing action, so pick the word that means squirming.

sc2.sentence: Because the scratchy wool sweater itched so badly, Leo began to _____ in his seat during the long concert, unable to keep his body still for even a minute.

traps.why: Relaxing means staying calm, but Leo could not keep still.
A long concert might make you sleepy, but Leo could not keep still.
People clap at concerts, but itching makes you squirm, not clap.

sc2.tip: "Because the scratchy wool sweater itched" is the cause, and "unable to keep his body still" is the effect: squirming.

saunter.hook: Picture a cowboy sauntering into town, thumbs in his belt, in no hurry at all.

traps.why: Dash means to run fast, the opposite of a slow, relaxed walk.
Marching is walking too, but stiff and purposeful, not relaxed.
Saunter is a kind of moving, but it means a slow, relaxed walk.

syn1.tip: Picture someone sauntering along a boardwalk eating ice cream, slow and in no hurry.

traps.why: Rushing is the opposite of a slow, easy walk.
Pacing nervously is walking with worry; sauntering is calm and carefree.
Marching is stiff and firm; sauntering is loose and lazy.

syn2.tip: Sauntering has a lazy, happy feeling, like a slow walk on vacation.

traps.why: Racing is what the others did; Felix did the opposite.
Stumbling is clumsy, but smiling lazily shows a relaxed walk.
Leaping takes a burst of energy; lazily shows he walked slowly.

sc1.tip: "While the other runners sprinted" sets up a contrast, and "smiling lazily" and "holiday walk" show a slow, casual walk.

sc2.sentence: With no homework due and the whole summer afternoon ahead, Maya would _____ down to the corner store, stopping to pet every dog and admire every flower she passed.

traps.why: Sprinting is fast, but stopping at every dog shows a slow walk.
You can drive to a store, but not while petting every dog.
Trudging is slow but tired and gloomy; Maya's afternoon is carefree.

sc2.tip: "No homework due" and "the whole summer afternoon ahead" make Maya relaxed, and stopping for every dog shows a slow, easy walk.

clamber.hook: Clamber sounds like climb plus clumsy; picture kids clambering up a snow pile on hands and knees.

traps.why: Gliding is smooth and easy, the opposite of a clumsy climb.
Clamor looks like clamber, but it means to shout noisily.
Hikers may climb, but clamber means climbing awkwardly with hands and feet.

syn1.tip: Clamber sounds like climb. Picture kids clambering over rocks at low tide, using hands and feet.

traps.why: Going down gracefully is the opposite of climbing up clumsily.
That is clamor, which looks like clamber but means shouting.
Clumsy climbers might fall, but clamber means climbing up.

syn2.tip: Hear climb inside clamber, then add clumsy: hands, knees and feet all working hard.

traps.why: Gliding is smooth, but they crawled on hands and knees.
Tumbling means falling down, but they were pulling themselves higher.
Strolling is easy walking; hands and knees shows a hard climb.

sc1.tip: "On their hands and knees" and "grabbing at roots and stones" show a clumsy climb using hands and feet.

sc2.sentence: The cat leapt gracefully onto the top bunk in one jump, but my little brother had to _____ up the wobbly ladder, gripping each rung and kicking his legs.

traps.why: Leaping is what the cat did; but shows your brother moved differently.
Gliding is smooth; gripping and kicking show a clumsy climb.
Clamor looks like clamber but means to shout noisily.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cat's graceful jump with your brother "gripping each rung and kicking his legs," a clumsy climb.

chide.hook: Chide rhymes with side; picture Mom calling you to her side to chide you for muddy shoes.

traps.why: Praise means to say good things, the opposite of scolding.
Hide rhymes with chide, but it means to keep out of sight.
Punishing goes further than chiding, which is only a mild scolding.

syn1.tip: Picture Mom chiding you for leaving shoes on the stairs: a mild scolding, not a big punishment.

traps.why: Praising is the opposite of criticizing.
Threatening is far too harsh; chiding is a mild scolding.
Teasing is for fun; chiding shows real disapproval.

syn2.tip: Chide has a disapproving but mild feeling, like a sigh and a head shake.

traps.why: You don't praise someone for forgetting; Grandpa is disappointed.
Teasing is playful, but his sigh shows real disapproval.
Punishing is too harsh; a head shake and sigh are mild.

sc1.tip: "Shaking his head and sighing" and "How many times must I remind you?" show gentle disapproval, a mild scolding.

sc2.sentence: Instead of yelling when I spilled juice on the new rug, Aunt Rosa would only _____ me softly, saying I should be more careful next time.

traps.why: No one thanks you for a spill; she wanted you to be careful.
Blasting someone is like yelling, and "instead of yelling" rules it out.
Teasing is joking, but she gave a serious warning.

sc2.tip: "Instead of yelling" means she did something milder, and "I should be more careful" shows she still scolded a little.

peevish.hook: A pet peeve is something that bugs you; a peevish person acts like everything is a pet peeve.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of peevish, which means grumpy and whiny.
Tired kids often get cranky, but sleepy is not the same thing.
Furious is far too strong; peevish is small, whiny annoyance.

syn1.tip: Think of a pet peeve, something that annoys you. A peevish person is easily annoyed.

traps.why: Always calm is the opposite of easily annoyed.
Sadness is a different bad mood; peevish means grumpy and irritable.
Rage is much too strong for small, whiny grumpiness.

syn2.tip: Peeve is inside peevish. Something that peeves you annoys you.

traps.why: Cheerful kids don't complain about cold milk and touching peas.
Missing a nap might make him sleepy, but the complaints show crankiness.
It was dinnertime, but complaining about food shows irritation, not hunger.

sc1.tip: The petty complaints, milk "too cold" and peas "touching his potatoes," show a boy who is easily annoyed and whiny.

sc2.sentence: My sister is usually sweet and patient, but after a long day at summer camp she turns _____, snapping at anyone who asks her a simple question.

traps.why: Gentle matches "usually sweet," but "but" signals a change.
A long day can tire you, but snapping shows irritation.
Quiet people don't snap at others; snapping shows she is irritable.

sc2.tip: "Usually sweet and patient, but" signals a change, and "snapping at anyone" shows she becomes easily annoyed.

careen.hook: Picture a runaway shopping cart careening down a hill, swerving wildly with nobody steering.

traps.why: Creeping is slow and careful, the opposite of careening.
Careening may end in a crash, but careen means swerving along.
Careening is a kind of moving, but wild and out of control.

syn1.tip: Picture a sled careening down an icy hill, rushing and swerving with no one steering.

traps.why: Gliding smoothly is controlled, the opposite of careening.
Careening can lead to a crash, but it means swerving wildly.
Speed is part of it, but careening means swerving, not going straight.

syn2.tip: Careen has a wild, scary feeling, like a cart lurching left and right with no driver.

traps.why: Gliding is smooth, but the cart was lurching wildly.
It crashes at the end, but first it swerves across the lot.
Freezing fits the ice, but the cart was moving wildly.

sc1.tip: "Runaway" and "lurching left and right" show the cart was rushing along out of control, swerving wildly.

sc2.sentence: Grandma drives her car slowly and steadily, but my cousin let his go-kart _____ around the track, bumping walls and sliding on every sharp turn.

traps.why: Creeping is slow, like Grandma, but "but" signals the opposite.
Parked karts don't bump walls or slide around turns.
An idling kart sits still, but this one was sliding around turns.

sc2.tip: "Slowly and steadily, but" sets up a contrast, and "bumping walls and sliding on every sharp turn" shows wild swerving.

qualm.hook: Having qualms means a queasy, uneasy feeling about a choice; no qualms means you feel completely fine doing it.

traps.why: Confidence is feeling sure, the opposite of a qualm.
Calm sounds like qualm, but it means peaceful and relaxed.
Terror is far too strong; a qualm is a small uneasy feeling.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "no qualms about it," which means having no doubts at all.

traps.why: Being certain is the opposite of having a qualm.
That describes calm, which sounds like qualm but means something else.
Sadness is a bad feeling, but a qualm is doubt or guilt.

syn2.tip: A qualm is a small nagging feeling that something might be wrong, like a twinge of guilt.

traps.why: A thrill is excitement, but Hiro felt an uneasy twinge of guilt.
Calm sounds like qualm, but Hiro was uneasy, not peaceful.
Confidence is the opposite of the guilt and doubt Hiro felt.

sc1.tip: "An uneasy twinge of guilt" restates the blank, so you need a word for a nagging feeling of doubt or guilt.

sc2.sentence: Although everyone else jumped off the high dive without a second thought, Priya had a _____ about the height and stood at the edge for ten minutes.

traps.why: A thrill would make her jump; she stood frozen with doubt.
Calm sounds like qualm, but a calm diver would just jump.
A dream about heights doesn't explain standing at the edge so long.

sc2.tip: "Although everyone else jumped without a second thought" contrasts with Priya waiting "for ten minutes," so she had an uneasy doubt.

appall.hook: Appall comes from an old French word meaning to grow pale; something appalling can drain the color from your face.

traps.why: Delight means to please greatly, the opposite of appall.
Appeal looks like appall, but it means to attract or ask.
Annoy is too weak; appall means to shock and disgust greatly.

syn1.tip: Think of the word appalling, used for something so bad it shocks and disgusts you.

traps.why: Please is the opposite of appall.
Applaud starts like appall, but it means to clap in approval.
A surprise can be pleasant; appall means a shocked, disgusted feeling.

syn2.tip: Appall has a strong negative feeling. Picture your face going pale at something disgusting.

traps.why: No one who loves sea turtles is delighted by trashy beaches.
Amuse is a happy feeling, but buried beaches are upsetting.
Annoy is too mild for beaches buried under plastic trash.

sc1.tip: Beaches "buried under plastic trash" would horrify "anyone who cares about sea turtles," so pick a word for strong shock and disgust.

sc2.sentence: The guests expected a tasty meal, but the moldy bread and the hair in the soup were enough to _____ even the least picky eaters at the table.

traps.why: Delight fits a tasty meal, but "but" signals a disgusting one.
Meals feed people, but moldy bread and hair would disgust them.
Applaud looks like appall but means to clap, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Expected a tasty meal, but" signals a letdown, and "moldy bread" and "hair in the soup" would shock and disgust anyone.

exhilarate.hook: Exhilarate shares a root with hilarious; both come from a Latin word meaning cheerful.

traps.why: Bore is the opposite of exhilarate, which means to excite.
Exhaust looks like exhilarate, but it means to tire out.
A big ride can frighten you, but exhilarate is a happy feeling.

syn1.tip: Picture the huge drop on a roller coaster that leaves every rider thrilled and cheering.

traps.why: Sadness is the opposite of the joyful excitement exhilarate means.
Exhilarate shares a root with hilarious, but it means thrill, not make laugh.
Fear is the wrong feeling; exhilarate is joyful excitement.

syn2.tip: Exhilarate is a strong positive word for the joyful rush you feel on a fast ride.

traps.why: Bored kids don't shriek with joy.
Exhaust looks similar but means to tire out, not to thrill.
Shrieking can mean fear, but these were shrieks of joy.

sc1.tip: The twins "shrieked with joy all the way to the bottom," so the sledding must have filled them with excitement.

sc2.sentence: Long car rides usually bore my little brother, but the first glimpse of the ocean through the window seemed to _____ him, and he bounced in his seat cheering.

traps.why: Soothing calms you down, but he bounced and cheered.
Exhaust looks like exhilarate but means tire out; he was full of energy.
Car rides can make kids sick, but cheering shows joy.

sc2.tip: "Usually bore..., but" signals the opposite of boredom, and "bounced in his seat cheering" shows the ocean thrilled him.

demure.hook: Picture a demure kitten tucked in a corner, eyes lowered, hoping nobody makes a fuss over her.

traps.why: Bold is the opposite of demure; bold people push forward.
Secure ends like demure but means safe, not shy.
Grumpy people may be quiet, but demure means modest, not bad-tempered.

syn1.tip: Think of a demure smile: small, quiet, and modest. Demure people avoid attention, just like shy people do.

traps.why: Boastful people brag; demure people do the opposite.
Mature looks a bit like demure but means grown-up.
Fearful is too strong; demure people are quiet, not afraid.

syn2.tip: Demure describes someone who keeps a low profile and doesn't show off. Ask which choice means not showing off.

traps.why: Outgoing matches the loud stage singer, not the quiet one at home.
Dramatic fits the stage, but the blank describes her quiet home life.
She may be famous, but the sentence describes how she acts at home.

sc1.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with "loud and flashy." The blank must match "quiet" and "rather than attract attention."

sc2.sentence: The new student was so _____ that she kept her eyes down, spoke softly, and blushed whenever the teacher praised her work in front of everyone.

traps.why: Confident people don't hide their eyes or blush at praise.
A boastful student would enjoy praise, not blush at it.
Gloomy is quiet but sad; nothing here says she is unhappy.

sc2.tip: The details after "so ... that" explain the blank: "eyes down," "spoke softly," "blushed" at praise. Those all describe a quiet, modest person.

fallible.hook: Fallible sounds like "fail-able": anyone who is fallible is able to fail or make a mistake.

traps.why: Flawless means without mistakes, the opposite of fallible.
Fallible isn't about falling down; it's about making mistakes.
Making mistakes is different from lying on purpose.

syn1.tip: The ending -ible means able to. Fallible people are able to fail, so they are not perfect.

traps.why: Never wrong is the opposite; fallible means you can be wrong.
Fall in fallible is misleading; it's about errors, not tripping.
Easy to break means fragile; fallible is about making errors.

syn2.tip: Its opposite, infallible, means never wrong. Take away the in- and you get someone who can be wrong.

traps.why: The teacher says machines give wrong answers, so they aren't always accurate.
Useful is too positive; the teacher is warning about mistakes.
Calculators may be complicated, but the point is that they can be wrong.

sc1.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with "trust calculators completely." Then "wrong answer" tells you the blank means able to make mistakes.

sc2.sentence: Since even expert weather forecasters are _____, Coach always keeps a backup plan ready in case the predicted sunny day turns into a sudden thunderstorm.

traps.why: If forecasters were certain, Coach wouldn't need a backup plan.
Cheerful fits sunny forecasts, but it doesn't explain the backup plan.
Being skilled wouldn't make Coach need a backup plan.

sc2.tip: "Since" gives the reason for the backup plan. Coach plans for a surprise storm because forecasters can be wrong.

malady.hook: Mal means bad, so a malady is something bad happening to your body: an illness.

traps.why: Health is the opposite of a malady.
Melody sounds like malady but means a tune.
Medicine treats a malady; it isn't the malady itself.

syn1.tip: Look for mal, meaning bad, as in malfunction. A malady is something bad wrong with your body.

traps.why: A cure ends a malady; it is the opposite.
Mal means bad, but malady is a bad illness, not evil behavior.
A symptom is a sign of a malady, not the malady itself.

syn2.tip: Mal means bad, and a malady is a bad condition of the body. Which choice names a sickness?

traps.why: A remedy cures illness; scurvy made gums bleed.
Vitamin C prevents scurvy; scurvy itself is a sickness.
Sailors suffered from it, but scurvy came from missing vitamins, not punishment.

sc1.tip: Scurvy was "caused by a lack of vitamin C" and "made their gums bleed." Something with a cause and symptoms like that is a disease.

sc2.sentence: The mysterious _____ spread quickly through the chicken coop, and within a week half the hens had stopped laying eggs and were too weak to stand.

traps.why: A remedy would make hens stronger, not weaker.
Melody sounds like malady, but a tune can't weaken hens.
A vaccine prevents sickness; it wouldn't make hens too weak to stand.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: hens "stopped laying eggs" and were "too weak to stand." Something that spreads and causes that is a sickness.

impertinent.hook: An impertinent kid talks back to the principal, rolls his eyes, and asks rude questions he shouldn't.

traps.why: Courteous means polite, the opposite of impertinent.
Impatient starts like impertinent but means unable to wait.
Violent is far too strong; impertinent is about rude words or manners.

syn1.tip: Think of a kid who talks back to a teacher. That cheeky, rude behavior is impertinent.

traps.why: Respectful is the opposite of impertinent.
Important looks like impertinent but means mattering a lot.
Playful teasing is friendly; impertinent remarks are rude.

syn2.tip: Impertinent has a negative feeling and is used for someone who talks back. Pick the choice that means bad manners.

traps.why: A polite reply wouldn't get Brady sent to the office.
Clever is too positive; his reply got him in trouble.
Important looks like impertinent but doesn't explain the punishment.

sc1.tip: Brady questioned whether the teacher "knew how to teach" and "was sent straight to the office." That effect shows his reply was rude.

sc2.sentence: Unlike her younger brother, who often made _____ remarks to their grandparents, Lila always said please and thank you and listened politely at dinner.

traps.why: Grateful remarks would be like Lila's, not unlike them.
Gentle remarks don't contrast with Lila's polite manners.
Pertinent means on topic, which doesn't contrast with being polite.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" signals a contrast. Lila is polite, so her brother's remarks must be the opposite of polite.

languid.hook: Picture a languid cat melting across a sunny windowsill, too relaxed to chase anything.

traps.why: Energetic is the opposite of languid.
Liquid looks like languid but means a runny substance.
Asleep goes too far; languid people move, just slowly.

syn1.tip: Picture someone lying around on a hot afternoon. Languid has a slow, droopy feel, like lacking the energy to do much.

traps.why: Full of energy is the opposite of languid.
Languid looks like language, but it isn't about speech.
Languid is relaxed and slow, not sorrowful.

syn2.tip: Languid sounds like languish, to droop or weaken. Think of a droopy, slow-moving body with little energy.

traps.why: Alert lions would lift their heads at food.
Hungry lions would jump up for food, but these barely moved.
Lions can be fierce, but these were barely moving.

sc1.tip: "Hottest afternoon" and "barely lifting their heads even when" fed show the lions had almost no energy.

sc2.sentence: At recess the twins raced around the playground nonstop, but by the end of the long, sticky afternoon they moved in a _____ way, dragging their feet to the bus.

traps.why: Lively describes recess, not the tired end of the day.
Dragging their feet is slow, not hurried.
Graceful is about movement, but dragging feet isn't graceful.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts racing "nonstop" with later. "Dragging their feet" confirms they moved slowly, without energy.

vindicate.hook: When the instant replay shows you were right all along, it vindicates you and clears your name.

traps.why: Accuse means to blame, the opposite of vindicate.
Indicate is inside vindicate but means point out.
Forgiving assumes someone did wrong; vindicating shows they didn't.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "clear your name." When evidence vindicates you, it proves you were innocent or right.

traps.why: Prove wrong is the opposite of vindicate.
That's vindictive, a lookalike; vindicate means prove someone right.
Arguing tries to win; vindicating comes from proof.

syn2.tip: People say they feel vindicated when they were doubted but turn out to be right. Pick the choice about being proven right.

traps.why: The discovery proved Aiden right, so it wouldn't embarrass him.
Finding the creek made things clear, not confusing.
Everyone mocked him at first; the "but" shows that changed.

sc1.tip: "Everyone laughed," "but" the stream was found. The contrast shows the discovery proved Aiden right.

sc2.sentence: When the security camera footage showed a raccoon tipping over the trash cans, it helped _____ our dog, who had been blamed for the mess all week.

traps.why: The footage showed a raccoon did it, so it cleared the dog.
The video proved the dog innocent, so punishing it makes no sense.
Training is about dogs, but the footage proved the dog innocent.

sc2.tip: The footage "showed a raccoon" did it, and the dog "had been blamed." So the video proved the dog innocent.

appraise.hook: On TV antique shows, experts appraise old treasures by telling owners what they're worth.

traps.why: Ignoring means paying no attention, the opposite of carefully judging.
Approve looks like appraise but means say yes to.
You might appraise before buying, but appraise isn't buying.

syn1.tip: Think of a home appraisal or a jewelry appraisal: an expert decides how much something is worth.

traps.why: Overlooking means not examining at all.
That's praise, which sounds like appraise but isn't judging value.
Appraising may come before selling, but it isn't selling.

syn2.tip: An appraiser studies an item and puts a price on it. Look for the choice about deciding value.

traps.why: Polishing cleans coins but doesn't tell what they're worth.
Ignoring the coins wouldn't tell the family their worth.
Praise sounds like appraise but doesn't tell how much coins are worth.

sc1.tip: The goal is "so they would know how much each coin was really worth." The expert's job is to judge their value.

sc2.sentence: Rather than simply guessing which used bike was the better deal, Dad asked the mechanic to _____ both, carefully judging their brakes, tires, and gears before he decided.

traps.why: The mechanic carefully judged the bikes, so he didn't ignore them.
Repairing fixes bikes; the sentence says the mechanic was judging them.
Praise sounds like appraise but means say nice things.

sc2.tip: The phrase "carefully judging their brakes, tires, and gears" restates the blank. Dad wanted the bikes' quality judged.

revelry.hook: Revelry is the noise of a party that goes all night: music, cheering, dancing, and fireworks.

traps.why: Mourning is sad grieving, the opposite of joyful revelry.
Revelation looks like revelry but means a surprising discovery.
A ceremony can be quiet and serious; revelry is wild and noisy.

syn1.tip: Revelry comes from revel, as in revelers at a party. It means lively partying.

traps.why: Sorrow is sadness, the opposite of revelry.
Rivalry sounds like revelry but means competition.
Parties have decorations, but revelry is the noisy fun itself.

syn2.tip: Revelers are people having a loud, happy time at a party. Pick the choice that means having fun together.

traps.why: People were dancing and celebrating, not grieving.
Fireworks boom like thunder, but the sounds came from people celebrating.
Traffic is noisy, but the noise came from dancing and singing.

sc1.tip: The examples "danced, sang, and set off fireworks to celebrate" tell you the sounds were lively partying.

sc2.sentence: The library was usually hushed, but after our team won the state spelling bee, the _____ in the study room grew so loud that the librarian asked us to quiet down.

traps.why: Silence can't grow loud.
Studying happens in libraries, but it isn't loud.
Grumbling is unhappy; the team had just won.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "hushed" with what happened after the team "won." Winners make loud, happy noise.

furtive.hook: A furtive glance is the quick, secret peek a kid sneaks at the cookie jar when Mom isn't looking.

traps.why: Open means done in plain view, the opposite of furtive.
Fertile looks like furtive but means able to grow things.
Guilty people may act furtive, but guilty means having done wrong.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a furtive glance": a quick look you hope nobody catches. That's sneaky.

traps.why: Obvious means easy to notice, the opposite of furtive.
Festive looks like furtive but means cheerful and party-like.
Criminal is too strong; furtive means trying not to be noticed.

syn2.tip: Furtive actions are done quietly so nobody sees. Look for the choice about hiding what you do.

traps.why: Bella hoped no one would notice, so her look wasn't bold.
Proud is too positive; she was hiding her phone.
Festive looks like furtive but means cheerful and party-like.

sc1.tip: "Hoping no one would notice," "under the desk," and "the teacher's back was turned" all show Bella was being secretive.

sc2.sentence: Unlike his brother, who grabbed snacks openly, Marcus made _____ trips to the kitchen at night, tiptoeing past his parents' door so the floor would not creak.

traps.why: Marcus tiptoed so the floor wouldn't creak, so he wasn't noisy.
Public means seen by all, which is like his brother, not Marcus.
Cheerful doesn't explain tiptoeing to avoid being heard.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts Marcus with his brother who acted "openly." Tiptoeing so the floor "would not creak" shows he was secretive.

contrite.hook: A contrite puppy with drooping ears after chewing your shoe looks truly sorry for what it did.

traps.why: Proud is the opposite of feeling sorry for doing wrong.
Contrary looks like contrite but means stubbornly opposing.
Devastated is far too strong; contrite means sorry, not crushed.

syn1.tip: Contrite people regret what they did and want to apologize. Think of a kid saying "I'm sorry" and meaning it.

traps.why: Defiant people refuse to admit wrong, the opposite of contrite.
Contrite contains trite, but it doesn't mean dull.
Polite people apologize, but contrite means feeling guilty, not good manners.

syn2.tip: Contrite is how you feel after doing something wrong: full of regret and ready to apologize.

traps.why: Pride wouldn't make Sam apologize and offer to pay.
Anger wouldn't lead to an apology.
Breaking the window was careless, but the feeling causing an apology is regret.

sc1.tip: Sam "apologized at once and offered to pay." People do that when they feel sorry for what they did.

sc2.sentence: Instead of making excuses for forgetting her best friend's birthday, Nora was genuinely _____, admitting her mistake and baking a cake to make up for it.

traps.why: Defensive people make excuses, which Nora didn't do.
Baking a cake can be fun, but she baked it to make up for a mistake.
Contrary looks like contrite but means stubborn, which doesn't fit admitting mistakes.

sc2.tip: "Instead of making excuses" sets up a contrast. "Admitting her mistake" and trying "to make up for it" show she felt sorry.

strategy.hook: A chess player thinking three moves ahead to trap the king is using a strategy.

traps.why: An accident is unplanned, the opposite of a careful strategy.
A strategy aims for victory, but it is the plan, not the win.
Tragedy ends like strategy but means a terrible event.

syn1.tip: Think of a coach drawing plays on a whiteboard before the big game. That drawing is the strategy.

traps.why: A sudden impulse is unplanned, the opposite of a careful strategy.
A strategy comes before the result; it is not the result itself.
Teams practice to carry out a strategy, but practice is not the plan.

syn2.tip: Generals and coaches make a strategy before acting. It is the thinking about how to win, not the winning.

traps.why: A trophy is the prize at a tournament, not a way to defend.
Careful study leads to a plan, the opposite of a mistake.
Studying past games gives her real knowledge, not gossip.

sc1.tip: "Studied her opponent's past games" and "worked out" a defense describe careful planning to win.

sc2.sentence: Instead of rushing the ball up the field as usual, our soccer coach drew a careful _____ on the whiteboard, showing exactly where each player should move.

traps.why: A guess is not careful, and it doesn't show exactly where players move.
Penalties happen in soccer, but a coach doesn't draw one to guide players.
A cheer pumps up a team but shows nobody where to move.

sc2.tip: "Instead of rushing" and "showing exactly where each player should move" tell you the coach made a careful plan.

relevant.hook: If your science fair talk drifts to your weekend at the beach, your teacher may ask, "Is that relevant?"

traps.why: Unconnected is the opposite of relevant.
Relaxed starts like relevant but means calm.
Interesting facts grab attention; relevant facts connect to the topic.

syn1.tip: Think of "relevant facts" in a report: they relate to your topic. Irrelevant ones wander off the subject.

traps.why: Off topic is the opposite of relevant.
Good writing can still wander from the topic.
Easy reading is about style, not about connecting to the topic.

syn2.tip: When a teacher says a detail is not relevant, she means it doesn't belong to the subject you're discussing.

traps.why: Random details are just what Jamal cut, so this is backwards.
Length isn't the problem; the pizza paragraph was off topic.
The pizza part may be funny, but it was cut for being off topic.

sc1.tip: Jamal cut his paragraph "about his favorite pizza" from an essay "about ocean life." Only details connected to the topic belong.

sc2.sentence: Because the debate topic was school uniforms, the judge stopped Mia when she started talking about her new puppy, saying the story was not _____.

traps.why: A short story wouldn't get her stopped; being off topic did.
A puppy story that's not boring wouldn't make a judge stop her.
Not irrelevant means on topic, so the judge would let her continue.

sc2.tip: "Because the debate topic was school uniforms" and the puppy story tell you the story did not connect to the topic.

elite.hook: Olympic gymnasts and top orchestras are elite: the small, best group picked from many.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of elite.
Polite rhymes with elite but means well-mannered.
Snobbish is a negative word; elite simply means the best.

syn1.tip: You hear "elite athletes" and "elite forces": the small group picked because they are the very best.

traps.why: Below average is the opposite of elite.
Rather good is too weak; elite means the very best.
Popular means well liked, not best at something.

syn2.tip: An elite team is chosen from many hopefuls, keeping only the strongest few.

traps.why: A basic program wouldn't pick only the twenty fastest.
Cost isn't mentioned; the clue is about being the fastest.
Only twenty swimmers made it, so the program is small, not crowded.

sc1.tip: "Only the twenty fastest" out of "thousands" were chosen, so the program is for the very best.

sc2.sentence: Although the chess club welcomes anyone who wants to play, its _____ team, which travels to national tournaments, accepts only the four strongest players.

traps.why: A casual team wouldn't accept only the four strongest players.
Being liked isn't the point; the team takes only the strongest.
The team travels to national tournaments, so local doesn't fit.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with "welcomes anyone." Taking "only the four strongest players" means the team is for the best.

valid.hook: A ticket stamped valid gets you in; an excuse that is valid has solid reasons behind it.

traps.why: A flimsy reason is weak, the opposite of valid.
Valued looks similar but means treasured.
Valid shares an old root with valor, but it doesn't mean brave.

syn1.tip: Think of a "valid excuse" or a "valid ticket": something with good reasons behind it that is accepted.

traps.why: Illogical means lacking good reasons, the opposite of valid.
Honest means truthful; valid means backed by good reasons.
An idea can be popular without good reasons behind it.

syn2.tip: Valid things pass a test: a valid ticket gets you in, a valid argument holds up. Invalid means not acceptable.

traps.why: The teacher accepted it with proof, so it wasn't suspicious.
A hospital visit sounds dramatic, but the clue is about proof.
Kai was sick, but an excuse can't be contagious.

sc1.tip: "Accepted" plus "a note from the hospital proving he had been sick" shows the excuse had good reasons behind it.

sc2.sentence: Maya insisted her reason for skipping practice was _____, but the coach disagreed, saying a sleepover was not a good enough excuse to miss the big game.

traps.why: The coach thought it was weak; Maya insisted the opposite.
Timing isn't the argument; they disagree about whether it's good enough.
Maya told the coach her reason, so it wasn't secret.

sc2.tip: "But the coach disagreed" by saying it was "not a good enough excuse," so Maya believed her reason was acceptable.

petition.hook: Picture a clipboard passed around the cafeteria, collecting names to ask the principal for longer recess.

traps.why: A refusal says no; a petition asks for something.
Partition looks similar but means a wall that divides a space.
People sign a petition, but a signature is just one name.

syn1.tip: A petition asks for something. Think of signing a petition to ask the town for a new skate park.

traps.why: A refusal turns something down; a petition asks for it.
A contract is an agreement, not a request for change.
A protest is louder; a petition politely asks in writing.

syn2.tip: A petition usually has a list of signatures at the bottom, all asking the same person for the same change.

traps.why: Rumors spread around, but nobody collects signatures for one.
A menu lists lunch food; it doesn't gather signatures.
A recipe explains cooking; it can't convince a principal with signatures.

sc1.tip: She "circulated" it and "collected signatures" to "convince the principal." A paper signed by many to ask for change is a petition.

sc2.sentence: Neighbors who wanted a stop sign on our busy street wrote a _____, a formal letter asking the city council for one, and two hundred families signed it.

traps.why: A warning tells of danger; this letter asks for something.
Two hundred families don't sign a postcard to ask the council.
The letter asks for a sign, so it isn't a refusal.

sc2.tip: The words after the comma, "a formal letter asking the city council," plus "families signed it," restate the meaning of the blank.

awkward.hook: Think of a middle school dance: two kids standing apart, arms stiff, nobody knowing what to say.

traps.why: Graceful is the opposite of awkward.
Backward ends the same way but means toward the back.
Rude means impolite on purpose; awkward means clumsy or uncomfortable.

syn1.tip: Picture a newborn giraffe trying to stand on wobbly legs. Its awkward steps are clumsy and unsteady.

traps.why: Relaxed is the opposite of an awkward, uneasy feeling.
Disastrous is far too strong; awkward moments are just uneasy.
An awkward silence is quiet, but quiet alone isn't the meaning.

syn2.tip: An "awkward silence" or an "awkward moment" makes everyone squirm. That uneasy feeling is the meaning here.

traps.why: Peaceful is too pleasant; the students were squirming.
Nobody laughed, so the silence was the opposite of joyful.
A welcome silence feels good, but the students felt uncomfortable.

sc1.tip: "Nobody laughed" and students "shifted uncomfortably in their seats," so the silence felt uneasy and embarrassing.

sc2.sentence: The puppy ran smoothly across the grass, but on the slippery kitchen floor its steps became _____, and it slid into the table legs.

traps.why: Sliding into table legs is the opposite of graceful.
Sound isn't the point; the puppy lost its footing.
Speed isn't the contrast; the puppy became clumsy, not fast.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "ran smoothly," and the puppy "slid into the table legs," so its steps turned clumsy.

eligible.hook: Eligible means able to be chosen: if you meet the rules, your name can go on the list.

traps.why: Barred means kept out, the opposite of eligible.
Legible looks similar but means easy to read.
Wanting to join is different from being allowed to join.

syn1.tip: The ending "ible" means able to be. Eligible means able to be chosen because you meet the rules.

traps.why: Not permitted is the opposite of eligible.
Being eligible lets you enter; it doesn't promise a win.
Skill isn't the point; eligible means you meet the rules.

syn2.tip: When a contest says who is "eligible to enter," it is listing who is allowed to take part.

traps.why: Pablo may be eager, but the age rule decides who may join.
Twelve-year-olds can join, so unable reverses the rule.
Fear isn't mentioned; the sentence is about an age rule.

sc1.tip: The rule "only students who have turned twelve" and Pablo having "to wait" show the blank means allowed by the rules.

sc2.sentence: Although Rosa wrote a wonderful story, she was not _____ to enter the writing contest, because the rules allowed only eighth graders and she was in seventh.

traps.why: Courage isn't the issue; the rules kept her out.
Her wishes don't matter here; the grade rule decided it.
Not forbidden would mean allowed, but the rules kept her out.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast, and "the rules allowed only eighth graders" explains that seventh grader Rosa was not allowed to enter.

mutual.hook: When you like your friend and your friend likes you right back, the feeling is mutual.

traps.why: One-sided is the opposite of mutual.
Mute starts like mutual but means silent.
Mutual feelings can be friendly, but mutual means shared by both.

syn1.tip: You've heard "the feeling is mutual," said when someone feels the same way back. Mutual means shared by both.

traps.why: Felt by only one person is the opposite of mutual.
Mutual feelings can be private, but mutual means shared.
Growth over time isn't the point; mutual means both sides share it.

syn2.tip: A "mutual friend" is a friend of both people. Mutual always points two ways, to both sides at once.

traps.why: They admired each other "just as much," so it was even.
Nothing says they hid it; the clue is that both feel it.
Weak respect wouldn't make them enjoy practicing together.

sc1.tip: Each admired the other "just as much," so the respect went both ways equally.

sc2.sentence: At first only Ben wanted to be friends, but by the end of camp the feeling was _____, and Carlos was asking to trade addresses too.

traps.why: "But" shows a change from one-sided to both boys.
Carlos wanting to trade addresses is warm, not awkward.
Privacy isn't the point; Carlos now feels the same way.

sc2.tip: "At first only Ben" changes with "but," and Carlos asking "too" shows both boys now felt the same.

tribute.hook: A band playing a famous singer's songs at a tribute concert is honoring that singer with music.

traps.why: An insult shows disrespect, the opposite of a tribute.
Tribe looks similar but means a group of related people.
An apology says sorry; a tribute shows respect.

syn1.tip: A "tribute concert" or "a tribute to our heroes" is held to show respect and thanks.

traps.why: Disrespect is the opposite of a tribute.
A warning alerts people to danger; a tribute honors someone.
Rules tell people what to do; a tribute honors someone.

syn2.tip: People pay tribute to someone they admire, the way a team wears a coach's initials on their jerseys.

traps.why: Grateful students wouldn't punish their beloved librarian.
A garden named for her honors her; it doesn't challenge her.
The garden shows gratitude, not something to pull attention away.

sc1.tip: "To show their gratitude" for her "forty years of service" tells you the garden honors the librarian.

sc2.sentence: The audience rose and clapped for five minutes as the old soldier walked onstage, for the whole assembly was a _____ to his bravery during the war.

traps.why: Long, standing applause shows respect, the opposite of an insult.
Nobody is competing; the assembly honors one man.
A complaint is negative, but the clapping shows admiration.

sc2.tip: The audience "rose and clapped for five minutes," a warm, respectful tone, so the assembly honored him.

toxic.hook: A skull and crossbones on a bottle under the sink warns you the cleaner inside is toxic.

traps.why: Harmless is the opposite of toxic.
Some poisons smell bad, but many toxic things have no smell.
Toxic things are unpleasant, but unpleasant is far too general.

syn1.tip: Toxic waste and toxic chemicals come with warning labels because they can poison you.

traps.why: Safe to eat is the opposite of toxic.
Taste isn't the point; toxic things can harm your body.
Dirt isn't poison; toxic means it can make you sick.

syn2.tip: Think of "toxic fumes" from paint or smoke. Breathing them can hurt your body, so toxic means harmful to health.

traps.why: Dogs may like chocolate, but the clue says it makes them sick.
A harmless chemical wouldn't make dogs very sick.
Being familiar doesn't explain why it makes dogs sick.

sc1.tip: The chemical "can make them very sick," which is what poisons do, so the blank means poisonous.

sc2.sentence: The shiny berries looked as sweet as blueberries, but the park ranger warned that they were _____ and that eating even a few could send someone to the hospital.

traps.why: "But" turns away from sweet looks; they are dangerous, not delicious.
Ripeness doesn't send people to the hospital.
Being rare isn't dangerous; the warning is about getting sick.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with looking sweet, and "could send someone to the hospital" tells you the berries are poisonous.
